en: Preface to the Combined Commentary on the Great Buddha-Usnīsa Śūraṅgama Sūtra:
The Śūraṅgama Sūtra has been transmitted to the world because it points out that the Tathāgata-garbha nature and the fundamental source of sentient beings are entirely without distinction;
yet, by being able to exhaust the deluded mind, the true vision naturally manifests. Therefore, I rejoice.
Out of joy, he established his questions from within the state where there is neither delusion nor enlightenment, and the Sugata responded with words that transcend verbal expression.

Like jade turning and pearls revolving, the sacred teachings were spread far and wide. Consequently, there appeared the secret indications of the seven examinations, the eight returns, the four conditions, the objects of the senses, and the two inversions;
as well as the detailed expositions on the five aggregates, the six entrances, the twelve bases, the eighteen elements, and the twenty-five perfect penetrations.
The *Discourse on the Seven Realms, the Three Advances, and the Four Illuminations* elucidates the various stages up to the fifty kinds of demons;

its principles are so penetrating that they are like the great sun shining brightly in the sky, yet those who are ignorant do not perceive them. Consequently, scholars of vast erudition have composed commentaries and sub-commentaries for it, none of which fail to explain it clearly.
However, when it comes to the innermost sanctum, red and purple dyes are confused with vermilion, and the original meaning is instead obscured.
Those who have obscured the intent of the Sage are many; thus, how could Jiyin’s treatise have been composed otherwise?

Observe how he employs the *jñānaprakāśa-samādhi* to distinguish between lineages and sects, and how he brings forth the Great Meaning amidst refutation and exclusion—there is no application for which it is not suitable.

Even if one were born at a distant time, what further refinement could be added? Some have said that no one except a Bodhisattva who has seen the Truth (*satyadarśin*) would be capable of such a work.
How could one know for certain that Jiyin was not, in fact, a seer of the Truth?
Being a fool, I have once taken his writings and arranged them to the right of the sutra, much like those of old who combined the treatises of Li Zhangzhe with the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*.

Fearing that there might be omissions, I have ventured to supplement them with my own wild and frivolous thoughts, and have further set forth their general outline at the beginning of this volume, hoping that it may serve as a place to settle the spirit.
"This text is clear and free from delusion, directly realizing the true and eternal; all else is fully contained within the original preface.

Written on the first day of the New Year in the Guihai year of the Jia Tai era by the śramaṇa Zhengshou, respectfully recorded for *The Great Buddha-Usnīsa Tathāgata’s Secret Cause, Cultivation, Realization, and Definitive Meaning of All Bodhisattvas*.
Preface to the Śūraṅgama-samādhi Sūtra Commentary:

The convergence of the myriad things is called the mind; the merging with the one mind is called the Way. As for the mind, it is empty and harmonious, vast and expansive, brilliantly manifest yet profoundly still.
Its responsive transformations are without fixed direction, its majestic spiritual power is unfathomable, and it is grand, remote, subtle, and wondrous—beyond all thought or deliberation.

How truly it is that from the great ocean of conditioned existence, clouds of ignorance gather in the vast void; the waves of consciousness surge boundlessly, and the dust of deluded emotions swirls in deep gloom.
For this reason, the One of Perfect and Universal Knowledge appeared in the Five Regions to open wide the gate of ultimate reality and extensively reveal the path of true cultivation.
Thus, those who recognize the truth may reach the pinnacle of wordless transcendence, and those who harbor the treasure within may avoid the misery of begging in poverty.
Regarding this diligent practice, neither the sages of antiquity nor those of later times have failed to attain awakening and entry through it.

The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* is the essential pivot for opening the Tathāgatagarbha and the direct path pointing to the wondrously luminous mind; it is the sublime instruction for understanding the faculties and their objects, and the profound principle for illuminating emotional delusions.
It is truly what is called the level highway for entering the One Vehicle and the grand strategy for dispelling divergent views.
It began when Ānanda, while begging for alms, encountered the influence of illusory arts; Mañjuśrī, responding to his words, proclaimed a divine mantra to protect him.

Thereupon, [Ānanda] earnestly requested the initial expedient means, and the Great Compassionate One revealed the primordial, eternal, and fundamental awakening—merely a direct mind devoid of any devious characteristics.
By means of this, through the seven internal and external locations, he shattered the deluded mind to manifest the true mind, clarifying the eight aspects of light and darkness.

Furthermore, by shattering deluded views, one reveals true vision; the five aggregates are seen as empty space, the elements and sense bases are vast and expansive, and the nature of the seven elements is perfectly complete.

Each and every mind is known to pervade the ten directions, like observing fruit in the palm of one's hand. One realizes that each and every nature is a profound, vast ocean, and no longer mistakes it for floating bubbles.
Thus, one attains the fundamental, wondrous mind, which is not obtained from another. Moreover, Pūrṇa Maitrāyaṇīputra harbored doubts regarding mountains, rivers, and the great earth.

Suddenly, a sense of joy arose within him as he requested that the Heavenly King of the Flowered Hall must enter through the gate. How could he have known that cataracts in the eyes cause the delusion of floating flowers?
That which was originally pure and perfect has become this turbid state; though the six elements and the one body are non-dual, one must investigate how bondage and liberation share the same source.
Thus, although the principle of liberation is subtle and perfect, its practice is manifested by the person. Consequently, he commanded those of the stage of no-more-learning (aśaikṣa) to each speak.
The perfect penetration of all dharmas is none other than the true Dharma-gate; they are all originally the ground for cultivation.

Manjushri’s great wisdom employs the eye that discriminates dharmas to observe without error, while Avalokiteshvara’s great compassion adapts to the capacities of beings in this Sahā world. The myriad Buddhas of the dust-motes of worlds concur in their realization of the True and Constant;

thus, the stages of understanding, practice, realization, and perfection are fully exhausted. Thereafter, as things were opened up and affairs accomplished, seekers requested further instruction and presented their doubts.
The prohibitions and precepts guard against error through four kinds of clear instructions; the pure cultivation and realization are arranged according to the stages of the ten bhūmis.

The emission of light proclaims the efficacy of divine mantras, while the inversion of conditions reveals the differences among the various classes of beings. One minutely investigates the seven destinies and extensively demonstrates the six modes of interaction.

Returning to the purple-golden mountain, he explains the meditative states (*dhyāna*) and their manifestations; he shows that the five kinds of deluded thoughts constitute the very root of these phenomena.

All demonic activities arise from causes; by relying on awakening, they are simultaneously dissolved. Through gradual progression, they are exhausted until none remain. This True Unsurpassed Treasure Seal is truly subtle and wondrous.

Like a lotus flower, it penetrates to the very core of both cause and fruit, fully exhausting both principle and phenomena. It removes the heavy obstacles of the ten evils and is illustrated by the seven treasures as being difficult to equal.
It reveals that future Bodhi can be attained; the essential purport of this single sutra is briefly set forth herein.

Regarding the subtle and coarse principles of the essential purport (*abhiprāya*), before explaining this sutra, one must first clarify its essential purport. While the commentaries of various masters differ slightly yet largely agree, that which is clarified here is as follows:
the universal *tathāgatagarbha* nature, wherein the holy and the ordinary are equal, constitutes the essence (*śarīra*);

the cultivation of the *śūraṅgama-samādhi* through the transcendence of thought constitutes the purport (*abhiprāya*). Furthermore, by means of the *śūraṅgama-samādhi*, all deluded views are shattered and the cycle of rebirth is forever severed.

Taking the turning [of the mind] as the primary principle (*mūla*) and the wondrously enlightened, luminous *tathāgatagarbha* nature as the ultimate goal (*prayojana*), according to the classification of the five teachings by the Great Master Xianshou and the deliberations of various masters, this belongs strictly to the Final and Perfect Teachings, while also encompassing the Sudden and Complete Teachings.

If one considers the function of this sutra, it does not transcend the two characters of "destroying" and "revealing": "destroying" refers to destroying all deluded views, and "revealing" refers to revealing the One [True Mind].

Although the true mind has many approaches, it does not exceed this meaning; yet throughout the entire *Prajñāpāramitā* section, there is only the negation of marks (*lakṣaṇa*), while the two chapters on *Amitābha’s Perfect Enlightenment* suddenly reveal the fundamental mind.

This sutra first states that [all phenomena] arise from ignorance of the eternally abiding true mind, and subsequently explains in detail and with subtle precision how the mind and the objects of the eyes—through the causes and conditions of the harmonious union of the three categories and seven elements—come into being.
The conjunction of false delusions is called birth through causes and conditions; their separation is called cessation.

Yet one does not realize that birth, cessation, going, and coming are fundamentally the Tathāgata-garbha, the wondrous nature of True Suchness (*tathatā*). Within this true and eternal nature, it is utterly impossible to find going or coming, delusion or awakening, birth or death.
There are extensive texts on this, which I do not wish to cite in full, for some may say that the commentaries composed by various masters already treat this at length.

"What do you mean by 'comprehensive illumination' (*sāmānya-prajñā*)? Let us now further discuss this point. He replied: "The wisdom and eloquence of the Tathāgata connect the principles of the Dharma like a continuous chain.

Master Fang’s profound writings possess refined literary elegance and concise expression. Those who cling to the literal text are mired in the study of the trap and snare [of words], while those who seek the fundamental principle disparage the profusion of characters.
One who has not yet been able to harmonize and adjudicate these matters is truly worthy of the highest vessel; I am merely one who does not presume to measure the ocean with a tube."

I have tentatively attempted to fathom the profound and the deep, meticulously rectifying the fundamental tenets and roughly dividing them into sections. Compared to previous commentaries and sub-commentaries, there is indeed something omitted here;

yet, by weeding out the weeds to reveal the fine grain and setting aside conventional meanings and images to focus exclusively on wondrous realization, those of like mind with me will surely not reproach this work.
The Combined Commentary on the Śūraṅgama Sūtra: The Ultimate Meaning of the Great Buddha-Uṣṇīṣa Tathāgata’s Secret Cause for Cultivation and Realization, and the Myriad Practices of All Bodhisattvas,
Volume One (also known as the Sūtra of the Great Maṇḍala of Nālandā in Central India, excerpted from the Abhiṣeka Section and circulated separately).
Translated by the Indian Śramaṇa Prajñāmitra;
translated orally by the Śramaṇa Migaśrī of the kingdom of Udyāna;
recorded in writing by Fang Rong, Grand Master for Rectifying Propriety, concurrently Minister of the Department of State Affairs and Vice President of the Secretariat.
Compiled by the śramaṇa Dehong of Jūnxī; revised by the śramaṇa Zhengshou of Eastern Wu,
with the treatise integrated into the sūtra and supplemented with deletions and additions.
I prostrate to the one of unimpeded wisdom, who manifests a wondrous form-body; To the peerless Dharma that transcends conceptual thought through the sublime Vajra-words;
To the treasury of merit, serene and focused, whose light of various compassionate vows subdues Māra and harmonizes the assembly;
May you secretly bestow your empowerment upon me, so that I may exhaust even the most subtle habitual tendencies of delusion.
Having extinguished views, pride, and inverted perceptions, One attains unimpeded eloquence. Entering the *Vikrīḍita-samādhi*, one explains the meaning that accords with the nature of reality;
Dispelling doubts and illuminating the darkness of error, One bestows this universally upon all sentient beings so that the lineage of the Buddhas shall never be severed.
The Treatise says: To manifest the certainty of attaining Buddhahood is solely to understand that the essential gateway for entering the Way is to accord with the essence of the mind.

What is meant by "accordance"? It is contemplative observation in accordance with the nature (*dharmatā*). What is meant by "understanding"? It is awakening to clarity that transcends conceptual emotions.

Therefore, this awakening to clarity does not obstruct precise and rigorous contemplative observation; this is called skillful means (*upāya*). Thus it was said by the ancients: [...]* *Note: The source text provided ends abruptly with "故古之" (Therefore, the ancients...). The ellipsis indicates the remainder of the original passage has been omitted.*

The Holy Master, in propagating the sutras, must necessarily establish their fundamental tenets (*zongqiu*). Since this sutra is the Honored Crown of the Dharma, it takes the clear vision of Buddha-nature as its tenet;

since it reveals Great Samādhi, it takes the extinction of dust and the unification with awakening as its purpose. As for "clearly seeing Buddha-nature," it is because one has departed from all views;
thus, among the sixty-two metaphors, the Crown of the Dharma is foremost. The Buddha himself does not...

Because it is seen as being free from the characteristics of one's own views, the *uṣṇīṣa* (crown protuberance) covers it; because it is free from the characteristics of others' views, it cannot be seen by oneself or others—this is called the "Secret Canopy.
It is the ground of the *samādhi* of the *Anantārtha-naya* (Infinite Meaning and Purpose), which dwells in its own *samāpatti*;
it is profound, firm, deep, and remote, such that no person can reach it. As the *Yi Jing* says: "Retreating and concealing within the secret," and this secrecy is like a lotus.
Regarding the term *mì* (the calyx), the *Shuowen Jiezi* states that the lotus is what can be used and seen, while its root alone retracts and hides within the useless;
its density is like that of the Tathāgata, who attained the Way by means of this. Therefore, it is called the "Profound Cause" (*mìyīn*) for the realization of the definitive meaning (*lǐoyì*).
Question: Since it is said that knowing one's own mind is itself the manifest resolution, why is it also said that there is cultivation and realization?

"Why is this? he asked. [The Buddha] replied: "It is because of Perfect Enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-bodhi*). All sentient beings, within the state of non-arising, falsely perceive arising and ceasing;

for this reason, it is called 'revolving in birth and death. When a Tathāgata cultivates Perfect Enlightenment on the causal ground, they know these are like flowers in the sky and thus there is no revolving.
Thus, it is clear that the Tathāgata takes thorough understanding as his cultivation. Furthermore, he said: "All sentient beings..."
All who are born shall realize Perfect Enlightenment; encountering a spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra), they rely upon that person’s practice of the Dharma for the causal stage.
At that time, as they cultivate it, there will be both sudden and gradual approaches; thus, the Tathāgata further employs cultivation as a skillful means—is this not a definitive revelation?
The Sūtra says: "The arising of all phenomena is manifested solely by the mind; all causes and effects, and even the minute dust motes of the world."

Since the body is formed by the mind, one knows that the power and function of sentient beings' own minds are exceedingly great; it is only because they are defiled by various sensory objects (*viṣaya*) that they are obscured and inferior.
One must certainly purify them through the skillful means of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*, concentration and wisdom, so that they accord with their original wondrous nature.
How is this known? Nāgārjuna said: "The Buddha taught that the power of the mind is the greatest; practicing the *prajñāpāramitā*..."

Because of the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), one disperses this great earth into subtle dust; because earth possesses color, fragrance, taste, and touch, and is heavy, it has no activity of its own.
Water has less fragrance and taste, so its activity surpasses that of earth. Fire has less fragrance and taste, so its heat surpasses that of water.
Wind has less color, fragrance, and taste, so its activity surpasses that of fire. The mind, however, lacks these four factors.
The power [of their minds] is great because they have many afflictions (*kleśa*), fetters (*saṃyojana*), and bonds; therefore, the power of their minds is slight.
Although the wholesome mind with outflows (*sāsrava*) is free from afflictions, its power is also slight because the mind grasps at the characteristics (*nimitta*) of phenomena.

Although the uncontaminated mind (*anāsrava-citta*) of the two vehicles does not grasp at characteristics, its power is limited because their wisdom is finite and because they have emerged from the state of being without outflows.
When practicing the Way, because the six sense-faculties follow worldly conventions to differentiate and grasp the characteristics of various phenomena, one does not exert the full power of the mind.

The wisdom of the Buddhas and great Bodhisattvas is immeasurable and boundless; they constantly abide in meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), making no distinction between the mundane world and *nirvāṇa*.
The true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena is in fact not different, but there is a distinction in the excellence or inferiority of their wisdom and practice.

The Prajñāpāramitā is ultimately pure and free from all obstructions; within a single thought-moment, it can disperse all the great earths, mountains, and lands of the trichiliocosm—equal in number to the sands of the Ganges—in the ten directions into subtle atoms.
Thus one knows that the true mind possesses such great power, yet sentient beings, obstructed by delusion, do not perceive it.
To know through the ear and yet be able to illuminate it with *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*—is this not the essential gateway? In the *Śūraṅgama-sūtra*, "Śūraṅgama" is translated as "Vigorous Form.
The *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* states: "Śūra" means 'all ultimate,' and "Gama" means 'firm. Firmness is precisely vigorous form, because it cannot be altered or destroyed;
"all ultimate" is because birth and cessation have been extinguished. This is like the *Yi* (Book of Changes).

Regarding the *Qian* hexagram among the various trigrams, it says: "How great is *Qian*! It is strong, vigorous, central and correct, pure, and refined. The *Xiang* (Image) says: "The movement of Heaven is vigorous;
the gentleman, accordingly, exerts himself with strength and does not cease. This is what is meant by "refined and solemnity.

Now, the myriad practices of a Bodhisattva increase through the six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*); the six perfections arise from meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*); and meditative concentration and wisdom are perfected through *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*. Stopping...
Because one contemplates the essence within the *Śūraṅgama*, the Sūtra says that the King of *Śūraṅgama* is "fully endowed with the ten thousand practices" (*sāhasrika-caryā*);
it is for this reason. Bodhisattvas study it in order to fulfill *bodhi*; therefore, it is called the *Śūraṅgama-sūtra of the Ten Thousand Practices of All Bodhisattvas*.

Regarding the term "Sūtra" (*jing*), the *Shuowen Jiezi* states: "In weaving, there is the warp (*jing*); it is made by collecting threads [lengthwise]. It is constant, while the woof (*wei*) is variable."
The Classics serve merely as the warp; it is through the woof that they are completed, for there are things the Classics cannot express.
Thus, Confucius valued the spiritual resonance, which resides in the person who illuminates it.
Thus have I heard: at one time the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove Monastery.
The commentary states: "Śrāvastī" is translated here as Shewei; its full form is Śrīrāvatī. "Jeta Grove" is translated as Sheduo;
its full form is Jita-huan, but it is abbreviated here. Nāgārjuna said: "The Tathāgata..."
When approaching the time of his parinirvāṇa, he addressed Ānanda, saying, "You must propagate the twelve divisions of the sūtras.
He further addressed Upāli, saying, "You must receive and uphold all the precepts. He addressed Anuruddha, saying, "You have attained the divine eye;

you shall constantly protect the śarīra relics and exhort others to make offerings. He then addressed the great assembly, saying, "If I were to remain in this world for an entire kalpa, even then [the Dharma would not be fully realized]."
Having thus extinguished all speech, he lay down with his head toward the north between the twin *śāla* trees and entered *parinirvāṇa*.
Ānanda, having not yet eliminated the habitual attachments of kinship, sank into an ocean of grief. Aniruddha said to Ānanda:
"You are the guardian of the treasury of the Buddha's Dharma; you should not, like an ordinary person, sink into an ocean of grief over conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*)."
"All these things are impermanent; why do you grieve? Furthermore, the Buddha, the World-Honored One, has entrusted the Dharma to you with his own hand.
Now, in your distress, you are neglecting what you have received. Although the World-Honored One is present today, tomorrow he will no longer be.

You must ask the Buddha about matters of vital importance for the future. Regarding the four matters to be asked as taught by Lu-dou: first, [ask] while the Tathāgata is still in the world and personally...
The first question was: "After the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa, what words should be placed at the beginning of all sūtras spoken by the Dharma-preacher?

The second question was: "While the Tathāgata was in the world, the bhikṣus took the Buddha as their teacher; after the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa, whom shall they take as their teacher? The third question was:
"When the Buddha was in the world, the community of bhikṣus dwelt in reliance upon the Buddha; after the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa..."

Regarding the four questions concerning who should be relied upon for dwelling [in the Dharma] after [the Buddha's passing]: while the Tathāgata was in the world, he personally disciplined the monks of evil character;
after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, how should one dwell together? Ānanda asked the World-Honored One according to the instructions. The World-Honored One replied:
"At the beginning of the sūtras, one should place the six characters 'Thus have I heard: at one time' as the first phrase. Second, it is called the *pratītyasamutpāda* (dependent origination).
First, the Buddha said that he took the *Prātimokṣa* as his teacher. Second, he said that all bhikṣus should dwell in reliance upon the four foundations of mindfulness (*catur-smṛtyupasthāna*).
Third, he said that bhikṣus of evil character should be disciplined through the "Brahma-penalty" (*brahma-daṇḍa*).

Fourth, after the Tathāgata had entered parinirvāṇa, Ānanda compiled the Dharma-piṭaka at the Seven-Leaf Cave; his body was like that of the Buddhas, endowed with all the marks and signs of excellence.
At that time, the great assembly gave rise to three kinds of doubt: first, the doubt that the World-Honored One, out of great compassion, had once again arisen to preach the Dharma;
second, the doubt that Buddhas from other directions had come here to preach the Dharma; and third, the doubt that Ānanda had attained Buddhahood and was preaching the Dharma for the assembly.
As soon as Ānanda proclaimed, "Thus have I heard: at one time," these three doubts were instantly extinguished.

He was accompanied by a great assembly of one thousand two hundred and fifty bhikṣus, all of whom were great arhats free from outflows, sons of the Buddha who upheld the Dharma and had skillfully transcended all realms of existence;

they were able to manifest majestic deportment within the lands, were worthy successors to the Buddha’s turning of the wheel of Dharma, and were entrusted with the sublime task of purifying the *vinaya* and establishing a grand model for the three worlds; through their immeasurable emanation bodies, they liberated sentient beings.
"Rescuing those of the future and transcending all worldly entanglements.
The Treatise says: "The great bhikṣus who were well-known to the assembly, numbering one thousand two hundred and fifty, constantly followed the World-Honored One.
Before the World-Honored One attained the Way, he first delivered the five bhikṣus of the Kausthila clan, and later delivered Śāriputra."

Maudgalyāyana and his two hundred disciples, as well as the three Kāśyapas and their one thousand disciples, and furthermore the householder Yaśas (alternatively called Yaṣa) and his fifty followers—these are cited here by way of their approximate numbers.
There are three outflows (*āsrava*): namely, the outflow of ignorance (*avidyā-āsrava*), the outflow of desire (*kāma-āsrava*), and the outflow of existence (*bhava-āsrava*).
Because he has completely severed all of these, he is an Arhat; this term means "one who is worthy" (*arhat*).
Third is the "Correspondence. The Tang dynasty master Xianshou inherited and developed the system established by Master Huayan Yanzong, establishing five teachings:
first, the Hīnayāna Teaching; second, the Initial Mahāyāna Teaching; third, the Final Teaching; fourth, the Sudden Teaching; and fifth, the Perfect Teaching.

First, the Hīnayāna is for those who, out of emotional attachment (*sattva-rāga*), maintain the precepts and cultivate merit to obtain rebirth in the heavens as their reward. Second, the Initial Teaching discusses emptiness to refute existence, yet still permits those with fixed natures.
1. Because those who rely on the [lesser] vehicles do not achieve Buddhahood, whereas the three [vehicles] ultimately exhaust the principle of the Mahāyāna;

2. Because those of the two vehicles who lack the Buddha-nature, as well as icchantikas, shall all attain Buddhahood; 3. Because [the sudden teaching] holds that the non-arising of a single thought is itself called "Buddha," rather than ascending through successive stages and positions;
4. Because it is perfectly complete, encompassing the Samantabhadra-dharmadhātu and the non-obstruction of phenomena within phenomena.

Because the Indra’s Net of obstacles is layered and complete with both primary and attendant elements, masters of doctrinal study have classified this sutra within the Five Teachings as belonging to the Final Teaching (Jiao) of the Mahayana, while also incorporating the Perfect and Sudden (Yuantun).
They claim it possesses both realization and cultivation because it shares certain features with the Hinayana;

however, this is decidedly not the case. For instance, the *Perfect Enlightenment Sutra* [involves] refining the three contemplations (*sanguan*) and washing away the four marks (*sishang*) to attain realization.
Is it not the case that prioritizing long-term practice over even half a verse implies the absence of realization and cultivation? Yet the World-Honored One personally judged this scripture, saying:
"This sutra is named the Mahāyāna of Sudden Teaching; sentient beings of sudden capacity awaken through it. Why is this so?
Students should infer the World-Honored One’s intention and know that because the matters of this sutra concern the *mūrdhan* dharma (the stage of the summit), it is also called the Sudden Teaching.
Question: In the *Sūtra of Perfect Enlightenment*, the assembly of virtues is described as including Mañjuśrī, Samantabhadra, Vajragarbha, and the great bodhisattvas of the various stages;

yet in this sūtra, the description of the assembly of virtues merely states: "those who have excellently transcended all realms of existence, who have accomplished majestic deportment, who strictly purify the *vinaya*, and who have surpassed all worldly defilements.
Wherein lies the reason for this difference? Answer: It is because [the former] is a sūtra... [text continues].
Each depends upon its respective object of focus; this is because it takes Ānanda as its causal condition. Regarding this, the World-Honored One said in the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*:
"It is for those of the Great Vehicle and the Supreme Vehicle that this is taught. Furthermore, examining the meaning of these words:

"Those who uphold the precepts and cultivate merit will be able to give rise to faith in these verses. Upholding the precepts and cultivating merit does not refer to the accomplishment of majestic power (*vibhūti*).
If one who studies according to the meaning of the Vinaya were to strictly adhere to formal purity, they would contradict the intent of the World-Honored One’s explicit teaching.
I have often deeply contemplated this sutra and grasped the World-Honored One’s intent; I know its essentials to be concise yet profound, subtle yet penetratingly clear.
The World-Honored One took pity on sentient beings wandering through the three realms, knowing that it is entirely due to attachment to desires regarding all objects of desire.
Because among these [sins], sexual misconduct alone is the most grave, the Sūtra introduces the story of the Mātangī girl at its outset specifically to explain this reason:
that being immersed in it is a great affliction, while severing it is a great benefit. It is like a shepherd who strikes the hindquarters of his flock;
thus, in matters of vital opportunity, one must apply oneself with painful intensity. The Bhikṣuṇī Ratnapadmagandhā, while upholding the Bodhisattva precepts, privately...

If one engages in sexual desire and falsely claims that such lust is neither killing nor stealing and thus carries no karmic retribution, a great, fierce fire will immediately arise from the female organ;
thereafter, one’s body will be burned by fierce fires limb by limb, and one will fall into the Avīci Hell.
Furthermore, Ucchuṣma heard the Buddha say that those who indulge excessively in lust become a mass of fierce fire through the Tejovatī Samādhi (Fire-Light Samādhi).

It is said that upon becoming an Arhat, as all outflows (*āsrava*) have been extinguished, one gives rise to the great jewel-flame and ascends to Unsurpassed Enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*).
Now, Unsurpassed Enlightenment is the stage of Buddhahood; yet by contemplating the nature of lust, one is able to ascend to it. The Avīci Hell is an evil path;
yet by following the affairs of lust, one can fall into it. Furthermore, when discussing the ten kinds of habitual causes (*vāsanā-hetu*), this is first set forth.
Regarding the habit of lust, it is said that first, the practice of sexual intercourse arises from mutual friction;
through this constant grinding, a great and fierce fire is ignited within. For this reason, the Tathāgatas of the ten directions designate the act of lust by the same name:
