thus we know that the World-Honored One spoke of this here because these conceptualizations are not real, and that there is cyclic wandering (*saṃsāra*). This serves as a clear instruction.
If you now wish to investigate the true nature of the luminous clarity of unsurpassed Bodhi, you should respond to my questions with a straightforward mind.
Because the Tathāgatas of the ten directions follow one and the same path, they all transcend birth and death by means of a straightforward mind;
since both their minds and words are straightforward, even throughout the stages from beginning to end, there is never any trace of crookedness or deviousness.
The Treatise says: Question: Regarding this, it specifically mentions the "nature of true illumination. Is there also a "nature of deluded illumination"?

Answer: There is. Question: How is this distinguished? Answer: That which spontaneously and universally knows the fundamental wondrousness and is eternally quiescent is the nature of true illumination.
As it is said, "The Tathāgatas of the ten directions follow one and the same path," for they have transcended birth.
Death in all cases consists in this very upright mind. To violate the proper timing and season, to falsely awaken and force knowledge, is to delusively manifest one's nature;
this is what is meant by "employing various false thoughts. Because these thoughts are not true, there is cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*). This is because they are fundamentally of one essence.
Since there is no inherent nature and no fixed time, they merely differ according to how they are employed. They are spontaneously quiescent.

If one knows [the mind] while it is in its constant state, one accords with the fundamental mystery; if one awakens to it when it deviates from its timing and loses its seasonal rhythm, one accords with delusive objects.

As Aśvaghoṣa said: "The original nature is pure and luminous, yet through non-awakening due to ignorance, the characteristics of the defiled mind appear. Although the defiled mind exists, the nature of the mind is always bright and clean.
The characteristics of the defiled mind are precisely the active manifestations of ignorance, while the nature of brightness and cleanliness is precisely the immovable wisdom."
Tiyu Seng asked: "The *Yun'an Zajah Lun* states that the active ignorance (*saṃudācāra-avidyā*) is itself the Tathāgata’s immovable wisdom (*acala-jñāna*).
This is truly difficult to believe; how can one attain understanding? At that time, there was a youth who happened to be sweeping the floor. Yun’an called to him.
The youth turned his head, and Yun’an said, "Is this not the immovable wisdom? He asked again, "What is it?"
"You, Child of Buddha-nature, look left and right with vacant stares and depart," Yun'an said. "Is this not the active manifestation of ignorance?
To truly manifest the nature is like the light of a bright pearl, which constantly illuminates the pearl itself.
Confucius said, 'Let your thoughts be without deviance'—this comes close to it. To falsely manifest the nature is like the east just before dawn, when the turbid sediment has not yet settled."
"Already there is the essence of clarity; the *Yi* says, 'The *Meng* hexagram is a mixture that becomes manifest,' which is close to this.
Ānanda, I now ask you: when you first resolved your mind upon the Tathāgata’s thirty-two marks, what did you see, and who was it that felt such love and delight?
Ānanda replied to the Buddha: 'World-Honored One, such love and delight were produced by my own mind.'"
Because the eyes perceive the sublime marks of the Tathāgata through the eyes, and because the mind gives rise to love and joy, I have resolved to abandon birth and death.
The Buddha told Ānanda: "What you say is true; the cause of this love and joy lies within the eyes and the mind.
If one does not know the location of the eyes and the mind, one will be unable to subdue worldly afflictions. It is like a king who is seized by a thief."
To dispatch troops for an offensive and eliminate them, one must first know where the enemy is located; it is your own wandering mind and eyes that are at fault.
I now ask you: where, precisely, are this mind and these eyes located?
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying, “World-Honored One, all ten types of ordinary beings in the world likewise maintain that the consciousness-mind resides within the body.
Even when observing the Tathāgata’s blue-lotus eyes, they see them situated upon the Buddha’s face.
Now, as I observe these four impurities of the physical eye-organ, they appear only on my face; thus, this consciousness-mind truly must reside within the body.”
The Buddha said to Ānanda, "As you are now sitting here in the Tathāgata’s lecture hall, look at the Jeta Grove; where is it now?
"World-Honored One, this great multi-storied pavilion and pure lecture hall is in Anāthapiṇḍada’s Garden, while the Jeta Grove is actually outside the hall.
"Ānanda, what did you see first when you were inside the hall just now? "World-Honored One, while I was in the hall, I first saw—"
The Tathāgata next observed the great assembly looking out in this manner toward the grove and garden. Ānanda, for what reason do you see the grove and garden?
“World-Honored One, because the doors and windows of this great lecture hall are wide open, I am able to look from within the hall and see them from afar.”
The Treatise says: The *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states that the purity of the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñājñāna*) opens the path of the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*).
Although the sixteen assemblies of this sūtra comprise tens of millions of verses, it addresses only the single phenomenon of form (*rūpa*) to dismantle it;

yet if even form, which possesses substance, is thus illusory and false, how much more so the four [aggregates] of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, which are merely names? This sūtra is for the purpose of clear vision.
The Buddha-nature is the nature of seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing, which is unborn.
Although the two assemblies discuss this for tens of thousands of words, they merely discourse on "seeing" one dharma—half of the whole. What is now indicated is precisely its source.

The words and meanings unfold brilliantly, connecting through conditions until we see that because of clarity, darkness constitutes non-seeing; yet when clarity does not arise, it manifests of itself, and thus all darkness [is dispelled].
The appearances can never again obscure it; it is like a gold-washer for whom the sand and ore have been entirely exhausted, and the gold manifests of itself.
If one still retains the "view of no-view," this is not possible. Why? Because it is not the true view. Therefore it is said: "Even seeing should be detached from seeing.
Furthermore, one must detach from hearing; therefore it is said: "The essence of mind leaves behind hearing. Furthermore, one must detach from cognition.
Therefore it is said: "The bodyless perceives touch, and one must further transcend cognition; thus it is called perfect, clear, and aware, not arising from mental thought.
Since seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing have already been transcended, is this not the principle of clearly perceiving the Buddha-nature?

Among sentient beings there are twelve classes; now, having excluded the two classes of those who are empty, scattered, dissolved, or submerged, as well as earth, wood, metal, and stone, it is therefore said:

Regarding the ten types of ordinary beings (the "inexhaustible" [category] consists of the six mundane and four noble ones; though called "noble," how could they be termed a mere "class" of deluded beings?): the natures of earth, water, fire, and wind are each fundamentally empty.
Because sentient beings fear the word "empty," the World-Honored One merely speaks of them as "pure," using this term to preclude the notion of emptiness;
hence it is said they are "pure. The characteristics of the four great elements—earth, water, fire, and wind—each and every one are in a state of constant motion.
Therefore, the World-Honored One designated them as the "four objects" (*catur-viṣaya*) by which the six sense organs (*ṣaḍ-indriya*) are accomplished;

hence they are called the "floating roots and four objects. Ānanda took "eye" to be the floating root of the four objects, but because the Indian language is inverted, it is called "floating roots and four objects.
Supplement: Whenever the Tathāgata preached the Dharma, there was nothing that did not originate from form (*rūpa*).
The mind gives rise to function in order to dispel the delusions of sentient beings and manifest that form and mind are non-dual.
Although this sutra speaks of "destroying the false to reveal the true," it also arises from the two dharmas of form and mind; therefore, it begins by posing the questions:

"What is it that is seen? and "Who is it that loves and delights? For what is seen is precisely form, and that which loves and delights is precisely mind. This is the essential purport of the entire sutra.
The general meaning does not go beyond this question regarding the four objects (*viṣaya*).

Yet, various masters have generally explained them by citing form, fragrance, taste, and touch, asserting that both the internal five sense organs and [the external objects] possess eight factors: internally, there are the four great elements (*mahābhūta*)—earth, water, fire, and wind;
externally, there are the four derivative objects (*upādāya-rūpa*)—form, fragrance, taste, and touch. I, the fool, have once offered this critique:
The four objects of the floating faculties differ slightly from the four derived objects;

whereas those four derived objects are paired with the four primary elements as form, odor, taste, and touch, these four objects of the floating faculties—referring to the eyes, ears, nose, and tongue—should properly be identified as form, sound, odor, and taste, and are likely not touch. Ānanda said: "I now..."
"Observe these four sensory objects of the floating faculties; they reside only upon my face. Reflect on this, and you will surely find it to be so.
At that time, the World-Honored One, amidst the great assembly, extended his golden-hued arm and stroked Ānanda’s head, informing Ānanda and the entire multitude:
"There is a samādhi called the Great Buddha-Crown Śūraṅgama King, which fully encompasses the myriad practices."
"The path of wondrous adornment through which the Tathāgatas of the ten directions transcend by a single gate—listen attentively now, Ānanda!
Ānanda prostrated himself and humbly received the compassionate instruction.
The treatise says: "When a Bodhisattva practices compassion of identical essence, they regard the body as a divergent path; therefore, regarding the body as..."

It is for this reason that the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, which fully embodies the myriad practices of the heterodox paths, describes the King Subhavyūha as one belonging to a family of wrong views, and he says to the Buddha: "World-Honored One, it is unprecedented!
The Dharma of the Tathāgata is fully accomplished with inconceivable, subtle, and wondrous merits. In this context, the term *samādhi* is also used as a support.
Only by entering the Samādhi of Transformation can one fully complete the myriad practices and adorn the Path with wondrous majesty;

yet this is merely the wisdom of skillful means (*upāya-jñāna*), not the Śūraṅgama Great Samādhi that fully completes the myriad practices. Therefore, it is said: "One transcends through a single gate. (Dinglin says:

"To stroke the head is to show affection by caressing; to prostrate at the feet is to show reverence by bowing down. The superior shows affection to the inferior, hence stroking the head; the inferior shows reverence to the superior, hence prostrating at the feet.)
The Buddha told Ānanda, "Regarding what you have said— that while the body is in the lecture hall and the doors and windows are wide open so that one can gaze far out at the groves and gardens,
there might be sentient beings within this hall who do not see the Tathāgata but do see those outside the hall— Ānanda replied, 'World-Honored One,
it is impossible for one to be in the hall and not see the Tathāgata yet be able to see the forests and springs. Ānanda, you too..."

In this way, your spiritual mind is all-encompassing and clearly aware. If the mind that you currently perceive as being clearly aware were actually located within your body, then you should first be able to clearly know the internal body.
Is there any sentient being who first sees what is inside the body and only afterwards observes external objects?
Even if you cannot see it, the heart, liver, spleen, and stomach, the growth of nails and hair, and the shifting of tendons and throbbing of veins—surely you ought to perceive these.
It is clearly understood that one who does not know what is within cannot possibly know what is without;
therefore, you should know that your claim that the mind capable of conscious cognition dwells within the body is impossible.
Ānanda bowed his head to the ground and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"I have heard such a Dharma-sound from the Tathāgata, and through it I have realized that my mind truly dwells outside the body. Why is this so? It is like a lamp burning within a room:

that lamp must first illuminate the interior of the room, and only after passing through the door of the room does its light reach the courtyard. Yet all sentient beings do not see [their own minds] within their bodies."
If you see only what is outside the body, it is like a lamp placed outdoors that cannot illuminate the interior of a room;
this principle must be clear so as to leave no room for delusion. Is this not the definitive meaning realized by the Buddha, free from error?
The Buddha said to Ānanda, "These bhikṣus have just now come from the city of Śrāvastī, begging for alms-food along the way and returning to the Jeta Grove.
I have already finished my meal. Observe, Ānanda: when one bhikṣu eats, are all these people satiated?
Ānanda replied, "No, World-Honored One. Why is this? Although these bhikṣus possess the bodies of arhats..."
"Since their destinies are different, how can one person cause many to be satiated? The Buddha told Ānanda:

"If your awakened mind that perceives and knows were truly outside the body, such that the body and mind existed externally to one another and did not interact, then what the mind knows the body could not perceive, and what the body perceives at its own boundaries the mind could not know. I shall now show you my hand, which is as soft as tūla-cotton."
"When seeing with the eyes, the mind discriminates. Ānanda replied, "It is so, World-Honored One.

The Buddha told Ānanda, "If they were mutually aware of one another, how could [the mind] be outside? Therefore, you should know that your claim—that the mind capable of awareness and cognition dwells outside the body—is impossible."
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying, "World-Honored One, as the Buddha has said, because one does not see within, it does not abide inside the body;
yet because the body and mind know each other and are not separate, it does not exist outside the body. As I now reflect, I know it must reside in one specific place.
The Buddha asked, "Where is that place now? Ānanda replied, "This cognizant mind, which is neither aware of the interior yet is able to see the exterior—"
As I contemplate this, it is as if the sense-faculties are hidden within, like someone taking a lapis lazuli bowl and covering both eyes;
although there is something covering them, it does not obstruct [vision]. Those faculties perceive according to their objects and immediately engage in discernment.
Yet, when I am aware and capable of knowing, that mind which knows does not see within, because it resides in the faculties; thus, it gazes clearly at the external without obstruction.
Because the faculties are hidden within. The Buddha told Ānanda: "As you say, that the faculties are hidden within is like the case of lapis lazuli.

That person should see the mountains and rivers through eyes covered by a cage of lapis lazuli; yet they do not see the lapis lazuli itself. "It is so, World-Honored One; that person should indeed see [the objects]."
The Buddha told Ānanda: "If your mind were truly joined with the lapis lazuli, you should see the mountains and rivers;
why do you not see your own eyes? If you could see your own eyes, the eyes would then be the same as the external objects, and it would not constitute 'following' [the gaze].
If you cannot see them, how can you say that this discerning mind is hidden within the faculties like the lapis lazuli?"
Therefore, you should know that your claim—that the mind capable of cognition lies hidden within the sense organs like a gem inside a lapis lazuli casket—is impossible.
Ānanda said to the Buddha, "World-Honored One, I now further reflect upon this: within the internal cavities of the bodies of these sentient beings..."
The viscera are within, while the apertures reside on the outside; where there are viscera, there is darkness, and where there are apertures, there is light.
Now, when I face the Buddha and open my eyes to see light, this is called seeing the outside; when I close my eyes and see darkness, this is called seeing the inside. What is the meaning of this?
The Buddha told Ānanda: "When you close your eyes and perceive darkness, does this realm of darkness face the eye or not?
If it faces the eye, the darkness is in front of the eyes; how can it be considered 'internal'?
If it were internal, then when you are in a dark room without the sun, moon, or lamps, the darkness within that room would all be your own entrails. If it does not face the eye,"

How can this be established as seeing? If one were to see internally by turning away from external objects, then when the eyes are closed and one sees darkness, it would be called seeing within the body;
yet when the eyes are open and one sees light, why does one not see one's own face? If one does not see one's own face, then internal perception is not established.

If this perception were established, one would know that the mind and the eye-faculty must reside in empty space; how then could they be said to be "within"? If they were in empty space, [how could they perceive the body?]
If your body were not identical to the Tathāgata’s, then when the Tathāgata now beholds your face, it would also be your own body.

Since your eyes already perceive it, your body ought not to be unaware of it; yet if you insist that both body and eyes possess distinct perceptions, then this single body of yours would become two Buddhas.
Therefore, you should know that your claim that seeing darkness is called "seeing within" is impossible.
Ānanda said, "I have often heard the Buddha reveal to the fourfold assembly that because the mind arises, all manner of phenomena arise;
and because phenomena arise, all manner of minds arise. Now, as I contemplate this very essence of contemplation, it is truly my own mind-nature.
Wherever it conjoins with something, the mind is present there accordingly; yet it does not exist within, without, or in between—none of these three locations."
The Buddha told Ānanda: "What you have just said—that because dharmas arise, various kinds of mind arise, and wherever they meet, the mind follows—is incorrect.

If this mind has no substance, then there is nothing with which it can meet. If that which lacks substance could nevertheless meet [with others], then the nineteenth sense-field would meet with the seven objects;
such a principle is not tenable. If it does possess substance, then consider, for example, when you use your hand..."
"Strike your own body. Does this mind that you know emerge from within, or does it enter from without? If it emerged from within, you would see what is inside your own body;
if it came from without, you should first have seen its face."
Ānanda said, "I see with my eyes; it is the mind that knows. It would not be logical for the eyes themselves to be what sees.
The Buddha said, "If the eyes were able to see, then when you are inside a room, would the door be able to see? Furthermore, among those who have already died, their eyes still remain;
they should all still be able to see objects. If they could still see objects, why would they be called dead? Ānanda, as for this mind of yours that perceives and knows—"
Does it necessarily have a body, or is it a single body, or does it have many bodies? Is it currently located within your body, or is it pervasive throughout the body, or is it not pervasive?
If it were a single body, then when you prick one limb with your hand, the other four limbs should feel it;
if they all felt it, there would be no specific location for the prick. If the prick has a specific location, then your "single body" cannot be established.

If [the self] were manifold in substance, it would constitute many persons. What substance, then, would belong to you? If it were omnipresent in its substance, it would be the same as the previous case of being struck.
If it were not omnipresent, then when you touch your head, you would also be touching your feet; yet while the head has sensation, the feet would be devoid of consciousness.
Since this is not the case for you, you should know that wherever there is contact, the mind is present there accordingly; it is impossible for it to be otherwise.

Ānanda said to the Buddha, “World-Honored One, I have also heard when the Buddha was discussing the true nature of phenomena with Mañjuśrī and other Dharma-princes, that the World-Honored One likewise stated that the mind is neither within nor without.

As I reflect upon this, since there is nothing seen within, the mind cannot be established as being inside; and since the body and mind do not know one another, it cannot be established as being outside.”
"Since the external is not the object and you now know it through mutual perception, and since there is no seeing within, it must be in between.
The Buddha said, "Regarding what you call 'in between,' that which is in between cannot be confused; it must have a specific location. Now, when you infer this 'middle,' where does it reside?

Does it reside in a place, or does it reside in the body? If it resides in the body, does it reside at the periphery or in the center? If it resides at the periphery, it is not the middle; if it resides in the center, [it is the middle]."

If that which is internal and occupies a location were either manifest (*vijñapti*) or non-manifest (*avijñapti*), and if the non-manifest were identical to the non-manifest [of other directions], then there would be no fixed determination.
Why? For example, when a person uses a marker to designate the center, looking from the east it is south, while looking from the west it becomes north;
since the substance of the marker is thus confused, the mind should likewise fall into disorder.
Ānanda said, "Among what I have spoken, it is not these two kinds [of location], as the World-Honored One has said: 'With the eye and forms as conditions, eye-consciousness arises.
Since the eye possesses discrimination and the object of form lacks consciousness, when consciousness arises between them, that must be where the mind resides.
The Buddha said, "If your mind were located between the faculty and the object, then would this essence of the mind encompass both, or would it not?"
Second, if it were to possess both [aspects], the substance would be a chaotic mixture; since a substance is not cognition and cognition is its opposite, how could they stand together as a middle?
Since possessing both is impossible, it would be neither cognition nor non-cognition, and thus would lack any essential nature. What, then, would constitute the characteristic of the "middle"?
Therefore, one should know that for there to be a "middle" in such a case is impossible.

Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying, "World-Honored One, in the past I saw the Buddha together with his four great disciples—Mahāmaudgalyāyana, Subhūti, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra, and Śāriputra—turning the wheel of Dharma.

He constantly spoke of the nature of the mind that perceives and discriminates, saying that it is neither within, nor without, nor in between; it has no location at all, and is entirely free from attachment."
"If you name it 'mind,' do you not then have an attachment to that which is called mind?
The Buddha told Ānanda, "You say that the nature of the mind that perceives and discriminates has no location whatsoever.
Now, the world, space, water, land, flying creatures, and all such objects and phenomena are called 'all things. If you have no attachment to them, do they exist or do they not exist?"
If it were non-existent, it would be the same as a tortoise’s hair or a rabbit’s horns; how then could there be non-attachment? That which is non-attached cannot be called non-existent.

If it lacks characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), it is not non-existent; if it is not non-existent, it possesses characteristics. If characteristics exist, they are present; how then can there be non-attachment?
Therefore, one should know that the claim that all non-attachment is the realization of the mind—that the mind has no such [characteristics]—is impossible.
The Treatise says: The subtlety of the mental dharmas cannot be sought through ordinary emotion, nor can it be discerned by consciousness;

yet students abandon emotion and consciousness, becoming bewildered and fearful. Out of compassion for them, the World-Honored One has peeled away their essential forms one by one, causing them to see clearly.
Once they see clearly, the mind will naturally abide in its own place. I shall now expand upon his words so as to exhaustively clarify this matter.

Regarding the understanding of this, it was first asked: "If the mind is within, then one cannot see the internal. It was further said: "If the mind is without, then the body and mind must know each other.
Again, it was said: "If it were hidden within the roots [of the sense organs], then it would be like the eye seeing mountains and rivers but not being able to see the eye itself;
thus, because the analogy of the glass covering the eye is not consistent, it was further said that the mind resides in the opening and closing [of the eyes]."
If the visual faculty were located within the eye itself, then in a dark room where there is no sun, moon, or lamp, it would become a mass of scorched entrails;
if you insist that perceiving the appearance of darkness constitutes seeing the interior, then when perceiving light, one should likewise be able to see one's own face.

Furthermore, if it were located wherever it happens to be joined [to the body], it should have a physical substance; yet when one presses on a single limb, the other four limbs do not feel it—how could this be?
"Does the mind have a location that is not pervasive? He replied, "It resides between the sense organs and their objects.

[The Master said: "If so, then knowing and not-knowing stand as opposing forces; how can this be verified as being 'in the middle' (of neither)? This implies that objects lack the essence of cognition while the body possesses it. Again he asked, "Does it reside in a place of non-attachment? [The Master said:
"If it were already in a state of non-attachment, it should then exist right now; why is it not so? Thus, he interrogated him thoroughly through these seven points."

When one does not see the place of return, the consciousness of emotion naturally withers. In the past, when the youth Sudhana ascended the peak of Mount Māyāgiri, he did not see the Bhikṣu Meghashvara;
yet when he saw the Bhikṣu Meghashvara, he was on a different peak.

In the assembly of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, for those being shown the way to the "transformed city," the location of the "Jewel Treasury" (the true destination) is not described by its direction, but is said to be near at hand.
If one were to see Mount De-yun (Cloud of Virtue) at the summit of Mount Miao-feng (Wondrous Peak), there would necessarily be a fixed direction;

likewise, the essence of the mind would have to possess both nature and characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*). This is analogous to the *Li* hexagram in the *Yi Jing*, which represents the mind: "Li" signifies attachment.
A supple line cannot stand alone and must have something to which it attaches. Although it attaches, it is visible, yet in reality, it possesses nothing. South.
The hexagram Fang corresponds to the image of fire. Since fire must not be trespassed upon, it is said: "If the first nine is treated with reverence, there will be ultimate good fortune.
As for the fourth nine, one trespasses upon it; therefore it is said: "It breaks forth suddenly like fire; it burns, it consumes, and it leads to death. Supplement:
The Buddhas of the three periods and the Bodhisattvas dwelling in the station of Great Sovereignty have realized this.
Because they exhaust the intrinsic nature of all phenomena and are of one essence with that very nature,
when a Buddha or a Bodhisattva eats a single meal, they can cause all sentient beings to be fully satisfied; this is like the rice in Subhūti’s bowl,
which was not given away because only those of the Two Vehicles have realized their own portion of nirvana, and thus their physical existence differs [from that of Buddhas].

The Tathāgata, wishing to cite this to refute Ānanda’s argument that he was outside [the assembly], first set him aside and barred him—fearing the fault of "incompleteness" (asiddha) regarding any one of the members—and thereby decisively severed the objections of the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*).

By using a metaphorical expression to show that he was not included within the count of those who had fasted, he said, "I have already completed my fast. Subsequently, he further excluded the rank of Maheśvara Bodhisattva...
Sakyamuni specifically refers to those of the Two Vehicles when he says, "Observe this bhikṣu, the Eye of the Inexhaustible Ocean.

This is not a teaching intended merely to exclude or reject; rather, it is simply for the sake of facilitating the act of giving. Therefore, phrases such as "I have already finished my morning meal" were omitted.

Changshui further explains "morning meal" (*suzhai*) as "preparatory meal," but neither interpretation accords with the original intent of the sutra. Since the Tathāgata likewise followed the practice of begging for alms, [the text was thus revised].
"Returning to the Jeta Grove, how could there be a prior arrangement for the midday meal? This simply means that after staying overnight, one arrives at noon to eat.

Furthermore, Changshui’s desire to emend "the outside does not know each other" (*wai buxiangzhi*) to "the outside also knows each other" (*wai youxiangzhi*), claiming it is an error in the character *zhi* (知), is all the more incorrect.
If one says "there is nothing seen within," this refers to what was previously called "even though... (*zong*).

It is because one cannot see the heart, liver, spleen, or stomach. As for the statement that "the external does not know [the internal]," this refers to what was previously called "certainly not knowing the internal";

how could it be that the external knows? Therefore, Ānanda cited the Tathāgata’s refutation of the position that [consciousness] is internal and established the argument of being "in the middle" as a response. Since there is nothing seen internally, the external does not know [the internal].
Because there is no cognition within, it cannot be established as being inside; yet since the body and mind cognize one another, it is not logical for them to be outside.
Now, although the body and mind cognize each other, because there is still no seeing within, this differs from the previous case of being "inside";
therefore, it must be in between. Whose error is this? As for the statement that "the mind follows what exists,"孤山 (Gushan) says: "Since the mind already conforms and joins [with its object]..."

If they exist, they must inherently lack self-nature; if they could combine while fundamentally lacking self-nature, then the nineteen realms and seven particles—both of which likewise lack self-nature—should also be able to combine. Since that is not the case, how could this be so?
For the realms are limited to eighteen, and the particles are limited to six.
At that time, Ānanda rose from his seat amidst the great assembly, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms in reverence, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"I am the youngest brother of the Tathāgata; having received the Buddha’s compassionate love, although I have now left the household life, I still rely upon his affectionate indulgence.
Consequently, despite my great learning, I have not yet attained the state of no-outflows (anāsrava) and am unable to subdue [my afflictions]."

"The *Sāṃvara* mantra has been turned against us by that [demon], causing us to drown in the brothels; this is surely due to our ignorance of the true destination of the ultimate reality (*bhūtakoṭi*).
We pray only that the World-Honored One, out of great compassion and pity, will reveal to us the path of *śamatha*, so that all those of the *icchantika* class may destroy their Mleccha ways.
Having spoken these words, they prostrated themselves with their five limbs touching the ground, while the entire great assembly waited expectantly with hearts full of longing.
I reverently heard these instructions.
At that time, the World-Honored One emitted various kinds of light from the gate of his face;

the radiance was so brilliant as to resemble hundreds of thousands of suns, causing the Buddha-world to quake in six ways, while lands as numerous as the motes of dust throughout the ten directions were simultaneously revealed.
By the majestic spiritual power of the Buddha, all worlds were merged into a single realm;
all the great bodhisattvas within those worlds remained in their own lands, joining their palms in reverent attention.
The treatise states: *Icchantika* is translated here as "one who burns away the roots of goodness.
In its correct form, it is *ācandika*, which means "one who has no desire [for nirvāṇa]. The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* defines an *icchantika* as one who lacks the faculties such as faith;
this is because the lack of such faculties as faith constitutes the burning away of the roots of goodness. *Mleccha* is alternatively said to mean "borderland dweller."
Some say these are those who delight in defilement, and others say they are those with evil views;
this is because those born in the borderlands where the Buddha-dharma does not exist are precisely those who delight in defilement. The borderlands are the retribution-ground of the icchantikas;
if an icchantika can attain this path of śamatha, they will destroy that ground of retribution. The World-Honored One, wishing to reveal this in the profound Vaipulya sutras, [said]:
Because form and mind are non-dual, the phrasing is cryptic while the meaning is manifest. How is this known? It is as stated in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*:
"The Buddha emits light from the white tuft between his eyebrows, illuminating eighteen thousand worlds in the eastern direction, such that there is nowhere it does not pervade.
This is cryptic in its phrasing. Yet, while the six sense-faculties are distracted and disturbed, the eyebrows have no [separate] function; the ten directions are at peace.
In stillness, the east is characterized by agitation; the golden *ūrṇā-kośa* (tuft of hair between the brows) represents the convergence of sense organs (*indriya*) and objects (*viṣaya*).

Within this convergence of organ and object, light is able to pervade everywhere—this is the manifest meaning [of the teaching]. The *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa Sūtra* states: "He took up the world-system of Abhirati as if it were a potter's wheel.
The phrasing of this passage is subtle. If a world-system can be taken up and moved like this, how could it be considered real?

How remarkable! This is where the meaning becomes manifest. Here it says that "the lands of the ten directions, as numerous as motes of dust, are all revealed at once," and again, "causing all worlds to merge into a single realm. These expressions are subtle;
if lands can be made to open and worlds can be made to merge, how could these be literal realities? This is its [meaning].

This is the explicit meaning of the passage. Supplement: Regarding Jiyin’s discussion of the ten directions' lands as numerous as motes of dust appearing simultaneously and all worlds merging into a single realm—it may be said that his phrasing is subtle and his intent is explicit;
however, it cannot be said that this is a literal reality. The purport of this section precisely clarifies the separation of the sense faculties.
Since the method of merging and opening is thus, it is not real. How else could it manifest the inconceivable power of the Tathāgata’s majestic spiritual authority?
Just as Vimalakīrti used his right hand to cut off and take up the world of Abhirati—inserting it into this world like a potter’s wheel—and displayed it to all the assemblies like a flower garland;
so too [did he show] the mountains, rivers, and valleys of that land of Abhirati.
The palaces of the rivers, sun, moon, stars, devas, nāgas, spirits, and Brahmās, as well as the assemblies of bodhisattvas and śrāvakas,
cities, villages, men and women, great and small, even up to the Tathāgata Akṣobhya and his bodhi tree with its various wondrous lotuses—
all those capable of performing buddha-work throughout the ten directions— [were seen] from Jambudvīpa via the three jeweled staircases.
From Jambudvīpa to the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, the various devas descended by means of these precious stairways to pay homage to the Tathāgata Acalā and listen to the Dharma.
The people of Jambudvīpa also ascended those stairs to rise up to the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven;
when they beheld those devas and the time came to lift up that land, those who had attained supernatural powers all raised their voices and addressed the Buddha.
I pray that you will grant protection to those who have not yet attained supernatural powers (*abhijñā*), for they do not perceive or know where they are going.
Although the world of *Abhirati* enters this land, it neither increases nor decreases; likewise, this world is not made cramped or narrow.
Since it is already named "inconceivable" (*acintya*), how could it ever be exhausted by intellectual cognition? What is meant by this?
The Buddha’s majestic power (*vibhūti*) is such that even thunder cannot rival it; this is called majesty. His spiritual power (*śakti*) is such that neither yin nor yang can fathom it;
this is called spirituality. Spirituality is that which wondrously governs all things while operating alone.
While spirituality within the myriad things may still be measurable, that which remains unfathomable is none other than the wondrous adaptability of our Buddha. As for the six kinds of earth tremors:
The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states that there are six kinds and eighteen types of miscellaneous tremors, namely: trembling (*calana*), universal trembling;
rising (*udaya*), universal rising; surging (*kṣobha*), universal surging; shaking (*prakaṃpana*), universal shaking; roaring (*nirghoṣa*), universal roaring;
and crashing (*vidhvaṃsana*), universal crashing. These are the [tremors].
The Buddha told Ānanda: "All sentient beings, from time immemorial, have accumulated various inverted karmic seeds that naturally cluster together like *akṣa* berries.

That practitioners of the Way are unable to attain unexcelled bodhi—whether they instead become śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, followers of external paths, devas, māras, or the retinues of māras—is entirely due to their lack of understanding."
The cultivation of these two fundamental delusions is like boiling sand in the hope of producing fine food;
even if one passes through kalpas as numerous as dust motes, one will never succeed. What are these two, Ānanda?

First is the root of beginningless birth and death, which is that very攀緣心 (pān-yuán-xīn—the mind that clings to objects) that you and all sentient beings now take as your own nature. Second is the root of beginningless Bodhi.
The fundamental essence of nirvana is originally pure; it is this very consciousness-essence, originally luminous, that is able to give rise to all conditions.

That which is lost amidst these conditions is due to sentient beings having abandoned this original luminosity. Thus, though they act throughout the day, they remain unaware of themselves and mistakenly enter the various realms of existence.
The Treatise says: Those who employ the攀緣心 (攀緣心, *pān-yuán-xīn*—the mind that grasps at objects) take that which arises and perishes moment by moment to be the producer of all conditions;
those who seek to learn take that clear and lucid awareness (*liǎoliǎo língzhī*) to be what is abandoned.

To take that which arises and perishes moment by moment as the truth and to discard that clear and lucid awareness is called "erroneous cultivation. As for the *ákchā* cluster, it has three fruits on a single stem and does not grow in isolation.
The mind-king, the mental factors (*citta-caitta*), and their objects arise simultaneously.
That which is called "lucid and numinous awareness" is termed the "pure ground of awakening" (*bodhi-bhūmi*) for sentient beings; to awaken to and cultivate this clearly is termed "unsurpassed bodhi.
Those who cannot awaken to it but cultivate in accordance with it are said to separately achieve divergent paths. The *Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment* states: "Sentient beings are deluded..."
Those who perceive the flow of saṃsāra and follow that flow harbor false views regarding nirvāṇa; because of this, they cannot enter pure awakening.
It is not that awakening rejects those capable of entering it, but rather that there are those capable of entering who do not enter through awakening.
For this reason, it is said they cannot achieve unsurpassed bodhi, but instead become śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas. As the *I Ching* says: "The wise one..."
When one perceives it, they call it wisdom; when a person of benevolence perceives it, they call it benevolence.
The myriad beings use it daily yet do not know it; therefore, the Way of the gentleman is rare. Now, the worthy person preserves the Way through their intention, thereby becoming benevolent and wise;
the ignorant person uses it daily yet does not know it. This distinguishes them from those who become Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas, as well as those who become non-Buddhists.
These are the various devas, Māras, and their retinues.
Ānanda, if you now wish to know the path of śamatha and desire to transcend birth and death, I shall now question you further.
At that moment, the Tathāgata raised his golden arm, bent his five fingers into a fist, and said to Ānanda: "Do you see this, Ānanda?"
The Buddha asked, "What do you see? Ānanda replied, "I see the Tathāgata raising his arm and bending his fingers to form a radiant fist that illuminates my mind and eyes.
The Buddha asked, "By what means do you see this? Ānanda replied, "Together with the great assembly, I see it with my eyes.
The Buddha said to Ānanda, "Now answer me: when the Tathāgata bends his fingers to form a radiant fist, what is it that sees?"
"Illuminate your mind and eyes for me. Your eyes can see; what do you take to be the mind? When Ānanda was thus illuminated by the Buddha’s fist, he said:
"The Tathāgata is now inquiring about the location of the mind. As I investigate and pursue it with my mind, that which performs this investigation—I shall take that to be the mind."
The Buddha said, "Alas, Ānanda! This is not your mind. Ānanda was startled; he left his seat, joined his palms, stood up, and addressed the Buddha:
"This is not my mind. What should it be called? The Buddha told Ānanda: "This is a false appearance and perception of the external objects before you, which deludes your true nature.
Because from time immemorial until this present life, you have mistaken a thief for your own son, you have lost your original [nature]."
Because of this constant [craving], one undergoes the cycle of rebirth.
Ānanda said to the Buddha, “World-Honored One, I am the beloved younger brother of the Buddha; because my heart loves the Buddha, he caused me to leave the household life.
Why should my mind alone offer sustenance to the Tathāgata? I shall even travel through lands as numerous as the sands of the Ganges to serve all Buddhas and...”
"Good spiritual friend, it is by means of this mind that one gives rise to great courage and vigor to perform all those dharmic deeds that are difficult to practice.
Even if one were to slander the Dharma and forever lose their roots of goodness, it would still be because of this mind.

If what I have now clarified were not the mind, then I would be without a mind, identical to wood or earth; apart from this awareness, there would be nothing else. How could the Tathāgata have said [that there is no self]?"

"This is not [the fault of] mind; I am truly terrified, and there is no one among this great assembly who does not harbor doubt. I pray that you will deign to show great compassion and reveal what we have not yet understood.
The treatise says: As stated previously in the text, the World-Honored One clearly declared the reasons why it is impossible to achieve unsurpassed bodhi.
None of them understood that these two kinds of roots were intended to point out the actual state of their own minds; thus, [the Buddha] raised his arm and bent his finger to demonstrate it.

Ānanda should have clearly understood the distinction between the true mind and deluded conditions, yet because Ānanda still identified with those deluded conditions, the World-Honored One rebuked him, saying:
"It is like a person who possesses a *maṇi* jewel and shows it off to a guest."
He said, "In my world, there is no jewel that can surpass this one. Yet the guest remained skeptical, asking, "Is it black or white?
Is it round or not round? Is it pure and lustrous or not pure and lustrous? The World-Honored One then said, "Alas! This is not your own mind.
It was as if he had taken a mani-jewel out and shown it to him, so that his eyes could personally witness it.
By way of conventional expression:

at that time, the World-Honored One, desiring to cause Ānanda and the great assembly to enter the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), rubbed the crown of Ānanda’s head while seated upon the lion throne and addressed him, saying: "The Tathāgata has always taught that all dharmas arise..."
All causes and effects, worlds, and even the finest atoms, are manifested solely by the mind; they derive their substance from the mind.
Ānanda, if one were to examine the root source of everything that exists within all these worlds—even down to blades of grass, leaves, threads, and knots—they would all possess an inherent nature.
Even empty space has a name and appearance; how much more so the pure, wondrously pure, and luminous mind-nature, which is fundamentally one?

If you insist that the nature perceived through the conceptualization and observation of the mind is itself the mind, then this mind should possess a complete, independent nature apart from all objects—the spheres of form, sound, smell, taste, and touch—and their activities.
Just as you now listen to my teaching, this [mind] arises through sound and possesses discrimination; even if that sound were extinguished, [the mind would still exist].
All that is seen, heard, sensed, and known, even when one maintains internal stillness in a secluded place, remains but the reflected shadow of the discrimination of dharma-objects.
I do not scold you for grasping at this as "not the mind," but rather, you must subtly examine the nature of the mind:

if there is a nature of discrimination that exists apart from these external objects, then that is your true mind; if this nature of discrimination has no substance apart from objects, then it is merely the discrimination of external objects.
"Reflections and sensory objects are not permanent; if they change and perish, this mind would be like the hair of a tortoise or the horns of a rabbit.
Thus, your Dharma-body would be subject to annihilation. Who then could cultivate and realize the patience of the non-arising of dharmas?
At that moment, Ānanda and the great assembly were silent and lost in self-reflection. The Buddha addressed Ānanda: "All practitioners in the world who are currently training..."
Although you have attained the nine successive concentrations, you have not yet exhausted the outflows to become an Arhat;

this is entirely because you have clung to these deluded thoughts of birth and death, mistaking them for reality. Therefore, although you have now acquired much learning, you have not achieved the fruit of sainthood.
Having heard this, Ānanda wept again with deep sorrow; prostrating himself with his five limbs touching the ground, he knelt with palms joined and addressed the Buddha, saying: "Since I..."
Having followed the Buddha to leave the household life, you relied upon the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power and constantly thought to yourself, "There is no need for me to practice;

I shall assume that the Tathāgata will bestow samādhi upon me. You did not realize that body and mind are fundamentally not interchangeable. Having lost your original mind, although you have left the household life in body, your mind has not entered the Way.
It is like a destitute son who abandons his father and flees; only today do you finally realize that although [the father] is present...
"O World-Honored One, though we have heard much, if we do not practice, it is equal to not having heard at all; it is like a person who speaks of food but can never satisfy their hunger.
We are now entangled by the two obstacles, precisely because we do not know the nature of the mind, which is quiescent and eternal.
We only pray that the Tathāgata, out of compassion for us who are destitute and exposed, will manifest the wondrous and luminous mind and open our eyes to the Way."
The Treatise says: That which has form yet is extremely subtle, such as grasses and trees, still possesses a substantial nature;

that which is formless yet is extremely vast, such as empty space, also possesses names and appearances. If Ānanda’s mind gives birth to empty space and contains the entire universe, how could it alone be subject to cessation?
It is like hearing a sound and having a discriminating mind; when the sound ceases, the mind does not.
Then, Ānanda, that which gives rise to empty space and contains the universe would arise and perish along with the auditory object;
how could such a principle possibly exist? Therefore it is said: "If there is a nature of discrimination apart from the external objects, then that is truly your own mind;

if this nature of discrimination has no substance apart from the objects, then it is merely a reflected image of the discrimination of those external objects. The objects themselves are not [the mind].
If it were permanently abiding, then at the time of transformation and cessation, this mind would be like the hair of a tortoise or the horns of a rabbit.
To be pure while apart from defilement is called "pure"; to be pure while being defilement itself is called "wondrously pure.
Because this mind is both identical to and separate from [defilement], it is called the "luminous mind of purity and wondrous purity. As for this mind, all minds receive their nature from it.

It is said that the nature of all minds—from the first dhyāna up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, as well as the meditative absorption of cessation—is called the nine successive attainments.
Ānanda lost his hold on these; he realized for himself that he was entangled by the two obstacles.

Regarding these two obstacles, the *Sūtra of Perfect Enlightenment* states: "The obstacle of principle obstructs right knowledge and vision; the obstacle of phenomena continues the cycle of birth and death."

Those whose correct knowledge and vision have not yet clearly manifested seek the Way through principles and meanings; having sought and attained it, they clarify what was known, which is called the "obscuration of the knowable" (*jñeyāvaraṇa*).
Furthermore, because those who have not yet severed birth and death take afflictions as their business, it is also called the "afflictive obscuration" (*kleśāvaraṇa*).
Since they are still within birth and death while seeking principles and meanings, it is said: "They think it will be like this."

"Come and bestow upon me samādhi. The *Pao-tsang lun* says: "To know existence as subject to destruction and non-existence as not subject to ruin—this knowing of existence and non-existence is beyond calculation.
Since it is said that existence and non-existence are not calculated, this is the spontaneously and eternally wondrous knowing of self-nature that is without conditions (*anālambana*).
The sages of the past merely used the skillful means (*upāya*) of great wisdom to bring this forth.
It is not that there is some dharma to be bestowed upon them. As the first line of the *Mong* hexagram in the *Yi Jing* states:
"To enlighten the ignorant, it is advantageous to employ punishment. The first line represents the *kan* trigram, which signifies moving through peril; thus, employing punishment is its image.
Only by being bound with shackles and subjected to humiliation can one fully realize and manifest one's own inner radiance.
Immediately, from the *svastika* mark on the Tathāgata’s chest, there surged forth a precious light.
This light was brilliantly radiant, possessing hundreds of thousands of colors, which simultaneously pervaded Buddha-worlds as numerous as the motes of dust in the ten directions.

It completely drenched the crowns of all the Tathāgatas in all the precious lands throughout the ten directions, and then returned to Ānanda and the great assembly. Addressing Ānanda, the Buddha said: "I shall now, for your sake..."

He erected the great Dharma-banner and caused all sentient beings throughout the ten directions to obtain the wondrous, subtle, and secret nature of pure and luminous mind, and to attain the eye of purity.
Ānanda, you previously answered me that you saw the light of my fist; from what source does this light of the fist arise?
How is it formed into a fist? And by means of what did you see it? Ānanda replied: "It was because the Buddha’s entire body was made of Jāmbūnada gold..."

The gold blazes like a mountain of jewels because it is born from purity; thus it possesses radiance. I truly observed with my own eyes that he clenched his five fingers into a fist to show them to people;
thus he possesses the mark of the clenched fist.
The Buddha told Ānanda, "I now speak these true words to you: those who possess wisdom must rely on parables to attain awakening.
Ānanda, it is like my fist: if there were no hand, my fist would not exist; if there were no eyes for you, your seeing would not exist.
If you take your faculty of sight as an analogy for the principle of my fist, is their meaning not the same? Ānanda replied, "It is so, World-Honored One."
Ānanda replied, "So be it, World-Honored One. Since there is no eye of mine, my seeing is not established; this is analogous to the case of the Tathāgata’s fist.
The Buddha told Ānanda, "Your claim that they are analogous is incorrect. Why is this?
Just as a person without hands has no fist at all, one who lacks eyes does not mean that seeing is entirely non-existent. Why is this so? You should try [this] on the road."
If you were to ask those blind people, "What do you see? they would surely answer you: "At present, before our eyes we see only darkness; we perceive nothing else.
By this principle, consider that the external objects themselves are dark; what impairment could there be to the seeing?
Ānanda said, "Those blind people see only darkness before their eyes; how can this be called 'seeing'? The Buddha told Ānanda: "All..."

A blind person without eyes perceives only darkness, and a person with eyes situated in a dark room perceives only darkness; is there any difference between these two kinds of darkness, or is there no difference?
Thus it was said, World-Honored One: "Between the person in the darkness and that group of blind men, when comparing the two types of darkness, there is never any distinction.
Ānanda, if a person without eyes who has been seeing only the darkness before them suddenly regains their faculty of sight, they return to the space before them.

If you claim that the eye sees various forms among the sensory objects, then a person in the dark who perceives only the blackness before them, upon suddenly obtaining the light of a lamp, should also be said to see those various forms before them by means of the lamp’s sight. If it were the lamp that sees, the lamp would possess the faculty of vision and could no longer be called a "lamp.
Furthermore, if it were the lamp that observes, what concern would that have with you? Therefore, you should know that the lamp can only reveal [objects].
"That which thus perceives form is the eye, not the lamp; the eye can manifest form, but that which thus perceives this nature is the mind, not the eye.
Although Ānanda had heard these words along with the great assembly, their mouths remained silent while their minds were not yet awakened.
Still hoping for the compassionate voice to be bestowed in the future, they joined their palms, purified their hearts, and waited expectantly for the Buddha’s merciful instruction.
The Treatise says: "From the *svastika* on his chest, a hundred-jeweled light surged forth" refers to the intention to reveal this mind-dharma.

That which is called "dust-motes" is a metaphor for the crowns [of the Buddhas]. That the light universally pervades the Buddha-worlds at once and completely drenches the crowns of all Tathāgatas in all the jeweled lands of the ten directions means that it is not only I, Ānanda, and the great assembly who are so drenched.
[The Buddha] said, "It is complete. When Ānanda and the great assembly arrived, it was not only the Tathāgatas who were complete.
Why is it that for the Tathāgatas he speaks of the "crown" (*mūrdhan*) while for Ānanda and the assembly he does not? He replied:
"Because the Buddha’s crown possesses the *uṣṇīṣa*, which is free from the characteristics perceived by others. The World-Honored One’s intention was as if to say: 'I shall now speak of this.'"
The Dharma of the Summit causes all sentient beings to clearly perceive the Buddha-nature; because it establishes the banner of the Dharma, it is said:
"I now establish for you the great Dharma-banner. The banner is used to subdue and overcome those of different classes, representing what I have established.
As for Jāmbūnada gold, it is named after the tree from which it originates; when the fruit juice enters the water, the sand and stones become gold. The Buddha-body is like this.
Because it is golden, it is said that the Buddha’s entire body is Jambūnada gold, blazing like a mountain of jewels.
What is called "attaining the wondrous, subtle, and secret mind of intrinsic purity and clarity" means that the student, relying on the Buddha's words, knows it is not extinguished;
yet in reality, they have not yet seen it clearly. It is like a person who, though their form is hidden, has not yet forgotten their tracks—so it is now observed.
When the external objects are naturally darkened yet seeing remains unimpaired, then all physical traces are utterly severed and one directly perceives the essence of the mind.

At that time, the World-Honored One extended his hand, which possessed the webbed fingers like soft cotton and radiated light, and with his five wheel-like fingers, he instructed Ānanda and the great assembly:
"When I first attained the Way, in the Deer Park, for the sake of Ājñātakauṇḍinya, the five bhikṣus, and others..."
Furthermore, you and your fourfold assembly have said that all sentient beings fail to achieve Bodhi and Arhatship solely because they are deluded by adventitious afflictions;
by what means did you yourselves then attain awakening and now achieve these holy fruits?

Then Kauṇḍinya rose and addressed the Buddha: "I am now the elder among this great assembly, and I alone have attained the name 'Kṣemaka' (the Liberated One) because I realized the two characters of 'adventitious dust.
As a result, I have attained fruition, World-Honored One. It is as if a traveler were to stay at an inn, either to sleep or to eat;
once the business of sleeping or eating is finished, he packs his bags for the road ahead and has no leisure to remain settled. If one is the actual host, they naturally have no such need."
Thus, that which moves on is called "not abiding"; it is called a "guest" and the "host" is that which does not abide. For the meaning of a "guest" is defined by its lack of abiding.
Furthermore, when the sky is newly cleared and the bright sun rises, light enters through a crack in a wall, illuminating the various forms of dust within the air.
The substance of the dust wavers, yet empty space remains tranquil. Thus, one should contemplate that what is clear and still is called "space," while what wavers is called "dust."
"Regarding what is called 'dust' (rajas), that which causes agitation is the meaning of 'dust. The Buddha said, 'It is so.
At that moment, the Tathāgata, in the midst of the great assembly, bent his five fingers; having bent them, he opened them again; having opened them, he bent them once more.
He then said to Ānanda, 'What do you see now? Ānanda replied, 'I see the Tathāgata’s palms, adorned with hundreds of precious wheels.'"
[The Buddha] opened and closed his hand in the midst of the assembly and asked Ānanda: "Do you see my hand opening and closing in the midst of the assembly?
Is it my hand that has the opening and closing, or is it your vision that has the opening and closing? Ānanda replied:
"World-Honored One, it is the precious hand of the Tathāgata that opens and closes before me; it is not my faculty of vision that has the opening and closing. The Buddha said:
"Who moves and who is still? Ānanda replied, "The Buddha’s hand does not remain still, yet my seeing-nature is not even still;
who, then, is 'not remaining'? The Buddha said, "It is so. Thereupon, the Tathāgata emitted a jewel-light from his palm that flew to the right of Ānanda.
Immediately, Ānanda turned his head and looked to the right. He then emitted another light to the left of Ānanda.
Again, Ānanda turned his head and glanced to the left. The Buddha asked Ānanda, "Why is your head shaking today?
Ānanda replied, "I saw the Tathāgata emit wondrous jewel-light coming from my left and right; therefore, as I looked left and right, my head shook of its own accord.
The Buddha said, "Ānanda, when you glanced at the Buddha’s light and moved your head left and right, was it your head that moved, or was it your vision that moved?"
“World-Honored One, my head moves, yet my nature of seeing has no cessation; what, then, could cause it to shake? The Buddha said, “It is so.
Thereupon, the Tathāgata addressed the great assembly: “If sentient beings take that which moves to be called ‘dust,’ [then they have not understood the true nature of phenomena].”
That which does not abide is called "guest. Observe, Ānanda: your head moves of its own accord, yet your seeing remains unmoved;
observe my hand opening and closing, yet your seeing has no expansion or contraction. Why is it that you now take movement to be the body and movement to be the object?
From beginning to end, moment by moment, you give rise to birth and extinction, losing the true nature and acting in delusion.
The fundamental nature of the mind has lost its true essence; by mistaking external objects for the self, one revolves within this cycle, undergoing transmigration by one’s own volition.
The treatise states: "Mṛgadāva" is fully called Mṛgāra-vana (Deer Park), also named Mṛga-ārāma (Deer Garden), and further known as Āmra-vana (Mango Garden).
When the World-Honored One was on the path to enlightenment, he served as the king of deer in this garden; now that he has attained the Way, he first preached the Dharma for the five bhikṣus here.
To demonstrate that he did not forget his origins, Ājñāta was called "He Who Understands the Meaning" and also "He Who Understands the Ultimate Limit.

Others were called Mahānāman, Aśvajit, Bhadrika, and Vāṣpa. As for what I have said regarding the nature of my vision being "without even a point of rest," this is because it has already transcended the characteristic of stillness.
