The "esoteric teaching" refers to that which is taught as being neither caused by conditions nor arising spontaneously, as in the original [text]; this is the esoteric teaching. Question: What is meant by the "exoteric teaching"? Answer:
As stated in the *Saṃpuṭa* (Flower Garland): "For example, like the waters in a river, rushing and flowing together in a torrent, each unaware of the others;
all phenomena are likewise. Furthermore: "Also like a great mass of fire, with its fierce flames arising simultaneously."

The arising of each [phenomenon] is mutually unknown; all dharmas are likewise. Furthermore, it is like a great wind rising that encounters objects and causes them all to vibrate, yet each is mutually unknown;
all dharmas are likewise. Furthermore, it is like the various earth-elements which abide by depending on one another, yet each is mutually unknown;
all dharmas are likewise—this applies to the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind.
The mental faculty and all the sensory organs thus constantly circulate, yet there is no agent that causes them to circulate;
the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is fundamentally without birth, yet it manifests as having birth. Within this, there is neither an agent of manifestation nor any object manifested.

The eyes, ears, nose, tongue, body, mind, and all sensory faculties are entirely empty and devoid of intrinsic nature. By forgetting the conceptualizing mind regarding existence, one realizes it is thus.
Observing that all things are without intrinsic nature and are *nirvāṇa*, it is further said that they are like a magnet; however, this meaning is not correct. Why?
Because the stone does not attract iron. For what reason? Because there is no mental activity (*citta-karma*).
Noble son, because a distinct phenomenon exists, a distinct phenomenon arises; because a distinct phenomenon is absent, a distinct phenomenon perishes. There is no agent.
There is no experiencer, son of good family. It is just as, for example, a fierce fire cannot burn the fuel;
rather, when the fire arises and the fuel is destroyed, it is called "burning the fuel. Son of good family, it is like sunflowers that turn toward the sun;
yet these sunflowers have no mind of reverence, no consciousness, and no karma—it is simply by the nature of their distinct dharmas that they naturally revolve. Son of good family...
Just as a plantain tree grows because of thunder, yet that tree has neither ears nor consciousness;
because of the presence of one phenomenon, another phenomenon grows, and because of the absence of one phenomenon, another phenomenon perishes.
Son of good family, it is like the *akāśa* tree, which produces flowers when touched by a woman; yet that tree has neither mind nor the sensation of touch.
Because a phenomenon exists, another phenomenon arises; because a phenomenon is absent, another phenomenon perishes.

Just as when a citron tree receives the fruit of a *śīrṣa* plant, its yield becomes abundant, so too does a citron tree—though it has no mind and no sensation—become abundant through the existence of one phenomenon and perish through the absence of another phenomenon.
Son of good family, it is like the pomegranate, brick, bone, and dung.
Therefore, when fruits grow in abundance, it is because the pomegranate tree lacks the intention to touch [them], yet because of the existence of one dharma, another dharma arises;
because of the non-existence of one dharma, another dharma perishes. Son of good family, the magnet attracting iron is also like this:
because of the existence of one dharma, another dharma arises; because of the non-existence of one dharma, another dharma perishes. Thus it is with all things.
The birth of the Buddha-nature is also like this: it cannot be drawn forth by *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Good son, ignorance cannot draw forth the formative forces (*saṃskāra*), nor can the formative forces draw forth consciousness (*vijñāna*).
This is called "ignorance conditions the formative forces; the formative forces condition consciousness," whether a Buddha exists or not, within the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*).
The meaning of the *Nityasthita-vicitrapuṣpa-sūtra* is that water, fire, wind, and earth all move and shift, yet they are without action and without creation;

who causes them to be so? From the beginning, it has never been heard that water, fire, wind, and earth undergo birth and death or receive karmic retribution, just as the faculties of the eyes, ears, nose, tongue, body, and mind are also all moving and shifting, without action and without creation—who [causes them to be so]?
If this is so, why do you say that only [sentient beings] undergo birth and death and receive the retribution of karma?

The intent of the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* is that although plants such as the plantain, the sunflower, the bean, the orange, and the pomegranate lack the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) to perceive touch and other sensations, they are nonetheless able to achieve growth and development.
Just as ignorance, formations, consciousness, and so forth, up to old age and death, function in this way—how could it be that only [beings with] discrimination possess such capacity? Great!
"How marvelous! This is what the World-Honored One has clearly expounded as the Dharma of non-arising.
Furthermore, Ānanda, how is it that the eighteen realms are fundamentally the Tathāgata-garbha, the wondrous nature of True Suchness?
Ānanda, according to your own understanding, the eye and forms serve as conditions to give rise to visual consciousness. Does this consciousness arise because of the eye?"

The eye is the cause of the realm [of consciousness] produced by form; form is the realm. Ānanda, if it were produced because of the eye, then in the absence of form and in emptiness, there would be nothing to distinguish.
Even if your consciousness existed, what would you have it serve? Furthermore, your seeing is not blue, yellow, red, or white, and having no representation, from what could a realm be established?
If it were produced because of form, then when there is emptiness and no form, your consciousness should [not exist].
Regarding extinction, how can you recognize it as being the nature of space? When form undergoes change, you likewise recognize that the characteristics of form are shifting;
yet your consciousness does not shift. From what basis could such a realm be established? If it follows from change, then the characteristics of the realm would themselves be non-existent;

if it does not change, then it is eternal. Since it arises from form, you ought not to recognize the location of space. If it were to combine both [form and consciousness], then the eye and form would be together.
If they were joined at birth, they would be separated in the middle; if they were separated, they would join together at both ends, causing a confusion of their essential natures.

How, then, could they constitute a "realm"? Therefore, one should know that the eye and forms serve as conditions to give rise to the eye-consciousness realm. Since these three locations do not exist [as independent entities], the eye, forms, and the eye-consciousness realm are fundamentally neither caused by conditions nor of a spontaneous nature.

Ānanda, furthermore, regarding what you have understood—that the ear and sound serve as conditions to produce ear-consciousness—does this consciousness arise because of the ear, taking the ear as its constituent element (*dhātu*), or does it arise because of sound, taking sound as its constituent element?

Ānanda, if it were to arise because of the ear, then since the two characteristics of motion and stillness are not present before it, the faculty would fail to constitute cognition; and if there is nothing known, then cognition itself cannot be established.
What is the form and appearance of consciousness? If it is apprehended through the ear’s hearing, since there is neither movement nor stillness, hearing cannot be established;
how then can the ear have a form? If the various colors and tactile objects are called the "element of consciousness," then from what would the "ear-consciousness element" be established?

If consciousness arises from sound and exists because of sound, then it has no relation to hearing; if there is no hearing, then the locus of the characteristics of sound perishes, and consciousness would not arise from sound.

If sound exists because of hearing, then the characteristic of sound should be heard by the auditory consciousness; yet it is not heard. If it were not a constituent element (*dhātu*), it would be identical to sound.

Once the auditory consciousness has been heard, who would know that auditory consciousness? If there were no knower, it would ultimately be like grass or wood. It should not be that sound and hearing are mixed together to form a middle constituent.
If a constituent lacks a middle position, then from what could the characteristics of internal and external be established? Therefore, one should know this.

With the ear and sound as conditions, the ear-consciousness element arises; yet in these three locations, none exist at all. Thus, the ear, the sound, and the consciousness element—these three—are fundamentally neither caused by conditions nor of spontaneous nature.
Ānanda, furthermore, regarding what you understand: with the nose and fragrance as conditions, nasal consciousness arises. Does this consciousness arise because of the nose?

That which arises takes the nose as its causal boundary, and that which arises from fragrance takes fragrance as its boundary. Ānanda, if it arises because of the nose, then within your mind, what do you take to be the nose?
Do you take it to be the physical form of the fleshy organ with its two nostrils, or do you take it to be the nature of the oscillating faculty of olfactory cognition?
If you take it to be the physical form, then that fleshy substance is merely the body; since bodily cognition is contact, it is called the "body" and not the "nose."
If "contact" is merely a name for the object, then since the nose itself lacks even a name, how can you establish a sense-field (*dhātu*)?

Furthermore, if you take the act of smelling as the cognition, then within your mind, what constitutes that cognition? If you claim the flesh constitutes the cognition, then the cognition of the flesh is fundamentally contact and not the nose.
If you claim space constitutes the cognition, then space would cognize itself, and the flesh would have no sensation; if this were so, then space would be you and your body would lack cognition.
Today, Ānanda, you should have no involvement with it; since the perception of fragrance belongs to the fragrance itself, what concern is it to you?

If the scents of fragrance and stench were necessarily produced within your nose, then those two kinds of flowing air—fragrance and stench—would not arise from the *eranda* and sandalwood trees respectively.
If those two objects did not come to you, yet you smelled your own nose, would it be fragrant or foul? If it is foul, it cannot be fragrant.
Fragrance should not be foul; if both fragrance and foulness could be perceived [by the same organ], then you, as a single person, should possess two noses.
I asked Ānanda, "There are two here before me; which of these is your essence? If the nose were one, then fragrance and foulness would not be two distinct things.

Since foulness becomes fragrance and fragrance becomes foulness, if these two natures do not exist, from what could the boundaries [of the sense organs] be established? If [the perception of smell] arises because of fragrance...

If consciousness exists because of fragrance, just as the eye exists because of seeing, then one would not be able to perceive it; for since the eye exists because of fragrance, it should not know fragrance.
If it knows it, it is not "arisen"; if it does not know it, it is not "consciousness. Since fragrance is not known, the fragrance-element (*gandha-dhātu*) is not established.

If consciousness does not know fragrance, then it is not established based on the element of fragrance. Since there is no intermediate state, the internal and external are not established; such is the nature of that which hears.
Since they are ultimately false and illusory, you should know that the nose, odors, and the nose-consciousness-element produced with them as conditions—these three locations are all non-existent;
thus, the nose, the odors, and the nose-element are fundamentally neither caused by conditions nor of a spontaneous nature.
Ānanda, furthermore, regarding that which you understand: with the tongue and flavors as conditions, the tongue-consciousness arises.
Does this consciousness arise because of the tongue, taking the tongue as its constituent element (*dhātu*), or does it arise because of the flavors, taking the flavors as its constituent element?
Ānanda, if it arose because of the tongue, then all the world’s sugarcane, *ume* plums, yellow myrobalan, rock salt, *śigru*, ginger, and cassia would have no flavor at all.
Taste your own tongue: is it sweet or bitter? If the nature of the tongue were bitter, who would come to taste it? Since the tongue does not taste itself, what is there to perceive?
If the nature of the tongue is not bitter, flavor does not arise; how then can you establish the sense-sphere?

If consciousness arises because of flavor and that consciousness itself becomes the flavor, then it would be identical to the tongue-organ and should likewise not taste itself; how then could it discern whether something is a flavor or not a flavor?
Furthermore, all tastes do not arise from a single substance; since tastes are manifold, the consciousness that arises from them should likewise be manifold in essence.

If the essence of consciousness were a single entity, then when salty, bitter, sweet, and pungent tastes arise together in combination and undergo various transformations, they would all become a single taste.
If there were no differentiation, it could not be called "consciousness. How, then, could it be termed the "tongue-taste-consciousness element"?
It should not be that space gives rise to your mind-consciousness; when the tongue and flavors combine, there is fundamentally no self-nature therein—how, then, could a realm arise?
Supplement: Gushan says, "If they were blended together, then one half would belong to sound and one half to hearing; therefore it is said..."
Since there is no intermediate state within the elements (*dhātu*), if there is no intermediate consciousness, then the meanings of "internal" and "external" objects are both untenable.

Furthermore, regarding the statement "it should not be like space," etc.: first, the tongue is used as the reason to refute arising from self; second, flavor is used as the reason to refute arising from other;

third, space is used as the reason to refute causeless arising; and fourth, the conjunction of the tongue and flavor is used as the reason to refute arising from both [self and other], as well as sequential arising.
All such passages are alike, yet this one is the most explicit among them. Therefore,

you should know that with the tongue and flavors as conditions for the arising of the tongue-consciousness element, when these three locations are entirely absent, then the tongue, the flavors, and the tongue-element— these three—
are fundamentally neither causes and conditions nor of a spontaneous nature.
Ānanda, furthermore, regarding that which you understand: body-contact serves as the condition for the arising of body-consciousness.
Does this consciousness arise because of the body and thus take the body as its constituent element (*dhātu*), or does it arise because of contact and thus take contact as its constituent element?

Ānanda, if it arises because of the body, there would necessarily be no dual conditions of conjunction and separation; what then would the body recognize? If it arises because of contact, there would necessarily be no such thing as your body.
Who is there that possesses a non-physical consciousness capable of knowing union and separation? Ānanda, objects do not know by touching; it is the body that knows through touch.
To know touch is the body; to know the body is touch. Thus, touch is not the body, and the body is not touch. These two characteristics—body and touch—are fundamentally without location.
When united with the body, they constitute the very nature of the body itself; when separated from the body, they are identical to the characteristics of empty space, both internally and externally.
If the middle does not exist, how can the middle be established? Since the nature of the internal and external is empty, from what could your consciousness arise?

How then could the sense-spheres (dhātus) be established? Therefore, you should know that with body and touch as conditions, the body-consciousness-element arises; yet these three locations are entirely non-existent.
Thus, the triad of body, touch, and the body-element are fundamentally neither caused by conditions nor of a spontaneous nature.
Ānanda, furthermore, regarding what you understand: with the mind and mental objects as conditions, the mental consciousness arises.
Does this consciousness arise because it takes the mind as its cause and the mind as its realm, or does it arise because it takes mental objects as its cause and mental objects as its realm?

Ānanda, if it arises because of the mind, then within your own mind there must be something being contemplated that brings forth your intention; if there were no preceding mental objects, the mind would have nothing from which to arise.

If separated from conditions, formless consciousness would have no function. Furthermore, is your conscious mind—the nature of deliberation combined with discrimination—identical to or different from the mental faculty (*manas*)?
If they are identical, it is simply the mental faculty; what then is produced? If they are different, the mental faculty would not be able to cognize anything.
If there is nothing cognized, how can the mental faculty arise? If there is something cognized, how can consciousness be distinct from the mental faculty? Is it merely identical or different?
If the two natures are unestablished, how can the realms be established? If the world arises from dharmas, then all worldly phenomena are not separate from the five sense objects.
Observe that the phenomena of form, sound, fragrance, taste, and touch have distinct characteristics;
they correspond to the five faculties and are not subsumed by the mind-faculty. Your consciousness definitely arises in dependence upon these dharmas. Now, observe this closely.

As for the nature of dharmas: if they are apart from form, emptiness, movement, stillness, penetration, obstruction, union, separation, arising, and ceasing, one ultimately finds nothing at all beyond these characteristics.
When they arise, form, emptiness, and all dharmas arise together; when they cease, form, emptiness, and all dharmas cease together.
Since their cause does not exist, what form or appearance could consciousness take that arises from it? Since such characteristics do not exist, how can the realms be produced?
Therefore, one should know that with the mind and dharmas as conditions, the mental consciousness-element arises; yet in these three locations, none exist at all.
Thus, the mind, dharmas, and the mental consciousness-element—these three—are fundamentally neither causes and conditions nor of a spontaneous nature.

Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, the Tathāgata has often said that all the various transformations in the world arise from the conjunction of causes and conditions, specifically through the manifestation of the four great elements in combination. Why then does the Tathāgata now reject both causes and conditions as well as spontaneity?
I do not yet understand to what this meaning refers; I only pray that out of compassion you will reveal it for the sake of sentient beings."
"This is the Dharma of the definitive meaning, free from conceptual proliferation.

At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Ānanda, saying: "Because you previously felt weary of and detached from the various Hinayana vehicles of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas, and resolved to diligently seek unsurpassed Bodhi, I shall now reveal the Ultimate Truth for you."

Supplement: The tenth fascicle of the *Wujin yi* (The Exhaustless Translation), from the section beginning with "From the source of delusion being originally causeless" (*wàng yuán wú yīn*) to the end of the passage on the "five false conceptions" (*wǔ wǎngxiǎng chéng*), together with the preceding twenty-eight characters and the addition of the two characters "Ānán" (Ānanda) above the phrase "source of delusion," totaling thirty-five lines, are included here under the heading of the "First Noble Truth" (*dìyī yìdì jù*).
This is done because it accords with the flow of the text. [End of] the *Yú* (Foolish/Inexperienced).
I humbly examine the preceding passage where Ānanda asks how the Tathāgata might simultaneously set aside both the views of causality and spontaneity,
and requests an exposition of the Middle Way— the definitive meaning free from conceptual proliferation—
whereupon the Tathāgata answers with the words "the nature of the seven elements," as seen in the section beginning with "delusion originally has no cause" in the tenth fascicle; Ānanda himself...

Question: Regarding the five kinds of delusion within the characteristics of the five aggregates, which serve as the original basis for the thought of the Tathāgata, [the text] then provides a detailed analysis using "delusion originally has no cause" and so forth. These two sets of questions and answers have no initial connection nor do they overlap;
what is inconsistent about their textual flow that you wish to change them? Moreover, Maitreya follows the Sanskrit original.
I fear that my translation may not have fully captured the nuances of the local dialects; yet, from beginning to end, it certainly shall not be as discordant as this.
Why, despite your great learning, do you further entangle yourself with worldly frivolity, conceptual proliferation, and delusive causes and conditions?
As it is said: "A man who possesses medicine, when the true medicine appears before him, cannot discern it; the Tathāgata calls such a person truly pitiable.
You should now listen attentively, and I shall analyze and reveal it for you, so that those who practice the Mahāyāna in the future may penetrate the true reality (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*).
Ānanda silently accepted the Buddha’s holy instruction. Ānanda, as you have said, regarding the four great elements...

The combination and manifestation of the various transformations in the world, Ānanda—if the substance of those great elements were not a combination, they could not intermingle with one another, just as empty space does not combine with forms.

If they were a combination, they would be identical to transformations, wherein beginning and end mutually constitute one another, and birth and cessation continue in succession: death after birth, and birth after death.
It is like a whirling firebrand that never rests, Ānanda; it is like water turning into ice, and ice returning to water. Observe the nature of earth:
grossly it is the great earth, subtly it is fine dust, down to the *paramāṇu* (the smallest particle).

If one analyzes that ultimate atom into its constituent parts of color and form, it is composed of seven parts; if one further analyzes the *paramāṇu*, it is simply the nature of empty space. Ānanda, if this *paramāṇu*...
When analyzed into emptiness, you should know that emptiness gives rise to the appearance of form.

As for your current question regarding how the various transformative phenomena of the world arise through combination: consider this—how much space is used in the combination of a single *paramāṇu* (subtle atom) so that it exists?
A *paramāṇu* cannot be formed by the combination of other *paramāṇus*. Furthermore, if a *paramāṇu* is analyzed and dissolved into emptiness...
By how many colors and forms is space synthesized? If it were synthesized by color, then what is joined with color would be color, not space;
if it were synthesized by space, then what is joined with space would be space, not color. Color can still be analyzed, but how could space be synthesized?

You fundamentally do not understand that within the Tathāgata-garbha, essential form is true emptiness and essential emptiness is true form. It is pure and fundamental, pervading the entire Dharma-realm, following the minds of sentient beings.
It manifests according to karma in accordance with the measure of what is known.
[Supplementary Note: The Tathāgatagarbha is the essence of quiescent illumination and wondrous clarity;

because it can contain and expel the ten voids, it is called "pervasive," and because it manifests the ten realms, it is called "according to karma. Guishan explains this in terms of the perfect fusion of the Three Truths.

Regarding the explanation of this "store-nature" as being neither identical nor different, Master Jingjue once remarked that its meaning is rich, vast, and all-encompassing, such that it is present everywhere.
Later commentators, merely wishing to appear clever and seek novelty, have instead lost the essential core of the principle. I, however, say this is not so.
When the Tathāgata was interacting with his close disciples, he frequently expounded and explained this meaning, saying: "I, by means of my wondrous clarity, which is neither extinguished nor..."

Being in union with the Tathāgatagarbha, and since the Tathāgatagarbha is solely wondrous, enlightened clarity that perfectly illumines the Dharma-realm, within it one becomes many and many become one; the small manifests the large and the large manifests the small;
without moving from the site of enlightenment, one pervades the worlds of the ten directions; the body contains the infinite space of the ten directions within a single hair-tip.

Manifesting the Jewel King Land while seated within a single mote of dust, he turns the Great Dharma Wheel; because he extinguishes the dust and unites with awakening, he brings forth the wondrously enlightened nature of True Suchness (*tathatā*).
Thus, the Tathāgatagarbha—the fundamentally wondrous, perfect, and circular mind—is neither mind nor emptiness, neither earth, water, wind, fire, nor anything else.
It is revealed in its true state as that which is detached from both "is" and "is not," and detached from both "is" and "is not."
Furthermore, in the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*, the Buddha said to Mahāmati Bodhisattva:

"There are times when such terms as emptiness (*śūnyatā*), signlessness (*animitta*), wishlessness (*apraṇihita*), the reality-limit (*bhūtakoṭi*), the dharma-nature (*dharmatā*), the dharma-body (*dharmakāya*), nirvāṇa, being devoid of self-nature (*niḥsvabhāva*), non-arising, non-ceasing, primordial quiescence, and natural nirvāṇa are used to speak of the Tathāgatagarbha. How could these fail to overturn and reveal its essential substance?"
Regarding the "Dinglin" [section], it says: Wind has no substantial entity; it manifests in dependence upon the earth, and is therefore called the "land" (*bhūmi*).

Water and fire serve as the utility for the world, and are therefore called the "world. The spheres of activity arising from consciousness and the six sense organs exist but are not real, and are therefore called the "ten voids.
Why does "form" (*rūpa*) not speak of the "world" and "land"? Because apart from form, there is no world or land.
Detached from worldly realms, it is perfected by formlessness and emptiness; it is neither merely a worldly realm, nor is it existent yet unreal.
Therefore it is said that in the ten directions there is no shifting or flowing, and emptiness is likewise so.

As for the limit of form, the "atom" (*paramāṇu*) refers to the smallest particle possessing spatial dimensions; the "neighboring atom" (*aṇu*) refers to the ultimate infinitesimal point devoid of spatial dimensions; this is analyzed from the dust-particle.
The ultimate, which cannot be broken down or analyzed, is true emptiness.
That the world is ignorant and deluded regarding causes, conditions, and inherent nature is merely the conceptualization and calculation of the discriminating consciousness;
it is nothing but words and lacks any real meaning.
Ānanda, the nature of fire has no self; it depends upon various conditions. Observe the households in the city that have not yet eaten:
when they wish to cook their food, they hold a magnifying lens in their hands and seek fire from the sun.

Ānanda, what you call "combination" is like myself and you, along with these one thousand two hundred and fifty bhikṣus, now forming a single assembly. Although the assembly is one, if you examine its fundamental basis, [it is composed of many individuals].
Each and every one has a body, all of whom have their own birth clans and names,
such as Śāriputra of the Brahmin clan, Uruvilvā-Kāśyapa of the Kāśyapa clan, and so on up to Ānanda of the Gautama clan. Ānanda,
if this nature of fire exists because of a combination of conditions, and someone holds a mirror in their hand and seeks fire from the sun— does this fire come from within the mirror?
If it emerges from the mugwort, then when it comes from the sun, Ānanda, if it were truly coming from the sun, it would naturally burn the mugwort in your hand;

the forests through which it passed on its way here should all have been consumed by fire. If it emerged from within the mirror, then as it emerged from the mirror to ignite the mugwort, why did the mirror not melt?
Even though you held it in your hand, it showed no sign of heat; how then could it have melted away?
If fire arises from the tinder, why does it require the conjunction of the sun and the mirror’s radiance before it is produced? You should observe closely:
the mirror is held by the hand, the sun comes from the heavens, and the tinder grows in its own place;
from where does the fire travel to reach here? The sun and the mirror are far apart; they neither blend nor combine, yet the fire cannot arise of itself without cause. You still do not understand.
In the Tathāgatagarbha, the nature of fire is true emptiness and the nature of emptiness is true fire; it is pure and fundamental, pervading the entire Dharma-realm.
It responds to the minds of sentient beings according to the measure of what they know. Ānanda, you should know that when people in one place hold up a mirror, fire arises in that one place;

if they were to hold mirrors throughout the Dharma-realm, fire would arise filling the entire world. Since this arising occurs everywhere throughout the world, how could it have a fixed location? It follows their karma.
One discovers that ignorance and delusion in the world, whether as causes and conditions or as inherent natures, are all merely conceptual constructions and calculations of the discerning mind;
they exist only as verbal expressions and possess no real meaning whatsoever.
Ānanda, the nature of water is not fixed; its flow and stillness are without constancy.

For instance, in the city of Śrāvastī, there were the mahāsiddhas Kapila, Jāṅgulī, Padma, and Mahāsatva, among other great illusionists, who sought the essence of the moon to mix with their magical elixirs.
These masters, during the day of the waxing moon, would hold a *fangzhu* (a concave mirror) in their hands to catch the water from the moon; as for this water—
Furthermore, does it emerge from within the pearl, or does it exist of itself in space, or does it come from the moon?

Ānanda, if it comes from the moon, then since it can cause water to emerge from the pearl even at a great distance, all the trees and forests it passes by should likewise discharge flowing streams. If they were to flow, why would one need to wait for the *fangzhu* (the concave mirror used to collect dew)?
Since they do not discharge water, it is clear that the water does not descend from the moon. If, on the other hand, it emerges from the pearl, then [it must already exist] within this pearl.

If water were always flowing, why wait for midnight to receive it under the white moon? If the water were produced from the sky during the day, then since the nature of space is boundless, the water would likewise be limitless.
From humans to the heavens, all would be submerged and drowned. How then could there still be those who travel by water, land, or air?
You should observe this further: the moon ascends from the heavens, the pearl is held in the hand, and the basin to receive the water from the pearl was originally set out by a person.

From what direction does the water flow into this moon-crystal? It is neither distant from it, nor is it a union, nor is it a combination; yet it cannot be that the crystal produced it spontaneously from nowhere.
You still do not understand that within the Tathāgata-garbha, the nature of water is true emptiness and the nature of emptiness is true water—pure and fundamental, pervading the entire Dharma-realm.
According to the minds of sentient beings and corresponding to the measure of their cognition, if one person grasps the crystal in one place...
If water were to emerge from a single place and fill the entire Dharma-realm, such that it fills every birth and every world, how could there be any fixed location?

It manifests according to karma; that the world lacks knowledge and takes delusion as its cause and condition, or that it possesses a nature of spontaneity—all these are merely calculations and discriminations of the conscious mind.
They are nothing but words and have no real meaning whatsoever.
Ānanda, the nature of wind has no substance; its movement and stillness are not constant.
When you regularly adjust your robes before entering the great assembly, the corner of your saṃghāṭī moves and touches those beside you, causing a slight breeze to brush against their faces.

Does this wind arise from the corner of the *kāṣāya*, or does it emerge from empty space, or is it produced on the faces of those people? Ānanda, if this wind were to arise from the corner of the *kāṣāya*...
When you wear this garment, its fabric flutters and sways; it ought to separate from your body. Now, as I preach the Dharma within this assembly, my robe hangs down still—look at my robe:

where is the wind? It cannot be that the robe contains a place where wind is hidden. If it were produced by empty space, then when your robe does not move, for what reason would there be no brushing against it?
Since the nature of space is eternally abiding, the wind should be constantly arising; yet when there is no wind, why is it absent?

If empty space were to be extinguished, then the extinction of wind could be perceived; what would be the appearance of the extinction of space? If there were arising and ceasing, it would not be called "empty space.
Being called "empty space," how could wind emerge from it? If wind arose of itself, then when you wipe your face, the wind should arise from that very face and wipe you yourself.
When you straighten your robes, why do you wipe them instead? Observe this carefully: it is you who are straightening your robes.
The face belongs to that person; empty space is quiescent and does not participate in movement. From which direction does the wind come to stir here?
Wind and space are distinct in nature; they are neither blended nor joined. It cannot be that the nature of wind exists spontaneously without a source.

Yet you, alas, do not realize that within the Tathāgata-garbha, the nature of wind is true emptiness and the nature of emptiness is true wind—pure and fundamentally so, pervading the entire Dharma-realm.
It accords with the minds of sentient beings and corresponds to the measure of what they can know. Ānanda, it is like when you, a single person, slightly move your robe and a subtle breeze arises;
though this wind pervades the entire Dharma-realm and brushes across the whole land, producing its presence throughout the world, how could it have a fixed location? It manifests according to karma.
That the ignorant of the world take delusion as their cause and condition, or conceive of it as having a nature of spontaneity—all such views are merely the discriminations of the conscious mind.
Such conceptual deliberations are merely words and possess no real meaning whatsoever.

Ānanda, emptiness has no form; it is manifested through form. For example, in the city of Śrāvastī, at a place far from the river, there dwell various kṣatriyas, brāhmaṇas, vaiśyas, śūdras, as well as pahlavas and caṇḍālas.
Supplement: *Ulu-piluo* (優盧頻螺) is translated here as "papaya"; *Yin-jia-she-po* (癊迦葉波) is translated here as "Great Tortoise.
*Gautama* is the name of a star; the clan name was established based on this star and was later changed to Śākya.
There are four types of clans in the Western Regions: *Kṣatriya*, the royal caste; *Brāhmaṇa*, those of pure conduct; and *Vaiśya*, merchants.
It is said that the Śūdras are farmers; thus, as in this land, among the four castes—scholars, farmers, artisans, and merchants—the noble and the humble each abide in their respective vocations.
Even in matters of marriage, they do not intermingle.
Since Śākyamuni stands outside these four castes, it is said that those who leave the home-life from among the four castes share the common name of Śākya. Pīlava is fully called Piṇḍola Pīlava.
Falling into this [category], they are called "swift," or "sharp-witted," or "violent and evil persons. Ci'en says:
"Among the eighteen clans of the Brahmins, this [clan] is one of them. Caṇḍāla means "one who adorns himself with insignia. Gu-shan says:
"They adorn themselves with evil karma and carry out their practices bearing these signs. Kapila and others were all masters of illusionary arts. *I*... [text ends].

The *Lan guan fo sanmei hai jing* (Sutra on the Ocean-like Samadhi of the Orchid Contemplating the Buddha) records in full the words of the Buddha Chou-shu (Udumbara), who used sandalwood as a counter-example to illustrate this principle;
it is akin to the Confucian metaphor of the fragrant ruan-herb and the putrid yu-herb, and is by no means comparable to the orchid of today.
As for the *yangshui* (sun-stone), its shape is like a mirror; it is fashioned from cast copper, and when held toward the sun with a tuft of mugwort placed upon it, fire is obtained.
Just as when oyster shells are refined with stones and placed before the moon, they exude moisture and water;
so too, when one newly establishes a dwelling and digs a well in search of water, for every foot of earth dug out, there is a foot of empty space within it.
This continues until ten feet of earth have been removed, at which point ten feet of empty space are likewise found in the middle. Such is the depth of this empty space.
To what does this space owe its emergence? Is it produced by the earth, or is it due to the excavation, or does it arise spontaneously without a cause?
Ānanda, if this space arose spontaneously without a cause, why was there no such unobstructedness before the earth was excavated?

Why did one see only the great earth, with no passage or penetration? If it were produced by the earth, then at the time the earth was being excavated, one should have seen the space entering; yet if [the space were already there]...
If space first emerges without entering [the earth], how can space emerge because of the earth? If there were no entering or emerging, then space and earth would fundamentally have no difference.
If they are not different, they are identical; thus, when the earth emerges, why does space not emerge as well?
If space emerges because of digging, then the digging should produce space rather than earth. If it does not emerge because of digging, yet the digging itself produces the earth, how is this so?
"Look at the empty space; examine it again with the utmost precision and scrutiny. The chisel follows the hand as it moves in various directions, and the earth shifts according to the ground.
From what source, then, does this empty space emerge? The chisel and the void—emptiness and solidity—cannot function for one another;
they are neither blended nor joined. It cannot be that empty space arises from nowhere on its own. If this empty space were by nature perfect and all-pervasive, it would fundamentally not..."
You should know that the moving [wind], and the present earth, water, fire, and wind—these five great elements—are all by nature truly perfect and harmonious;
they are the Tathāgata-garbha, fundamentally without arising or ceasing. Ānanda, your mind is deluded and confused, failing to realize that the four elements are originally the Tathāgata-garbha.
You should contemplate whether space comes out of it or enters into it, or whether it neither comes out nor enters; you have no understanding at all regarding the Tathāgata-garbha within.
The nature of awareness is true emptiness, and the nature of emptiness is true awareness; it is pure and fundamental, pervading the entire Dharma-realm.
It accords with the minds of sentient beings and responds to the measure of what they know. Ānanda, it is like a single well: when a well is dug, space arises within it;

the empty space of the ten directions is likewise so. Perfectly filling the ten directions, how could it have a fixed location? It manifests according to karma, yet the ignorant of the world are deluded by it.
Causes and conditions, as well as inherent nature, are all merely conceptual constructions and calculations of the discerning mind; they exist only as verbal expressions and possess no real meaning.
Ānanda, you perceive that seeing is devoid of cognition, yet it exists in dependence upon form and space, just as you are now in the Jeta Grove at the break of dawn.
At twilight it abides in the center; at midnight, when there is a white moon, it is luminous, and in the black fortnight, it is dark.

Thus, through the perception of light and darkness, this vision is analyzed. Furthermore, is this vision combined with light and darkness? Is it of the same substance as the great void of space? Or is it not of the same substance?
Is it both the same and not the same, or different and not different? Ānanda, if this vision were again combined with light and darkness...

If light and space were originally one entity, then light and darkness—these two entities—would mutually negate one another; when it is dark, there would be no light, and when it is light, there would be no darkness.
If light were identical to darkness, then seeing would cease to exist. If they were necessarily one with respect to light, then at the time of darkness, [seeing] should perish.
If it perishes, how could one see light or see darkness? If light and darkness are distinct from seeing, then seeing would be without arising or ceasing; how then could "oneness" be established?

If this essence of seeing were not of one substance with darkness and light, then when you separate it from light and darkness as well as from empty space and analyze the source of seeing, what form or appearance would it have?
Separated from light, separated from darkness, and separated from empty space, this source of seeing would be like the hair of a tortoise or the horns of a hare.
Since these three things—light, darkness, and empty space—are all distinct, from what could seeing be established? Light and darkness are mutually opposed.

How could they be identical? They are equally free from the three elements and fundamentally non-existent. How could they be different? The division of emptiness and the division of vision are originally without boundaries.
How are they not identical? One sees darkness while the other sees light; their natures do not undergo change. How are they not different?

You should examine this further—examine it minutely, examine it thoroughly, examine it with precision, and observe it clearly—that light follows the great sun, darkness follows the dark moon, and both belong to empty space.
When the jar returns to the great earth, from what source does this essence of seeing emerge? This faculty of seeing perceives emptiness as inert;
it is neither a composite nor a fusion. Thus, it cannot be that the essence of seeing arises spontaneously without a source.

If the nature of seeing, hearing, and knowing is perfect and all-pervading, fundamentally unshakable, then you should know that the boundless, unmoving void, together with the shifting elements of earth, water, fire, and wind, are all equally termed the "Six Great Elements."
The nature of reality is truly perfect and harmonious; all are the Tathāgata-garbha, fundamentally free from arising and ceasing.
Ānanda, your nature is mired in saṃsāra because you do not realize that your seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing are fundamentally the Tathāgata-garbha.

You should examine this seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing: do they arise or cease? Are they the same or different? Are they neither arising nor ceasing, or neither the same nor different? You have never known the Tathāgata’s [true nature].

Within the storehouse-consciousness, the nature of seeing is the luminosity of awareness; this luminous awareness is the essence of clarity. It is pure and fundamental, pervading the entire Dharma-realm.

According to the minds of sentient beings, it responds to the measure of what they know. Just as with the faculty of seeing, where seeing pervades the Dharma-realm, so too do hearing, smelling, tasting, touching, and the awareness that perceives—these wondrous virtues are brilliantly clear, pervading the entire Dharma-realm and filling the ten voids. How could they have any fixed location? They follow the course of karma.
One discovers that ignorance and delusion in the world, whether as causes and conditions or as inherent natures, are all merely conceptualizations and calculations of the discerning mind;
they exist only as verbal expressions and possess no real meaning whatsoever.
Ānanda, the nature of consciousness has no source; it arises falsely from the six kinds of sense organs and their objects.
Now, as you survey this assembly of noble ones with your eyes, following them one by one, your eyes look all around like a mirror, without further analysis.
Within that [mirror-like vision], your consciousness sequentially identifies and points out: "This is Mañjuśrī," "This is Pūrṇa," "This is Maudgalyāyana," "This is Śāriputra..."
"Bodhi! Śāriputra, does this consciousness that cognizes arise from seeing, or from forms, or from empty space, or does it emerge suddenly without any cause?
Ānanda, if the nature of your consciousness were to arise within seeing, then in the absence of darkness, light, form, and emptiness—these four conditions—it would necessarily not exist;
yet even your seeing would have no basis, for the nature of seeing itself would be non-existent."

From what does consciousness arise? If the nature of your consciousness arises from within the objective forms (*nimitta*) and not from the faculty of vision, then since you do not perceive light nor do you perceive darkness, and light and darkness are not being gazed upon, there would be neither form nor emptiness. Since those very forms do not even exist, from what could consciousness arise?

If it were to arise from within emptiness—being neither form nor vision—then, lacking the faculty of vision, there would be no discernment, and you yourself would be unable to know light, darkness, form, or emptiness.

It is not that the conditions for the cessation of marks have been extinguished; rather, seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing have no place of establishment. If these two—place and non-place—were not empty, they would be identical to non-existence;
they are not identical to material objects. Even if you were to activate your consciousness, what would there be to differentiate?

If it emerged suddenly without any cause, why do you not perceive a bright moon while differentiating it during the day? Examine this further and scrutinize it minutely: seeing relies upon your pupils.
They mutually push one another toward external objects; these can be manifested as existent, yet they cannot be established as non-existent. From what source, then, does this consciousness arise?

When the consciousness moves, the vision remains clear; they are neither a composite nor a union. Hearing, listening, sensing, and knowing are likewise so. It should not be that consciousness arises from no source on its own.
If this conscious mind originally has no source from which it comes, then one should know that it is the faculty of discernment that perceives, hears, senses, and knows.
The perfect, tranquil nature does not arise from anything external; together with space, earth, water, fire, and wind, these are all equally called the "Seven Great Elements.
Their nature is truly perfect and harmonious, all being the Tathāgata-garbha, fundamentally free from birth and extinction. Ānanda, your mind is coarse and restless;

you do not realize that the clarity and awareness of seeing and hearing are fundamentally the Tathāgata-garbha. You should contemplate whether these six consciousnesses of the sense-bases are identical [to the Tathāgata-garbha].
Is it different? Is it empty? Is it existent? Is it neither identical nor different? Is it neither empty nor existent?

You fundamentally do not know that within the *tathāgatagarbha*, the nature-consciousness is clearly aware; the awareness of clarity is the true consciousness, and the wondrous enlightenment is profound and still, pervading the entire dharma-realm.

It contains and exhales the ten voids; how could it have a fixed location? It manifests according to karma. The world lacks knowledge and is deludedly attached to causes and conditions, as well as to the self...
However, their nature is entirely that of the mind of consciousness (*vijñāna*) engaging in conceptualization and discrimination; they are merely verbal expressions and possess no real meaning.
The treatise says: What are called earth, water, fire, and wind rely upon space (*ākāśa*) as the five elements of the vessel-world (*bhājana-loka*).
Seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting, and touching rely upon consciousness as the five elements of the root-body (*mūla-śarīra*). Together, the root-body and the vessel-world constitute ten.
If one speaks of the Dharma now in terms of its fundamental nature (*dhātu*), it consists of the ten great natures; yet why does the Sūtra refer to them merely as the "seven greats"? It is said:
because earth, water, fire, wind, and space are the physical forms of the vessel-world (*bhājanaloka*), they are each described in detail.

However, as for the conventional designations of seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting, touching, cognition, the sense-faculties (*indriya*), and their objects (*viṣaya*), they are treated here simply by way of "seeing" [and so forth].

When awakening and consciousness are abbreviated, they constitute seven [faculties]. Therefore, it is said that "seeing and awakening are without knowledge, pure and fundamental, pervading the entire dharma-realm," and then it proceeds to describe:

"Just as the faculty of seeing pervades the dharma-realm, so too hearing, smelling, tasting, touching, and the awareness of touch—this wondrous virtue is luminously clear, pervading the entire dharma-realm. Furthermore, when one examines the various sages in the subsequent text...
The human witnesses have established the twenty-five kinds of perfect penetration regarding the dharmas of the six sense bases, twelve bases, eighteen elements, and seven great natures.
When it came to Mahāsthāmaprāpta, the Dharma Prince, and his fifty-two fellow Bodhisattvas, he said:
"When the Buddha asked about perfect penetration, I made no selection; I simply gathered all six sense faculties together, and pure mindfulness succeeded one another."
Entering samādhi, one uses it to seal and confirm that what is seen, heard, sensed, and known relies upon consciousness as the six sense organs;
when there is no selection among them, the ten great natures are free from doubt and obstruction. Nāgārjuna said:

"If phenomena truly exist, they should not be known to have characteristics by means of the mind-consciousness. If they are known to have characteristics by means of the mind-consciousness, then they do not truly exist."
The characteristic of solidity in earth is known through the body-faculty (*kāyendriya*) and body-consciousness (*kāyavijñāna*);
if these were absent, there would be no perception of solidity. Question: Whether the body-faculty and body-consciousness perceive it or not, the characteristic of solidity always exists in earth.
Answer: If one first perceives the characteristic of solidity for oneself, or hears of it from another, then one knows that solidity exists. If...

If one has previously neither known nor heard of it, then there is no characteristic of solidity. Furthermore, if earth were permanent as a characteristic of solidity, it should not abandon that characteristic;

yet, just as congealed butter, wax, honey, or tree resin abandon their characteristic of solidity and fall into the characteristic of moisture when melted, so too is it with gold, silver, copper, iron, and the like.
Water, having the characteristic of moisture, transforms into the characteristic of solidity when cold.
All such various characteristics are entirely abandoned. Furthermore, it is said: if fire truly possessed the nature of heat, why would some people enter fire without being burned?
Why does the fire within the human body not burn the body? And why can water not extinguish the fire in the clouds?
It is because fire lacks a fixed nature of heat; and by the power of supernormal faculties (*ṛddhibala*), fire cannot burn.
Due to the causes and conditions of bodily karma, the five viscera do not become hot; due to the power of the divine dragon, water cannot extinguish them.
If the nature of heat were different from fire, then fire would not be hot. If the nature of heat were identical to fire, how could one say that heat is the nature of fire?
It is the same for other natures as well. Thus, because the general characteristic and the specific characteristic are both non-existent, it is called the emptiness of nature (*svabhāva-śūnyatā*).
Inferring the natures of earth, water, and fire through this principle is like tracing a stream to find its source;

since all things are empty, how much more so wind and space? That which the World-Honored One taught—phenomena arising from their own nature—is called "the manifestation of phenomena according to karma" (xun-ye-faxian), corresponding to the capacity of what is known.
That which Nāgārjuna discussed—thoroughly investigating nature through its phenomena—is [the same].
This is merely to specially reveal that form and mind are non-dual. Regarding space, it says: "Your mind is deluded and obscured, yet the nature of space is awakened. Regarding seeing, it says:
"Your nature is submerged and sinking, yet the nature of seeing manifests externally. Regarding consciousness, it says:

"Your mind is coarse and floating, yet the essence of consciousness is hidden within. This is because when one is floating, one only recognizes the floating sense-roots; when one is coarse, one does not penetrate the essence of consciousness.
Supplementary Note: Zhenji says, "The nature of form is true emptiness, detached from all marks; the nature of emptiness is true form, which is all marks.
Yuyu says, "Form and marks can be detached from and can be identified with, just as it is with fire and water.
But regarding emptiness, awakening, and consciousness, how should one discern them? One must know that earth, water, fire, wind, and so forth are all [of this same nature]."

Because these objects manifested within the essence of the wondrous mind are what you perceive, it is said that "your mind is deluded and confused, failing to realize that the four great elements are fundamentally the Tathāgatagarbha.
It is further said: "You should know that the boundless, unmoving void, together with the shifting earth, water, fire, and wind, are all collectively termed the six great elements.
Their nature is truly perfect and harmonious; they are all the Tathāgatagarbha, fundamentally devoid of arising or ceasing. Furthermore:
It is said: "Including those [elements], space, earth, water, fire, and wind, they are all uniformly named the 'Seven Great Elements. Their natures are truly and perfectly interfused;

all are the Tathāgata-garbha, fundamentally devoid of arising and ceasing. Viewed from this perspective, they are not external objects. It clarifies that when there is light, there is no darkness; the *Jijie* (Collected Explanations) reads it as: "When it is light, it is not dark."

At that time, Ānanda and the great assembly, having received the subtle and wondrous instruction of the Buddha-Tathāgata, found their bodies and minds completely cleared away, attaining freedom from all obstructions.
Each member of the assembly individually realized that the mind pervades the ten directions;
they perceived the emptiness of the ten directions as clearly as looking at a leaf held in the palm of one's hand, such that all things existing within all worlds were immediately seen to be Bodhi.
The wondrously luminous original mind is the essence of the mind, all-pervasive and perfect, encompassing the ten directions.

When you turn back to contemplate the body born of your parents, it is like a single mote of dust blown into the empty space of the ten directions—whether it exists or perishes, it is as if a single bubble were to rise and vanish upon a vast, tranquil ocean, with no trace of its origin or destination.
Thus, you clearly know for yourself that you have attained the fundamental wondrous mind, which abides eternally and is never extinguished.
Prostrating before the Buddha with palms joined, he attained what he had never experienced before and spoke these verses in praise of the Tathāgata before him:
"O Wondrous, Profound, and All-Holding Lord of Immovability, Suraṅgama King, rare in this world! Eradicate my inverted thoughts of billions of kalpas;
Without passing through the aeons of the saṃgha, may I attain the Dharmakāya."

Supplement: Regarding the two characters "not passing through" (bù lì), the interpretations of the various masters above all fail to trace back to the Tathāgata’s direct revelation of the dharma-gate of sudden realization;
instead, they are confined by mere names and words, obscuring the great purport. Some claim it is a discourse of skillful means (*upāya*);
some claim it is a manifestation through supernatural power (*ṛddhi*); some claim it is merely a sequential narration of awakening and understanding; and some claim it is not a description at all.
If even a single individual were as insistent as various masters in establishing inconsistent doctrines, how could those practicing *samādhi* ever reach a state free from doubt?
I, the ignorant one, refute their dogmatic attachments by means of the two principles of gradual cultivation and sudden realization,
just as the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* describes the cultivation of the six perfections over three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas* and the planting of the marks over a hundred kalpas.

Only after cultivating wholesome causes does one attain the fivefold Dharma-body (*pañcadharmakāya*). Regarding the theory of Consciousness-Only (*vijñaptimātra*), it is said that one passes through the first *asaṃkhyeya-kalpa* prior to the stages (*bhūmi*), the second at the completion of the first stage (*prathamabhūmi*), and the third from the eighth stage up to the level of Equal Enlightenment (*samyaksambodhi*);

only then does one attain the ultimate Dharma-body. This is the meaning of gradual cultivation. When this sutra describes the point where the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñānaskandha*) is exhausted, it says: "the various faculties..."
Through mutual application, from within this mutual application, one is able to enter the Bodhisattva’s adamantine *khaṇḍa-prajñā* (dry wisdom).
With a perfectly luminous and refined mind, transformation arises therein like a precious moon contained within pure lapis lazuli.

In this way, one transcends the ten faiths, the ten abodes, the ten practices, the ten transferences, and the four stages of preparatory application (*prayoga-citta*), as well as all that is practiced by Bodhisattvas up to the adamantine ten grounds and the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samya-sambodhi*).
"Perfect clarity enters the Tathāgata’s ocean of wondrous adornment; when bodhi is perfected, one returns to non-attainment. It is further said:
"Conceptual appearances are dust, and the consciousness-mind is defilement; when both are left far behind, your dharma-eye will become clear and bright at that moment.
Why then would you not achieve unsurpassed perfect enlightenment? This is the meaning of sudden realization. To speak of it in terms of gradual progression:

If one practices this, then from the subtle to the manifest, through self-confidence, one passes through the stages of abiding, practice, and direction until reaching Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*), where one finally realizes the ultimate fruit.
From the perspective of the Sudden Teaching, however, when not a single thought arises and the boundaries of past and future are severed, one is immediately named a Buddha;

since one does not even ascend through the successive stages and positions, how could one pass through incalculable eons (*asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*)? The subsequent text states that for those with non-perfect faculties, [the attainment] takes as long as days and kalpas.

This is precisely what is meant by "doubling. When Ānanda personally realized this sudden gate, he said, "I clearly know for myself that I have attained my original wondrous mind," which is no different from the perfectly luminous mind of Equal Enlightenment (*samyaksambodhi*). Could one say that he did not attain it?
Furthermore, this Dharma-body is possessed by every person; it is merely obscured by ignorance and turbid with delusive thoughts.
It was as if something long hidden had been lost and suddenly found; ignorance was abruptly shattered and delusive thoughts followed suit in their dissolution.

Even a creature as small as an ant or an ant-eater can attain realization—how much more so for this body? Why should it alone not be a cause for celebration? Long ago, the butcher Wide-Face came before the Buddha’s seat, where his ignorance was instantly extinguished.
He set down his knife and said to the Buddha, "World-Honored One, I am counted among the number of the thousand Buddhas."

The Buddha immediately confirmed this, saying: "Is it not permissible that he was already among them? For one such as Wide-Forehead (Panthaka), who cast down his butcher’s knife and had his ignorance suddenly stilled, is now numbered among the thousand Buddhas.
Now, since Ānanda has exhausted his emotional perceptions and his Dharma-eye is clear and bright, it is only fitting that his words were granted [confirmation].
However, while his awakening is equal to that of the Buddha’s awakening, his merit has not yet reached that level."
Because it is the ultimate fruit, one does not speak of the five branches or the final consummation. Pūrṇa said:
"I and the Tathāgata’s precious awakening, perfect luminosity, and truly wondrous pure mind are non-dual and complete.
Yet, though I have long been in saṃsāra due to beginningless delusion, I have now attained the Holy Vehicle and am still not yet at the ultimate end. How is this different from that meaning?"
I have been deluded by the profundity of names and words.

I now vow that upon attaining the fruit [of Buddhahood] and becoming a Treasure King, I shall return to deliver as many beings as there are grains of sand in the Ganges. With this profound resolve, I shall serve every atom of every land;
this is what is called repaying the Buddha’s kindness. I humbly entreat the World-Honored One to bear witness to my vow to save the world of the five turbidities.
I shall first enter [the path] such that as long as even a single sentient being has not attained Buddhahood, I will never take *nirvāṇa* here.

O Great Hero, of Great Power and Great Compassion, I pray you will further examine and eliminate my subtle delusions, so that I may quickly ascend to Unsurpassed Enlightenment and sit at the site of awakening throughout the worlds of the ten directions.
Even if the nature of empty space (*śunyatā*) should perish, my diamond-like mind (*vajracitta*) shall never waver.
The Treatise says: The "Forest of Samādhi" states that the essence of consciousness is water; when this water does not ripple, it is called "stillness" (*zhan*).
What is meant by "perfect stillness" (*yuan-zhan*) is that which is pure and fundamental, pervading the entire Dharma-realm; when it is not divided into six, it is perfectly still.

What is meant by "wondrous stillness" (*miao-zhan*) is that through wondrous power it maintains total stability without movement, and thus it is wondrously still. What is meant by "awakening" (*jue*)...
The nature of profound clarity is the union of awakening with the essence of consciousness, like the sun uniting with water to produce luminosity.

What is called the "profoundly pure, perfect, and eternal" refers precisely to the perfectly clear essence of consciousness. Because it has extinguished all arising and ceasing, it is termed "eternal.
As for this statement that "this profundity is not stagnant, like a rushing torrent appearing tranquil from a distance," the Sūtra says:
When consciousness moves and the vision becomes clear, consciousness possesses a nature of movement; this is called the source of perception (*saṃjñā*).

Unless one attains the wondrous stillness of total mastery (*dhāraṇī*), then moment-to-moment craving, karma, and habitual tendencies form a violent torrent that produces all conditioned formations (*saṃskāra*).

The Sūtra uses the metaphor of a flowing stream for these formations; yet compared to these formations, consciousness is still called "still. This so-called stillness refers to the entry into stillness that merges with stillness.
When the waves have subsided and transformed into clear water, it is called the exhaustion of the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*).

When one enters inwardly into inner stillness and clarity, reaching a state where there is nowhere to enter, this is the domain of the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*). Thus, what is called "entering into stillness" is the aggregate of consciousness.

Since entering into stillness constitutes the aggregate of consciousness, that which is still is the nature of consciousness; the clarity of consciousness is wisdom (*jñāna*), and the clarity of wisdom is itself wisdom. Wisdom and consciousness—this is consciousness.
Because they represent the ultimate limits, the five aggregates are spoken of; yet it is said that "the entry into stillness merges with stillness, returning to the limit of consciousness.

Why is the nature of consciousness not called "entry into stillness"? Because it pervades the Dharma-realm and thus has no coming or going. What is called "innermost, innermost, and luminous entry" refers to having nowhere to enter;
when stillness emerges as activity, it is like flowing water, whereas when stillness enters as consciousness, consciousness ceases and activity ends.
When the *āyatanas* (senses) are withdrawn inward, they become profoundly clear within, entering until one reaches the source of perception (*saṃjñā*), beyond which there is nowhere further to enter.

That which is called the "essence of consciousness" (*vijñāna-ghana*) is precisely the *ādāna-vijñāna*. That which is called "adhering to the profound clarity" refers to this essence of consciousness adhering [to objects].

This essence of consciousness is like pure water, which by nature has no quality of adhesion; it is only because of the arising of deluded discrimination and its conjunction with form (*rūpa*) that the water [becomes turbid].
When soil is mixed with water, it becomes viscous; yet if one recognizes this consciousness, it is like pure, clear water that is inherently free from viscosity.
It does not combine with form, and its detachment from viscosity lies latent within.

There is the perfectly lucid, the wondrously lucid, the awakened lucid, the refined lucid, the lucid penetration, and the viscous lucid—each distinguished by the subtlest nuances as explained previously. This is the exhaustive analysis of all phenomena.
This is an analogy. Aśvaghoṣa said: "To rely on the non-awakened mind has movement as its activity; awakening is non-movement.

Indeed, awakening is non-movement, which is termed the wondrous, profound, and all-sustaining state (*samādhi*). Movement constitutes activity, flowing on to become the various conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*).
As for what is called the *Śūraṅgama-rāja*, it is because Bodhisattvas of the ten stages are able [to abide] in the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi*.
Because he attained this, the Buddha is thus [called] a King. *A-saṃkhyeya* (阿僧祇) should be translated as "incalculable eons" (*asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*);
the translator has omitted the word for eon. *Asaṃkhyeya* here means "innumerable"; *kalpa* here means "period of time.
There are long and short durations of time; what is generally called a *kalpa* refers to an extremely long period. *Śūnyatā* (舜若多) is the wind-deity; its nature is movement. *Śakya*... [text ends].
"Luo" (羅) here means "firm and solid," which refers to the adamantine, firm mind. The old commentary states:
"Śūnyatā" (舜若多) means "empty space. Ānanda’s intention was as follows:
"If the nature of empty space, which cannot be destroyed, could yet be destroyed, then my firm and solid mind could not be moved or shifted. It further states: "The nature of Śūnyatā has not yet..."

yet although the Buddha has proclaimed this clearly to remove our delusions, we still do not fully understand the ultimate meaning of this principle and have not yet reached the ground of being free from doubt.

At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Pūrṇa and all the Arhats in the assembly whose outflows were exhausted and who were beyond training:
"Today, for the sake of this entire assembly, the Tathāgata shall proclaim the true nature of the ultimate meaning within the ultimate meaning,
so that the śrāvakas of fixed nature in your assembly, as well as all the Arhats who have not yet attained the two kinds of emptiness and have turned toward the Mahāyāna, may understand it."
"All have attained the ground of the single vehicle’s tranquil extinction, the true *āraṇyaka* place for correct practice.
Listen attentively now, and I shall speak for you. Pūrṇa and the others, revering the Buddha’s voice of Dharma, listened in silence.
The Treatise says: Zao Bo said, "That which has a beginning and an end is like a person who, within a brief moment, dreams of immeasurable kalpas;
when they suddenly awaken from the dream, all those durations of immeasurable kalpas within the dream can no longer be found.
The beginning and the end are likewise so. Although Pūrṇa was still within the dream, the dream is sustained by memory."

Due to the power of the conceptualization of solitary shadows (*pratibimba*), one falsely perceives various mountains, rivers, and worlds; due to the power of ignorance (*avidyā*), these are illusorily formed as the three branches.
This is similar to the doctrine of the Vijñānavāda school regarding the three types of habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*): first, the habitual tendency of conceptual proliferation (*prapañca-vāsanā*);

second, the habitual tendency of the links of existence (*bhavāṅga-vāsanā*); and third, the habitual tendency of names and words (*nāma-kāya-vāsanā*). Question: What is meant by "conceptual proliferation"? Answer: It is, for example, like...
In the world there is a grass called the "Lady Yu" (*yumeiren*). This Lady Yu was the beloved consort of Xiang Wang;
because she died an untimely death, the world mourned her and composed songs for her. When people lean against the grass and sing with such piteous emotion, the grass invariably sways.
Though the grass possesses no consciousness, when it first appeared while Chu still existed, the beloved consort likewise did not exist—how much less could there have been this grass?
All sentient beings, through their own delusions and inversions, constitute the three realms. He asked again: "What is meant by the 'limbs of existence' (bhava-aṅga)?
He replied: "It is like a magnet in the world; when it encounters iron, it attracts it. Although the stone has no consciousness, it moves, shifts, and turns as if there were something directing it.
Likewise, the three types of suffering of all sentient beings act as causes for one another, forming the twelve [links of dependent origination]."
Sentient beings are formed through the conditions of false planting and grafting; it is thus. He asked again: "What is meant by 'name and phrase'? [The Master] replied:
"For example, when people of the world bury their ancestors in an auspicious location, the family receives blessings for generations; otherwise, there is calamity.
Although one's relatives and the land are not sentient consciousnesses, the response of fortune and misfortune is swifter than a shadow or an echo. All things are like this.

The karmic fruits of sentient beings arise from the power of false conceptualization regarding killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct. Regarding these two emptinesses—person-emptiness (*pudgala-śūnyatā*) and phenomenon-emptiness (*dharma-śūnyatā*):
one who attains person-emptiness knows that sentient beings lack intrinsic nature; one who attains phenomenon-emptiness knows that all phenomena lack intrinsic nature.
Therefore, it is said: "Within your assembly, let the śrāvakas of fixed nature and all others who have not yet attained these two [emptinesses]..."
Turning back toward the emptiness of the Mahāyāna, Arhats and others all attain the ground of quiescent extinction of the One Vehicle,
the true site of *araṇya* for correct practice. *Araṇya* (also *āraṇya*) is here translated as "free from clamor and contention," and also as "a place of leisure and stillness."
The Buddha said, "Pūrṇa, as you have said, it is pure and fundamental by nature; how then could mountains, rivers, and the great earth suddenly arise?
Have you not constantly heard the Tathāgata proclaim that the nature of awakening is wondrously luminous, and that fundamental awakening is luminously wondrous?
Pūrṇa replied, "Indeed, World-Honored One, I have constantly heard the Buddha proclaim this meaning. The Buddha said, "You refer to the luminosity of awakening as..."
"Furthermore, when the nature is manifest, it is called 'Awakening' (jue); when Awakening is not manifest, it is called 'Luminous Awakening' (mingjue).
Pūrṇa said, "If this non-manifestation is called Awakening, then there would be nothing that is luminous. The Buddha said, "If there were nothing luminous, then there would be no Awakening.
To have something is not Awakening; to have nothing is not Luminosity. Furthermore, non-luminosity is not the nature of profound Luminosity. This nature is necessarily Awakened."
"To take delusion as clarity is called 'clarity-awareness' (*ming-wang wei ming-jue*).
The Treatise says: "When nature is spoken of in terms of awareness, that awareness must be clear. Yet there are three names for it. What are these three? They are:

'wondrous clarity' (*miao-ming*), 'clarity-wonder' (*ming-miao*), and 'awareness-clarity' (*jue-ming*). Regarding the nature of awareness, it is called 'wondrous clarity'; regarding the fundamental..."
If one speaks of awakening, it is called "wondrously bright" (*miaomiao*); if one speaks of the awakening within delusion, it is called "awakening-brightness" (*jueming*).

Why is it that "awakening-brightness" alone is not said to be wondrous? It is said: the fundamental awakening (*xingjue*) does not establish beginning or end; it stands alone and is eternally quiescent.

If, however, it encounters conditions for realization and the confusion is resolved, then its wondrousness is made manifest. Therefore, it is said that fundamental awakening is "bright and wondrous. Yet, once "fundamental" (*ben*) has been established...
"Beginning" is another name for this. That which is "intrinsic awakening" (xing-jue) is essentially wondrous and perpetually luminous from the outset;

its luminosity does not depend on anything else to exist. "Original awakening" (ben-jue) refers to the capacity to clearly know that one possesses this wondrous intrinsic awakening, by virtue of the power of inconceivable perfuming and cultivation.
"Awakened luminosity" (jue-ming) refers to the luminosity that arises because of awakening.
"If awakening ceases, then clarity vanishes; are his words not subtle? Maming replied: "The time of initial awakening (*ādi-bodhi*) is itself original awakening (*mūla-bodhi*);

there is no separate awakening that arises to establish initial awakening. It is because of original awakening that non-awakening exists, and it is based on non-awakening that initial awakening is said to exist.
Inferring Maming’s intent and comparing it with this sutra, it appears that [the sutra] elevates original awakening.
Because the awakening of nature (*xingjue*) takes initial awakening (*shijue*) as its basis for becoming original awakening (*benjue*), they appear distinct.
What is here termed "awakening of nature" is what Asvaghosa regards as original awakening; what is here termed "original awakening" is what Asvaghosa regards as initial awakening.
However, the World-Honored One specifically states that returning to the luminosity of one's nature and designating it as such is called "awakening."
This phrase serves to distinguish and define the meaning of what Pūrṇa has understood; it is like saying, "O Benevolent One, are you called a worthy man?
To which he replies, "Indeed, I am a worthy man. Again, it is like saying, "To call that which is not enlightened 'enlightened awareness' (prajñā) [is it so]?
To which he replies, "Is it reasonable to call one who is unworthy 'benevolent'? There is no such principle. However, Pūrṇa did not realize the essence of the nature of enlightenment.

That which is inherently wondrous and eternally luminous is called the "nature of awakening" (*prakṛti-bodha*) because it is capable of luminosity; it is due to the existence of an object of awakening that [the term] "awakening" arises.
Herein lies a doubt: if the World-Honored One were to take a body that is not luminous as being awakening itself, that would be impossible.

How do we know this? Because he responds by stating that there is no need for an object to be illuminated. From this, we know that it must be due to the presence of an object to be illuminated that it constitutes awakening.
[Ananda] said: "If one who does not possess such illumination is called an awakened one, then there would be nothing at all to illuminate.

The World-Honored One took up these words to exhaust the matter, saying: "Pūrṇa, if you mean that because there is nothing to illuminate, there is consequently no illumination-awakening, this interpretation is not correct.
