Fundamentally, one cannot know the false roots and objects; since one does not even know where the inversion lies, how can one subdue it to attain the rank of Tathāgata?
Ānanda, observe those in the world who untie knots: if they do not see what was knotted, how could they know how to untie it?
You have not heard of empty space being torn asunder by you. Why is this? Because space has no form or appearance.
Because of the binding and the unbinding, your present eyes, ears, nose, tongue, as well as body and mind—these six serve as the intermediaries for thieves who plunder the family’s own treasures.
From this beginningless time, the world of sentient beings has given rise to entanglements and fetters; therefore, one cannot transcend the vessel-world (*bhājana-loka*).
Ānanda, what is meant by the "world of sentient beings"? "World" (*loka*) refers to constant flux and change; "realm" (*dhātu*) refers to spatial dimensions.
"Subhūti, you should now know that east, west, south, north, southeast, southwest, northeast, northwest, above, and below constitute the directions;
the past, future, and present constitute the time periods. Thus, there are ten directions and three periods of time.

All sentient beings, through the interweaving of their delusive thoughts, construct their bodies and trade and migrate between worlds, interacting with one another. Yet, although the nature of these directions consists of ten,"
When the positions are established, the world may be clearly defined as merely east, west, south, north, above, and below; yet in the center there is no fixed direction.

These four numbers must be clearly understood as interacting with the world: three times four and four times three turn into twelve, which flow and transform through three cycles to total one thousand two hundred.
Within each of the six sense faculties, these respective merits number one thousand two hundred.
"Ānanda, you should further distinguish the relative superiority and inferiority among these. For instance, when the eye observes, the back is dark while the front is bright;

the front is entirely bright while the back is entirely dark; when looking sideways to the left or right, two-thirds are visible. Generally speaking, the meritorious function of the eye is incomplete by one-third;
thus, if we speak of its efficacy, it possesses only one-third of merit. You should know that the eye possesses only eight hundred merits."
The ear listens all around to the ten directions without omission; whether in motion, it reaches both the near and the far, and in stillness, it is boundless.

You should know that the faculty of hearing is endowed with one thousand two hundred merits. As for the nose, its smelling is connected to the inhalation and exhalation of breath; there is out-breathing and in-breathing, yet it lacks the intermediate junction.
When examined, the faculty of the nose lacks one-third of its three parts. You should know that the nose possesses only eight hundred merits. As for...

The tongue proclaims all mundane and supramundane wisdom; its expression has boundaries, yet its principle is inexhaustible. You should know that the faculty of the tongue is perfected with twelve hundred merits. Just as the body perceives touch—discerning the disagreeable and the agreeable when in contact, yet being unable to discern them when separated—the faculty of the body is verified through three aspects: when one is missing, it is deficient. The same applies to the tongue. When it is in contact with food, it can perceive flavors; when separated from food, it cannot perceive them. Thus, the faculty of the tongue is also verified through these three aspects. If one aspect is lacking, it is deficient. Therefore, you should know that the faculty of the tongue is perfected with twelve hundred merits. Furthermore, when the tongue is in contact with food, it can perceive flavors; when separated from food, it cannot perceive them. However, the textual meaning concerning the essential characteristics of the six sense organs as they are set forth therein is quite clear. It is vulgar for some to recently compare the female organ to the front of a waist drum.

From the shoulders to the hips constitutes the trunk; the rest are merely the limbs and the head. Since the shoulders and hips are broad while the middle is narrow, is this not like a waist-drum (*yaogu*) or a frontal globe?
If one claims that the female organ represents the image of the body, it is but one of the nine apertures.
If one claims that the waist-drum and the frontal globe are metaphors for the two apertures of water and fire, then the bamboo pipes of a musical instrument should likewise resemble them. Indeed.
If it were as you say, then one could only speak of the female organ as the image [of the body] and not the body itself; how then could it be called the "body"?
It is like a waist-drum or a forehead—speaking from this perspective, the original intent was specifically to use these as metaphors for physical form.

As stated in the first fascicle regarding the refutation of the sense organs (*indriya*) and their objects (*viṣaya*), it says: "Is it because of grasping the physical form that one perceives the marks of the two claws, or is it because of grasping the act of smelling that one perceives movement?"
To shake out its nature is to know that the Tathāgata uses the nose of his physical form as a metaphor for the mark of the two hands;

if so, what doubt can there be regarding the body being likened to a waist-drum? As for the "four objects" (*catur-viṣaya*), these refer to the four derivative objects of form, fragrance, taste, and touch.
Someone asked: "In the old commentaries, *jue-ming* (awakened clarity) was sometimes taken to mean true clarity (*zhen-ming*); how do you regard this? He replied: "That is not correct."
This is merely the clarity of deluded capacity; the manifest clarity of consciousness and the essence of the aforementioned deluded capacity are both delusions.
Because one thereby loses the wondrous clarity of true realization, it is said that regarding the deluded, one follows that [delusion], while regarding the true, one has lost it.
Furthermore, "darkly forming non-seeing" means that the cause of seeing is destroyed by conditions; it is not a self-arising clarity.
This refers to the breaking of darkness to achieve "no-seeing. Since seeing exists because of light, then in the presence of darkness, this seeing would logically become non-existent.
If, however, seeing arises spontaneously without depending on light, then when the appearance of darkness manifests before you, it constitutes "seeing darkness" rather than "no-seeing.
Once seeing darkness has been established, how could this essence of seeing be obscured by darkness? Thus, since the sense organ and its object have already...
When these are eliminated, the awakened clarity also becomes perfectly wondrous.

Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying: “World-Honored One, as the Buddha has said, if one seeks the permanently abiding awakened mind at the causal stage, it must correspond in name and designation with the fruition stage.
World-Honored One, if within the fruition stage there are bodhi, nirvāṇa, true thusness, and the Buddha...”

The fundamental *āmalaka*-consciousness, the empty Tathāgata-garbha, and the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom—though these seven names differ, their pure and perfect essence is firm and solid like a diamond-king, eternally abiding and indestructible.

If one views this hearing-faculty as being free from light and darkness, movement and stillness, and penetration and obstruction, it ultimately has no substance; it is like the mind of recollection being separated from its preceding objects.
Dust is fundamentally non-existent; how can one take this ultimate annihilation as a cause for cultivation in order to obtain the fruit of the Tathāgata’s sevenfold eternal abiding?
World-Honored One, if one is separated from light and darkness, seeing that all is ultimately empty, then with no external objects before one, the nature of thought itself is extinguished.
Whether advancing or receding, through subtle investigation in this cycle, one finds that there is fundamentally no self-mind nor any mental factors associated with the self.

Who would establish a cause to seek unexcelled enlightenment if the Tathāgata’s previous teaching that [the nature] is profound, pure, perfect, and eternal were to contradict his truthful words and ultimately become mere frivolous discourse?
How can the Tathāgata be said to speak words of truth? We pray only that you will bestow great compassion and dispel our ignorance and stinginess.
The Buddha said to Ānanda, "Though you have studied much and possess great learning, you have not yet exhausted all outflows (*āsrava*).

In your mind, you merely know the causes of inversion, but when true inversion actually manifests before you, you truly cannot recognize it. I fear that despite your sincere heart, you have not yet attained full conviction and submission.
I shall now test you with matters of the mundane world to remove your doubts. Immediately, the Tathāgata commanded Rāhula to strike the bell once.
The Buddha asked Ānanda, "Do you hear it now? Ānanda and the great assembly all replied, "I hear it.
When the bell ceased and there was no sound, the Buddha asked again, "Do you hear it now? Ānanda and the great assembly all replied, "We do not hear it.
Then Rāhula struck it once more; the Buddha asked again, "Do you hear it now? Ānanda and the great assembly all replied, "We hear it."
The Buddha asked Ānanda, "How do you hear? How do you not hear? Ānanda and the great assembly together replied to the Buddha, "If the bell is struck, we hear it;
when the striking has long ceased and the sound has faded so that both resonance and echo are cut off, this is called 'not hearing.
The Tathāgata then commanded Rāhula to strike the bell again and asked Ānanda and the great assembly, "Do you hear the sound now? Ānanda and the great assembly [replied].
[The Buddha] said, "There is sound. After a short while, the sound ceased. The Buddha asked again, "Ānanda, is there now sound? Ānanda and the great assembly replied, "There is no sound.
After a moment, Rāhula came again and struck the bell. The Buddha asked again, "Ānanda, is there now sound?
Ānanda and the great assembly both replied, "There is sound. The Buddha asked Ānanda, "In what way is there sound, and in what way is there no sound?"
Ānanda and the great assembly together addressed the Buddha, saying: "If a bell is struck, it is called 'having sound';
when the striking has long ceased and the sound has faded so that both resonance and echo are cut off, it is called 'having no sound. The Buddha said to Ānanda and the great assembly:

"How is it that you now speak with such self-contradictory confusion? The great assembly and Ānanda simultaneously asked the Buddha: "In what way, O Buddha, do we speak with such self-contradictory confusion?"
The Buddha said, "I ask you about what you hear, and you say 'I hear. I ask you about the sound, and you say 'It is a sound.
Since your answers regarding hearing and sound are not fixed, why do you not call this evasive confusion? Ānanda, when the sound has vanished and there is no resonance, you say there is no hearing.
If indeed there were no hearing, the nature of hearing would have already ceased, and you would be like a withered tree; yet when the bell is struck again—"
How do you know? You know there is [sound] and you know there is not; this is simply because the object of sound either exists or does not exist.
How could that nature of hearing itself be subject to existence or non-existence for you? If you truly say there is no hearing, who is it that knows there is none?
Therefore, Ānanda, it is within the sound that there is arising and ceasing, not that the arising and ceasing of the sound causes your nature of hearing to become existent or nonexistent.
If you are already so deluded as to mistake sound for hearing, how much more strange is it that you are confused enough to take the permanent to be intermittent?
You must never say that hearing has no inherent nature apart from movement and stillness, or closure and openness. It is like a person in deep sleep, lying comfortably on a bed and pillow;
while they sleep, someone in the house pounds silk or husks rice. In the dreamer's dream, they hear the sound of the pounding and husking.
He was making another object, perhaps striking a drum or tolling a bell, when during his dream he marveled at the sound of the bell, wondering if it were made of wood or stone.
Suddenly waking up, he immediately recognized the sound of the pestle and told his family, "While I was dreaming, I was confused by this sound of pounding rice and took it for the sound of a drum.
Ānanda, how could that person, while in a dream, have recalled whether [the bell] was still or moving, or open or closed?

Whether unimpeded or obstructed, though your physical form may be in sleep, the nature of hearing does not grow dim. Even if your form were to dissolve and your life-force were to pass away, how could this nature ever be extinguished for you?
Since beginningless time, all sentient beings have followed after forms and sounds, flowing along with every thought;

they have never awakened to the pure, wondrous, and eternal nature of their own being, but instead fail to follow that which is constant while pursuing what arises and perishes. It is because of this...
The continuous flow of birth and death is defilement; if you abandon this arising and ceasing and maintain the True Constant, the eternal light will manifest before you.
The sense organs, objects, consciousness, and mind will then dissolve in their proper time. Conceptualizations and appearances constitute the dust, while the conscious emotions constitute the grime.
When both are removed, your Dharma-eye will become clear and bright at that very moment. How could you then fail to achieve unsurpassed enlightenment?

The Treatise says: Regarding what is called "vision dependent on light," it is established through the presence of light and darkness; "non-vision" does not arise spontaneously in the absence of light.
Thus, if these various dark forms could never again obscure [vision], then since vision exists because of light, it must necessarily be absent because of darkness.
Now, as for that which arises spontaneously without depending on light—if one clearly perceives the nature of darkness, then this essence of vision neither depends on light nor on darkness.

Yet it arises spontaneously; how then could the latent characteristics of darkness ever obscure it? Ānanda understood this meaning but remained in doubt, thinking it was a doctrine of annihilationism.
Thereupon, [the Buddha] had the bell struck to answer him, so that he might know for certain that it does not perish.
In the preceding passage, the World-Honored One said: "If, during the stage of the causal ground, one takes a mind of arising and ceasing as the basis for cultivation..."
Therefore, to seek the Buddha-vehicle (Buddhayāna) while remaining subject to birth and death is impossible; hence it is said:

"If, within the state of fruition, there were Bodhi, Nirvana, True Suchness (Tathatā), Buddha-nature (Buddhadhātu), the Amala-vijñāna, the Empty Tathāgatagarbha, or the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom—though these seven names and designations differ, their pure and perfect essence is firm and solid like gold."
The King of Firmness eternally abides in the indestructible *amala*—here translated as "stainless"—the empty *tathāgatagarbha*. The *Ratnakūṭa Sūtra* states:
"The empty *tathāgatagarbha* is free from all afflictions that are not liberated by wisdom;
the non-empty *tathāgatagarbha* possesses inconceivable qualities and the wisdom of liberation of Buddhas exceeding the sands of the Ganges. Thus it is called the non-empty *tathāgatagarbha*.
The *tathāgatagarbha* that accords with form is empty, universally responding to all things while remaining empty;

the *tathāgatagarbha* as the eternal fruit is the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom (*mahā-ādarśa-jñāna*), which clearly perceives all things without discrimination. The *amala-vijñāna* discriminates all things without being stained by attachment.
As the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* says: "Discrimination is consciousness (*vijñāna*); non-discrimination is wisdom (*jñāna*). [Consciousness] arises and ceases."
This consciousness is non-arising and non-ceasing; it is wisdom. Because it is without arising or ceasing, it is called the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom (*ādarśa-jñāna*).
Because it possesses discernment, it is called the *amala-vijñāna*. Because it is eternally abiding, it is called the Empty Tathāgatagarbha.
Because it is clear and lucid spiritual awareness, it is called Buddha-nature (*buddhadhātu*). Since this clear and lucid spiritual awareness is ultimate awakening, it is so named.
"Bodhi" is named as such; here it is translated as "Awakening. Because the essence of ultimate awakening is fundamentally quiescent from the beginning, it is called "Nirvana.
"Nirvana" is here translated as "Quiescence. Since quiescence cannot be touched by any deluded mind, it is called "True Suchness" (*tathatā*).
To state the essential point: the essence of ultimate awakening is the quiescence of all deluded minds.
It is that which cannot be touched, yet is clearly aware and knowing. This spiritual awareness is without birth or extinction; though it possesses discernment, it is free from defiled attachment.
Therefore, the World-Honored One emphasized this earnestly, saying: "You need only abandon that which is subject to birth and extinction, and maintain the true and eternal. Alas!
Among the World-Honored One’s intimate and clear instructions, there are none more profound than these words—who could possibly [fail to heed them]?

Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying, "World-Honored One, although the Tathāgata has explained this second gateway of meaning, when I observe those in the world who attempt to untie knots, if they do not know the origin from which the knot was tied, I believe such people will ultimately never be able to untie it.
World-Honored One, I and the śrāvakas in this assembly are likewise so; since beginningless time, we have been with all [sentient beings]..."

"Though I have attained such roots of merit from extensive learning through the simultaneous cessation and arising of clarity, I am still called a renunciant only by name; I am like one suffering from a quotidian malaria.
Therefore, I implore your great compassion and pity for me who am drowning in the depths. How is it that today my body and mind are bound? From what do they arise, and how are they liberated?
May you also cause future sentient beings in hardship to escape saṃsāra and not fall into the three realms of existence. Having spoken these words, he—

Having already spread this to the great assembly, they prostrated themselves with their five limbs touching the ground, raining down tears as they waited with uplifted sincerity for the unsurpassed instruction of the Buddha,
the Tathāgata. At that time, the World-Honored One, out of compassion for Ānanda and all those in the assembly who were still learners, as well as for the sake of future generations...
As the cause for all sentient beings to transcend the world and as the eyes for the future, he stroked the crown of Ānanda’s head with his hand, which was like Jāmbūnada purple-gold light.
Immediately, the worlds of the Buddhas throughout the ten directions shook in six ways;

and from the crowns of the heads of the Tathāgatas dwelling in those worlds—each as numerous as motes of dust—there issued forth precious lights, which simultaneously appeared in those respective worlds.
Coming to the Jeta Grove to sprinkle water upon the Tathāgata’s crown, this great assembly attained what they had never experienced before.
Thereupon, Ānanda and the entire assembly heard the Tathāgatas of the ten directions, as numerous as motes of dust, speaking with one voice and in unison:
"Excellent, Ānanda! If you wish to recognize and know the co-arisen ignorance that causes you to revolve in birth and death and constitutes the root of your fetters..."

"It is only your six faculties and nothing else; there is no other thing. Furthermore, if you wish to know the unsurpassed Bodhi that will cause you to swiftly realize peace, liberation, tranquility, and wondrous permanence—it is also your six faculties and nothing else.
Although Ānanda heard these words of the Dharma, his mind was still not clear, and he bowed his head to the Buddha, saying: "How can it be that my cycle of birth and death..."

Peace, bliss, the wondrous, and permanence are all identical to these six sense faculties and are nothing other than them. The Buddha told Ānanda: "The faculties and their objects share the same source;

bondage and liberation are not two. The nature of consciousness is false and illusory, like flowers in the sky. Ānanda, knowledge arises from the objects, and characteristics exist because of the faculties.
These characteristics and the seeing-nature have no inherent substance; they are like two bundles of reeds leaning against each other."

Supplement: Jingjue says that those who explain this "mutually supporting reed" (jiaolu) metaphor by means of the sense organs (*indriya*), objects (*viṣaya*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*) are mistaken.
They do not realize that the phrasing of the sutra is skillful, proceeding from the broad to the narrow: first, it subsumes the eighteen *dhātus*;

second, it subsumes the twelve bases (*āyatana*); and third, as in the following passage, it further abbreviates the objects and speaks only of the organs, hence saying, "To establish knowledge within seeing and knowing."
Dengyü said: "The principle that the faculties and their objects meet implies there is nothing that does not encompass one another.
Yuanjue said: "If this deluded mind did not have the six sense-objects, it could not exist. Does he not mean by "deluded mind" the *vijnana* that discriminates phenomena?
Furthermore, the preceding text clearly demonstrates that the faculties and objects share the same source, and that bondage and liberation are non-dual; this refers to consciousness (*vijñāna*).
The nature [of things] is false and illusory, like flowers in the sky. It is further said that cognition arises from objects, and appearances exist because of the sense faculties;

yet these appearances and the seeing [faculty] lack inherent nature. Do you not possess clarity regarding these three—faculties, objects, and consciousness? Why then do you specifically employ such clever artifice to grasp for yourself, and use such narrowness as your own standard?
Therefore, you should now know that when one establishes knowledge upon seeing and knowing, this is the very root of ignorance;

when one realizes that there is no seeing within seeing and knowing, this is *nirvāṇa*, the untainted, true purity. How could any other thing be admitted therein? At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
The true nature is empty of the conditioned because it arises dependently, like an illusion; the unconditioned has no arising or ceasing and is unreal, like flowers in the sky.
To speak of "delusion" is to manifest the various truths, yet delusion and truth are both equally false. Since neither is truly real, how can there be a seer and something seen?
Between them, there is no substantial nature, like two reeds leaning against each other. Thus, bondage and liberation share the same cause; for the holy and the ordinary, there is but one path.
Observe that within the nature of their intersection, both existence and emptiness are absent; when obscured and darkened, it is ignorance, but when clarity and illumination arise, it is liberation.

The method for untying the knots follows a sequence of six, yet once they are all untied, even the "one" vanishes. By selecting the most perfect faculty among the sense-roots, you shall enter the stream and achieve true enlightenment.

The Treatise says: "In this regard, the World-Honored One has shown that the six sense organs possess the cause for both the simultaneous arising of ignorance and the unraveling of the knots. Furthermore, it is asked:

"If there are subtle particles of light from the Tathāgatas dwelling in various worlds, each emitting a precious radiance from their crowns, why do these lights arrive simultaneously in the Jeta Grove to drench the crown of the Tathāgata’s head? It is replied: "This is because [the Buddha] desires to make [the truth] profound."
The discourse on the "Summit Dharma" (mūrdha-dharma) is for the purpose of causing all sentient beings to clearly perceive the Buddha-nature;

because the Summit Dharma is itself without seeing, it entrusts Ānanda with the task of specifically analyzing the faculty of sight. When the conditions of seeing—such as light and darkness—are established, one reaches the state of non-seeing;

when non-seeing arises spontaneously without dependence on light, then the various phenomena of darkness can never again obscure him. Abiding in true seeing, the numinous manifestation appears, and deluded seeing is instantly severed.
The Abandonment says: "To establish knowledge upon what is seen is the very root of ignorance; to see no seeing is itself nirvana, the untainted and true purity.
How could any other thing be admitted within this? Thus, the efficacy of seeing nothing is clearly manifest.
However, as the World-Honored One is the bestower of the Dharma, that which he shows takes the faculty of sight as primary; Ānanda received [the teaching] accordingly.

Since this concerns the Dharma, one takes awakening through hearing as the priority; when master and disciple take seeing and hearing as the secret instruction for transmission, the other faculties may be understood without being explicitly mentioned.
The opening verse designates "True Nature" (bhūtatathatā) to indicate that the essence of the *Cūḍā-bhāṣita* is being shown.
What follows states that "conditioned phenomena are empty" in contrast to the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
That which is without arising or ceasing is established through the mutual opposition of the two dharmas of existence and non-existence;

these are both merely figurative designations (*adhivacana*). If "existence" and "non-existence" are but figurative designations, then how could the single word "True" (*zhen*) be established by manifesting the false?
Since the manifestation of words and forms is itself defilement, when one is free from all defilements, there is nothing at all that exists; how then could any view remain?
Therefore it is said: "Since that which is not truly real is not truly real, how can one see what is seen? Now it is said: "That which is able to see is the eye;
yet the eye does not possess seeing. Nāgārjuna said: "This eye cannot see its own substance.
If it cannot even see its own substance, how can it see other things? If the eye were to have seeing, it should first see itself."
The eye cannot see itself; therefore, to say it can see all objects is contrary to reason.
Yet these three—sense organ, object, and consciousness—exist only through the provisional borrowing of deluded conceptualization and ultimately lack reality, being like a dream or an illusion.
The World-Honored One used the metaphor of the interlaced reeds to illustrate this, for they are neither existent nor non-existent. Thus he said: "Observe the nature within the interlacing."

Both emptiness and existence are neither; to be obscured by delusion is to regard them as existent, while to be enlightened by clarity is to regard them as non-existent—how could these be definitive meanings?

One who enters the stream is like a small river whose current inevitably reaches the sea; this serves as a metaphor for the Small Vehicle, showing that one who has entered the stream of the sages will necessarily reach the great ocean of nirvana and extinction.
What is called "entering the stream" refers to attaining perfect enlightenment—that is, Buddhahood.
The distance between this stage and the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna) is like that between heaven and an abyss; how could one attain perfect enlightenment through the Lesser Vehicle?

It is said: "This is the definitive teaching of the Single Buddha Vehicle. As the subsequent passage states, "By a mere snap of the fingers, one transcends those beyond training"—this is precisely for this reason.
It is, for example, like a prince born to an emperor: from his very birth, he is fully endowed with nobility and does not belong to the ranks of commoners.
The subtle *ālayavijñāna* has its habitual tendencies forming a violent torrent; fearing that [disciples] might confuse the real with the unreal, I have never openly expounded it.
To grasp one's own mind with one's own mind is a non-illusory phenomenon becoming an illusory dharma. If one does not grasp it, there is nothing that is not illusory;
since even the non-illusory does not arise, how could illusory dharmas be established? This is called the Wondrous Lotus, the Vajra King, the Jewel Awakening, and the Illusion-like Samādhi.
"In a single snap of the fingers, one transcends to the stage beyond training; this Abhidharma is the single path to Nirvana for the Bhagavāns of the ten directions.

Thereupon, Ānanda and the great assembly, hearing these unsurpassed compassionate instructions of the Buddha-Tathāgata—composed of both *geya* and *gāthā*, refined and crystalline, exquisite and lucid—felt their minds and eyes opened and enlightened, exclaiming that such a thing had never before occurred.
The Commentary states: In the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*, the Bhagavat spoke of two kinds of consciousness:

namely, the coarse consciousness, which is the *vikalpa-vijñāna* (discriminative consciousness of phenomena), and the subtle consciousness, which is the *ālaya-vijñāna*. What is here called the *ādāna-vijñāna* is the *amala-vijñāna*.
In full, it is called *ādhāna*, which means "that which grasps and maintains. Among the three stages [of consciousness], it is that which continuously grasps [the seeds].
To regard this state as real is to defile the whole; to regard it as illusory is to imply that the Tathāgatagarbha has no distinct essence.
As Maitreya said: "Based upon the Tathāgatagarbha, the mind of birth-and-death evolves;
its union with the unborn and undying is neither identical nor different, and is called the ālayavijñāna. This is the subtle consciousness. The Saṃdhinirmocana Sūtra states:
The *ādāna-vijñāna* is extremely subtle; it contains all seeds and flows like a torrent.

I do not reveal this to the ignorant and foolish, fearing they would falsely grasp at it as a self. Yet, since all phenomena are transformations of consciousness alone, the mind itself grasps its own mind.
Because there is grasping, all illusory phenomena are established. If one were to constantly abide in the perfect clarity of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), [these delusions would cease].
Within this, they are unstained like a lotus flower; all are empty like the Vajra King. The Vajra King is the emptiness of dharmas. As Aśvaghoṣa said:
"All that is conceptually differentiated is the differentiation of one's own mind; the mind does not see the mind, for there is no characteristic to be apprehended.
*Abhidharma* is translated here as "Incomparable Dharma" (*Anupama-dharma*). *Bhagavat* is translated here as "Accomplished in Virtue" (*Guṇasiddha*).
It possesses six meanings, namely: sovereignty, brilliance, majesty, renown, auspiciousness, and nobility. The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states:
"Because it is based on the original sūtra and expressed in verse, it is called *geya* (re-statement). Others say that four-line verses are called *gāthā* (stanza);
this [type of] verse spoken based on the original sūtra is called *geya-gāthā*. Supplement: *Geya*.

"Night" refers to *geya*, which is also called *saṃgīti* (repeated verse); it consists of verses that repeat the preceding prose (*gadya*). *Gāthā* means "recited verse" (*bhaṇitaka*), also called *śloka*;
it does not depend on prose but merely recites and praises in verse. Because these two types of verse are combined and explained together, they are called "intermingled" (*miśraka*).

Ānanda joined his palms, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and said to him: “I have now heard the World-Honored One’s words on the unobstructed great compassion, the pure, wondrous, and eternal nature of reality—true and authentic words that my mind has not yet fully grasped.

Regarding the sequence for loosening the knots so that the six are resolved and the one is extinguished, I pray that you will again bestow your great compassion upon this assembly and those of the future, and grant us the sound of the Dharma to wash away our deep-seated defilements.”
At that moment, the Tathāgata, upon his lion throne, adjusted his inner robe (*nirvāṇasaṃghāṭī*), gathered his outer robe (*saṃghāṭī*), and took hold of a seven-jeweled armrest.
Reaching out his hand over the armrest, he took the flowered cloth offered by the *Kāpila* deva and, before the great assembly, tied it into a single knot.
He pointed to it and asked Ānanda, "What is this called? Ānanda and the entire assembly together replied to the Buddha, "This is called..."
The Tathāgata then tied the folded flower-cloth into another knot and asked Ānanda once more, "What is this called?
Ānanda and the great assembly again addressed the Buddha, saying, "This too is called a 'knot'. In this same sequence, he tied the folded flower-cloth until six knots were formed in total.
As each knot was completed, he took the knot formed in his hand and held it up to ask Ānanda.
[The assembly] challenged this, asking: "What is this called, Ānanda? The great assembly likewise responded to the Buddha in succession:
"This is called a knot. The Buddha said to Ānanda: "When I first tied the cloth, you called it a knot. This folded flower-cloth was originally a single strip;
as for the second and third [folds], why do you and the others again call them knots? Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One..."
"This precious layered flower has been woven together to form a headcloth;

though it was originally a single entity, as I contemplate it, when the Tathāgata ties one knot, it receives the name 'one knot,' and if he ties a hundred, it will ultimately be called 'a hundred knots.
How much more so for this cloth, which has only six knots—it never reaches seven, nor does it remain at five. Why, then, does the Tathāgata permit only the first, second, and third [knots]?"
"It is not called 'knots,' the Buddha told Ānanda. 'This precious flowered cloth—do you know that this cloth originally consists of only a single strand?
When I tied it six times, it was called "six knots. Examine this closely: the substance of the cloth is the same, yet because of the knots, there are differences.
What do you think? When the first knot was tied, it was called the "first"; and so on, until the sixth knot arose.'"
"I now wish to designate the sixth knot as the first. "No, World-Honored One. If the six knots still exist, this name 'sixth' can never become 'first.
Even if I were to exhaust my eloquence throughout successive lifetimes, how could I cause these six knots to change their order?
The Buddha said, "It is so. These six knots are not the same; yet if one traces them back to their original cause, they were all fashioned from a single piece of cloth."
If they are allowed to remain in disorder, they will ultimately never be accomplished; so it is with your six sense-faculties as well—how can you ultimately produce identity from within difference?
The Buddha said to Ānanda: "If you truly loathe these six knots for not being accomplished and wish to joyfully attain a single unity, how might that be achieved?
Ānanda replied: "If these knots persist, arguments over right and wrong arise; from within them, this [conflict] naturally arises."
The fetters are neither those fetters nor these; for this Tathāgata today, whether he collectively dissolves the fetters or they do not arise, there is neither "that" nor "this.
Since even one cannot be named, how could there be six? To speak of "the six being dissolved and the one vanishing" is likewise so.

Because from beginningless time your mind-nature has been deluded and chaotic, your cognition has falsely arisen; as the arising of delusion does not cease, the wearying vision gives rise to [further] manifestations.
Dust is like a strain upon the eye; it causes the appearance of floating flowers. Within the serene, brilliant, and pure consciousness, there is no cause for such disorder to arise.

All that exists in the world—the mountains, rivers, and great earth, as well as birth-and-death and nirvana—is itself a manifestation of these delusory, exhausted, and inverted flower-like appearances.
Ānanda said, "This exhaustion is like a knot; how can it be untied? The Tathāgata took the knotted cloth in his hand and pulled its left side to one side.
He asked Ānanda, "Is it thus untied? "No, World-Honored One. Then, turning his hand back, he pulled the right side again and asked Ānanda, "Is it thus untied?
"No, World-Honored One. The Buddha told Ānanda, "I have now pulled at both the left and right sides with my hands, yet I cannot untie it.
If you employ skillful means, how would you untie it? Ānanda addressed the Buddha.
The World-Honored One said, "One should untie a knot at its very center; then it will immediately disperse. The Buddha told Ānanda, "So it is, so it is.
If one wishes to remove a knot, one must do so at the center of the knot. Ānanda, I teach that the Buddha-dharma arises from causes and conditions;

it does not grasp the coarse, composite appearances of the world. The Tathāgata illuminates mundane and supramundane dharmas, knowing their fundamental causes and following their respective conditions."
From here outward, even to the point beyond worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, he knows the number of drops of rain;

he perceives before him all varieties—the straightness of pines, the crookedness of thorns, the whiteness of cranes, and the blackness of crows—and understands their fundamental causes. For this reason, Ānanda, choose whichever of the six faculties you prefer from within your own mind.
Once the knots of the faculties are untied, the appearances of external dust will naturally vanish, and all delusions will perish. What would there be that is not true?
"Wait, Ānanda, I shall now ask you this: regarding these six knots in this *karpāsa* cloth that appear before us, can they be untied and removed simultaneously?
No, World-Honored One; these knots were originally tied in succession, and today they must be untied in succession.
Since the six knots share the same substance but are not tied at the same time, how could they be removed simultaneously when they are untied?"
The Buddha said: "The liberation of the six sense organs is also like this. When this organ is first liberated, one first attains the emptiness of persons.
When the nature of emptiness becomes perfectly luminous, it constitutes the liberation of dharmas. Once both [persons and dharmas] have been liberated, they are both empty and do not arise;
this is called a Bodhisattva attaining the patience of non-arising from samādhi."
The Commentary states: *Nirvāṇa-saṃghāṭī* is translated here as "inner garment," referring to the skirt worn next to the body.

*Saṃghāṭī* is translated as "great robe" (*mahāsaṃghāṭī*), consisting of twenty-five strips. *Kāpāla* is translated as "time-portion," referring to the Yāma Heaven. Regarding the statement, "This faculty is first understood;

one first attains the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*)," the emptiness of persons refers to being free from the grasping of pervasive conceptualization (*parikalpita*). This is due to the six knots.
When they are tied into a single knot, if one understands this with the mind, one will know that the remaining knots are not definitively knots.
By analogy, if one discerns that the six knots are devoid of inherent nature and that all are empty, then there is no need to reconcile differences or level out sounds and forms.
Furthermore, it is said that the perfect luminosity of emptiness constitutes the liberation of phenomena.

This is the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*). Having abandoned the attachment to the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) through the exhaustion of the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*), because there is still attachment to phenomena, one must realize that the root of phenomena is empty.
Since the distinct functions of the six sense organs are originally one refined spirit, it is called "liberation.

When both [subject and object] are already empty and do not arise, this is named the Bodhisattva’s attainment of the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) from samādhi. As for "patience," it means...

Regarding the meaning of "movement," it is not called "immovability" but rather "patience" (*kṣānti*), because there is a wondrous power of *dhāraṇī* that maintains [the mind] so that it does not move.
Thus, Ānanda’s verse says: "The Wondrously Profound, the *Dhāraṇī*, the Immovable Honored One" is merely another name for the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* states: "The Bodhisattva Sarvasattvapriyadarśana said: 'Although I, by means of my spiritual...'"
Making offerings to the Buddha through material power is not as good as making offerings with one's own body— namely, by consuming various fragrances such as *candana*,
*kunduruka*, *turuṣka*, *pilikā*, *agaru*, and resin incense; furthermore, for twelve hundred years, drinking the fragrant oils of flowers such as *campaka*, and after that period,
anointing the body with these fragrant oils before the Buddha Candrasūryavimalaprabhāsaśrī, using heavenly...

Wrapping his body in precious robes and pouring over himself various fragrant oils, by means of his supernatural power and his vow, his own bodily radiance spontaneously illuminated worlds as numerous as the sands of eight hundred million Ganges Rivers. Therein, all the Buddhas simultaneously praised him, saying:
"Excellent, excellent, son of good family! This is true diligence; this is called the true Dharma-offering."
They came and, having spoken these words, each remained silent; their bodies burned for twelve hundred years, and only after this period had passed were their bodies finally consumed.
This refers to those whose faculties are initially liberated and who share the same realization.
Furthermore, it says that after the Bodhisattva Sarvasattvapriyadarśana had performed this Dharma-offering, he passed away and was reborn once more.
In the land of the Buddha Candrasūryavimalaprabhāsaśrī, he was suddenly born by transformation, sitting cross-legged within the household of King Śuddhadeva.
He immediately spoke a verse for his father, and so on, until he addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, World-Honored One, you still remain in the world.
At that time, the Buddha Candrasūryavimalaprabhāsaśrī addressed the Bodhisattva Sarvasattvapriyadarśana.
The Buddha said, "Good son, the time for my parinirvāṇa has arrived; the moment of my final extinction is at hand.

You should prepare a seat, for tonight I shall enter parinirvāṇa. Then this Bodhisattva thought further, "I should once again make offerings to the śarīra," and before eighty-four thousand stūpas, he set ablaze his arm, adorned with the hundred merits, seven times over.
Having made offerings for twelve thousand years, one achieves the Dharma-liberation; this is also in accord with that principle.
For when the body is already empty, attachment to dharmas is also exhausted—this is the purport of "the six dissolving and the one perishing."
Ānanda and the great assembly, having received the Buddha’s instruction on the perfect penetration of wisdom and awakening, were freed from all doubt.
At once, they joined their palms, prostrated at his feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying: "Today our bodies and minds are radiant and clear; we have swiftly attained unimpeded understanding.
Although we have realized that the 'one' and the 'six' are devoid of inherent meaning, we have yet to reach the fundamental root of perfect penetration, World-Honored One."

We have drifted through the ages, orphaned and exposed for countless kalpas; what heart or concern could we have anticipated becoming kinsmen of the Buddha? We are like infants who have lost their mother’s milk and suddenly encounter a compassionate mother.

If, through this present convergence, the Way is realized and the secret words obtained are identical to our original awakening, then there will be no difference between having heard them now and never having heard them at all.
May you deign to bestow upon us, out of great compassion, the secret adornment that brings about the realization of the Tathāgata.

Having finally revealed this teaching and spoken these words, he prostrated himself with his five limbs touching the ground, withdrawing to conceal his secret intent as he hoped for the Buddha’s silent transmission.
[Supplementary Note: Although Ānanda and the great assembly had realized the meaning of the "one" and the "six" being lost, they had not yet reached the fundamental root of perfect penetration.
In their lamentation over being left alone and exposed, he said: "If we can achieve the Way through this present encounter, it would be a great blessing."
It is ultimate! Yet, what can be done? The secret words one has obtained are identical to the Dharma-principles originally realized; how do they differ from what was not yet heard?

However, this fundamental root is not something that can be transmitted through the mind or grasped through silent resonance by anyone unless the Tathāgata’s great compassion reveals it through the ultimate exposition of the Secret Adornment (Guhyasamāja). Therefore, I have withdrawn and concealed this secret mechanism, rather than setting it forth openly.
Regarding the questions posed, I hope only that the Buddha will grant me his secret transmission.

As for the two phrases "the various masters" and "not being detailed in their reclusion," these are both the words of the compilers and not the speech of Pūrṇa; therefore, many have raised groundless criticisms.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed all the great Bodhisattvas and the Arhats whose outflows were exhausted within the assembly:
"You Bodhisattvas and Arhats, having been born into my Dharma and attained the state of no-more-learning, I now ask you:
regarding your initial generation of the mind, through the awakening to which of the eighteen realms did you realize perfect penetration? By what skillful means did you enter samādhi?"
The Commentary states: Zao Bo said, "Generally, if there is a holy teaching but no one to testify to it, it cannot be called 'circulating.
Likewise, if there is a teaching spoken by an ordinary person but no one to testify to it, it also cannot be called 'circulating. Therefore, the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* speaks of fifty-three stages:
the ten faiths, the ten abidings, the ten practices, the ten transferences, the ten grounds, the eleventh ground, and up to the stage of wondrous enlightenment."
This sutra establishes the stages through the realization and confirmation of fifty-three spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*).
Regarding the dharmas of the six sense bases, twelve bases, eighteen elements, and seven great natures, it extensively discusses the non-arising of faculties and objects;
it then uses the entry into perfect penetration by twenty-five sages to provide confirmation. Thus, it demonstrates the standard model for the practice of cultivation.
Then the five bhikṣus, including Kauṇḍinya, rose from their seats, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and said to the Buddha:
“While we were in the Deer Park and at the Kukuṭārāma, we observed the Tathāgata when he first attained enlightenment; through the Buddha’s voice, we awakened to clarity.”
Regarding the Four Truths, the Buddha asked the bhikṣus, "I was the first to declare my understanding; the Tathāgata named me Ājñāta.
My wondrous voice is subtle, secret, and perfect; through sound, I attained arhatship. When the Buddha asked about the most perfect penetration, according to what I have realized, sound is supreme.
Upāniṣada then rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:

"I too, upon observing the Buddha when he first attained enlightenment, contemplated the signs of impurity and gave rise to great revulsion. I realized the nature of all forms through this contemplation of impurity;

as they returned to white bones, then to subtle dust, and finally to empty space, both form and emptiness became non-existent, and I attained the path of no-more-learning. Thus was I certified by the Tathāgata."
"My name is Niṣadha. When all coarse forms have been exhausted, wondrous forms become subtle and perfect. I attained Arhatship through these characteristics of form.
When the Buddha asked about the most perfect penetration, according to what I have realized, the causal factor of form is supreme."
The youth Ghrāṇarati immediately rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:

"I heard the Tathāgata instruct me to contemplate carefully the characteristics of all conditioned phenomena. At that time, having taken leave of the Buddha, I was dwelling in quiet seclusion and pure fasting.
I saw bhikṣus burning aloeswood incense; the fragrance was tranquil as it entered my nostrils. I observed this scent: it was neither wood nor empty space."
It was neither smoke nor fire; it departed without attachment and arrived from nowhere. Through this, my conceptual mind dissolved and the untainted light of realization shone forth.

Thus, I received the seal of the Tathāgata and was named "Incense Purity" (Gandhavimala). Dusty vapors suddenly vanished, and wondrous fragrance became subtle and pervasive. Through this Incense Purity, I attained Arhatship.
When the Buddha asked about the perfect penetration, according to what I have realized, Incense Purity is supreme.

The two Dharma princes, Bhaiṣajyarāja and Bhaiṣajyasamudgata, along with five hundred Brahmās present in the assembly, immediately rose from their seats, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Throughout beginningless kalpas, we have served as skilled physicians for the world.
We have tasted the plants, trees, minerals, and metals of this Sahā world; their names and numbers total one hundred and eight thousand, all of which we know completely."
Whether tastes be bitter, sour, salty, bland, sweet, or pungent; whether they arise from combinations or through transformation;

whether they be cold or hot, poisonous or non-poisonous—he is able to know them all completely. Having served the Tathāgata, he thoroughly understands the nature of taste as being neither empty nor existent, neither identical to the body and mind nor separate from the body and mind.
By discerning the causes of taste, he attained awakening and was thus enlightened by the Buddha, the Tathāgata.
"I certify to the names of my brothers, the two Bodhisattvas Bhaiṣajyarāja and Bhaiṣajyasamudgata, who are now among those in this assembly as Dharma-sons.

Because they awakened to clarity through the sense of taste, their rank attained that of Bodhisattva. When the Buddha asked about the perfect penetration, [Bhadrapāla] said, "As I have realized it, the cause of taste is supreme.
Then Bhadrapāla, together with his sixteen companions, rose from their seats, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and said:

They addressed the Buddha, saying: "In the past, under the Buddha Vimalasvararāja, we heard the Dharma and left the household life. At the time of bathing the Sangha, we followed the custom of entering the bathhouse;
there, we suddenly awakened to the cause of water—realizing that it neither washes away defilement nor cleanses the body—and in that interval, we attained a state of tranquil non-existence.
Our former habits were not forgotten, and thus even until this present time, we have followed the Buddha to leave the household life and attained the stage of No-more-learning."
That Buddha’s name was I-bhadra-pāla (I-Bhadrapāla), who attained Buddhahood through the manifestation of sublime touch and dwelt as a son of the Buddha.
When asked about the perfect penetration of the faculties, he testified that, according to his realization, the faculty of touch is supreme.
Then Mahākāśyapa, the Bhikṣuṇī Golden Light, and others rose from their seats and prostrated at the Buddha’s feet.
He addressed the Buddha, saying: "In a past kalpa, within this world-system, there was a Buddha who appeared in the world named Candrasūryapradīpa.

I was able to draw near to him, hear the Dharma, and practice its study. After that Buddha passed into parinirvāṇa, I made offerings to his relics, lit lamps to continue the illumination, and coated the Buddha’s image with purple-gold light.
From that time until now, in birth after birth throughout successive lives, my body has always been perfect and complete."
"The Bhikṣuṇī Jinguangju (Gathering of Purple Golden Light) and others like her were my kinsmen who awakened their resolve at the same time as I.

I observe that the six sense-objects in this world are subject to decay; by cultivating cessation through emptiness and stillness alone, one can transcend hundreds of thousands of kalpas in the space of a finger-snap.
By means of the dharma of emptiness, I have attained Arhatship. Thus did the World-Honored One speak of me.

The dhūta practices are the most wondrous dharma for illuminating and extinguishing all outflows. When the Buddha asked about the perfect penetration [of the faculties], I testified that the faculty of dharma is supreme.
The commentary states: Kauṇḍinya (his clan name) means "Fire-vessel" in this language; Ājñāta (his personal name) means "Understood"; Niṣa... [is his surname].
*Tuṣita* (the meaning is seen in Volume One); *Bhadrapāla* is translated as "Worthy Protector" (*Xiánhù*), though correctly it should be "Worthy Guardian" (*Xiànsǒu*).

*Dhūta* is translated as "Abandoning" (*Chūqì*) or "Shaking Off" (*Dǒusǒu*). These six sages are those who realized perfect penetration by relying upon the six sense objects—form, sound, fragrance, taste, touch, and dharmas.
Yet, [the text] first designates Kauṇḍinya; Kauṇḍinya [realized it] through sound.

This refers to those who have attained understanding. [The] supplement states: Regarding sound, form, and fragrance, it says "mysterious perfection" (*miyuan*), describing the mysterious realization of the perfect principle.
Regarding flavor, touch, and mental objects (*dharma*), it says "awakened clarity," "proclaimed clarity," and "opened clarity," describing the manifest development of the causal entry.
The meaning of "mysterious perfection" is spoken of in terms of what is realized; the distinction between Great and Small [Vehicles] arises from this.
It is not necessary to compare these in terms of provisional and ultimate truth; "Chicken Garden" (Kukkutārāma) is simply another name for a vihāra.
Then Āniruddha rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and said to the Buddha: "When I first left the household life, I was always fond of sleep.
The Tathāgata rebuked me, saying I was of the same class as animals. Hearing the Buddha’s rebuke, I wept and reproached myself."
For seven days I did not sleep, and I lost both my eyes. The World-Honored One showed me the Vajra Samādhi of Joyful Vision and Illumination;
I no longer rely on the eyes to perceive the ten directions, for the essential purity is brilliantly clear, like looking at fruit in the palm of one's hand.

The Tathāgata sealed my attainment as an Arhat. When the Buddha asked about perfect penetration, according to what I have realized, to revolve the seeing and return to the source is the foremost method.
Cūḍapanthaka immediately rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and said to the Buddha: “I lacked the capacity for recitation and retention, and possessed no nature of great learning.
When I first encountered the Buddha, heard the Dharma, and left the household life, I attempted to remember a single verse of the Tathāgata;

yet for a hundred days, I could only retain what preceded while losing what followed, or retain what followed while losing what preceded. The Buddha took pity on my folly and taught me the *śamatha*.”

While dwelling in the practice of mindfulness of inhalation and exhalation, I observed the breath until it became subtle and reached its ultimate limit; I perceived the arising, abiding, changing, and ceasing of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) within every moment (*kṣaṇa*).
My mind then opened wide, attaining great non-obstruction, until finally, with the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya*), I became an Arhat.

Seated beneath the Buddha’s seat, I was certified as one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*). When the Buddha asked about the perfect penetration of the Way, according to what I have realized—returning the breath and following it into emptiness—this is the foremost method.
Supplementary Note: The *Wujinlun* (Treatise on the Inexhaustible) and the *Ahan Dajilun* (Great Treatise on the Āgamas) both state: "Instruct me to guard the mouth and restrain the mind.

Furthermore, the *Zengyi Ahan Jing* (Ekottarika Āgama) and the *Faju Jing* (Dharmapada) do not mention "regulating the breath" (*tiaoxi*); rather, they change "breath" (*xi*) to "thought" (*si*). Moreover, the *Ershiwumen* (Twenty-five Gates) omits "thought" while including the nose;
now, by reducing "breath" and incorporating "thought," the gates of contemplation are made complete. This is as if one did not know how to regulate [the practice].
Breathing is the fundamental basis for guarding the mouth and restraining the mind. When breathing is regulated and the mind is restrained, discursive thought naturally fades away;

how much more so when one enters into contemplation within the eighteen realms? To engage in thought while breath is lacking is a deficiency; to diminish the breath while thought persists is an excess.
Kauṇḍinya immediately rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying: "I have committed verbal karma;
in past kalpas, I habitually mocked śramaṇas, and thus in every successive birth I have suffered from the disease of ruminating like an ox.

The Tathāgata has shown me the Dharma-door of the single-flavor, pure mind-ground. Having attained this, I have extinguished the discursive mind and entered samādhi, observing the cognition of flavors."

Neither a substantial entity nor a material object, one should, through mindfulness, transcend all worldly outflows (*āsrava*). Internally detached from body and mind, externally leaving behind the world, and far removed from the three realms of existence (*tridhātu*), one is like a bird escaping its cage.
Free from defilement and with dust extinguished, the Dharma-eye becomes pure, and one attains Arhatship.

Sealed by the Tathāgata himself, one ascends the path of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*). When the Buddha asked about perfect penetration, that which I have realized is the returning of the flavor and the revolving of the faculty of cognition.
This is the first [point]. Supplement:
This noble one already suffers from the ailment of "ox-chewing" (*go-mukha*), and furthermore, his physical characteristics are like those of an ox;

oxen are among the animals of the intermediate state, knowing only the taste of grass. Now, although Pāṭali’s tongue-organ resembles that of an ox, he is nonetheless able to discern and distinguish various [flavors].

Because of the nature of taste, the Tathāgata reveals the Dharma-gate of the single-flavor pure mind-ground, causing one to contemplate taste at the root of the tongue until the awareness of it arises spontaneously;
thus, the mind of discursive thought ceases and one enters right concentration. Looking back upon the awareness of tongue and taste, one finds it is neither perception nor a physical object;
then the subtle truth manifests before one, and all worldly outflows are transcended in a single thought-moment.
The *deyi shengshen* (body born of mastery) is like a bird escaping its cage, soaring and flying with unimpeded freedom.

The *Dazhidu lun* states that the Tathāgata taught the contemplation of the tongue-root tasting flavors as a means of entering the Way; one should thereby attain the Dharma-gate of the single flavor within the mind-ground.

Thus, we know that there is some omission regarding the contributory causes (*yuan-yin*) described in this sutra. The preceding text speaks of "a distinct tongue knowing flavors," while the subsequent verse says "the tongue is not... [the rest of the verse].
Entering into that which has no causal origin, the arising of awareness through flavors is identical in meaning to the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*.
Pindola Bharadvāja then rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:

"When I first resolved to attain the Way, I followed the Buddha and entered the Path. I frequently heard the Tathāgata speak of the various things in the world that are not to be enjoyed. While begging for alms in the city..."
While contemplating the Dharma-gate at the center [of my being], I was unaware that a thorn had pierced my foot on the road, causing my entire body to ache.

I reflected that there must be a cognizer who knows this deep pain; though I am aware of the awareness of the pain, the awareness is pure, and in the mind there is neither pain nor the awareness of pain.
I further contemplated: "How could there be two simultaneous awarenesses within this single body? Before long, as I focused my mindfulness, my body and mind suddenly became empty for twenty-one days.
Within this, all outflows were exhausted and I became an Arhat; I received the Seal of Intimacy and realized the state of No-more-learning.
When the Buddha asked about the perfect penetration of the faculties, as I have realized it, the pure awakening that leaves behind the body is the foremost.
Subhūti immediately rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying: "For many kalpas past, my mind has attained non-obstruction.
I recall as many lifetimes as there are sands in the Ganges; from the very moment I was in my mother's womb, I already knew emptiness and stillness.
Thus it continued until the ten directions became empty, and I caused sentient beings to realize the nature of emptiness, having been inspired by the Tathāgata to manifest their inherent nature."

Awakening to the true emptiness wherein emptiness is perfectly luminous, I attained Arhatship and entered suddenly into the Tathāgata’s ocean of jewel-like clarity and emptiness, becoming one with the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.
Sealed as one beyond further training, I realized that the nature of liberation is empty of self. When the Buddha asked me about the most perfect penetration, I replied:
"As I have realized it, all phenomena enter into non-existence; when even that 'non-existence' is exhausted, the dharmas revolve back into the state of nothingness. This is the foremost."
The Treatise says: Aniruddha—also called Aniruddha, or alternatively Anuruddha—is translated as "Unextinguished" (Wumie).
He is also said to mean "As One Wishes" (Ruyi). He was the younger brother of the Buddha and the son of King Śuklodana.
Cūḍapanthaka means "Snake-Slave" (She Nu) or "Successor of the Path" (Jidao). Gavāmpati (as seen in Volume Four) and Pilindavatsa.

Vatsa is here translated as "Subhūti, who has eliminated habitual tendencies" (see Volume One). This passage describes the six faculties of seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting, touching, and cognizing;
however, it mentions only five. The Noble One [the author] does not list the nature of hearing realized by Avalokiteśvara among these.
Supplement: Regarding seeing, smelling, and tasting, the terms used are "revolving," "returning," and "reverting."

The meaning is one and the same. Jingjue said: "When the foot is pricked, although there is a mind capable of awareness that perceives the sensation of pain, if one turns back to observe the aware mind itself, it is fundamentally pure and devoid of subject and object. If one examines this thoroughly, it accords with the concluding text below, which says:
'Body and mind suddenly become empty. It should not be the case that there is a perception of pain within a state where there is no pain."
It says: "How could there be two perceptions? and so forth; this is to know that one is personally experiencing bodily pain.
When one thinks, "I have a cognition," and knows this profound pain, this describes what is perceived. Although perception perceives pain, the pure mind of perception is itself without pain;

when it is said that "pain is perceived by perception," this describes the perceiving faculty. At first, there is only the knowledge of the profound pain perceived by oneself; in the middle, regarding...
Although there is pain, when one investigates the locus of the sensation of pain, one finds that the pure mind capable of perceiving it has never possessed pain from the very beginning;

therefore, it is said that there is "double awareness" regarding what is perceived. To speak of "awareness of pain" refers to the object of perception, while to speak of "pain-awareness" refers to the subject capable of perceiving.
Subsequently, one collects the mind and observes, asking: "How could my single body possess two distinct perceptions? Then, regarding the body which is the object of perception...
When awakening occurs, thoughts suddenly vanish entirely; hence it is said that body and mind are suddenly empty.
Once body and mind are empty, the nature of pure awakening manifests, and the body that was previously known is forgotten.

To claim that "pure awakening" refers to taking the pure mind as pure awakening while forgetting the awareness of pain as the forgetting of the body is an error. This applies to all other holy ones as well.
The textual conventions are as follows:
Śāriputra immediately rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying: "Since the beginningless kalpas, my mind and vision have been pure;
thus have I undergone births as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, manifesting various transformations of both the mundane and supramundane realms."

Upon seeing him, I immediately attained unobstructed penetration. While on the road, I encountered the Kāśyapa brothers as they were traveling together expounding the causes and conditions [of their realization].

There, I awakened to the boundlessness of the mind and followed the Buddha into the homeless life. Having witnessed the perfection of enlightened clarity, I attained great fearlessness and became an Arhat. As the eldest son of the Buddha, born from the Buddha’s own mouth and transformed by the Dharma, when the Buddha asked about perfect penetration, I replied: [The text continues: "I attained unobstructed penetration upon seeing him. While on the road, I encountered the Kāśyapa brothers as they were traveling together expounding the causes and conditions [of their realization]. There, I awakened to the boundlessness of the mind and followed the Buddha into the homeless life. Having witnessed the perfection of enlightened clarity, I attained great fearlessness and became an Arhat. As the eldest son of the Buddha, born from the Buddha’s own mouth and transformed by the Dharma..."
"The mind that I have realized sees the radiance of light, and this supreme knowledge and vision is the foremost.
Samantabhadra Bodhisattva then rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:

'I have already served as a Dharma Prince to Tathāgatas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges; the Tathāgatas of the ten directions have instructed me, their disciples, regarding those with the faculties of a bodhisattva.'"
"World-Honored One, I have established my name based on my cultivation of the practices of Samantabhadra. With a mind that hears and discriminates all the knowledge and views of sentient beings,

if there should be a single sentient being in worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges in other directions who brings forth the realization of the practices of Samantabhadra within their own minds,
at that time I shall mount my six-tusked elephant and manifest hundreds of thousands of bodies, reaching every such place— even if it be beyond those realms."
"Because their hindrances are deep, they have not yet been able to see me; I shall secretly place my hand upon their heads to protect and comfort them, enabling them to achieve success.
The Buddha asked about the perfect penetration, and I spoke of its fundamental cause: the mind-hearing that illuminates and brings mastery over discernment—this is the foremost."
Sundarananda immediately rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:

“When I first left the household life and entered the Path under the Buddha, although I was fully endowed with the precepts, my mind was constantly distracted and agitated within samādhi, and I had not yet attained the state beyond outflows (*anāsrava*).
World-Honored One, you instructed me and Cūḍapanthaka to contemplate the white [spot] at the tip of the nose. I began to observe it intently for three weeks.”
Daily I saw the breath entering and exiting my nostrils like smoke; the interior of my body and mind became luminous and clear, and the world became a pervasive, empty purity like lapis lazuli.
As the appearance of the smoke gradually vanished, the breath from my nostrils turned white; my mind opened and my outflows were exhausted.
All incoming and outgoing breaths transformed into light, illuminating the worlds of the ten directions, and I attained Arhatship. The World-Honored One then prophesied that I shall attain Bodhi.

Pūrṇa Maitrāyaṇīputra rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying: "When the Buddha asked about the most perfect penetration, I relied upon the method of the cessation of mental activity.
Once that activity had long ceased, clarity arose; this clarity was perfectly pervasive and extinguished all outflows. This, I believe, is the foremost."
Since the beginningless kalpas, my eloquence has been unimpeded as I have proclaimed suffering and emptiness, profoundly penetrating the true reality (*dharmatā*).
Thus, even regarding the secret dharma-gates of Tathāgatas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, I have skillfully revealed them within the great assemblies, attaining fearlessness.
World-Honored One, knowing that I possess great eloquence, You have instructed me with the wheel of Your voice to bring these forth; thus, before the Buddha...
"Assisting the Buddha in turning the wheel of Dharma, I achieved Arhatship through the Lion’s Roar. The World-Honored One has certified my unsurpassed preaching of the Dharma.

When the Buddha asked about the perfect penetration of the faculties, I replied that by means of the sound of the Dharma, I subdue demonic adversaries and extinguish all outflows; this is the foremost.
Upāli then rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and said to the Buddha: "I personally followed the Buddha across..."
Leaving the city to renounce the world, he personally beheld the Tathāgata’s six years of diligent austerity;
he personally saw the Tathāgata subdue all Māras and restrain all non-Buddhists, attaining liberation from the worldly taints of greed and desire.

Receiving the Buddha’s teachings and precepts, he thus purified everything down to the three thousand modes of deportment and the eighty thousand subtle natures of active and prohibitive karma, achieving the tranquility of body and mind.
"O Tathāgata, among the assembly, I am the leader who personally seals my own mind; I maintain the precepts and cultivate the body, and the multitude ranks me as supreme.

When the Buddha asked about perfect penetration, I replied that by focusing on the body, I attained mastery over the body; then, by successively focusing on the mind, I attained penetration of the mind.
Thereafter, both body and mind became universally beneficial and proficient; for this reason, I am ranked first."
Mahāmaudgalyāyana immediately rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:

"When I first encountered the three Kāśyapa brothers—Uruvilvākāśyapa, Gayākāśyapa, and Nadīkāśyapa—while begging for food along the road, they were proclaiming the profound meaning of the Tathāgata’s causal conditions.
Instantly, I attained the Dharma-mind and achieved great penetration. The Tathāgata then bestowed upon me a *kāṣāya* robe, which I have worn upon my body."

My beard and hair fell off naturally as I traveled through the ten directions, attaining unimpeded supernatural powers and manifesting spiritual illumination; I was ranked supreme and attained Arhatship.
Not only did the World-Honored One praise me, but the Tathāgatas of the ten directions also extolled my spiritual power as perfect, bright, pure, sovereign, and fearless.
When the Buddha asked about the perfect penetration, I replied that by turning back the stillness, the light of the mind was manifested and proclaimed, like clearing a turbid stream.
Having long ago achieved such pure clarity, this is considered the foremost.

The Treatise says: These six sages attained perfect penetration by relying on the six consciousnesses; however, regarding Puxian, it is said that "the hearing of the mind penetrates the ten directions.
As previously noted, among the six objects (*viṣaya*), sound was first mentioned, but among the six faculties (*indriya*), none has yet been mentioned.
To hear [the teachings] through the six consciousnesses is called "Samantabhadra as mental hearing.
It is clear that his showing this to new learners is intended to ensure they realize the principle of awakening through hearing; this purpose is profound and manifest.

Since Samantabhadra’s universal conduct possesses great power, the discernment manifested by the six sense organs is none other than the Dharma-nature (li). Therefore, he rides upon a six-tusked elephant.
Maudgalyāyana said: "I have rotated my tranquil mind-light to manifest its power, like clearing a turbid stream until it becomes long-established in its crystalline purity.
All supernatural powers (*abhijñā*) rely on mental conditions; for instance, when Vimalakīrti entered samādhi, he first formed a mental intention.

However, because such intention is subject to arising and ceasing, there can be failure in attaining supernatural powers, as was the case with the heretic who lost his divine power upon seeing the woman Nandā."
The Bodhisattva Tong could fly through the air because he was free from lust; were it not for the long accumulation of pure karma, such a feat could not have been achieved.

The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* (Yuanjue jing) states: "The samādhi like an illusion is like a sprout gradually growing. Therefore, it must be accumulated over a long period before one can attain clarity and purity.
When the Monk Baozhi first practiced meditative concentration (*samādhi*), after a long duration, he suddenly attained supernatural powers (*abhijñā*). Indeed, as for concentration—
If one practices for a long time, will not the turbid flow suddenly become clear and radiant? [Supplementary Note: Killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, and lying are inherently sinful by nature;

they do not require external prohibition, for their commission immediately constitutes karma. Therefore, these are called "natural offenses" (*prakṛti-sāvadya*). Other matters are prohibited only because of subsequent transgressions;

since there is no offense prior to the establishment of the prohibition, these are called "prohibited offenses" (*pratikṣepaṇa-sāvadya*). As for *Sundarananda*, the first three characters are [the name].
His wife’s name was *Sundarī*, which in this language means "Good Love"; the latter two characters are her own personal name, which means "Joy.
Because he was confused with Nanda the cowherd, he prefixed his wife’s name to his own to distinguish himself.
This is like the Chinese having two Du Zixia, one of whom distinguished himself by the "Small Crown" (*Xiaoguan*).
Consequently, he was styled "Little-Crowned Du Zhi-xia"; this type of person is Upāli, which here means "Foremost" or "Close Attendant.
Gayā is a name for a mountain, also called a city, and Nadi is the name of a river.
Ucchuṣma joined his palms before the Tathāgata, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"I always first recall that in the distant past, during many kalpas ago, there was a Buddha who appeared in the world named Śūnyarāja.
He taught that those with excessive lust become a mass of fierce fire, and he instructed me to contemplate everywhere throughout the hundred members and four limbs the various cold and warm breaths."
Divine light condensed within me, transforming my many lustful thoughts into the fire of wisdom;
for this reason, all Buddhas called me by the name Huatou (Fire-Head). By the power of the Fire-Light Samādhi, I attained Arhatship and made a great vow:

"When the Buddhas attain the Way, may I serve as a powerful attendant to personally subdue their demonic enemies. When the Buddha asked about perfect penetration, I replied that through my diligent contemplation—
When the warmth of body and mind flows unimpededly, all outflows are extinguished, giving rise to the great jewel-flame and ascending to unsurpassed enlightenment;
this is the foremost.
The Bodhisattva Earth-Holder then rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying: "I recall the distant past."

When the Tathāgata Samantaprabhā appeared in the world, I was a bhikṣu. Constantly at all major thoroughfares, ferry crossings, fields, and narrow passes, wherever there were irregularities that obstructed or damaged carts and horses, I leveled and filled them all;
I constructed bridges or carried sand and earth. Thus, through such diligent toil, immeasurable Buddhas appeared in the world. Among these, there were sentient beings...

In the midst of bustling marketplaces, when someone needed another to carry an object, I would first carry it for them to the destination; once the object was set down, I would depart without accepting any payment.
During the time when Vipaśyin Buddha was present in the world, there was widespread famine; I served as a porter for people, taking only one coin regardless of whether the distance was far or near.
Furthermore, if a cart or ox became mired in mud or water, I possessed the supernatural power [to rescue them].
When he pushed his wheel to pull them from their suffering, the Great King of that land invited the Buddha to partake of a meal. At that time, I leveled the ground to await the Buddha.
Viśvabhū Tathāgata placed his hand upon my head and said to me: "If you level the ground of your own mind, then the ground of the entire world will be level.
My mind was immediately opened, and I perceived the subtle atoms of my own body as well as all the atoms used to construct the world.
