In the nature of atoms, which are equal and without distinction, there is no mutual contact or friction; even by weapons of war, nothing is touched.
Having awakened to the patience of non-arising within the dharma-nature and attained arhatship, I have now turned my mind to enter the stage of a bodhisattva.
Hearing the Tathāgatas proclaim the ground of the Buddhas’ wondrous Lotus wisdom and vision, I was first among those who witnessed and verified it, serving as their leader.

The Buddha asked about the perfect penetration of the Way, and I replied: "By contemplating with clarity that the two objects—the body and the sensory realm—are equal and without distinction, fundamentally the Tathāgata-garbha from which delusion gives rise to these objects;
when these objects are extinguished, wisdom becomes perfect and the unsurpassed Way is realized. This is the foremost."
The Commentary states: These noble ones have realized perfect penetration through ten great natures;
in describing the vessel-world, one should speak of earth, water, fire, wind, and space.
Now, why is it that Ucchuṣma—translated here as "Fire-Head," signifying entry through fire—is placed before the Bodhisattva Earth-Holder? It is said that this sutra provides an illustration.
Because the sin of lust causes sentient beings suffering, and in order to remedy it, Ucchuṣma is listed first;
by contemplating its conditions, he transforms the mind of excessive lust into the fire of wisdom.

From this arises the Great Jewel Flame, whereby one ascends to Unsurpassed Enlightenment—the Buddha-way of the Unsurpassed—which not even the twenty-four sages were able to realize through their own attainments.
"Can this holy one alone ascend [to enlightenment] simply by contemplating that the nature of lust is unborn?
He replied, "Indeed. Therefore, Mañjuśrī spoke these verses: "Is it not through the skillful means of the initial mind? When one is in the midst of lust, it becomes a great mass of fire;
yet when one departs from it, it again becomes a great jewel-flame. Why is this so? He replied, "Lust is named 'feverish affliction' (*paridāha*). All [things] are thus.
Because all sentient beings are consumed by [passion], Maitreya Bodhisattva said: "Men and women engage in mutual union, two by two, and impurity flows forth.
Although the various devas of the desire realm practice sexual desire, they do not have this impurity;
rather, from their sense organs, a wind-like vapor issues forth, and the feverish affliction is thereby stilled. Among the devas of the Four Great Kings, there is likewise mutual union, two by two."
The torment of heat subsides; it is the same for the gods of the Four Great Kings and the Trāyastriṃśa heaven.
For the Yāma gods, the torment of heat subsides merely by holding one another in embrace. For the Tuṣita gods, the torment of heat subsides merely by holding hands.
For the Nirmāṇarati gods, the torment of heat subsides by looking at one another and smiling. For the Paranirmitavaśavartin gods, [the torment subsides] by gazing with their eyes.
Upon seeing this, their feverish affliction was immediately stilled. Alas! If even the devas are thus, how much more so those in the human realm?
Viśvabhū—translated here as "All-Pervading Sovereignty"—was a Buddha who appeared in the world prior to the Bhadrakalpa, alongside Śikhin.
The youth Candraprabha rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:

"I recall that in the past, as many eons ago as there are grains of sand in the Ganges, a Buddha appeared in the world named Jalamdhara. He taught the bodhisattvas to practice the contemplation of water (*āp-dhyāna*) and enter samādhi.
They contemplated the watery nature within the body as being indestructible, beginning with the nasal mucus and saliva, and thus investigating it thoroughly."
The bodily fluids, essence, ditches, and the large and small excretions within my body circulate and turn back like water; their nature is identical.
When I see this water, there is no difference between it and the various fragrant oceans of the Floating Banner King Lands outside the world.
At that time, when I first accomplished this contemplation, I saw only the water and had not yet attained the state of being bodiless; I was then a bhikṣu practicing meditation in my chamber.
"I had a disciple who looked into my room through a window and saw nothing but clear water filling the entire space;
being ignorant and childish, he took a piece of tile and threw it into the water, which caused a splash and a sound, after which he looked around and departed.
After I emerged from samādhi, I suddenly felt a pain in my heart, like that experienced by Śāriputra when he was struck by a malevolent spirit. I reflected upon this:"
"Now that I have attained the path of Arhatship and have long been free from the conditions of illness, why does a heartache suddenly arise today?
Could it be that I am falling away?
At that time, the youth quickly came before me and related the aforementioned matter. I then told him, "Do you see the water again?"
"You may immediately open the door and enter this water to remove the tiles and debris. The youth followed these instructions;

when he later entered meditative concentration (*samādhi*), he again saw the water, and the tiles and debris were still there exactly as before. He opened the door and removed them, but after I emerged from concentration, my physical body was restored to its original state.
Thus he encountered immeasurable Buddhas, until finally, under the Tathāgata King of Sovereign Power over Mountains and Seas, he attained the dissolution of the self.
I am of one nature with the vacuity that permeates all the seas of fragrant water throughout the worlds of the ten directions, being non-dual and without distinction.

Now, having received the name "Childlike Innocence" from the Tathāgata and joined the assembly of Bodhisattvas, when the Buddha asked about the perfect penetration of the Way, I replied that through the single flavor of the water-element’s universal flow, I attained the patience of non-arising and perfected Bodhi; this is the foremost.
The Dharma Prince Vairocanaraśmiprabha rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"I recall that in the past, after kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, a Buddha appeared in the world named Amitaghoṣa.

He revealed to the bodhisattvas the wondrous clarity of fundamental enlightenment, teaching that this world and the bodies of sentient beings are all transformations driven by the power of the wind of false conditions. At that time, I..."

At that time, I contemplated the establishment of the realms, contemplated the movement of the world, contemplated the movement and stillness of the body, and contemplated the movement of thoughts in the mind.
Seeing that all movements are non-dual and without distinction, I then realized the nature of these various movements: they come from nowhere and go nowhere;
the sentient beings within the dust motes of the ten directions, though inverted, are of one and the same delusion. Thus it extends even unto the three thousandfold world system.

All sentient beings within a single world-system of the great trichiliocosm were like a hundred mosquitoes and gnats contained within a single vessel, chirping and clamoring together, creating a frantic noise within a mere fraction of space.
Upon encountering the Buddha for but a short while, they attained the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharmakṣānti*).

At that moment, their minds opened and they beheld the land of Akṣobhya Buddha in the eastern direction; they served as Dharma princes under the Buddhas of the ten directions, their bodies and minds [in harmony with them].
"Radiant and penetrating, unimpeded—when the Buddha asked about the means of perfect penetration, I observed that the power of wind has no basis;
thus I awakened to the Bodhi-mind and entered samādhi. In harmony with the Buddhas of the ten directions, we transmit this one wondrous mind. This is the foremost."
The Bodhisattva Ākāśagarbha rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:

"I and the Tathāgata attained the body of boundlessness under the Buddha Dīpaṃkara. At that time, I held four great precious jewels in my hands, which illuminated the Buddha-fields as numerous as motes of dust throughout the ten directions, transforming them into empty space.
Furthermore, within the Great Perfect Mirror manifested from my own mind, I emitted ten..."
The light from various exquisite jewels flowed and poured throughout the ten directions to the very limits of empty space;
all the lands of the Sovereign Banners came into the mirror and entered my body. My body was identical to empty space, without mutual obstruction.

My body was able to skillfully enter lands as small as motes of dust to extensively perform the Buddha-work, attaining great accordance. This great spiritual power arose because I contemplated that the four great elements are non-existent.
"Based on the arising and ceasing of deluded thoughts, space appears; yet space and the Buddha-lands are non-dual, being fundamentally identical.
By realizing this identity, I attained the patience of the non-arising of dharmas. When the Buddha asked about perfect penetration, I observed that space is boundless and thereby entered samādhi;
its wondrous power is perfectly clear and bright, and this is the foremost."
The Commentary says: It would be reasonable for the youth Candraprabha, once his meditation on water was accomplished, to see the appearance of water himself;
yet he said, "When my disciple peers through the window and looks into the room, he sees only clear water. How could it be that there is a fixed form and color visible to others? [The answer is:

At the beginning, when one forms a mental image, one sees only within one's own mind. However, as the power of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) becomes increasingly superior, the resulting objective form (*rūpa*) also becomes superior; therefore, others can see it.
One can also perceive what is called "matter resulting from meditative concentration" (*samādhi-phala-rūpa*). Śāriputra once entered meditative absorption on the banks of the Ganges;
when a malevolent spirit struck him, he emerged from concentration feeling a headache. The Buddha said, "You lacked the power of concentration; otherwise, your body would have been shattered.
In the past, the monk Bhāviveka once debated with non-Buddhists; the non-Buddhist stubbornly clung to his own [position].

He saw that it suddenly transformed into stone, yet his clear eloquence remained as he inscribed the titles upon the rock. When he went to look at it the following day, there was also a response inscribed there.
After a long time, it suddenly shattered of its own accord, and a roaring sound resounded through the air.
If one can become stone through a mind of fixed resolve, why could a concentrated mind alone not become water? As for what was said regarding the place of movement in the East—
The Buddha is named "Immovable. How is it known that he who perceives immobility within the realm of movement is [the Buddha]?
It is said: wind has, in truth, never moved. A questioner asked: "Is it not the case that what now blows upon the myriad things is wind? He replied:
"If wind were truly in motion, then from antiquity until now it would never have ceased or been extinguished, nor would it ever move again. Therefore, the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa Sūtra* says:
Mañjuśrī comes without the characteristic of coming, and sees without the characteristic of seeing;
that which is visible cannot be seen again—this is likewise so. [Supplement]:
According to the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*, within the Flower Treasury World-Ocean there are various fragrant water-oceans, and each of these fragrant water-oceans constitutes a Buddha-field world-system.

The phrases "elements" (*dhātu*), "seeds," and so forth, are used here to explain that this Floating Banner King realm is not the domain transformed by the present Buddha, but rather the sphere of transformation of the Tathāgata Jalamdhara as he recounted his past deeds. Therefore, he said to the Buddha:
"I recall that in the past, during kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, there was a Buddha who appeared in the world named Jalamdhara, who taught all the bodhisattvas to practice..."
By practicing the contemplation of water and entering samādhi, one contemplates the watery nature within the body as being indestructible;
it is then seen to be no different from the various fragrant water-oceans of the Floating Banner King world-system beyond this world.
Judging by this, how could this not be the transformative realm of the present Buddha? Those who would become bhikṣus should reach this state, just as Candraprabha did in past lives.
Even before he had become a monk, he had already accomplished this contemplation, and after becoming a monk, he again entered this contemplation with ease.

This is like Chan Master Chou entering the fire-light samādhi (*jvalana-samādhi*), such that his room was ablaze yet no different from being in meditative concentration. "Ding-guang" (定光) refers to Dīpaṃkara Buddha; "ding" (定) is originally written as "dìng" (錠).
In my time, it was transcribed as "I then clearly awakened" (*wǒ shí liǎo jué*); the *Jíjiě* (集解) edition reads "I then awakened and realized" (*wǒ shí jué liǎo*).
Maitreya Bodhisattva immediately rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"I recall that in the past, after the passing of as many eons as atoms of dust, a Buddha appeared in the world named Candrasūryapradīpa. From that Buddha, I attained renunciation;
however, my mind was heavy with worldly fame, and I delighted in frequenting noble families. At that time, the World-Honored One instructed me to practice the cultivation of consciousness-only."
Having entered samādhi for kalpas past, through the practice of this samādhi, I have served Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges;
my worldly mind for fame has ceased and vanished. Upon the appearance of Dīpaṃkara Buddha in the world, I attained the unsurpassed, wondrous, perfect samādhi of the cognitive mind.
Even unto the exhaustion of empty space, throughout all the lands of the Tathāgatas—whether pure or defiled, existent or non-existent—all are but myself.

"World-Honored One, I have realized that what is manifested by the transformations of the mind is but the mind itself; because I understand this as mere consciousness, the nature of consciousness flows forth as immeasurable Tathāgatas.
I have now received the prediction that I shall next succeed to the Buddha’s place. When the Buddha asked about the most perfect penetration, I replied:

'By clearly observing that the ten directions are but consciousness, my conscious mind became perfectly luminous. Entering the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*), I remained far removed from the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) and the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*).'"
"Endurance of the Non-arising of Dharmas is the foremost.
The Dharma Prince Mahāsthāmaprāpta, together with fifty-two bodhisattvas of his same rank, rose from their seats, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
'I recall that in the past, during kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, there was a Buddha who appeared in the world named...'"
Twelve Tathāgatas of Immeasurable Light will appear in succession throughout one kalpa; the last of these Buddhas is named Surpassing the Sun and Moon.
That Buddha taught me the samādhi of mindfulness of the Buddha. It is like two people, one who is single-mindedly mindful of another and one who is single-mindedly forgetful of that person:
even if they meet, it is as if they do not meet; even if they see each other, it is as if they do not see. When these two people are mindful of one another, their mutual mindfulness is profound.
In this way, from birth to birth, they are like a form and its shadow, never diverging or differing.
The Tathāgatas of the ten directions cherish sentient beings as a mother remembers her child; though the child may flee and hide, what can the mother’s remembrance do?

But if the child remembers the mother, just as the mother remembers the child, then throughout successive lives the mother and child will not be far apart. If sentient beings, with their own minds, remember the Buddha and recite his name...
In the present and in the future, you will certainly see the Buddha; you are not far from him. Without relying on further expedient means, you will spontaneously attain the opening of the mind.
It is like a person who has been perfumed with incense: their body carries the fragrance. This is what is called "Adornment by Fragrant Light.

In my own stage of practice, I entered the patience of non-arising through the mind of mindfulness of the Buddha. Now, within this world, I gather those who mindfully recite the Buddha's name and lead them back to the Pure Land.

The Buddha asked about the perfect penetration of the faculties, and I replied that I have no preference; by completely gathering the six sense-faculties and maintaining a continuous flow of pure mindfulness, I attained samādhi—this is my foremost method.
The commentary states: from the preceding passage on Ucchuṣma up to the Bodhisattva Ākāśagarbha, there are five sages in total.
Having previously enumerated the five dharmas of the vessel-world—earth, water, fire, wind, and space—I now enumerate the five dharmas of the sense-faculties and the body.

One might ask: since it should first have been stated that seeing, hearing, awareness, and cognition arise through consciousness—as Maitreya realized perfect penetration by means of consciousness—why are they mentioned here first?
The answer is: because seeing, hearing, awareness, and cognition exist only through the discrimination of consciousness; therefore, they are listed at the outset.
"All objective spheres are merely transformations of consciousness; they lack reality yet appear as precious staffs. The *Treatise* says:

"It is like a person who sees a moving object and takes it for a snake; upon looking at it for a long time, he realizes it is but a rope. Then the mind that suspected it was a snake ceases of its own accord.
This is like being free from the grasping of the *parikalpita-svabhāva* (imagined nature). Yet the rope still remains. Then, looking more closely, one says: 'It is not even a rope. For it is..."
The mind that previously grasped at the rope as being hemp does not cease through deliberate effort but subsides of its own accord;

because grasping at the dependent nature (*paratantra*) is likewise abandoned, it is said that one "removes the grasping at the dependent and the imagined (*parikalpita*)," thereby attaining the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
As for the Dharma Prince Mahāsthāmaprāpta, he speaks on behalf of his peers—the fifty-two bodhisattvas—representing the entire assembly; furthermore, he says:
When the Buddha asked about perfect penetration, I had no preference; rather, I gathered all six sense faculties and maintained a continuous flow of pure mindfulness.
This is fully realized within seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting, touching, and cognizing. As for the six faculties: in the eye, it is said to depend on two kinds of false objects—light and darkness;
in the ear, it depends on two kinds of false objects—motion and stillness; in the nose, it depends on openness.
Regarding the two kinds of false objects that obstruct the body, it is said they depend on the two kinds of false objects of conjunction and disjunction;

regarding the two kinds of false objects that obstruct the mind, it is said they depend on the two kinds of false objects of arising and ceasing. Therefore, when using human experience as evidence, these are all matched one-to-one;

yet, for the tongue alone, it is said it depends on the two kinds of false objects of sweet, bitter, and bland—whereas sweet and bitter constitute two distinct characteristics that can be categorized accordingly.
It is through the categories of cessation and arising, separation and union, penetration and obstruction, motion and stillness, and light and darkness that [the nature of phenomena] is understood;

yet, as there remains the characteristic of "fading away" (*tánxiàng*), the World-Honored One spoke of it by means of the two bodhisattvas Bhaiṣajyarāja and Bhaiṣajyasamudgata. Thus we know that the words established in the sutra are not arbitrary.
Supplement: Zizhong says: "To recklessly conceptualize [them] as a sentient being, a living soul, or a life-principle."

Furthermore, the imputation of a real entity that is pervasive throughout all things—ranging from "I" and "mine" to sentient and insentient beings—and the conceptualization of such distinctions is called the *parikalpita-svabhāva* (imagined nature).

To conceive of the world as established through the conjunction of causes and conditions, and to cling to these conventional signs (*nimitta*) as being definitively produced from seeds—despite the absence of a self—is to grasp at the seeds of one's own innate disposition as producing conventional form and mind. This is the imagined nature.

The dharmas such as the five aggregates are called the *paratantra-svabhāva* (dependent nature). The essence of untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*) and the *dharmadhātu-tathatā* (the realm of reality as suchness) are called the *pariniṣpanna-svabhāva* (perfected nature).
Maitreya is correctly called *Maitreyīna* [in Sanskrit], which is translated here as "Compassionate One" (*Cishi*).

This name "Compassionate One" is established based on three meanings: first, based on his mother, because she possesses a compassionate nature; second, based on his conduct, referring to his own practice; and third, based on his vows, referring to his aspiration for the benefit of others.

Because of his compassion, he relies on three vows; since these have now been fulfilled through his past vows, from the very first moment he entered the Path and realized the Samādhi of Compassion, all his manifested births have been identical to this name.

At that time, Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying: “World-Honored One...”
"Venerable One, please remember that in the past, countless *gaṅgā-nadī-vāluka* kalpas ago, there appeared in the world a Buddha named Avalokiteśvara.
Under that Buddha, I gave rise to the bodhicitta. That Buddha taught me to enter *samādhi* through hearing, contemplation, and cultivation.

First, within the process of hearing, I entered the stream and forgot the objects; once that which was entered had become still, the two characteristics of movement and stillness were clearly understood."
However, when such [gradual increase] does not arise, what is heard reaches its end; as hearing is exhausted, it does not abide. What is perceived becomes empty;
as perception is emptied, it reaches ultimate perfection. When that which empties is extinguished, both arising and ceasing are extinguished, and quiescent extinction manifests before one.

Suddenly transcending the mundane and supramundane worlds, one attains the ten directions' perfect luminosity and achieves two extraordinary excellences: first, one's upward union with the fundamental source of all Buddhas of the ten directions.

The mind of wondrous enlightenment and that of the Buddha-Tathāgata share the same power of compassion; second, they merge downward with all sentient beings of the six realms throughout the ten directions, sharing the same sorrowful longing as all such beings.
The Treatise says: The Tathāgatas of the three periods and the Bodhisattvas of the ten directions, by means of great skillful means, destroy ignorance and draw near to the method of Prajñā;

this method must necessarily enter through *śamatha* (calm abiding) and *vipaśyanā* (insight). Therefore, it is called the "Skillful Means for the Initial Mind. The opening of the *Dharmadhātu-vipaśyanā* states:
"To cultivate the *dharmadhātu-vipaśyanā*; 'cultivation' refers to *śamatha*. When one is in the state of *śamatha*, there is also..."
When observing the directions, at the time of observation there is likewise stillness, just as in the *Yījīng* it is said that within the yin there is yang, and within the yang there is yin.

What is called "proceeding from hearing, reflection, and cultivation" refers to the method of achieving stillness (*śamatha*) through the process of hearing; it is termed a "skillful means" (*upāya*).
Thus, one enters the profound from the shallow, and reaches the subtle through the coarse; this is called entering *samādhi*, Maitreya.

It is said: Whenever a single dharma arises, it is immediately endowed with three meanings. What are these three meanings? They are: the sudden (sū-er), the seeking (xún-qiu), and the resultant flow (děng-liú).
For example, when first hearing a sound, the awareness of it is the sudden; being startled and searching for its source is the seeking;
and knowing it to be the sound of a bell is the resultant flow. Since the sound itself constitutes the object of entry, it is called the "initial" [moment].
"Entering the stream within hearing and losing the object": since that which is entered has become still, the two characteristics of movement and stillness clearly do not arise.
This refers to the meaning of the preceding passage: "This faculty first resolves itself; one first attains the emptiness of persons.

Because one begins by entering the stream within hearing and losing the object, eventually reaching the point where the essence of the mind leaves behind hearing, it is said: "In this way, gradually increasing, both hearing and that which is heard are exhausted."
"Exhausting hearing so that it does not abide, one realizes that the perceiver and the perceived are empty.

This preceding passage explains the meaning of how the perfect clarity of emptiness constitutes liberation through the dharmas. As for what is called "Avalokiteśvara," can sound, which is without form, be seen?
Since visible forms have never reached the ear, how could sound possibly touch the eye? Inferring from this, it appears that the sense organs and their objects are fundamentally [non-dual].
Because one realizes that all things are simultaneously quiescent and extinguished, it is said that "when birth and extinction are both extinguished, quiescent extinction manifests before one.
This refers to the meaning of the previously mentioned liberation-dharma, wherein both are empty and do not arise. Question:
If there is quiescent extinction, then is this not the state of annihilation? Answer: What is meant by "quiescent extinction" is not "annihilation. Annihilation refers to death and cessation.

That which is quiescent extinction (*śānti-nirvāṇa*) is that which is eternally living yet extinguished. Thus, the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa-sūtra* says: "Attaining the extinction of ambrosia (*amṛta*), one realizes the path of awakening.
The *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* says: "The nature of ambrosia causes people not to die; even when combined with other substances, it can likewise prevent death.
Therefore, what is called the "extinction of ambrosia" refers to the non-extinction of eternal life. Now, when the drums and bells sound together—
When struck, there is sound, yet they do not know that these sounds are different; this difference is the nature of arising and ceasing.
However, the bell cannot become the drum, and the drum cannot become the bell. The sounds of these two are heard simultaneously, yet they never intermingle—this is quiescent extinction (*śamatha*).
Therefore it is said: "Suddenly transcending the mundane and supramundane worlds, it is perfectly pervasive throughout the ten directions."
This clarifies the meaning of the preceding passage concerning attaining the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharmakṣānti*) through samādhi. The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* states:
"For what reason is he named Avalokiteśvara? The Buddha told the Bodhisattva Akṣayamati:
"Good son, if there are immeasurable hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis of sentient beings who undergo various sufferings and afflictions, and they hear of this Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara..."
If one single-mindedly recites the name of Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva, he will immediately perceive their voices and they shall all attain liberation.

Thus it is said in verse: "True Contemplation, Pure Contemplation, Vast and Great Wisdom Contemplation, Contemplation of Compassion and Contemplation of Loving-kindness— May I always vow to and forever gaze upon them.
What is called "True Contemplation" refers to this: that the two aspects of movement and stillness clearly do not arise.
What is called the contemplation of purity refers to the state where hearing ceases entirely and that which perceives is empty of what is perceived; this is it.
What is called the contemplation of vast wisdom refers to the state where emptiness and awakening are perfectly complete, such that both the emptiness and that which is emptied are extinguished;

when birth and death are thus extinguished, quiescent extinction manifests before one—this is it. That which is said to share the same power of compassion as the Buddha-Tathāgata refers to the contemplation of compassion.
One who shares the same compassion and longing as all sentient beings is called an Avalokiteśvara. Supplement:

The Sanskrit term *Avalokiteśvara* is translated here as "Guān-yīn" (Contemplating Sound) or "Guān-shì-yīn" (Contemplating the Sounds of the World). The older translation was "Guāng-shì-yīn" (Light of the World's Sound).
Because this Bodhisattva first gives rise to the wisdom of reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*) through the faculty of hearing, he begins with listening.

"Entering the stream of the Noble Truths, one loses the nature of that which is heard. This means that once what is entered is already stilled, the two characteristics of movement and stillness clearly do not arise;
this establishes the meaning of "entering the stream and losing the object" mentioned above.

"Thus gradually increasing until both hearing and that which is heard are exhausted" means that both the subject who hears and the object that is heard are simultaneously discarded. "Exhausting hearing and not abiding therein" [is as follows].

Furthermore, regarding the elimination of its traces: when that which perceives and that which is perceived are both empty, since the perceiver and the perceived have already been eliminated, the perceiving-consciousness and the perceived-object must likewise be made empty.
When the emptiness of consciousness is perfected, observation transcends discursive thought.
When that which is emptied is itself extinguished, body and mind can no longer reach it. When birth and death are extinguished, these two—birth and death—[are brought to an end].

"Perfectly detached" means that quiescent extinction is manifest; this is the eternal reality. "Suddenly transcending the mundane and supramundane" means that the emotional attachments of both sages and ordinary beings have been exhausted.
"The ten directions are perfectly luminous" means there is no place left unilluminated.
"Attaining two kinds of excellence" will be fully explained in the following text. As for what is called "being one and the same with all sentient beings," it refers to...
Regarding "sorrowful longing" (*bei-yǎng*): "sorrow" (*bei*) refers to the Bodhisattva’s compassionate mind that rescues sentient beings, like a mother yearning for her child;
"longing" (*yǎng*) refers to sentient beings’ admiring devotion toward the Bodhisattva, like a child yearning for its mother.
Because mother and child yearn for one another and do not part, it is said they share a single sorrowful longing. Thus, through this shared power of compassion, one enters all lands.
The earth manifests as the thirty-two transformation bodies; when these share the same compassion and longing, they cause all sentient beings to obtain fourteen kinds of fearlessness.
Because various masters explain "compassion and longing" (*bi-ang*) as having a single meaning, their forced syntheses fall short of the mark.
World-Honored One, because I made offerings to the Tathāgata Avalokiteśvara and received from that Tathāgata the transmission of the Vajra Samādhi of Hearing-Perfuming and Hearing-Cultivation—
which is like an illusion— and because I share the same power of compassion as the Buddha-Tathāgatas, my body has become capable of manifesting thirty-two transformations to enter all lands.
World-Honored One, if Bodhisattvas enter samādhi and advance in the cultivation of the untainted (anāsrava),...
If those with resolute conviction manifest perfection, I manifest the body of a Buddha before them and preach the Dharma to bring them liberation.

If those who are still in training (*śaikṣa*) have attained the tranquil, wondrously luminous, and supremely excellent manifestation of perfection, I manifest the body of a Pratyekabuddha before them and preach the Dharma to bring them liberation.
If those who are still in training have severed the twelve links of dependent origination and the nature of that severance has manifested as supremely excellent perfection...
Before them, I manifest the body of a Pratyekabuddha and preach the Dharma for their liberation.

If there are those in training who have attained the emptiness of the Four Truths and entered cessation through the cultivation of the path, such that their supreme nature is fully manifested, I appear before them in the body of a Śrāvaka and preach the Dharma for their liberation.
If there are sentient beings who desire to awaken their minds and do not transgress the dust of desire, [I likewise act for their liberation].
If sentient beings desire purity of body, I appear before them in the form of a Brahma King and preach the Dharma to bring about their liberation.
If sentient beings desire to become lords of heaven to rule over the devas, I appear before them in the form of Śakra and preach the Dharma to enable them to achieve that goal.
If sentient beings desire bodily mastery to travel throughout the ten directions, I appear before them...
Before those beings, I manifest the body of Maheśvara and preach the Dharma to them so that they may achieve accomplishment.
If there are sentient beings who desire bodily mastery to fly through the void, before them I manifest the body of Maheśvara and preach the Dharma to them so that they may achieve accomplishment.
If there are sentient beings who love to govern spirits and deities and protect their lands...
To those before whom I manifest the body of a Great Heavenly General, I preach the Dharma so that they may achieve success.

To those sentient beings who desire to govern the world and protect all living beings, I manifest the body of one of the Four Heavenly Kings before them and preach the Dharma so that they may achieve success.
To those sentient beings who desire to be born in celestial palaces and command spirits and deities, I—
To those before whom I previously appeared in the form of a crown prince of the Four Heavenly Kings, I taught the Dharma so that they might achieve success;
to those sentient beings who delight in being human kings, I appeared before them in the form of a human king and taught the Dharma so that they might achieve success;
and to those sentient beings who cherish their noble lineage and are esteemed by the world, I appeared before them as an elder...
For those who delight in the body, I manifest as a teacher of the Dharma to bring them to fulfillment.

If there are sentient beings who delight in discussing names and terminology and dwell in self-purification, I appear before them in the form of a layperson (*gṛhapati*) and teach the Dharma to bring them to fulfillment.

If there are sentient beings who delight in governing territories and adjudicating the affairs of states and districts, I appear before them in the form of a high official (*kṣatriya-rājāmātya*) and...

I preach the Dharma so that they may achieve accomplishment. If there are sentient beings who delight in various arts and sciences and dwell in self-protection, I manifest before them in the body of a Brahmin and preach the Dharma for them so that they may achieve accomplishment.
If there are men who enjoy study and have left the household life to uphold the various precepts, I manifest before them in the body of a Bhikṣu and preach the Dharma for them.

Regarding their accomplishment: if there is a woman who delights in study, leaves the household life, and upholds the various prohibitions and precepts, I will manifest before her in the body of a bhikṣuṇī and preach the Dharma for her so that she may achieve accomplishment.

If there is a man who delights in upholding the five precepts, I will manifest before him in the body of an upāsaka and preach the Dharma for him so that he may achieve accomplishment. If there is a woman...
If there are those who abide by the five precepts, I will appear before them in the form of an upāsikā and preach the Dharma for them so that they may achieve fulfillment.

If there are women who manage internal affairs and establish themselves as pillars of their families and states, I will appear before them in the form of a queen, a noble lady of the court, a titled wife, or a great matron and preach the Dharma for them so that they may achieve fulfillment. If there are...
If there are sentient beings whose male organs are unimpaired, I manifest before them in the form of a young boy and preach the Dharma to them so that they may achieve accomplishment.

If there are virgins who love their own bodies and do not seek to violate others, I manifest before them in the form of a young girl and preach the Dharma to them so that they may achieve accomplishment. If there are devas who desire to leave their celestial ranks, I manifest...
If there are those with celestial bodies who wish to hear the Dharma so that they may achieve accomplishment, I manifest a celestial body and preach the Dharma for them to bring about their success.
If there are nāgas who delight in remaining within the class of nāgas, I manifest a nāga body and preach the Dharma for them to bring about their success.

If there are yakṣas who wish to transcend their own class, I manifest a yakṣa body before them and preach the Dharma for them to bring about their success. If there are gandharvas who wish to attain liberation...
If those belonging to the class of gandharvas desire liberation, I manifest before them in the form of a gandharva and teach the Dharma to bring them to accomplishment.
If those belonging to the class of asuras desire liberation, I manifest before them in the form of an asura and teach the Dharma to bring them to accomplishment.
If those belonging to the class of kinnaras desire liberation, I manifest before them in the form of a kinnara.

If there are those who take the form of *mahoragas* and delight in liberation from their own kind, I manifest before them in the body of a *mahoraga* and preach the Dharma to bring them to fulfillment.
If there are sentient beings who delight in being humans and practicing as humans, I manifest in a human body and preach the Dharma to bring them to fulfillment. As for those non-humans...
Whether they have form or no form, whether they possess thought or no thought, I appear before them all in their respective forms to preach the Dharma and enable them to achieve realization.
This is called the "Exquisite Purity" of the thirty-two manifestations entering various lands;
all are accomplished through the sovereign power of effortless wondrous efficacy, cultivated through the constant hearing and practice of Samādhi.
World-Honored One, I further rely on this power of the effortless, wondrous Samādhi of the Vajra, cultivated through hearing and practicing what has been heard;

because I share in the same compassion and yearning as all sentient beings throughout the ten directions and the three periods of time across the six realms, I cause those beings to obtain fourteen kinds of meritorious virtues of fearlessness within my body and mind. First, because I do not observe myself, but rather observe [others]...
First, by contemplating the sounds, it causes all suffering beings throughout the ten directions who hear them to attain immediate liberation.
Second, by the revolving of knowledge and vision, it causes all beings—even if they enter a great conflagration—to remain unburned by the fire.

Third, by the revolving of hearing and sound, it causes all beings—even if they are adrift upon a great flood—not to be drowned by the water. Fourth, it brings about the cessation and extinction of deluded thoughts.
Fifth, their minds are free from the intent to kill, causing all sentient beings to enter the realms of hungry ghosts where the ghosts cannot harm them;

they cultivate hearing until it becomes perfected hearing, and as the six faculties are dissolved and restored, they become identical to the auditory faculty, enabling them to face imminent slaughter so that when blades sever them limb from limb, their weapons are like slicing through water or blowing across light—their nature remains unshakable. Sixth...
When the fragrance of hearing is refined until it is luminously pervasive throughout the Dharma-realm, then the nature of all dark obscurations can no longer prevail;
it can cause yakṣas, rākṣasas, kumbhāṇḍas, pretas, piśācas, pūtanas, and the like to be unable to see even when they draw near its side.
Seventh, when the nature of sound is perfectly dissolved and the faculties of seeing and hearing return inward, one becomes free from all defilements and delusions, and is able to...

Eighth, though bound by the shackles and fetters of sentient beings, they cannot be constrained; by extinguishing sound and perfecting hearing, they universally generate the power of compassion, enabling them to lead sentient beings through perilous paths where bandits cannot plunder them. Ninth, as their cultivation of hearing leaves behind sensory dust, they cannot be robbed by forms;
they can cause all sentient beings with excessive lust to distance themselves from greedy desires. Tenth, their pure sound is free from dust.

Eleventh, the sense faculties and their objects are perfectly interfused, such that there is no longer subject or object; this enables all sentient beings harboring anger and resentment to be free from all hatred.
Twelfth, by dissolving the dust of the senses and revolving the light, the body and mind become like lapis lazuli—luminously penetrating and unobstructed;
this enables all those of dull nature and obstructed character, including the icchantikas, to forever leave behind the darkness of ignorance. Thirteenth, the forms are melted away...
Furthermore, he heard that while remaining in the Immovable Bodhimanda, he enters into the mundane world without destroying it;
he is able to universally make offerings to Buddhas as numerous as motes of dust throughout the ten directions, acting as a Dharma Prince at the side of each Buddha;

he can cause those sentient beings in the Dharma-realm who have no sons and desire a male child to give birth to a son endowed with merit and wisdom; and thirteenth, his six sense faculties are perfected.
With pervasive clarity illuminating the non-dual, encompassing the realms of the ten directions, it establishes the Great Perfect Mirror as the *Tathāgatagarbha*.
It accords with and receives the secret Dharma-gates of Buddhas as numerous as motes of dust throughout the ten directions without fail.

It enables those beings within the Dharma-realm who have no offspring—and those who desire daughters—to give birth to children of upright appearance, endowed with merit, gentleness, and compliance, whom all people love and respect, and possessed of auspicious marks.
The Fourteenth Daughter: Within this trichiliocosm, there are ten billion suns and moons;

among the various Dharma Princes currently dwelling in the world, there are those numbering as many as sixty-two Ganges-sands who cultivate the Dharma and establish models to teach and transform sentient beings.

Their skillful means and wisdom, which accord with the capacities of sentient beings, are each different. From the fundamental root of perfect penetration that I have attained, [this power has been issued forth].
Through the gateway of the Sublime Ear, my body and mind become subtle and wondrous, encompassing and pervading the entire Dharma-realm. I am able to cause sentient beings to hold my name;
if they and those who hold the names of the sixty-two *gaṅgā-nadī-vāluka* numbers of Dharma-princes were to do so together, the merit of these two individuals would be exactly equal and no different.
World-Honored One, my single name is no different from those many names, because...

To the point: I have cultivated and attained true perfect penetration; this is called the fourteenth power of bestowing fearlessness, providing all beings with merit.
