When the essence of the mind abandons hearing, this samādhi is called the Vajra Samādhi, because it destroys phenomena that are like illusions.
Therefore, the text below says: "From the mind of dry wisdom up to Equal Enlightenment, one has begun to realize; within this realization, one attains the Vajra Mind.
The Vajra Mind is so named because it also destroys and extinguishes the preceding stages. [Question: Because it is identical to the Buddha...
Because they share the same power of compassion, the thirty-two bodies should enter all lands—namely, the four types of noble bodies:
those of Buddhas, Pratyekabuddhas, Śrāvakas, and [Bodhisattvas]. May these be called "liberation"?

They may indeed be called "liberation" because they awaken the minds of sentient beings from desire and do not transgress the dust of sensual passion. Is this not so? The World-Honored One distinguished the matter of sexual conduct in this sutra.
Regarding the merits and faults of observing or violating the precepts: if one guards against even the slightest transgression, then even the five pungent roots (pañca-garaka) must not be consumed;

yet when considering the gravity of the offense, such prohibited karma (*pratikṣepa-śikṣāpada*) is not exempt from punishment. However, if one reaches the point of being able to remain free from violation, then it is not an error to rank them among the ranks of the various holy ones, as they are equally named "liberated" (*vimukti*).
It is said that the various masters have explained the thirty-two transformation bodies (*nirmāṇakāya*) and the fourteen kinds of... [text fragment].
"Wei, do you rely on principle to establish your interpretation? Can you understand the Buddha’s intention? He replied, "These people do not know the Buddha’s intention;
they merely possess discussions that are refined and extensive enough to be observed, yet in reality, their interpretations have no foundation.

It is like what the world calls Zhao Chang, who was renowned for his flower paintings and styled a master of *xiasheng* (life-like depiction); while such works appear excellent when viewed, they are not actual flowers.

Regarding what is called the "accomplishment of the sovereign power of the wondrous force of non-action," this refers to the *Samantabhadra-avabhāsa-rūpa-kāya-samādhi* mentioned in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, and the *Sarva-rūpa-kāya-darśana-samādhi* mentioned in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*.

Can the *Sarva-rūpa-kāya-darśana-samādhi* ever be fully exhausted by means of mere principles? For its subtle permeation of the Dharma-realm and the power of the roots of goodness of compassion are inconceivable.
He who moves within the true limit manifests traces throughout the ten directions. By means of the compassion of the Holy Conduct, he responds to those with inferior capacities;
thus, he holds a refuse bucket as if in a state of fear. By means of the compassion of the Celestial Conduct, he responds to those with middling capacities;

thus, like a swift horse that runs the great straight path at the mere sight of the whip’s shadow, he is without fear. For this reason, by means of the compassion of the Brahma Conduct, he responds to those with superior [false] capacities.
The *kīṭa* (spiritual power) sits upon a lion throne with a precious footstool supporting its feet; merchants and traders travel throughout other lands, engaging in profit and loss wherever they go.
These three kinds of *kīṭa* are manifested through the provisional spontaneity within the void, causing all sentient beings to see such things.
This is the Lotus Sūtra’s *rūpakāya-samādhi* (samādhi of the physical body). Such is the divine function of the Tathāgata throughout the ten directions.

Because they do not abandon sentient beings through the power of their vows of great compassion as they manifest in accordance with the faculties [of those beings], they are able to pervade everywhere in a single thought-moment without a creator.
As in the eleventh stage, the sentient beings benefited are equal to the dharma-realm;
they manifest form-bodies in accordance with faculties and timing, acting without effort and responding without deliberate doing by means of the wisdom of universal radiance.
Not belonging to any specific location, it shares the same mind as sentient beings, manifesting forms according to things because it is without coming or going.
Just as when the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī turned back to look at the youth Sudhana with the majestic gait of an elephant king, he manifested himself in accordance with their faculties;
thus he did not turn his back on sentient beings, and all those who were to see him according to their capacity perceived him as if facing them directly. And yet...
Sentient beings do not know one another; each thinks that the Sage is speaking to them alone. This is the "Manifestation of the Physical Body" (Rūpakāya) through the *Avataṃsaka* Sūtra.
When Chan Master Rang resided at Mount Nanyue, there was a monk who managed the communal affairs for twenty years.
When the county magistrate investigated his accounts of income and expenditure, the monk found no records. While lying in prison, he thought of the Master, saying: "O Upādhyāya..."
"Can you save me? One night he attained sudden enlightenment; over twenty years' worth of provisions, item by item, were not left behind, and thus he was released.
Master Ràng was initially unaware of this, which is why the world later hailed Ràng as an incarnation of Avalokiteśvara.

This [title] is translated as "Terrifier of Māras" (*bhayabhairava*), and also as "Remover of Hunger" (*kṣudhapanodana*); it refers to removing the hunger of desire and form. *Nī* means woman. *Upāsaka*—this...
*Upāsaka* (layman) is translated here as "one who attends" (*jìnshì*). *Upāsikā* (laywoman) is translated here as "one who attends" (*jìnshì nǚ*).
*Yakṣa* is translated here as "light and agile," and is also called "the observer," because they guard the gates of the celestial city and its portals.
*Gandharva* refers to the celestial musicians; it is translated here as "seeking fragrance. *Asura* is also called *Āxūlún* or *Āsùluò*. This...

Asura is translated as "Cloud-No-Rain" and also as "Non-God. Kinnara is translated as "Doubtful Human," so called because they have human bodies with horns, causing those who see them to doubt their identity.
Mahoraga refers to the dragons (*nāga*) who guard the grounds of the *ārāma*.
Rākṣasa are man-eating demons; Kumbhāṇḍa are demons that cause nightmares; Piśāca are demons that consume vital energy; and Pūtana are demons of feverish diseases.
*Kṣīṇāśrava* is also called *Acchanda*, which means "free from desire.

World-Honored One, because I have further attained this perfect penetration and realized the unsurpassed Way, I am also well-able to attain the four inconceivable, unconditioned, and wondrous virtues:
First, because when I first attained the wondrous and subtle faculty of hearing, the essence of the mind left behind all hearing.
Because seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing cannot be partitioned off from one another to form a single, perfectly integrated, pure, and precious awakening,
I am able to manifest many wondrous forms and preach boundless secret mantras. Among these, I may appear with one head, three heads, five heads, seven heads, nine heads,
eleven heads, and so on, up to one hundred and eight heads, a thousand heads, or ten thousand heads.
There are eighty-four thousand *śakara* heads, with two arms, four arms, six arms, eight arms, ten arms, twelve arms, fourteen, sixteen, eighteen, twenty, up to twenty-four;
and so on, even unto one hundred and eight arms, a thousand arms, ten thousand arms, and eighty-four thousand *mudrā*-arms; with two eyes, three eyes, or four eyes.

Ninth: Thus, from nine eyes up to one hundred and eight eyes, a thousand eyes, ten thousand eyes, or eighty-four thousand pure jewel-eyes—whether through compassion, majesty, meditative concentration, or wisdom—they rescue and protect sentient beings, attaining great sovereignty. Second:
Because I have been liberated from the six sense objects through hearing and reflection, just as sound passes through a wall without obstruction, I am thus wonderfully capable.
Manifesting each individual form and reciting each individual mantra, these forms and mantras are able to bestow fearlessness upon all sentient beings;
for this reason, throughout the lands as numerous as motes of dust in the ten directions, I am known as the "Bestower of Fearlessness.
Thirdly, because I have cultivated the fundamental, wondrous, perfect, and penetrating root of purity, I cause all sentient beings in the worlds where I travel to relinquish their bodies.

Fourth, regarding the seeking of precious jewels with a plea for my compassion: having attained the Buddha-mind and realized the ultimate, I am able to provide various kinds of precious jewels as offerings to the Tathāgatas of the ten directions, extending also to all sentient beings within the six realms of the Dharma-realm. For those who seek a wife, they shall obtain a wife;
for those who seek a son, they shall obtain a son; for those who seek samādhi, they shall obtain samādhi; for those who seek long life, they shall obtain long life—and so on, even unto...

Seeking Great Nirvana and attaining Great Nirvana, when the Buddha asked about the perfect penetration of the faculties, I replied: "I attained the Samādhi of Perfect Illumination through the gateway of the ear;
by gaining mastery over the conditioned mind and entering the stream of the Dharma, I attained Samāpatti and achieved Bodhi—this is the foremost method.
World-Honored One, that Buddha-Tathāgata praised me for having well-attained the Dharma-gate of perfect penetration and bestowed a prophecy upon me in the midst of the great assembly.
I am named Avalokiteśvara because, through my observing and listening, the ten directions are perfectly luminous; thus, the name "Avalokiteśvara" pervades the worlds of the ten directions.
The treatise says: Because the essence of the mind transcends hearing, seeing, smelling, tasting, touching, and knowing, it cannot be partitioned by these; this is to be free from discrimination.

When the pervasive conceptualization of marks is exhausted, one becomes a perfectly integrated, pure, and precious awakening; when attachment to dharmas is abandoned and dependence on others is exhausted,
then how could there be anything from the single head up to eighty-four thousand *śakara* heads,
from the two arms up to eighty-four thousand *mudrā* arms, or from the two eyes up to eighty-four thousand pure [eyes]?
O Jewel-Eyed One, although one may have immeasurable heads, immeasurable arms, and immeasurable eyes, this is permissible. For where there is thought, there is obstruction;
where there is obstruction, there is fear. It is like a person sitting in a dark room who hears a sound:

though the sound has no form, the mind of the hearer is obstructed by it, and thus they become afraid. Through my hearing and contemplation, I have escaped the six sense-objects, just as a sound passes through [the air].

A "wall" (yuan) refers to being detached from all conceptual thoughts; thus, it manifests forms and recites mantras so that sentient beings may thereby leave suffering behind and attain happiness—hence it is called "bestowing fearlessness.
The "pure fundamental root" means being without grasping and without affliction;
because this is so, one can cause sentient beings to relinquish their bodies and precious treasures, seeking my compassion to realize ultimate liberation, which is the state of wishlessness.
Because he was free from seeking, he was able to cause all the wishes and desires of sentient beings to be fulfilled.
Master Dushun once hung his sandals on the door of his dwelling; for three years, no thieves came. When people asked him the reason, he said:
"Throughout kalpas past, I have never stolen anything from others; therefore, others cannot trouble me. [Supplementary Note: East]
Suzhou’s record of the Beidi Pavilion in Chengdu states: "The Great Compassionate One (Mahākāruṇika) is a transformation of Avalokiteśvara.

Avalokiteśvara attains awakening through hearing; he begins with hearing yet is able to be without anything heard. He begins with being without anything heard yet is able to hear everything that can be heard.
Being able to have nothing heard, though he may lack a physical body, he is nonetheless able to hear everything."
It is permissible even for there to be thousands of myriads of koṭis of bodies, let alone hands and eyes.

Nevertheless, it is not without a body that one can raise thousands of myriads of koṭis of beings; nor is it without thousands of myriads of koṭis of bodies that one can demonstrate the ultimate state of bodilessness.
Thus, they disperse to become thousands of myriads of koṭis of bodies, yet they gather together to become the eighty-four thousand *śakāra* [teeth].
The head has eighty-four thousand arms like the *mudrā* gesture and eighty-four thousand pure jewel-eyes; their way is one and the same.
Long ago, I once observed this: my hair is beyond counting, and the pores of my body are likewise beyond counting.
If one pulls a single strand of hair, the head moves with it; if one plucks a single pore-hair, the entire body [trembles].
Such are the transformations! Thus, hair is all my head and every pore is my body;
yet though all that is my head, it cannot perform the functions of a head, and though all that is my body, it cannot possess the intelligence of a body—this is because things have confused them.
I shall cause the people of the world to wield an axe with their left hand while holding a plane with their right.

To count flying geese with the eyes while discerning the beating of drums with the ears, to nod in agreement to a bystander while simultaneously recognizing the rungs of a ladder—this would leave even the wisest person with no leisure;
how much more so when a thousand hands grasp different objects and a thousand eyes look in different directions?
When I sit in quiet meditation, my mind is concentrated in silence, as still and clear as a great bright mirror, reflecting people, ghosts, and birds alike.
Animals are arrayed before me, and forms, sounds, fragrances, and flavors reach my body; though the mind does not arise [to grasp them], there is nothing that does not come into contact.
There must be a way for this, such that a thousand hands emerge and a thousand eyes function; though these may not yet be visible, the principle is already complete.
It is the same with those Buddhas and Bodhisattvas: though they do not manifest as a single body, it is not that they do not exist.
Although there are two Buddhas, one Buddha is able to manifest as Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges; there is no other besides him. Though touched by phenomena, he is not disturbed;
when conditions arrive, he responds accordingly. Since it is a matter of principle that he must necessarily appear, why do you alone harbor doubts regarding his great compassion?

At that time, from his five limbs, the World-Honored One emitted precious light which reached far to moisten the crowns of the heads of the Tathāgatas as numerous as motes of dust throughout the ten directions,
as well as the Bodhisattvas who are Dharma Princes. Those Tathāgatas likewise emitted precious light from their five limbs,
which came from the motes of dust in all directions to moisten the crown of the Buddha’s head and to moisten the crowns of the heads of the great Bodhisattvas in the assembly.
Furthermore, for the Arhats, the groves, ponds, and marshes all resounded with the sounds of the Dharma; their interlacing lights were like a net of precious threads.
This great assembly attained what they had never experienced before, universally obtaining the Vajra Samādhi.

Immediately, the heavens rained down lotus flowers of a hundred jewels—blue, yellow, red, and white—intermingling and blending together, until the voids of the ten directions became the color of the seven treasures.

In this Sahā world-system, the great earth, mountains, and rivers all vanished simultaneously, and only the lands of the ten directions, as numerous as motes of dust, were seen merged into a single realm, where the chanting of Brahma-songs and hymns was spontaneously performed.
Thereupon, the Tathāgata addressed the Dharma Prince Mañjuśrī: "Observe now these twenty-five great Bodhisattvas beyond training and the Arhats..."
The various patriarchs of the Han dynasty each spoke of their initial expedient means for attaining the Way, all claiming they had cultivated true and perfect penetration (*yuan-tong*).
In their actual practice, there was truly no distinction of superiority or inferiority, nor of priority or sequence. Now I wish to cause Ānanda to attain awakening;

which of these twenty-five practices is suited to his faculties? Furthermore, after my parinirvāṇa, which among the sentient beings of this world who enter the Bodhisattva Vehicle and seek the Unsurpassed [Enlightenment] shall find it?
Asking by what skillful means the Way may be easily accomplished, Mañjuśrī, the Dharma Prince, having received the Buddha’s compassionate command,
rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and, sustained by the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power, spoke these verses in response to the Buddha:

The Commentary states: Seeking the underlying intent of the preceding sutra passages, which desire to extinguish the dust of the senses and unite with awakening to demonstrate the principle of the Unseen Summit (Anavalokitamūrdha), one must first describe the six sense organs.

Since the manifestation of light necessarily accompanies the description of the six organs, [the Buddha] first used his own hand—adorned with Jambūnada purple-golden light—to stroke Ānanda’s crown, whereupon all the worlds of the Buddhas in the ten directions immediately shook in six ways.
The Tathāgatas dwelling in worlds as numerous as motes of dust each have jewel-light radiating from their crowns;
these lights simultaneously arrive at the Jeta Grove in that world and drench the crown of the Tathāgata’s head. Thereupon, he says to Ānanda:
"That which causes you to revolve in birth and death is rooted solely in your six faculties; it is these that enable you to swiftly realize peace and liberation."

"Transcending quiescence, wondrous permanence, as well as your six faculties"—this refers to the preceding discussion on the faculty of sight (*cakṣur-indriya*), with a brief mention of the faculty of hearing (*śrotra-indriya*).
From "the conditioned is empty within its own true nature" up to "selecting the perfect penetration of the faculties to enter the stream and achieve right enlightenment," this is precisely that.
However, in this [passage], it merely distinguishes the modes of activity (*ākāra*) of the six faculties; now, furthermore, [the text] recounts...
Furthermore, as the six sense organs emitted light, the World-Honored One likewise emitted precious radiance from his five limbs,

which reached far to moisten the crowns of the heads of Tathāgatas as numerous as motes of dust throughout the ten directions, as well as the Dharma-Prince Bodhisattvas. Those Tathāgatas also simultaneously emitted precious radiance from their five limbs,
coming from those motes of dust in all directions to moisten the crown of the Buddha’s head and to moisten the crowns of the heads of all those in the assembly.
Only after the great Bodhisattvas and Arhats [have attained this] can it be said that "the forests, trees, ponds, and marshes all proclaim the sounds of the Dharma.
This first discusses the faculty of hearing and briefly touches upon the faculty of sight;

from the point where the interpenetrating lights cross one another until now, when the great earth, mountains, and rivers of this Sahā world simultaneously cease to appear—this is it. Whether it be the World-Honored One’s description of the six faculties or...
To prioritize either the faculty of sight or the faculty of hearing is not for any other purpose;
it is simply because one wishes to know through one's own seeing and hearing how the functions of the six faculties interact and mutually fulfill one another. Question:

As previously stated, when light was emitted to distinguish the characteristics of the activities of the six faculties, why is light now emitted as a portent? Answer: It is to manifest and clarify [the meaning].
Because the six sense faculties are purified, the faculty of hearing is first described to demonstrate the realm of wisdom;
subsequently, the faculty of seeing is mentioned to demonstrate that both realm and wisdom have vanished. It is asked: "What is meant by the 'realm of wisdom'? It is said:

The *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states, "The knowledge of all-knowledge is pure, non-dual, not divided into two, without distinction, and uninterrupted. Therefore, it says: "forests, groves, ponds, and marshes."
All are the manifestation of the sound of the Dharma. The *Dharmadhātu-vipaśyanā* states: "In time and space, the Indra-net manifests in successive layers;
because the wisdom of all-knowledge penetrates without obstruction, it is said that 'the interlacing lights are mutually entwined like a net of precious threads.

This is because the wisdom still remains, like polishing a mirror: when the grime is removed, the light remains. It asks: "What is meant by 'both object and wisdom are extinguished'? It answers: "Gold."
The Diamond Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra says: "Whether born from eggs, born from wombs, born from moisture, or born by transformation;

whether possessing form or being formless; whether possessing perception, lacking perception, or neither possessing nor lacking perception—I shall cause them all to enter *nirvāṇa* without remainder and bring them to liberation.
Therefore it is said: 'In this Sahā world, the great earth and its mountains...'"
The *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā* states that if sentient beings are already empty, how much more so are the mountains, rivers, and the great earth?

If the skin is absent, where could the hair remain attached? To say that the mountains, rivers, and the great earth do not manifest simultaneously makes it unnecessary to even mention sentient beings.

The nature of the ocean of awakening is clear and perfect; this clarity and perfection of awakening is fundamentally subtle and wondrous. Fundamental luminosity shines forth, giving rise to the "object" (the perceived);

once the object is established, the nature of the shining light itself vanishes. Through delusion and falsehood, there arises empty space; relying upon space, worlds are established. When thought becomes clear, it forms the land;

when cognition arises, it becomes sentient beings. Within the Great Awakening, emptiness arises like a single bubble emerging from the sea; all these minute, defiled lands arise entirely dependent upon emptiness.
When the bubble has vanished, emptiness is fundamentally non-existent; how much more so the various realms of the three existences?
The Treatise says: That which is called the "wondrous origin" is that which is inherently wondrous and eternally luminous.

Because it discriminates external objects, it is called "originally luminous. Once this original luminosity has fallen into the ground of the faculty of mental consciousness (*manas*), it becomes what resembles valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

If one establishes [reality] through what resembles direct perception (*pramāṇa*), then the perfect clarity of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) vanishes; hence it is said that "the nature of illumination perishes when established.
Dinglin said: "To 'perish' means simply to enter into non-existence. The desire realm, the form realm, and the formless realm dwell in dependence upon space;

these are called the "three existences" (*tridhātu*). Yet even space arises within the Great Awakening like the rising and ceasing of waves in the ocean—how much more so, then, the so-called three realms?
Since this is so, how much more so for those within the three realms of existence!
Returning to the source, the nature is non-dual; as for expedient means, there are many gates. The sagely nature has no obstruction; whether following or reversing, all are expedient means.

For those at the initial stage entering samādhi, the speed varies and cannot be categorized as equal; the fetters of form and thought solidify into dust, such that refined discernment cannot penetrate through them.

How can one not clearly penetrate this and yet claim to have attained perfect penetration? Sound is mixed with language; it merely relies on names, phrases, and meanings, and as a single entity, it does not contain all things.
How can one attain perfect penetration through this? As for fragrance, it is known when in contact, but when separated, it is fundamentally non-existent;

its perception is not constant. How can one attain perfect penetration through this? The nature of taste is not inherent; it exists only at the time of tasting. How can one attain perfect penetration through this?
That awakening is not constant; how can it attain perfect penetration? Touch is clarified by that which is touched, yet there is nothing it does not clarify;
the nature of contact and separation is not fixed—how can it attain perfect penetration? Mental objects are called internal dust;

relying on dust necessarily involves the subject and the object, and thus cannot pervade all things—how can it attain perfect penetration? Although the nature of seeing is penetratingly clear, it sees what is before but not what is behind.

The four intermediate directions lack half [of their full extent]; how can one attain perfect penetration? The inhalation and exhalation of the nose are manifest before one, yet there is no meeting of these breaths;
being fragmented, they do not interpenetrate; how can one attain perfect penetration? The tongue has no fixed point of entry, for it gives rise to discernment because of flavors;

when the flavor perishes, discernment ceases to exist; how can one attain perfect penetration? The body and its objects of touch are identical, yet neither is the contemplation of Perfect Enlightenment.
If the limits of the sense-objects do not harmonize with the ultimate, how can one attain perfect penetration? When the faculties are confused and thoughts are turbid, there is ultimately no seeing;

since ideation cannot be escaped, how can one attain perfect penetration? When consciousness, seeing, and the three-fold harmony are conflated, one interrogates their source and finds them to be without characteristics;
since their own essence has no fixed basis from the start, how can one attain perfect penetration? When the mind’s hearing penetrates the ten directions, it arises from the power of the Great Cause.
Those with a beginner’s mind cannot enter; how could they attain perfect penetration? The practice of nose-observation is fundamentally a provisional device intended only to cause the mind to abide;

once the mind has attained abiding, it becomes merely a mental state—how could this lead to perfect penetration? Expounding the Dharma involves playing with sounds and texts, which may awaken those who are already somewhat matured;

yet names and phrases are not themselves untainted—how could this lead to perfect penetration? Observing precepts and transgressions merely constrains the body; where there is no body, there is nothing to constrain.

Originally not pervading all things, how could you have attained perfect penetration? Spiritual powers are fundamentally due to past causes; what relation do they have to the discrimination of dharmas?

If mental objects are not apart from material things, how could you have attained perfect penetration? If you contemplate the nature of earth, its solidity and obstruction prevent thorough penetration;
as it is conditioned and not the nature of the sages, how could you have attained perfect penetration? If you contemplate the nature of water, thoughts and perceptions are not ultimately real.

Since Suchness is beyond thought and deliberation, how can one attain perfect penetration? If you contemplate through the nature of fire, you will grow weary of existence; yet this is not true transcendence.
Since it is not the initial skillful means, how can one attain perfect penetration? If you contemplate through the nature of wind, motion and stillness are not without opposition;

since there is opposition, it is not the supreme awakening. How can one attain perfect penetration? If you contemplate through the nature of space, dullness and ignorance were already present before awakening.

Without awakening, how can one differ from Bodhi? How then could one attain perfect penetration? If one uses the nature of consciousness as the object of observation, observing that consciousness is not permanent, yet maintaining a mind that is fundamentally illusory—how then could one attain perfect penetration?
All conditioned phenomena are impermanent; the nature of thought is inherently subject to arising and ceasing.
Since cause and effect now produce such disparate responses, how then could one attain perfect penetration?

Supplement: Wujin said, "The World-Honored One stated that their practices are truly without superiority or inferiority, yet Mañjuśrī refuted them one by one, asking, 'Which of you has attained perfect penetration? This was established as a model for future generations;
while the twenty-four sages each realized perfect penetration, regarding the expedient means for beginners, there is concern they might fall into biased views."
I now address the World-Honored One: When a Buddha appears in this Sahā world-system, the true essence of the teaching here consists in purity found within sound and hearing.
To attain samādhi, one must truly enter through the faculty of hearing; thus one leaves suffering behind and attains liberation. How excellent is Avalokiteśvara!
Throughout kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, he has entered Buddha-lands as many as motes of dust, attaining the power of great mastery and bestowing fearlessness upon sentient beings.
The wondrous voice, the Avalokiteśvara-voice, the Brahma-voice, the ocean-tide voice—saving the world and bringing all peace, transcending the world to attain eternal abiding.
I now address the Tathāgata as Avalokiteśvara has described: suppose a person dwells in stillness while drums are struck simultaneously in the ten directions;
they hear them all at once in those ten places. This is the perfection of true reality. The eyes do not see beyond obstructions, nor is it so with the mouth or nose.
Only through the union of body and mind does one know that mental thoughts are chaotic and without order. By listening to sounds across a wall, one can hear them both from afar and nearby;
yet the five sense organs are not uniform in their capacity. This is the penetration of true reality: within the hearing of movement and stillness, sound exists as having and not having.

To claim there is no hearing when there is no sound is not true non-hearing, for it lacks inherent nature. Since sound is non-existent, it cannot be extinguished; since sound is existent, it is not born.
When one is perfectly free from both arising and ceasing, this is the true permanence; even within dreams, one is not subject to non-thought or the absence of investigation and analysis.

This transcends discursive thought, such that body and mind cannot reach it. In this Sahā world, the principles of sound and discourse can be clearly proclaimed, yet sentient beings are deluded regarding their fundamental hearing;
by following sounds, they wander through the cycle of existence. Ānanda, even with your powerful memory, you cannot avoid falling into deviant thoughts.
Is it not so that by following the whirlpool of what one has sunk into, one attains non-delusion? Ānanda, listen attentively!
Relying on the Buddha’s majestic power, I shall proclaim the Vajra King, the Illusory and Inconceivable Mother of Buddhas, the True Samādhi.
The Treatise says: The Vajra King is the Dharma of emptiness; that which is like an illusion and inconceivable is the Dharma of the provisional;
it is the Dharma within true samādhi. Nāgārjuna said: "All phenomena that arise through conditions, I declare to be empty;

they are also called provisional names, and they are also called the meaning of the Middle Way. These three dharmas—emptiness, the provisional, and the middle—are the path of the Tathāgatas of the three periods of time for entering [reality].
This is the track of the Dharma-realm. A question was asked: "Why is it called the 'Mother of Buddhas'? He replied:
"The primary tenet of this sutra is the clear vision of Buddha-nature. This tenet is the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi*, the supreme dharma.
The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states: 'Buddha-nature is precisely the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi*; it is the mother of all Buddhas. Thus have the various masters judged it."

To establish the doctrine of this sutra as the final teaching of the Mahayana while simultaneously incorporating the sudden and perfect teachings, asserting its central tenet to be the *tathāgatagarbha* nature—
or alternatively, "Great Samādhi"— is to miss the Buddha’s true intent.
"You have heard of the secret gates of all the subtle-dust Buddhas, yet you have not first eliminated the outflows of desire; by hoarding what you have heard, you have created error.
Since you hold onto hearing from Buddha to Buddha, why do you not hear your own hearing? Hearing does not arise spontaneously; it exists because of sound and names.
When hearing turns away from sound, you are liberated. Once one faculty returns to its source, all six faculties achieve liberation."
Supplement: [The commentary] states: Because the defiled mind harbors attachments, it is called the "outflow of desire" (*kāma-āsrava*).

Because one seeks extensive learning and possesses strong memory, it is called "accumulated hearing. The phrase "intending to hear and maintain" refers to Ānanda taking sound as his hearing, seeking outwardly, and grasping at the Buddha as being the Buddha.
Why not instead hear the "hearer"? This means to cease following sounds and return to hearing the fundamental hearing.
This means that the nature is inherently endowed with hearing, which does not exist because of sound; therefore, the subsequent phrase says, "Turning the hearing back to hear one's own nature.
That "hearing is not produced spontaneously" refers to being deluded regarding this original hearing and flowing along with sounds, thereby claiming that hearing exists because of sound;
thus, the following phrase says, "Because of sound there are names. When one turns the hearing and detaches from sound, one is able [to realize the nature].
"Who can name that which is liberated from desire? This line reverses the two preceding phrases to cause one to turn back and hear the sound of liberation.
It means that if one is able to remain unattached to the sounds one hears, then as for the hearing that arises because of those sounds—who could possibly name it?

Since hearing cannot be grasped and thus cannot be named, one returns to the source and reverts to the fundamental; in its very essence, this constitutes liberation. Therefore, the following line says: "Once one faculty has returned to the source..."

When the six sense-faculties (*ṣaḍ-indriya*) originate from liberation and pure awakening is realized, it is said that one should employ the three types of wisdom (*tri-prajñā*) to revolve these faculties and their objects, causing both to be freed from their attachments.
Once what is grasped has been dissolved, what further name or form could there be for the wisdom that performs the liberation? I venture to ask:
when one employs these three wisdoms to revolve these faculties and objects in order to detach from their clinging, what is the nature of this wisdom? Does wisdom possess any [form]?
Such is the nature of things.

Seeing and hearing are like illusory cataracts; the three realms are like flowers in the sky. When hearing is restored and the cataracts of the faculties are removed, the dust is extinguished and awareness becomes perfectly pure.
When purity reaches its limit, light penetrates everywhere, and tranquil illumination encompasses empty space. Returning then to observe the world, it is like an event in a dream.

When Mātanga appears in a dream, who can retain your form? Like a skilled worldly illusionist who conjures various men and women—though their faculties appear to move, they are pulled by a single mechanism;
when that mechanism ceases, all illusions become devoid of nature. The six sense-faculties are also like this:
originally derived from one brilliant essence, they divide into the union of six; once they are unified in one place, there is restorative peace.

The six faculties are all rendered non-functional; defilements are dissolved upon reflection, becoming perfectly luminous, pure, and wondrous. When remaining traces of dust are further purified through study, and clarity reaches its ultimate limit, one is a Tathāgata.

The Commentary states: A Bodhisattva at the initial stage perceives the medium-grade function because they have attained deep faith in True Suchness (Tathatā), thereby gaining a small portion [of realization].
They perceive that the body of the Tathāgata neither goes nor comes, is without interruption, and is manifested solely by the mind, never departing from True Suchness (*tathatā*).
Nevertheless, because this Bodhisattva has not yet entered the stage of the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*), they have not yet been able to abandon subtle conceptualization.
A Bodhisattva of pure mind perceives these subtle functions as thus progressively superior, until the Bodhisattva reaches the ultimate.
When one has completely exhausted all subtle perceptions within the ground of consciousness, it is then called the Enjoyment Body (*saṃbhogakāya*).
If one possesses the karmic consciousness, one perceives the Enjoyment Body; yet if one is separated from the karmic consciousness, nothing can be seen.

All Tathāgatas are the Dharma Body (*dharmakāya*), and the Dharma Body is devoid of distinctions such as "self" and "other," for its forms do not perceive one another. This is because, having exhausted all that is subtle...

That which is called the *saṃbhogakāya* (enjoyment body) exists because of the subtle characteristics of the *karmavijñāna* (karma-consciousness), which are said to persist within the stages of the Bodhisattvas;

thus it is said, "If there remains even a trace of dust, one is still a learner. If one is separated from the *karmavijñāna*, there is nothing further to be seen, which is called the *dharmakāya* (dharma body) of the Tathāgata;
thus it is said, "When clarity reaches its ultimate limit, that is the Tathāgata."
O Great Assembly and Ānanda: Turn back the inverted hearing-faculty and listen instead to the nature of hearing itself.
When this nature is perfected, the Unsurpassed Way is attained; such is the true, perfect penetration. This is the single path to Nirvana for countless Buddhas;
all Tathāgatas of the past have accomplished it through this gate, all Bodhisattvas of the present now enter its perfect clarity, and those who practice and study in the future [shall do the same].
One should rely upon such dharmas; I too have realized them therein. It is not only Avalokiteśvara who is thus;

as the Buddha, the World-Honored One, questioned me regarding the various skillful means for saving those in the final age who seek to transcend the world and achieve the mind of nirvana, I replied that Avalokiteśvara is supreme.
All other skillful means are the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power, which, through specific matters, causes one to abandon worldly afflictions.
This is not for those who have long practiced; it is a teaching on the profound and the shallow alike. I prostrate to the Tathāgata-garbha, the untainted and inconceivable.
I pray that you will bestow your grace upon future generations so that they may be free from delusion regarding this gateway, easily achieving accomplishment through skillful means.

It is fit to be taught to Ānanda and to those sinking in the depths during the final kalpa. By cultivating perfect penetration through this faculty alone, one transcends all others; such is the true mind.
Thereupon Ānanda and the great assembly attained clear understanding in both body and mind, receiving a profound revelation.
They perceived that the Bodhi of the Buddha and Great Nirvāṇa were like a person who, having traveled far on business, has not yet returned home but clearly knows the path leading back to his house.
This included the entire assembled multitude: devas, nāgas, and the eight classes of beings; those still in training and those of the two vehicles; and all others.
The number of newly resolved bodhisattvas was equal to ten Ganges-sands; they all attained their original minds, became free from dust and defilement, and achieved the purity of the Dharma-eye.

Upon hearing these verses, the bhikṣuṇī Śrīprabhā attained arhatship, and immeasurable sentient beings all resolved to attain the peerless, unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment (anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi).
Ānanda adjusted his robes, joined his palms in homage before the great assembly, and with his mind and its traces perfectly clear, he was filled with a mixture of sorrow and joy.
Desiring to benefit all sentient beings of the future, he bowed his head to the Buddha and addressed the World-Honored One of Great Compassion:
"I have now realized the Dharma-gate of attaining Buddhahood; practicing within it, I have attained freedom from doubt and confusion. I have often heard the Tathāgata speak in this manner."

"To say that one who has not yet crossed over oneself first crosses others refers to the Bodhisattva’s initial resolve; to awaken oneself fully and then be able to awaken others refers to the Tathāgata appearing in the world.
Although I have not yet crossed over myself, I vow to deliver all sentient beings of the final age. World-Honored One, these sentient beings are gradually moving further away from the Buddha;
false teachers preach the Dharma as numerous as the sands of the Ganges River. [I wish] to gather their minds and lead them into..."
"How does one, through samādhi, establish oneself at the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa), remain far removed from all demonic activities, and attain non-retrogression in the mind of awakening?
At that time, the World-Honored One, in the midst of the great assembly, praised Ānanda, saying: "Excellent, excellent! It is as you have asked."
"Establishing the site of enlightenment to rescue and protect sentient beings drowning in the final age—listen attentively now, and I shall explain it for you.
Ānanda and the great assembly responded, "Yes, we respectfully accept your instruction.
The Buddha told Ānanda: "You have often heard me, within the Vinaya, proclaim the three definitive meanings of spiritual practice."
What is called "gathering the mind as the precept" means that because of the precept, concentration arises; because of concentration, wisdom is produced.
This is what is known as the Threefold Training in the Outflow-free (Anāsrava). Ānanda, what is meant by gathering the mind? I call this the precept.

If the beings of the six realms throughout all worlds do not harbor lustful hearts, they will not follow the continuity of birth and death. Your cultivation of samādhi is fundamentally for the purpose of emerging from worldly toil.

If the lustful mind is not eliminated, one cannot transcend the dust of the world; even if one possesses great wisdom and meditative concentration manifests before them, if they do not sever lust, they will inevitably fall onto the path of demons.
There will be high-ranking demon kings, middle-ranking demon subjects, and low-ranking demonesses.

These various demons will each have their own followers, and every one of them will claim to have attained the Unsurpassed Way. After my parinirvāṇa, during the period of the Final Dharma, [this shall come to pass].

These many followers of Māra flourish in the world, widely practicing greed and lust while posing as spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*), causing all sentient beings to fall into the pit of craving and false views and lose the path to Bodhi.
You should teach the people of the world that when they cultivate *samādhi*, they must first sever sexual desire in the mind;
this is called the foremost, definitive, pure, and clear instruction of the Tathāgata and the Buddhas of the past. Therefore, Ānanda, [you must uphold this].
If one who has not severed lust practices meditative concentration, it is like steaming sand and gravel in hopes of producing cooked rice;
even after hundreds of thousands of kalpas, it will remain nothing but hot sand. Why is this? Because it is not the fundamental substance of rice, being composed of sand and gravel.

If you seek the Buddha’s wondrous fruit with a body of lust, even if you attain wondrous awakening, it will all be rooted in lust. Since its foundation is lust, you will inevitably revolve through the three miserable realms.

If one cannot emerge from the Tathāgata’s nirvāṇa, by what path can one cultivate and realize it? One must ensure that the mechanism of lust is severed in both body and mind, and that even the nature of this severance is absent;
only then may one hope for the Buddha’s bodhi. What I have spoken thus is called the Buddha’s teaching;
if it were not spoken thus, it would be the teaching of Pāpīyān.
Ānanda, furthermore, among the sentient beings of the six realms in all worlds, if their minds do not kill, they will not follow along with the continuity of birth and death.
When you cultivate samādhi, its purpose is fundamentally to escape from worldly toil; if the mind to kill is not eliminated, you cannot escape from the dust of the world.

Even if you possess great wisdom and meditative concentration manifests before you, if you do not sever the act of killing, you will inevitably fall into the realm of spirits. Those of the highest grade will become great [spirits].
Those of middling power among the *bala-rākṣasas* shall become flying *yakṣas* and various ghost generals; those of inferior power shall become earth-walking *rākṣasas*.
These ghosts and spirits also have their own followers, each claiming to have attained the Unsurpassed Way.
After my parinirvāṇa, during the period of the Final Dharma, many such ghosts and spirits will flourish in the world, declaring that by eating meat one attains Bodhi.
"Ti lu, Ānanda, when I permitted bhikṣus to eat the five kinds of pure meat, those meats were all produced through my supernatural power;
they originally had no life-force. You, O brāhmaṇa, live in a land where the soil is mostly damp and humid, further compounded by sand and stones such that grasses and vegetables do not grow.
Through the application of my great compassionate supernatural power, and because of my great kindness and pity, I provisionally designated them as 'meat' so that you might obtain their flavor."
How can it be that after the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa, those who eat the flesh of sentient beings call themselves disciples of the Śākya?
You should know that such meat-eaters, even if they attain mental clarity resembling *samādhi*, are all great rākṣasas;

when their retribution ends, they will inevitably sink into the bitter sea of birth and death and are not disciples of the Buddha. Such people kill one another, devour one another, and eat one another without end.
"How does such a person escape the three realms? You teach the people of the world to cultivate *samādhi*, and next to that, to sever the taking of life;
this is called the second definitive, pure, and clear instruction of the Tathāgata and the World-Honored Buddhas of the past.
Therefore, Ānanda, if one cultivates meditative concentration without severing killing, it is like a person who blocks their own ears while shouting at the top of their voice."
To seek out others while remaining ignorant of these things is called "desiring to conceal what is manifest.
Pure bhikṣus and bodhisattvas do not tread upon living grass even when walking on a forked path, much less would they pluck it with their hands.

How could those of great compassion take the flesh and blood of sentient beings to serve as food? Furthermore, if bhikṣus do not wear silks, cotton, or fine fabrics from the East, nor those produced in this land...

"Boots, leather shoes, furs, wool, milk, curd, and clarified butter—thus, a bhikṣu who has attained true liberation from the world repays his karmic debts from past lives and no longer wanders within the three realms. Why is this?
Because by using their physical parts, they become conditions for those beings; it is like a person whose feet do not leave the ground while eating the various grains grown in that soil.
"He must cause his body and mind, as well as the various parts of his body, [to serve all sentient beings]."
One whose mind is free from the two taints, who neither wears [the robes] nor eats [the food], I declare such a person to be truly liberated.
What I have spoken thus is called the teaching of the Buddha; what is not spoken thus is the teaching of Pāpīyān.
Ānanda, furthermore, if the minds of sentient beings within the six realms of this world do not harbor theft, they will not follow along with the continuity of birth and death.
When you cultivate samādhi, it is fundamentally for the purpose of emerging from worldly toil; if the thieving mind is not eliminated, one cannot emerge from the dust of the world.

Even if you possess great wisdom and meditative concentration manifests before you, if you do not sever the thieving mind, you will inevitably fall into the paths of the heterodox, becoming a superior-grade spirit or a medium-grade one.
Possessed by demons of the lower grade and various malevolent spirits, these wicked people and their hordes of followers each claim for themselves that they have attained the Unsurpassed Way.
After my parinirvāṇa, during the period of the Final Dharma, such demonic and perverse beings will flourish in the world;

hiding their deceit and fraudulence while claiming to be "Good Knowledge-holders" (Kalyāṇamitra), they each assert that they have attained the Dharmas of a Superior Person (Āryadharma) and thereby delude and mislead others.
Those without wisdom fear that their minds will be lost; wherever they pass, their households fall into ruin.
My teaching is for bhikṣus to wander from region to region begging for food, so that they may abandon greed and achieve the path to Bodhi.

These bhikṣus do not cook for themselves, but rely on the remnants of others' meals as they journey through the three realms, demonstrating a single coming and going, after which there is no returning. How can these thieves falsely claim to be my followers?
Those who trade in clothing and profit from the Tathāgata, performing all manner of such deeds while claiming it is the Buddha-dharma,

yet instead revile bhikṣus who have left the household life and observed the precepts for the sake of the Hīnayāna path— thereby misleading immeasurable sentient beings and causing them to fall into the Avīci Hell—
if, after my parinirvāṇa, there should be bhikṣus who resolve their minds to cultivate samādhi and [pay homage] before an image of the Tathāgata...
If in a previous life one lit a lamp, burned a finger joint, or heated a single incense stick upon one's body, I say that such a person has at once repaid their karmic debts from beginningless time;
they shall long enjoy the world and forever be liberated from all outflows (*āsrava*).

Although they have not yet clearly seen the path to unsurpassed enlightenment, their mind is already resolved regarding the Dharma. If one does not perform such acts of self-sacrifice, [one cannot attain this].

Even if subtle causes were to result in the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), one would inevitably be reborn as a human to repay past debts; this is no different from my own experience with the horse-barley, which was exactly the same.

Your teaching that people of the world should first cultivate *samādhi* and only then sever the taking of what is not given is called the third definitive, pure, and clear instruction of the Tathāgata and the Buddhas of the past. Therefore, Ānanda, if you do not sever the taking of what is not given while practicing dhyāna...

One who is settled in concentration is like a person who enters the water to fill a leaking cup with the intent of making it full; even if they pass through kalpas as numerous as dust motes, it will never be restored.

If a bhikṣu does not store so much as a fraction of what remains from his robes and bowl, gives away the remnants of his alms-food to hungry sentient beings, joins his palms in reverence toward the assembly at a great gathering, and treats those who strike or revile him as if they were praising him—[he shall surely... make it so that...

Abandoning both body and mind, sharing one’s own flesh, bones, and blood with all sentient beings, and not misinterpreting the Tathāgata’s teachings of provisional meaning as definitive for oneself so as to delude beginners—such a person is sealed by the Buddha. They have attained true samādhi;
what I have thus described is called the Buddha’s teaching, and what is contrary to this is the teaching of Pāpīyān.

Ānanda, although the beings of the six realms in worlds such as these may have already perfected their physical and mental conduct by being free from the three acts of killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct, if they engage in great falsehood, their *samādhi* will not attain purity. They become demons of craving and views, losing the seed of the Tathāgata.

This refers to those who claim to have attained what they have not attained, or say they have realized what they have not realized, or who seek to be the most honored, supreme, and foremost in the world.
To say to another, "I have now attained the fruit of a Srotāpanna, a Sakṛdāgāmin, an Anāgāmin, the path of an Arhat,
or the vehicle of a Pratyekabuddha," or to seek the prostrations and offerings of Bodhisattvas at the stages prior to the ten bhūmis,
is a pāyattika that extinguishes the seed of the Buddha; it is like a person cutting down a tāla tree with a sword.
The Buddha has prophesied that such persons have forever destroyed their roots of goodness and lack further wisdom or insight;

they sink into the sea of the three sufferings and shall not attain samādhi. After my parinirvāṇa, I shall command the bodhisattvas and arhats to manifest bodies within that age of the final dharma, assuming various forms to deliver those wandering in saṃsāra—whether appearing as śramaṇas, laypeople, householders, kings, or officials.

Whether with young men or women, even down to prostitutes, widows, thieves, butchers, or merchants, he associates with them and praises the Buddha Vehicle, causing their bodies and minds to enter samādhi.
Yet, until his death, he never says of himself, "I am a true Bodhisattva" or "I am a true Arhat.
He does not leak the secret causes of the Buddhas nor speak lightly of those who have not yet studied, except when, at the end of life, he has something to entrust to them in secret.

"How is it that this person deludes sentient beings and commits a great falsehood? You have taught the people of the world to cultivate samādhi, yet afterwards they continue to sever all great falsehoods;
this is called the fourth definitive, pure, and clear instruction of the Tathāgata and the World-Honored Buddhas of the past.
Therefore, Ānanda, if one does not eliminate such great falsehoods, it is like carving a human figure out of excrement."

To take the form of sandalwood while seeking its fragrance is impossible. I teach my bhikṣus that within the field of the straightforward mind, even amidst all actions during the four modes of deportment, there is not even the slightest pretense; how then could they claim to have attained the dharmas of a superior man?
It is like a destitute person who falsely calls himself an emperor, only to bring about his own execution—how much more so for one who would falsely usurp the title of Dharma King!
If the ground is not true, the fruit will be circuitous; seeking the Buddha’s Bodhi is like a man trying to bite his own navel—who can achieve it?
If bhikṣus have minds as straight as bowstrings, being entirely truthful and entering samādhi, they will forever be free from demonic affairs.
I certify that such people shall achieve the unsurpassed awakening of a bodhisattva. What I have spoken is called the Buddha’s teaching.
To speak otherwise than this is the speech of Pāpīyān.
The treatise states: Māra is fully termed *māra*; this is translated as "the slayer" (*ghātaka*), and also as "one who obstructs the three definitive meanings of practice.
When the mind is gathered as precept and the characteristics of the precepts are complete, then concentration and wisdom increase like horses under a bridle.
The instruction says: "If the mind wanders and scatters, you must immediately gather it back and dwell in the present mindfulness.

Since there is only mind and no external objects, one should draw near to and accord with Prajñā; this requires neither strenuous effort nor painful struggle, but merely applying the mind with utmost sincerity and compassion.
The four types of karmic nature—killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, and lying—are thieves that slay the life-force of wisdom."
The World-Honored One has severed the mountains that obstruct the Right Path as a definitive teaching for pure clarity;

yet to advance toward the three poisons before [this realization] is something the Great Compassionate Father never forgets even in his most casual moments, providing intricate instructions for the sake of novice Bodhisattvas—this is what those who should know their debt of gratitude ought to understand.
Among the monks of the Five Indias was one named Dharmadatta, a master possessed of eloquence and wisdom.
The Venerable Siṃha, knowing that [Bodhidharma] had attained realization, proclaimed it before the assembly;

however, when it came to the transmission of the Dharma and the succession to the Patriarchate, he designated Vasubandhu as the successor. Bodhidharma harbored deep resentment in his heart and said, "The Venerable One surely knows me profoundly;
yet, as for the position of the Patriarchal Successor, he does not grant it to me—how can there be any explanation for this? After a long time...
One day, while walking alone across a stream, he saw a woman washing her feet and her legs were exposed. Dharmada thought to himself, "How exceptionally white and fair these shanks are!
Suddenly, Venerable Siṃha appeared at his side and said, "Whenever you think of me, I do not bestow the position of the Patriarch upon you.
Can the mind of this very day be granted the position of the Patriarch? Dharmada—
He gathered his mindfulness, prostrated at [the Buddha’s] feet, and sought compassion, saying: "Is such a subtle transgression so difficult to overcome? [The commentator] supplements:
"Since the mind is not lustful, the body naturally commits no offense; how could it be merely a matter of restraining the body alone?

In various sutras, the five kinds of meat are defined as those that have not been seen, heard, or suspected [to have been killed for oneself], as well as meat left by birds or that which died of itself; these are now referred to as the five pure meats.
This is likely because it differs from what is taught in other sutras, as it concerns those transformed by the Tathāgata.

Wujin said: "Indeed, burning one's body or fingers is difficult for others to practice; yet if one practices with faith, the body is not to be begrudged. If one preserves the body, past causes remain obscured;
if one forgets the body, there is no basis for karmic retribution. Thus, one is forever liberated from all outflows (*āsrava*). [The text ends with] "Shi."
Regarding the "navel" (*qi*): the *Zuo Zhuan* states, "If you do not plan early, the successor will bite his navel;
will it be too late to plan then? Du Yu’s commentary explains: "Biting the navel of the belly is a metaphor for something that cannot be reached. In the *Vinaya*, this is translated as *lǜ*;
*pāpīyas* is correctly rendered as "the evil one," whereas *pāpīyan* is a corruption.
