Fāng (the lower part is read as fǔ or yù; second tone). Yuán (yīn yuán). Dài (yīn dài). Tà (tú há qiè). Chuì (chǐ bǐng qiè). Huǐn (gǔ quǎn qiè). Bì (yīn [biàn]). Chuí (yīn zhǔ). Shì (yīn shì). Huàn (yīn huǎn). Xī (yīn xī). Niè (wǔ jié qiè).

The Combined Commentary on the Śūraṃgama Sūtra: The Ultimate Meaning of the Secret Cause for Cultivating and Realizing the Myriad Practices of All Bodhisattvas, Based on the Great Buddha-Uṣṇīṣa Tathāgata. Volume Seven.
"Ānanda, regarding your question on the gathering of the mind, I shall first explain the wondrous gate of practice for entering samādhi and seeking bodhi."
The path of a bodhisattva must first maintain these four kinds of discipline as clearly as ice and frost;
then, one cannot give rise to any branches or leaves of mental activity, nor can the three [actions] of mind or the four [actions] of body arise, for there would be no cause for them.

Ānanda, if these four matters are not lost, the mind will not even take as its object form, sound, smell, taste, or touch; how then could any demonic affairs arise? Even if there were residual habits from the past...
If one who cannot extinguish your teachings recites with single-minded devotion this unsurpassed divine mantra of my Buddha-Uṣṇīṣa-Vijaya-Mahā-Satvata-Patara,
this heart-mantra spoken by the Tathāgata from his Unseen Crown (Anavalokitamūrdha) when he sat upon a precious lotus flower,
emitting radiance from his crown as the Unconditioned Mind-Buddha— then consider that in your past lives, you and Mātangi...
The karmic conditions of countless eons and the habitual tendencies of affection are not the result of a single lifetime or a single kalpa.

When I proclaimed that those with hearts of love could forever be liberated and become arhats, even she—a courtesan—was without the intent to practice, yet she was secretly aided by my spiritual power and swiftly realized the stage of no-more-learning (aśaikṣa).
How much more so for you, the śrāvakas assembled here, who seek the Supreme Vehicle and are determined to attain Buddhahood!
For example, if one scatters dust while facing a favorable wind, what difficulty or danger could there be?

Likewise, if anyone in the final age wishes to sit at the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa), they must first uphold the pure prohibitions of a bhikṣu; they must certainly select a preceptor who is foremost among śramaṇas and whose precepts are pure.
If they do not encounter a truly pure monk, their observance of the Vinaya discipline will surely not be accomplished.
After the precepts have been completed, don new, clean robes, burn incense, and dwell in seclusion reciting this divine mantra spoken by the Mind-Buddha one hundred and eight times.

Thereafter, establish the boundary and set up the *maṇḍala*, seeking that the Unsurpassed Tathāgatas currently residing in the lands of the ten directions will emit the light of great compassion and descend to anoint your crown. Ānanda, in this way, one shall be pure in the final age.
Ānanda, if a bhikṣu or a bhikṣuṇī, or a lay donor, extinguishes the mind of greed and lust, upholds the pure precepts of the Buddha,

and within the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa) makes the vow of a bodhisattva, entering and leaving for ablutions and practicing the path during the six periods of the day and night without sleep for twenty-one days,
I shall manifest my own body before that person, stroke their head to comfort them, and cause them to attain awakening.
He addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, having received the unsurpassed compassionate instruction of the Tathāgata, my mind has already been awakened.

I know for myself that I have cultivated and realized the path of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*). Now, as I establish a site of practice (*bodhimaṇḍa*) during the age of the final dharma, how should I perform the ritual of delimiting the boundary (*sīmābandha*) in accordance with the pure rules of the Buddha, the World-Honored One?"

The Buddha told Ānanda: "If people in the final age wish to establish a site for the Way, they should first seek a powerful white ox from the Snowy Mountains that eats the lush, fatty fragrant herbs of those mountains.
This ox drinks only the pure water of the Snowy Mountains; its dung is fine and subtle.
One may take this dung and mix it with sandalwood to plaster the ground. If it is not from the Snowy Mountains, the ox's dung will be foul and impure."
It is not fit to be smeared upon the ground.
The treatise states: *Mahā-satvata-pratara*, which is translated as "White Parasol" (*Sitātapatra*).

This scripture is the sovereign crest-ornament of dharmas and mantras, possessing the meaning of providing protection by covering the crown of the head. Furthermore, that which is spoken by the mind, the Buddha, and the manifestation cannot be [otherwise].
"It is attained through contemplation. He asked: "The expedient means for extinguishing dust and unifying with awakening are not uniform;

yet the ritual procedures of the *dharmapūjā* (*daochang*) are invariably complex and minute. Is this not essentially no different from toil and labor? Could it be that the World-Honored One has forgotten his previous words about having nothing to rely upon?
He replied: "The World-Honored One’s intention was truly one of profound compassion. It is precisely because of this true compassion that he regards [beings as his own children]."
Because sentient beings are without partiality, being regarded as one's only child, and because of his profound compassion, whenever he preaches the Dharma,

he invariably uses wisdom to extensively gather those of diverse faculties and does not abandon any sentient being. Thus, while the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā* opens by expounding the path of the dharma of emptiness,
it subsequently compares the merit of various deeds to demonstrate the superiority [of this path]— showing the dharma of emptiness while also addressing merit— is this not so?
To prevent Bodhisattvas who are attached to merit from developing doubt and aversion toward the meaning of emptiness, this is the principle for extensively gathering those of diverse faculties.
For example, when the great ocean is drunk by mosquitoes, gadflies, and asuras, they all become fully satiated;
yet though the World-Honored One has compassion for them, those whose minds have attained faith and realization lack the power of self-mastery, even if their understanding is clear.

Because he was still being overcome and distressed by the latent tendencies of past sexual habits, the Buddha spoke to him in esoteric language, intending to repel and sever them through inconceivable power.
Kumārajīva of the Yao Qin dynasty was a great Bodhisattva who propagated the *Sūtra on the Four Reliances*.
Once, when he sought a wife, [the Buddha] said: "There are two small children climbing upon my shoulders," which was intended as a protective barrier.
Thereupon Yao Xing summoned palace women and presented them to him; from a single union, two sons were born.

If Kumārajīva had been made to hear this *dhāraṇī* and have it held and recited with precision, would he then have allowed the fragrance of his knowledge and vision of liberation to be eclipsed by the five-colored filth?
He established a *bodhimaṇḍa*, embodying the spirit of sublime solemnity within ritual and dharma.
Whether walking, standing, sitting, or reclining, or in seeing, hearing, speaking, or remaining silent, all these are conditions for purity;
this is the meaning of being free from thirst and craving. When one suffers from thirst and craving, the mind becomes dull and inferior.

With a mind that is dull and inferior due to thirst and craving, when confronted with the realms of coarse sounds and forms, how could one avoid becoming deluded, intoxicated, and overturned? The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* says: "One should [respond] with the Dharma..."
One should irrigate one's own mind with water; one should support one's own mind with wholesome dharmas;
and one should purify one's own mind through objects of experience—this is for the purpose of providing an antidote to this [affliction]. Question:

How is it known that even those who have already attained faith and realization are still broken and distressed by the latent tendencies of past sexual habits? Answer: It is known by means of the phenomena and events demonstrated by the World-Honored One.

Regarding the manifestation of the intended meaning, know that his words first take up the great powerful white ox of the Snowy Mountains, which feeds on the rich, fragrant herbs of those mountains and drinks only the pure water of the Snowy Mountains—this "mountain soil" refers to the Snowy Mountains, which signify vast faith.
Having such vast faith, one is able to accord with it; yet there remains the affliction of feverish distress.
It is simply that residual habits have not yet been exhausted. Furthermore, it is said that their excrement is so subtle that it can be gathered and mixed with sandalwood to plaster the ground;
this "excrement" refers to the subtle remnants of residual habits. Although these are but the dregs of residual habits, they are nonetheless the final vestiges of compliant faith.
Sandalwood by nature removes feverish affliction; it is intended to be used as... [the text continues].
The mantra-power of *dāna* (generosity) sweeps away the excrement of the afflictions of desire and purifies the powerful faculty of faith (*śraddhendriya*).
Question: How is it verified that this does not universally purify the obstacles of desire for all sentient beings?
Answer: All sentient beings have formed their very nature through greed and desire; it is not merely an obstacle of desire. Therefore it is said: "If it were not for the Snowy Mountains..."

The meaning is this: cow dung that is foul-smelling and unfit for smearing the ground is called "subtle" when it is the dung of a large, white bull, whereas the dung of a bull that is not large and white is described as "foul-smelling. This is the intended sense.
Apart from the level plain, one should dig down five feet into the earth and take the yellow soil from below;
this is mixed with sandalwood, agallochum, *suhak*, frankincense, saffron, resin, *candana* wood, *ling-lang*, sweet spikenard, and *keshetara* incense.
These ten ingredients are finely ground into powder and blended with the soil to form a paste, which is then used to smear the site of the ritual ground.

The Commentary says: As for the previous statement that the cow is foul-smelling and unfit for smearing the ground, this refers to one who has not yet developed the great power of the faculty of faith (*śraddhendriya*).
If the faculty of faith has not yet arisen, one should cause it to arise. "Level plain" refers to a vast and impartial mind.

Once this mind is established, one should cultivate the fivefold dharma-body (*pañcāṅga-dharmakāya*) consisting of precept, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation.

Because it is perfumed by these fragrances, it is said that one takes yellow earth and mixes it with *candana*, agallochum, *sūhaka*, *guggulu*, *uragasāra*, *śrīveṣṭaka*, *sāla*, *jātī*, *kālānusārya*, and *kakkolaka*.
Previously, it was only mentioned that *candana* was mixed with the dung of a white ox; this was merely to clear away the feverish afflictions of residual habits. Now, however—
If one possesses a vast and impartial mind, one shall gather all merits, just as *śrīveṣṭaka* incense can remove foul odors from the body and eliminate sores;
likewise, the fragrance of the precepts removes unwholesome states from the body, attaining liberation free from the blemish of sores.
Furthermore, regarding the color of these precepts, one adds the fragrance of diligence, which is like *tagara* incense, capable of awakening those who are in a swoon.
While sleeping, this incense of diligence leaves behind the hindrance of drowsiness; even in sleep, one remains constantly awake.
Like *guggulu* (frankincense), it can alleviate pain and stabilize the power of concentration (*samādhi*), enabling one to endure all afflictions without harboring a desire for retaliation.

Furthermore, this incense of patience is like *sahakāra* (sandalwood or storax), which destroys malevolent spirits, eliminates evil influences, and communicates with the divine; so too does this patience.
Incense serves to ward off all demonic activities. For example, *ling-zheng* (nagakesara) can arrest seminal essence and clarify the eyes;
likewise, "wisdom-incense" (*hui-xiang*) can store up the essence of wisdom and give rise to clear vision.

Furthermore, there is the application of incense such as *candana* (sandalwood), which may be red, black, or white; the superior sandalwood—what is called the "one-zhu" variety—is said to be fragrant for forty li.
This is because this gift of fragrance—whether consisting of internal wealth, external wealth, or the Dharma—is fully endowed with the power of giving and is able to reach far away.
Just as *gandhaka* (sweet flag) can harmonize various fragrances, liberation (*vimukti*) can harmonize all merits;
furthermore, to this liberation, one adds the fragrance of the Dharma (*dharmagandha*), such as *uragasāra-candana* (saffron).
This incense of the Dharma removes poison and expels evil, extinguishing darkness and shattering attachments;

like *kakkola* (clove) incense, it may be blended with other fragrances to make the body fragrant, yet the knowledge and vision of liberation can, through all skillful means, universally enter all realms.
Upon this knowledge and vision of liberation, one further adds the fragrance of Bodhi, which is like *agaru* (aloewood).
It can sink to the bottom of the water, yet this power of the Bodhi-fragrance reaches the very depths of the ocean of Dharma;
among blended fragrances, it is called "Liberation. Speaking of it in terms of pine fragrance, it is called "Liberation-Knowledge-and-Vision" among all fragrances that can be entered.
This is similar to what is said in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*: "O Son of the Buddha, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva practices giving..."
When applying scented ointments, one should dedicate all roots of goodness in this way:
namely, may all sentient beings be universally perfumed by the fragrance of giving and be able to relinquish all that they possess;

may all sentient beings be universally perfumed by the fragrance of ethical discipline and attain the ultimate pure precepts of the Tathāgata; may all sentient beings be universally perfumed by the fragrance of patience and be free from...
May all beings with minds inclined toward all manner of perilous harm be universally perfumed by the incense of diligence, always donning the armor of Mahāyāna diligence;
may all beings be universally perfumed by the incense of meditative concentration, dwelling securely in the samādhi of the presence of all Buddhas;
may all beings be universally perfumed by the incense of wisdom, attaining the realization of the Unsurpassed in a single thought-moment.
O King of Wisdom, may all sentient beings be universally suffused with the fragrance of the Dharma, attaining fearlessness in the unsurpassed Dharma.
May all sentient beings be universally suffused with the fragrance of virtue, accomplishing all great merits and wisdom.
May all sentient beings be universally suffused with the fragrance of Bodhi, attaining the ten powers of a Buddha and reaching the further shore. May all...

When all sentient beings are perfumed by the wondrous fragrance of pure, white dharmas and forever extinguish all unwholesome dharmas, this is the dedication of roots of goodness when a bodhisattva bestows scented ointments. As stated in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*:
"The Bodhisattva Sarvasattvapriyadarśana made offerings to the Buddha Candrasūryavimalaprabhāsa; when the Buddha arose from samādhi, the Bodhisattva reflected to himself:"
He said, "Although I may provide offerings to the Buddha through supernatural powers, it is not as good as making offerings with my own body.
Thereupon, he consumed various incenses—*candana*, *kunduruka*, *turuṣka*, *bhallātaka*, and *agaru*—as well as resinous incense.
He also drank the fragrant oils of the *campaka* flower for twelve hundred years. Having done so, he anointed his body with these fragrant oils before the Sun and Moon Pure Radiance [Buddha].
Before the Buddha, he wrapped his body in celestial precious garments and poured over it various fragrant oils;
by means of his supernormal powers and vows, the radiance of his own body naturally shone throughout worlds as numerous as the sands of eighty billion Ganges Rivers.

Tiantai’s commentary states: He was clothed in the fragrance of the precepts, meditative concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation, and anointed with the oil of the *cintāmaṇi* (wish-fulfilling jewel).

Question: In the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, the five kinds of incense are used as metaphors for precepts, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation; I dare not offer further words on that. However, regarding the use of ten kinds of incense, is there a specific intent behind it? Answer: This sutra intends to cause ordinary beings to realize the truth. Therefore, it necessarily adds [preliminary stages] to the Dharma, such as adding the three gradual steps before the ten levels of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*), and [the preparatory stages] before the ten grounds (*daśa-bhūmi*). Thus, it is here that the ten kinds of incense are employed. Furthermore, the five incenses represent the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), while the five fragrant substances represent the five roots of goodness (*pañca-kuśala-mūla*). Because these two groups of five are combined, they constitute the ten kinds of incense. Moreover, the ten kinds of incense represent the ten perfections (*daśa-pāramitā*). The ten perfections are the causes for attaining Buddhahood, and the ten incenses are the causes for attaining the ten perfections. Because the ten perfections are the causes for attaining Buddhahood, the ten incenses are the causes for attaining the ten perfections. Consequently, the ten incenses are the causes for attaining Buddhahood. For this reason, the ten kinds of incense are used as metaphors. Furthermore, the ten kinds of incense represent the ten stages of the Bodhisattva path. The ten stages of the Bodhisattva path are the causes for attaining Buddhahood, and the ten incenses are the causes for attaining the ten stages of the Bodhisattva path. Because the ten stages of the Bodhisattva path are the causes for attaining Buddhahood, the ten incenses are the causes for attaining the ten stages of the Bodhisattva path. Consequently, the ten incenses are the causes for attaining Buddhahood. For this reason, the ten kinds of incense are used as metaphors. Furthermore, the ten kinds of incense represent the ten powers (*daśa-bala*) of the Tathāgata. The ten powers of the Tathāgata are the fruit of attaining Buddhahood, and the ten incenses are the fruit of attaining the ten powers of the Tathāgata. Because the ten powers of the Tathāgata are the fruit of attaining Buddhahood, the ten incenses are the fruit of attaining the ten powers of the Tathāgata. Consequently, the ten incenses are the fruit of attaining Buddhahood. For this reason, the ten kinds of incense are used as metaphors. Furthermore, the ten kinds of incense represent the ten stages of the Buddha’s ground (*daśa-buddha-bhūmi*). The ten stages of the Buddha’s ground are the ultimate fruit of attaining Buddhahood, and the ten incenses are the ultimate fruit of attaining the ten stages of the Buddha’s ground. Because the ten stages of the Buddha’s ground are the ultimate fruit of attaining Buddhahood, the ten incenses are the ultimate fruit of attaining the ten stages of the Buddha’s ground. Consequently, the ten incenses are the ultimate fruit of attaining Buddhahood. For this reason, the ten kinds of incense are used as metaphors. Furthermore, the ten kinds of incense represent the ten aspects of the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*). The ten aspects of the Dharma-body are the essence of attaining Buddhahood, and the ten incenses are the essence of attaining the ten aspects of the Dharma-body. Because the ten aspects of the Dharma-body are the essence of attaining Buddhahood, the ten incenses are the essence of attaining the ten aspects of the Dharma-body. Consequently, the ten incenses are the essence of attaining Buddhahood. For this reason, the ten kinds of incense are used as metaphors. Furthermore, the ten kinds of incense represent the ten virtues of the Tathāgata. The ten virtues of the Tathāgata are the merit of attaining Buddhahood, and the ten incenses are the merit of attaining the ten virtues of the Tathāgata. Because the ten virtues of the Tathāgata are the merit of attaining Buddhahood, the ten incenses are the merit of attaining the ten virtues of the Tathāgata. Consequently, the ten incenses are the merit of attaining Buddhahood. For this reason, the ten kinds of incense are used as metaphors. Furthermore, the ten kinds of incense represent the ten realms of the Buddha’s wisdom. The ten realms of the Buddha’s wisdom are the function of attaining Buddhahood, and the ten incenses are the function of attaining the ten realms of the Buddha’s wisdom. Because the ten realms of the Buddha’s wisdom are the function of attaining Buddhahood, the ten incenses are the function of attaining the ten realms of the Buddha’s wisdom. Consequently, the ten incenses are the function of attaining Buddhahood. For this reason, the ten kinds of incense are used as metaphors. Furthermore, the ten kinds of incense represent the ten directions of the Buddha’s light. The ten directions of the Buddha’s light are the manifestation of attaining Buddhahood, and the ten incenses are the manifestation of attaining the ten directions of the Buddha’s light. Because the ten directions of the Buddha’s light are the manifestation of attaining Buddhahood, the ten incenses are the manifestation of attaining the ten directions of the Buddha’s light. Consequently, the ten incenses are the manifestation of attaining Buddhahood. For this reason, the ten kinds of incense are used as metaphors. Furthermore, the ten kinds of incense represent the ten types of sentient beings. The ten types of sentient beings are the objects of attaining Buddhahood, and the ten incenses are the objects of attaining the ten types of sentient beings. Because the ten types of sentient beings are the objects of attaining Buddhahood, the ten incenses are the objects of attaining the ten types of sentient beings. Consequently, the ten incenses are the objects of attaining Buddhahood. For this reason, the ten kinds of incense are used as metaphors. Furthermore, the ten kinds of incense represent the ten stages of the Bodhisattva’s practice. The ten stages of the Bodhisattva’s practice are the process of attaining Buddhahood, and the ten incenses are the process of attaining the ten stages of the Bodhisattva’s practice. Because the ten stages of the Bodhisattva’s practice are the process of attaining Buddhahood, the ten incenses are the process of attaining the ten stages of the Bodhisattva’s practice. Consequently, the ten incenses are the process of attaining Buddhahood. For this reason, the ten kinds of incense are used as metaphors. Furthermore, the ten kinds of incense represent the ten paramitas of the Bodhisattva. The ten paramitas of the Bodhisattva are the means of attaining Buddhahood, and the ten incenses are the means of attaining the ten paramitas of the Bodhisattva. Because the ten paramitas of the Bodhisattva are the means of attaining Buddhahood, the ten incenses are the means of attaining the ten paramitas of the Bodhisattva. Consequently, the ten incenses are the means of attaining Buddhahood. For this reason, the ten kinds of incense are used as metaphors. Furthermore, the ten kinds of incense represent the ten stages of the Buddha’s transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*). The ten stages of the Buddha’s transformation body are the manifestations of attaining Buddhahood, and the ten incenses are the manifestations of attaining the ten stages of the Buddha’s transformation body. Because the ten stages of the Buddha’s transformation body are the manifestations of attaining Buddhahood, the ten incenses are the manifestations of attaining the ten stages of the Buddha’s transformation body. Consequently, the ten incenses are the manifestations of attaining Buddhahood. For this reason, the ten kinds of incense are used as metaphors. Furthermore, the ten kinds of incense represent the ten stages of the Bodhisattva’s vows. The ten stages of the Bodhisattva’s vows are the aspiration for attaining Buddhahood, and the ten incenses are the aspiration for attaining the ten stages of the Bodhisattva’s vows. Because the ten stages of the Bodhisattva’s vows are the aspiration for attaining Buddhahood, the ten incenses are the aspiration for attaining the ten stages of the Bodhisattva’s vows. Consequently, the ten incenses are the aspiration for attaining Buddhahood. For this reason, the ten kinds of incense are used as metaphors. Furthermore, the ten kinds of incense represent the ten stages of the Bodhisattva’s merit. The ten stages of the Bodhisattva’s merit are the accumulation for attaining Buddhahood, and the ten incenses are the accumulation for attaining the ten stages of the Bodhisattva’s merit. Because the ten stages of the Bodhisattva’s merit are the accumulation for attaining Buddhahood,
Adding the four kinds of preparatory practices, prior to the stage of Sublime Awakening (Miao-jue), one establishes the Vajra-Dry Wisdom Ground (Vajra-śuṣka-prajñā-bhūmi).
A square altar sixteen feet in circumference is made with eight corners; at the center of the altar, place a lotus flower fashioned from gold, silver, copper, or wood.
Within the flower, set a bowl; within the bowl, first fill it with dew collected during the eighth month, and upon the water, place whatever flowers and leaves are available.
Take eight circular mirrors and place them each in its respective direction surrounding the flower bowl;

outside the mirrors, establish sixteen lotus flowers and sixteen incense burners, interspersed with flowers and arranged as an adornment. Burn only aloeswood incense in the burners so that the flames are not visible.
Take white cow’s milk and place it in sixteen vessels; prepare milk pancakes along with various granulated sugar cakes, oil cakes, and milk porridge.
Sūhaka resin, honey, ginger, pure ghee, and pure honey each surround the lotus flower sixteen times on the outside;
these are offered outside the flower to the Buddhas and the great Bodhisattvas.
The Commentary states: "The World-Honored One speaks here extensively of 'sixteen dharmas,' which refers to the Eightfold Noble Path and the eightfold wrong path."
The power of mantras is considered correct, while sexual desire is considered deviant. As for the "octagonal altar," the altar symbolizes the Eightfold Noble Path;

its square and circular dimensions of one zhang and six chi represent the eight paths of deviation. The *Vimalakīrti Sūtra* states: "If one can practice through what is not the path, this is called penetrating the Buddha-way.
This is because it is accomplished through correct faith; therefore, it is said that "the metal [altar] represents correct faith."

When accomplishment is attained, right mindfulness is pure; therefore it is said to be "silver. When right mindfulness is pure, one is then able to unite with awakening; therefore it is said to be "copper.
When one unites with awakening, the power of the roots of wholesome compassion is complete; therefore it is said to be "wood.
When the roots of wholesome compassion are complete, one is unstained by the mud of desire; therefore it is said to be a "lotus flower. Being unstained by the mud of desire is—
Because one can peacefully partake of the flavor of the joy of the Dharma and the delight of dhyāna, it is said that the bowl contains the flavor of the joy of the Dharma and the delight of dhyāna;

because one thereby attains the knowledge of the path leading to all destinations, it is said that one first fills [the bowl] with dew collected during the eighth month, placing whatever flowers and leaves are available within the water, whereby they are moistened and brought to bloom according to their respective natures. Thus, in every place...
Because it clearly understands and is free from both the correct and the deviant, it is called "taking up.

Eight circular mirrors are placed, each in its respective direction, surrounding the flower bowl to serve as vessels for containing the joy of the Dharma and the delight of dhyāna. Interspersed between them are incense burners for the fragrance of precepts, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation;
therefore, it is said that outside the mirrors, sixteen lotus flowers and sixteen incense burners are established in alternation.

Regarding the arrangement of flowers and the setting out of incense burners to adorn this *maṇḍala*: because one first employs the knowledge and vision of liberation (*vimukti-jñāna-darśana*), it is said that one should exclusively burn aloeswood (*agaru*) so as not to see the fire. In this way, all demonic activities (*mārakarma*) are warded off and severed, for there is meditative concentration (*samādhi*).

Furthermore, regarding *sugandha* (sandalwood resin), the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states: "From milk comes curd; from curd, fresh butter (*navanīta*) is produced. Thus, [the sequence of refinement is established].
The mention of "milk" and "pure ghee" refers to the progression from the coarse to the refined.

The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* further states that "stone honey treats heat, while black honey treats cold. The mention of "honey" and "pure honey" here indicates that pure honey removes feverish affliction, whereas black honey does not.
Fried cakes, oil cakes, milk porridge, and granulated sugar all possess the quality of providing nourishment.
Ginger has the significance of harmonizing various differences, dispersing impurities and evils, and thereby enabling the spiritual intelligence to manifest.
Whenever at mealtime or during the middle of the night, take half a *sheng* of honey and three *he* of clarified butter (*ghṛta*).
Before the altar, set up a small fire-pit separately, and using *turuṣka* incense, boil it to extract scented water with which to bathe the charcoal, kindling it until it blazes fiercely.
Heat this ghee and honey in a blazing furnace until the smoke has vanished, and offer it to the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.

Hang banners and flowers everywhere on the four exterior sides of the altar chamber. Within the four walls of the hall, arrange all the images of the Tathāgatas of the ten directions and their various Bodhisattvas;
specifically, you should display Vairocana, Śākyamuni, Maitreya, Akṣobhya, and Amitābha facing directly toward the front.
One should place various great transformed images of Avalokiteśvara, together with Vajragarbha, on the left and right;
furthermore, Śakra, Brahmā, Ucchuṣma, and Lambodara, along with the Cāmuṇḍīs, Vijayā, the Four Heavenly Kings, and Vināyaka, should be arranged on the left and right sides of the entrance.
Moreover, one should take eight mirrors and suspend them inverted in the air.
Place the mirror installed within the ritual mandala so that it faces directly toward the void, allowing its forms and reflections to interpenetrate one another in successive layers.
During the first seven days, prostrate with utmost sincerity to the Tathāgatas of the ten directions, the great Bodhisattvas, and those bearing the titles of Arhats.

Constantly recite mantras throughout the six periods of the day and night, circumambulating the mandala with a sincere heart to practice the Way. At all times, perform this practice one hundred or eight hundred times.
Throughout the second seven-day period, they should single-mindedly and exclusively resolve upon the Bodhisattva vow without interruption;

this is because within my Vinaya there is a prior teaching on the power of vows. During the third seven-day period, they should at all twelve times of the day single-mindedly maintain the Buddha’s *pāṭala* mantra.
By the seventh day, the Tathāgatas of the ten directions will simultaneously appear at the place where the mirrors reflect one another's light, and they shall receive the Buddhas' touch.
Atop the site of enlightenment, one cultivates samādhi, enabling those who practice and study in this final age to purify their bodies and minds until they are as clear and bright as lapis lazuli.
Ānanda, if among the preceptor who originally conferred the precepts upon this bhikṣu,
or among the ten bhikṣus in the assembly, even one is impure, then such a site of enlightenment will for the most part not be accomplished.

After twenty-one days, he sat upright in meditative seclusion for one hundred days; those of keen faculties attained the *śīrṣa-srotāpanna* (the "stream-enterer at the summit") without rising from their seats.
Even if their physical and mental bodies had not yet fully realized the holy fruit, they knew with certainty that their attainment of Buddhahood would be unerring.

You asked about the establishment of the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*); it is thus, Ānanda. Having prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying: "Since my own emergence..."
Relying on the Buddha’s compassionate love, I sought extensive learning; yet, because I had not yet realized the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), I was obstructed by the malevolent arts of that Brahmā.
Although my mind was clear, I lacked the power of freedom. Fortunately, I encountered Mañjuśrī, who enabled me to attain liberation.
Though I have received the secret power of the Tathāgata’s *Uṣṇīṣa* dhāraṇī, I have not yet heard it directly from you. I pray that, out of great compassion, you will proclaim it once more for me.
The Buddha spoke of compassion to save those practitioners in this assembly, as well as those in the future who remain within saṃsāra;

through the Buddha’s secret voice, their bodies and minds attained liberation. At that time, the entire great assembly in the gathering universally prostrated themselves, waiting expectantly to hear the Tathāgata’s secret verses.
At that time, from within the *uṣṇīṣa* on the crown of his head, the World-Honored One emitted a hundred jewel-lights;
from within these lights, thousand-petaled jewel lotuses emerged, upon which transformation-Buddhas sat amidst the precious flowers.

From their crowns issued ten streams of hundred-jewel radiance, each stream universally manifesting ten *gaṅgā*-sands of Vajrapāṇis, Secret-Knights of the Vajra, who bore mountains and held vajras, filling the entire realm of empty space.

The great assembly looked up in awe and affection, seeking the Buddha’s compassionate protection as they listened with single-minded devotion to the Tathāgata Emitting Light from His Invisible Crown as He proclaimed this divine mantra: *Namastathāgatāya arhate samyaksaṃbuddhāya.* (1)
