From this mantra-heart, all Buddhas of the ten directions are born; by means of this mantra-heart, the Tathāgatas of the ten directions have attained unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
By upholding this mantra-heart, the Tathāgatas of the ten directions subjugate all māras and restrain all heterodox paths.
By mounting this mantra-heart, the Tathāgatas of the ten directions sit upon jeweled lotuses and respond to lands as numerous as motes of dust.
When one brings forth this mantra-heart, it turns the Great Dharma Wheel within lands as numerous as motes of dust;

the Tathāgatas of the ten directions, by means of this mantra-heart, can bestow the prophecy of enlightenment by touching the crown of the head throughout the ten directions; even those whose own fruits are not yet perfected receive the Buddha’s prophecy throughout the ten directions;
and the Tathāgatas of the ten directions, relying upon this mantra-heart, can rescue and deliver beings from the various sufferings of the ten directions, namely those of the earth... [and so forth].

The suffering of hell-beings, hungry ghosts, and animals; the suffering of being blind, deaf, or mute; the suffering of encountering those one hates; the suffering of separation from those one loves; the suffering of not obtaining what one seeks;
and the intense burning of the five aggregates—all such great and small calamities shall be simultaneously liberated.

May the perils of bandits, armies, kings, prisons, wind, fire, and water, as well as hunger, thirst, and poverty, be dissolved upon mere thought. Thus do the Tathāgatas of the ten directions respond to this mantra.
The mind is able to serve spiritual friends throughout the ten directions during the four modes of conduct, making offerings as desired;

it is ranked among the great Dharma-princes within the assemblies of Tathāgatas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges. When the Tathāgatas of the ten directions practice this mantra-heart, they are able to gather and sustain their karmic affinates throughout the ten directions, ensuring that those of the Hīnayāna, upon hearing the secret treasury, do not give rise to alarm or fear. The Tathāgatas of the ten directions...
Come, recite this mantra-heart; you shall achieve unsurpassed enlightenment, sit beneath the Bodhi tree, and enter Great Nirvana.

The Tathāgatas of the ten directions transmit this mantra-heart so that, after their parinirvāṇa, the affairs of the Buddha-dharma may be maintained to ultimate completion and the precepts may be strictly purified, all becoming utterly stainless.
If I were to speak of this Buddha-Usnīṣa-Raśmi-Sañcaya-Pāṭala-Mantra from dawn until...
The sounds of these words resonate in succession, their syllables and phrases not overlapping even for a single moment;
though one were to recite them for kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, one could never reach the end. This mantra is also called the "Crown of the Tathāgata.

You who are still in training and have not yet exhausted saṃsāra, if you resolve with sincerity to attain arhatship, do not sit in the place of awakening without holding this mantra, lest your body and mind remain far removed from the various māras.
Such a thing is impossible.
The Treatise says: The World-Honored One’s intention was as follows: regarding the essential means for governing past habits, nothing compares to diligence.
Even while eating or sleeping, one does not forget to gather the fragrance of all merits and to ripen the honey of the wisdom of various skillful means. It is like [the scent of] many fragrances...
Regarding "concentrated," it refers to the excellence of ghee, milk, and curd; regarding "honey," the number five refers to the fivefold collection;
regarding "ghee," the number three refers to the threefold refinement. Therefore, it says: "At every mealtime, or if it is midnight, take half a *śoṇa* of honey and three *karṣas* of ghee.
*Turuṣka* incense is a red-colored fragrance, a coarse variety of *agaru* (aloe) or *candana* (sandalwood).
Maitreya said: "One should contemplate the light of the Dharma, for it can cure the three kinds of darkness.

Because one does not know all phenomena as they truly are, one gives rise to much doubt regarding the past, future, and present; it is likewise so with respect to the Buddha-dharma and other matters. He further said:
"When sleeping, one should place the feet one upon the other and form the perception of light; thus, by contemplating the light of the Dharma, one forms the perception of light."
The expedient means for treating the habitual tendencies of delusion are not true knowledge and vision.

Bathing with water infused with *turuṣka* incense and contemplating those embers—since all sublime practices do not naturally manifest in one's conduct—it is merely through the power of diligence established at the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*) that they are brought forth;
yet, it is by means of contemplation of the Dharma that one causes them to blaze fiercely.

When one perceives light as light, and the fragrance of merit has already accumulated and the wisdom of skillful means has matured, then the light of the Dharma and the perception of light are both abandoned;
thus it is said that "this ghee and honey are cast into the furnace and burned until the smoke is exhausted.
Ratnakūṭa said: At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Bodhisattva Anantamati.
The Mahāsattva said: "O Boundless Wisdom, there are gateways of the Dharma-light for Bodhisattvas that can give birth to skillful means regarding the principles of all phenomena;
they can also give birth to the seals of all phenomena and enter the gates of the seals of all phenomena, such that one may understand and enter into the dharmas that ought to be performed."

Through light, one is able to attain and expound it; by means of the light of the Dharma, one enters into the gateways of illumination regarding all phenomena (*dharmāloka-mukha*) in accordance with reality.
What are called the gateways of illumination regarding all phenomena that are able to give rise to skillful light? They are:
the teaching-gate of synonyms, the teaching-gate of secrets, the gate of synonymous matters, the gate of encompassing matters, and the various distinctions.

The Separate Gate asks: How is it that by attaining knowledge of this, one is able to give birth to the gateways of samādhi, the gateways of the principles of all dharma-gates, and enter into the single meaning? It is the radiance of all dharmas that can be understood accordingly:
it is the Reward Buddha Vairocana; it is the silence of Śākyamuni; it is the compassion of Maitreya; and it is Akṣobhya in the East.
Amitābha Buddha is the West; Avalokiteśvara is compassion; Vajragarbha is wisdom.
The East represents the agitation of delusion, which Vajragarbha destroys; the West represents the severity of suffering and affliction, which Avalokiteśvara rescues from.
As for Śākyamuni, he gazes serenely upon that very agitation.
Regarding Maitreya, he regards their suffering with compassion; he is the master of this site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*). The root of deluded habituation is the mechanism of lust;
it is this that is the source of suffering. Greed and desire are its essence. As for what is called Śakra, Brahmā, or Ucchuṣma:
Brahmā attained clear awakening through his mind of desire, yet without violating the dust of desire, he became identical to a Buddha. Alone.
Those who awaken through conditions—namely the Pratyekabuddhas and Śrāvakas—are called "liberated.
Ucchuṣma, however, is one who ascends to unsurpassed awakening by being able to contemplate the mind of lust and transform it into the fire of wisdom.

Otherwise, why would these two sages alone be mentioned in the sequence following the five Buddhas and two Bodhisattvas? Furthermore, the *Dhāraṇīsaṃgraha-sūtra* contains the ritual for the maṇḍala site, including the [monastery] grounds.
In the *Karuṇāpuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, there is the Rākṣasa Lendika, who possesses great supernatural power and great radiance;

"Lendika" is indeed the same as "Lampaka. In the *Susiddhikara-sūtra*, there is the wrathful Krodhakumāra, who must be this very same holy being. In the *Buddhoṣṇīṣa-vijaya-dhāraṇī-sūtra*, there is...
The *Vikūṭi-bodhisattva-anya-dhāraṇī-sūtra* and the *Sena-bhadra-bodhisattva-anya-vairocana-rddhi-vikurvaṇa-sūtra* state:
"On the right side is Vikūṭi, whose hand hangs down holding a rosary garland; he has three eyes and wears his hair in a topknot.
His honored form is pure white, and the color of his halo is incomparable. This is what is called Vikūṭi. This must indeed be him.
This holy one is Vināyaka, the deity who creates obstacles. He asked: "If one recites mantras with utmost sincerity, do the Buddhas of the ten directions truly appear?
He replied: "In the Jin dynasty, there was a monk named Tanyi who resided at Changgan Temple in Jiangning.
Diligently seeking śarīra relics, he placed a golden vase before it during a vegetarian feast and worshipped it day and night. Suddenly—"
A nocturnal light emerged from within a bottle, its five colors illuminating the entire chamber as if it were day.

He further redoubled his diligent practice to seek a response regarding the Auspicious Image (Śāriputra), bowing toward the ten directions from morning until evening and saying: "May images fill the void of space; I pray for an early manifestation.

On the eighth day of the second month of the nineteenth year of the Taiyuan era, a light suddenly burst forth at the Baima Monastery north of the city. When the monks went to see the image, they wished to lift it up.
When the image was about to descend, he said, "This is an image of King Aśoka; it is descending upon me," and as he lifted it up, it became cool and still.
Beside its side were inscribed characters which, when translated, read: "On such-and-such a month and day, made by the Lord Aśoka.
Because the inscription on the side testified with such sincerity, one could verify that the Tathāgata must have indeed placed his hand upon his head.
Ānanda, if in any world, according to whatever land, all sentient beings born in that land were to write this dhāraṇī on birch bark,
conch leaves, paper, silk, or white woolen cloth, and store it in a fragrant pouch; or if, because their minds are dull and they are unable to recite or memorize it,
they carry it upon their bodies or inscribe it within their homes— it should be known that for all such people, throughout the entirety of their lives, [all obstacles shall be eliminated].
It cannot be harmed by any poisons.
Ānanda, I now speak this mantra for you once more to protect the world, to attain great fearlessness, and to bring about the supramundane wisdom of all beings.
If, after my parinirvāṇa, there are sentient beings in the final age who can recite it themselves or teach it to others...
He recited: "One should know that for those who thus recite and uphold [this], fire cannot burn them, water cannot drown them, and neither great nor small poisons can harm them.
Likewise, even all evil spells of dragons, devas, ghosts, spirits, *piśācas*, and *mārās* cannot take hold;
their minds attain right concentration (*samādhi*), and all curses, sorcery, toxic drugs, and gold poisons [are neutralized]."
If the poisonous vapors of silver, mercury, plants, trees, insects, snakes, or any other myriad things enter this person’s mouth, they will turn into the flavor of ambrosia (*amṛta*).
Even malevolent stars, various ghosts and spirits, or those with cruel hearts and poisonous intent cannot give rise to evil toward such a person.
The *vināyakas* and all the evil kings of ghosts, along with their retinues, shall all acknowledge their profound kindness and constantly provide protection, Ānanda.

It should be known that this mantra is always attended by eighty-four thousand nayutas of *gaṅgā-nadī-vāluka* *koṭis* of the family of Vajragarbha-rāja Bodhisattvas; each of these is accompanied by a retinue of vajra-beings who serve them day and night.
Should there be sentient beings who, even with a distracted mind or a mind not in *samādhi*, remember and recite this [mantra] with their mouths...
The Vajra King constantly follows those sons of good family, let alone those who have resolved upon the Bodhicitta.
These Vajra Bodhisattvas, Kings of the Treasury, through their refined essence and subtle speed, swiftly awaken the divine consciousness of such a person.
At that moment, this person’s mind is able to remember eighty-four thousand Ganges-sands of kalpas, knowing them all-pervasively and attaining freedom from doubt. From the first...
For one kalpa or even until their final birth, they will not be born among yakṣas, rākṣasas, pūtanas, kaṭapūtanas,
kumbhāṇḍas, piśācas, and other such hungry ghosts— whether with form or without form,
with perception or without perception— in such evil states. This is so for these sons of good family who read, recite, copy, transcribe, or wear [this scripture].
If one conceals all manner of offerings throughout kalpa after kalpa, one will not be born into states of poverty, lowliness, or unpleasantness;

all the merits of the Tathāgatas of the ten directions shall be bestowed upon this person, by virtue of which they shall, for *asaṃkhyeya* eons as numerous as the sands of the Ganges—unspeakably unspeakable—constantly [attain... (Note: The source text appears to be a fragment from a Mahayana sutra concerning the merit of making offerings.
The final clause "常" likely connects to a subsequent verb such as "常受安樂" or "常不離佛," but based strictly on the provided text, the translation reflects the available syntax.)
Born together with all Buddhas in one place, their immeasurable merits—like clusters of akṣa fruits—are cultivated in the same location so that they never disperse.
Therefore, they can cause those who have broken the precepts to purify the roots of their discipline;
those who have not yet attained the precepts to attain them; those who lack diligence to attain diligence; and those who lack wisdom to attain wisdom.
Those who are pure will swiftly attain purity; those who do not observe the precepts of fasting and abstinence will naturally fulfill them.

Ānanda, when these sons of good family maintain this mantra, even if they have violated the prohibitive precepts prior to receiving them, all transgressions of the precepts—regardless of whether they are light or heavy—are extinguished at once after maintaining the mantra.
This remains true even if they have subsequently consumed alcohol or eaten the five pungent roots.
All Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, Vajras, celestial immortals, ghosts, and spirits are purified; they will not regard one as having committed a transgression even if one wears impure or tattered clothing.
Whether walking or standing still, one is entirely equal to those who are pure.

Even if one does not construct an altar or enter a *maṇḍala*, nor practices the Way, by reciting and upholding this mantra, one’s merit will be no different from that of entering an altar and practicing the Way.
Furthermore, if one has committed the grave offenses of the five heinous crimes of immediate retribution, or the four *pārājika* and eight *saṃghāvaśeṣa* transgressions of monks and nuns,
upon reciting this mantra, such heavy karma will be entirely eliminated— just as a fierce wind blows apart a heap of sand until not even a hair’s breadth remains.
Ānanda, if there are sentient beings who, from immeasurable and incalculable kalpas past, have possessed all manner of...

All heavy and light karmic obstacles accumulated from previous lives that have not yet been repented—if one can read, recite, copy, or wear this mantra upon one’s person, or place it in one’s dwelling, house, garden, or villa—then such accumulated karma will vanish like snow melting in hot water;
before long, all shall attain the realization of the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*). Furthermore, Ānanda, if there is a woman who has not yet borne a son...

If a woman who desires to conceive can recollect this mantra with a sincere heart, or can wear this *Sītātapatrā* (White Parasol) [dhāraṇī] upon her body, she will give birth to a son or daughter endowed with merit and wisdom. Those who seek long life shall immediately obtain long life;
those who seek the swift fulfillment of karmic rewards shall quickly attain such fulfillment, as shall their physical vitality and strength.
Thus, after the end of life, one will be reborn in accordance with one's vows in the lands of the ten directions;
one will certainly not be born in border regions or among the lowly, much less in mixed forms.

Ānanda, if in any land, prefecture, county, village, or hamlet there be famine, pestilence, or even the calamities of swords and weapons, bandits, strife, and all other such places of misfortune, one should write out this divine mantra.

At the four gates of Ancheng and at all the caityas, one should cause the sentient beings within that land to welcome this mantra with offerings, prostrating and paying respect with single-minded devotion.
Furthermore, one should have the people each wear it upon their persons or place it in the grounds of their respective dwellings; thus, all calamities and misfortunes will be entirely extinguished.

Ānanda, wherever there are sentient beings in any land who possess this mantra, the devas and nāgas will rejoice, wind and rain will follow their proper seasons, the five grains will be abundant, and the masses will live in peace and happiness.
Furthermore, it can suppress all malevolent stars and the strange portents that manifest in various directions;
calamities and obstacles shall not arise, and no one shall suffer untimely death. Shackles, fetters, and cangues shall not touch their bodies, day or night.

One shall sleep peacefully and never have evil dreams. Ānanda, in this Sahā world there are eighty-four thousand calamitous and malevolent stars, with twenty-eight great malevolent stars as their leaders.
Furthermore, there are eight great malevolent stars that act as their sovereigns;
they manifest in various forms when appearing in the world, capable of producing all manner of calamities and anomalies for sentient beings. This dharani [is able to quell them].
The entire ground shall be purified for twelve *yojanas*, becoming a consecrated boundary (*sīmābandha*) such that no evil portents or calamities can ever enter.
Therefore, the Tathāgata proclaims this mantra to protect beginners and practitioners in future ages,
so that they may enter *samādhi* with body and mind at ease, attaining great peace and security, free from all demons and malevolent spirits.
O gods, and you who have been harmed by beginningless grudges, calamities from past lives, or the lingering debts of old karma that come to afflict and injure you—
and all those among the assembly who are still in training, as well as all practitioners of future ages— who rely upon my maṇḍala,

maintain the precepts according to the Dharma, receive their precepts from a preceptor, and encounter pure monks, should harbor no doubt or regret regarding this dhāraṇī-heart-mantra. O virtuous sons...
"If you, my son, do not attain mental penetration within this body born of your parents, then the Tathāgatas of the ten directions would be speaking falsely.

Having spoken these words, immeasurable hundreds of thousands of *vajra*-beings in the assembly simultaneously joined their palms before the Buddha, prostrated with their heads at his feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"In accordance with what the Buddha has taught, we shall protect with sincere hearts those who thus cultivate bodhi."
At that time, Brahmā, Śakra Devendra, and the Four Great Kings also simultaneously prostrated before the Buddha and addressed him,
saying: "If there are indeed such virtuous persons who practice and study in this way, we shall protect them with all our hearts and with the utmost sincerity."
May all that they have done throughout their lives be fulfilled according to their wishes.

Furthermore, immeasurable yakṣa generals, rākṣasa kings, piśāca kings, kumbhāṇḍa kings, piśāca kings, vināyaka kings, and various great ghost kings and demon commanders also joined their palms before the Buddha, prostrated themselves with their heads at his feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying: "We also make this vow."

"Protecting these persons so that their bodhicitta may swiftly reach fulfillment, there are also immeasurable Sun and Moon Devas, Masters of Wind, Masters of Rain, Masters of Clouds, Masters of Thunder, along with the Lord of Lightning and the various stellar deities who oversee the years;
these members of the retinue also prostrated at the Buddha’s feet within the assembly and addressed the Buddha, saying: 'We, too, shall protect these practitioners.'"
Having established the site of enlightenment and attained fearlessness, there were further immeasurable mountain deities,
ocean deities, and all the spirits of the earth, water, land, marshes, and air, as well as the wind kings and the gods of the formless realm,
who simultaneously bowed their heads before the Tathāgata and addressed the Buddha, saying: "We, too, shall protect these practitioners so that they may attain Bodhi."

"From now on, there shall be no more demonic interference. At that time, eighty-four thousand nayutas of *koṭis* of *Gaṅgā*-river-sands of Vajragarbha-rāja Bodhisattvas, within the great assembly, rose from their seats, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One, as for the meritorious deeds we have cultivated, we have long since accomplished Bodhi; yet we do not take up *nirvāṇa*, but constantly follow [the Buddha]."
This mantra shall protect and rescue those who, in the final age, cultivate *samādhi* and practice correctly.

World-Honored One, for such persons who thus cultivate the mind and seek right concentration—whether they are in a place of practice (*maṇḍala*), walking for meditation, or even wandering with a distracted mind through villages—we, the members of our assembly, shall constantly follow and attend to them. Even if Māra or Maheśvara...

Though one seeks a means to do so, it can never be found; even the minor spirits and ghosts will remain ten yojanas away from such a virtuous person, except for those who have resolved their minds to joyfully cultivate dhyāna.

World-Honored One, if an evil Māra or his retinue should wish to come and harass this virtuous person, I shall shatter their heads with my precious mallet until they are like fine dust, ensuring that—
"What this person has done shall be as wished.

The Treatise says: There are various methods for translating scriptures; for instance, *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* is translated as "Unsurpassed Perfectly Equal and Right Enlightenment," yet it is not translated [in other contexts] because there are remaining meanings that have not been fully exhausted. As for...

"Bhagavān" is translated here as "Buddha," which possesses six meanings. This statement means that by the power of reciting mantras, even all evil spells—whether belonging to devas, nāgas, ghosts, spirits, earth-dwellers, or māras—cannot affect the mind;
one attains *samādhi*. Commentators say that *samādhi* is "right reception. *Samādhi* is translated as "right concentration"; it is indeed right concentration.
To say that "correct reception" (*samyak-samādhi*) refers to the objects of perception is incorrect; rather, it refers to *samādhi* and "correct reception.
These two meanings are as stated in the *Awakening of Great Perfect Enlightenment Sūtra*: "Entering the treasury of great radiant light of supernormal powers, in correct reception";
and as stated in the *Ratnakūṭa Sūtra*: "In *samādhi* and correct reception, evil cannot invade. This is what is called "correct reception," *kaṭha*.

*Kaitaka-pūtana*—here translated as the "Oddly Foul-Smelling Ghost"—is the track for entering the city of Great Nirvāṇa, as previously described in the detailed and subtle ritual methods for practice within the *maṇḍala*. Students should therefore exert themselves in this.
Even if one is unable to construct a ritual altar, it is sufficient to recite, copy, wear, preserve, or make offerings to [this text].

If entering the *maṇḍala* and practicing the Way were no different from entering the altar and practicing the Way in terms of their merit, it would be because the World-Honored One’s great compassion feared that those who hear this might again fall into literalism and fail to understand the wisdom of skillful means.
*Caitiya* is translated here as "a place worthy of offerings" (*kōkyōsho*); it is also transcribed as *reimyō*. *Dhvaja* is translated as "banner" (*tō*). [Supplementary Note]
Wujin said: "The so-called 'evils' do not refer to the evil of malevolence, but rather to the evil of becoming [evil].

The celestial phenomena all receive the refined vital energies of the four great elements and the five phases; when these become obstructed and fail to circulate freely, they are not like the Buddha, who possesses compassion.
If one violates that nature, calamities respond accordingly because things are moved by their own kind. Thus, a lack of benevolence results in the wood [element]."
If one punishes that which is contrary to ritual propriety, it is punished by fire; if one punishes that which is contrary to righteousness, it is punished by metal.
All other cases follow this pattern. Wherever this incantation exists, calamities do not arise. As for "calamity and auspiciousness," they are in fact simply "inauspiciousness."
Ānanda immediately rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying: “We are dull-witted and fond of mere erudition;

our minds were still burdened by outflows (*āsrava*) and had not yet sought liberation. Having received the Buddha’s compassionate instruction, we have attained correct cultivation, and our bodies and minds are filled with joy, gaining great benefit.
World-Honored One, such is the cultivation and realization of the Buddha’s *samādhi*, though we have not yet reached *nirvāṇa*.”
"What is meant by the stage of 'Dry Wisdom' (*śuklavidarśanā-bhūmi*)? How many minds are there up to the forty-fourth? Through what gradual sequence does one attain the vision of cultivation?

To what destination must one go to be said to have entered the stages (*bhūmi*)? And what is meant by the Bodhisattva of Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*)? Having spoken these words, he prostrated himself with his five limbs touching the ground.
The great assembly, with single-minded devotion, waited for the Buddha’s compassionate voice, gazing upward with wide-open eyes in reverent anticipation.
At that time, the World-Honored One praised Ānanda, saying: "Excellent, excellent!

You have been able to universally provide for the great assembly and all sentient beings of the future ages who cultivate *samādhi* and seek the Great Vehicle—from ordinary persons up to the ultimate Great Nirvāṇa—a provisional demonstration of the unsurpassed path of correct cultivation. Listen attentively now; I shall speak for you."
Ānanda and the great assembly joined their palms, hollowed their hearts, and silently received the instruction.
The Treatise says: Nirvāṇa is the ultimate fruit of all Buddhas, while the "dry wisdom" (śuṣka-prajñā) is the initial cause. Dry wisdom is like a river originating at Mount Min;

its flow begins as a mere trickle but, upon reaching the land of Chu, it merges with ten thousand tributaries. Thus it is with dry wisdom reaching the tenth stage (bhūmi): it flows together with myriad streams.
Furthermore, it is like the Great Ocean which, having already arrived, possesses the flavors of the hundred rivers.

Other sutras all begin with faith; from the ten levels of faith (*śraddhā*) arise the ten abidings (*vihāra*); from the ten abidings arise the ten practices (*caryā*); from the ten practices are perfected the ten transferences (*pariṇāmanā*);
from the ten transferences one immediately enters the ten stages (*bhūmi*). After the ten stages, the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*) is established. Thus...

Furthermore, this sutra uses diligent effort (*vīrya*) to inspire and awaken [beings], intending to cause ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*) to manifest protection in the present life—just as Sudhana attained the Way in a single lifetime, or as the Dragon Girl attained Buddhahood at the age of eight. Within the category of ordinary persons, there are three gradual stages:

first, the stage of Dry Wisdom (*śuṣka-vipaśyanā*) where the initial mind arises; then, from the ten levels of faith (*śraddhā*) up to the end of the ten levels of transference (*pariṇāmanā*), four further stages are added.
According to their respective capacities and practices, they enter the ten stages (*bhūmi*) and proceed to Equal Enlightenment (*samyaksambodhi*);

furthermore, by adding the stage of Vajra-Dry Wisdom (*vajra-śuṣka-prajñā*), one finally realizes Wondrous Enlightenment (*tathāgata-buddhatva*). Therefore, it does not speak of the duration or brevity of kalpas, but rather speaks of "from ordinary beings to the Great Nirvāṇa" as a remote demonstration of the path of supreme, correct practice.
The Buddha said, "Ānanda, you should know that the wondrous nature is perfectly luminous and free from all names and marks; it has originally no worlds or sentient beings.
Because of delusion there is birth, and because of birth there is extinction. Birth and extinction are called delusion; the cessation of delusion is called reality.
This is what is termed the Tathāgata’s unsurpassed Bodhi and Great Nirvāṇa—the two designations for the transformation of the basis."
The Treatise says: As Aśvaghoṣa stated, because one does not know that the dharma of *tathatā* (suchness) is one as it truly is, the mind moves without awakening;
thus, in every thought-moment, there is the characteristic of arising and the characteristic of ceasing. Therefore it is said: "Because of delusion there is arising;
because of arising there is ceasing. Arising and ceasing are called "delusion. If one can understand the dharma of *tathatā* as one as it truly is, then...
Delusion is fundamentally non-existent, yet it is like a person who becomes confused by relying on directions; this confusion has no inherent characteristic of its own.
To mistake the east for the west, while the west itself does not actually change—sentient beings are also like this.

Because they are deluded by ignorance, they claim the mind is moving when in reality it is unmoving. If one realizes that the moving mind is itself neither arising nor ceasing, one immediately attains entry [into the truth].
Because it pertains to the gateway of *tathatā* (suchness), it is said that the cessation of delusion is termed "the True.

However, because internally there are differences in the strength or weakness of the power of the perfuming of *tathatā*, and externally there are differences in the power of the external conditions for sentient beings, the World-Honored One is titled the "King of Physicians," who administers medicine according to the illness;
thus, there are stages and positions, as well as gradual and sudden [attainments]. As the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* says: "Distinguishing..."

The cessation of the distinct consciousnesses is called *nirvāṇa*. It is also said that realizing the realm of one’s own wisdom and transforming the *ālayavijñāna*—the storehouse consciousness—is *mahāparinirvāṇa*.
*Mahāparinirvāṇa* and unsurpassed *bodhi* are like sound and its resonance;
they are neither identical nor different. Because the transformation of delusion is termed awakening, it is called unsurpassed *bodhi*; because of this transformation...

Regarding the two transformations of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*) within Great Nirvāṇa—both the named and the nameless—there is first the transformation from defilement to purity, and second, the transformation from delusion to awakening.
"Bodhi" (Awakening) is termed "arisen" because it was previously obstructed by the two hindrances (*āvaraṇa*) and thus could not arise; now that the hindrances are severed, it is called "arisen.
"Nirvāṇa" is termed "attained" because its intrinsic nature is pure, yet it was obscured by adventitious dust; now that this is severed, it is manifested.

This is called "the stage of manifesting the transformation": there are six [stages]. First, the transformation through the weakening of power and the strengthening of capacity, which refers to the first two stages.

By means of the power of resolute conviction (*adhimukti*), shame (*hrī*), and dread of blame (*apatrāpya*), one weakens the force of the defiled seeds within the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*) and strengthens the functional capacity of the pure seeds;

thus, one gradually subdues the active manifestations (*samudācāra*). This is also termed the "transformation of the basis" (*āśrayaparāvṛtti*). Second, the transformation through penetration, which is attained by means of the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*).

The first is the transformation through true power (*tathatā-bala*), which refers to the realization of a portion of the true basis-of-existence (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*) by severing the two obstacles (*āvaraṇa*) in their coarse forms.

The third is the transformation through cultivation (*bhāvanā-parāvṛtti*), which refers to the gradual severance of innate [afflictions] stage by stage, realizing the transformation of the basis into reality.

The fourth is the transformation of the fulfillment of the fruit (*phala-paripūri-parāvṛtti*), which refers to the ultimate stage where, by means of the diamond-like concentration (*vajropama-samādhi*), all heavy residues (*dausthulya*) are forever severed, and the perfect fruit of Buddhahood is suddenly realized.

The fifth, the inferior transformation, refers to the two vehicles (śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas) who, weary of suffering and longing for quiescence, realize true analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*);

because they lack superior capability, [it is called inferior]. The sixth, the vast transformation, refers to the stage of the Mahāyāna, wherein there is neither longing nor weariness, one penetrates both types of emptiness, simultaneously abandons both obstacles, and suddenly realizes unsurpassed bodhi; because it possesses superior capability, [it is called vast].

Ānanda, if you now wish to cultivate the true samādhi and proceed directly to the Great Nirvāṇa of the Tathāgata, you must first recognize these two causes of inversion regarding sentient beings and the world; when inversion does not arise, this is the true samādhi of the Tathāgata.
Ānanda, what is meant by the inversion of sentient beings? Ānanda, it arises from the luminous nature of the mind; the nature of the mind is luminous.
Because it is perfect, the nature of causality arises; this nature of nature is born from deluded vision. From absolute non-existence, there is established ultimate existence.
This existence and its objects are not causes, nor are they that which is caused; they do not abide, nor are they the locus of abiding.

When one realizes that these have no fundamental root, and that this lack of abiding establishes the world and all sentient beings, then one is deluded regarding the fundamentally perfect luminosity. Thus, this gives rise to the false; this false nature has no substance and is not existent.
The basis. [The supplementary note says: "Inexhaustible" is deleted from below this point.

Regarding the seven phrases from "about to return to truth" to "neither mind nor dharma," totaling twenty-eight characters, it is not known that the first five phrases are intended to dispel the previously mentioned arising and ceasing called "deluded cessation."
To call the false "true" is what is meant here; these [two] phrases are also words spoken by the Tathāgata out of necessity.
The following two lines are terms that introduce a successive unfolding of the argument. If they were deleted, the intended meaning would not continue.
As for saying it has no cause, this refers to the preceding text which asks: "Since it is called false, how could it have a cause? That which is the cause is simply the self.
All deluded thoughts are mutually dependent upon one another.

If one wishes to return to the truth, yet that which is sought as "true" is already not true; the nature of True Suchness is not something to be sought through truth. Thus, what is sought after turns out to be a non-characteristic:
it is neither arising, nor abiding, nor mind, nor dharmas.
The Treatise says: "If one wishes to cultivate true samādhi, it must reach the state that is neither arising nor abiding, neither mind nor dharma.
This is because the World-Honored One has just now explained to Pūrṇa that delusion is not the fault of the intrinsic clarity of awakening;

rather, it is the three factors of sentient beings, worlds, and karmic fruits, as well as their habitual tendencies. To be detached from these is to be detached from what is not, and this is to be neither attached to nor detached from what is."
This is a brief summary of that meaning. A question is asked:

"Since you have already explained this in detail for Pūrṇa, what is the intention behind not yet answering regarding the characteristics of the forty-four mental states—the ten faiths, ten abidings, ten practices, ten dedications, heat, summit, patience, and the supreme mundane dharma—and instead first citing the previous brief summary? [The answer] says: "Where there is illness, there is medicine."
It remedies the illnesses of sentient beings; it is the medicinal medicine of the methods for cultivation and realization across the various stages of conditioned existence (*saṃskāra*).

Therefore, one must first identify the source of the illness before administering the appropriate remedy. As the *Zhoutai Dingshuo* (Explanation of the Hexagram Ding) states: "Ding is an image. It further says: "Fire upon wood is Ding.
The legs of the Ding distinguish its base, and the ears distinguish its top; with a lid covering it and its interior filled, such is the image of Ding.
However, a cauldron requires both water and fire before the act of cooking can take place; the forty-four minds are like the cauldron, and sentient beings are like the water and fire.
To say "neither arising nor abiding, neither mind nor dharma" is another designation for the preceding meaning.
The preceding meaning states that "separation is precisely non-arising," and "separation from what is not" further causes one not to abide.
Because it is detached [from all extremes], it is further said: "That which is not abiding is precisely that which is not identical. This means it is not the mind;
furthermore, that which is not identical is intended to prevent one from abiding in non-identity. Therefore, it is further said: "It is not the Dharma. Supplementary Note:

The true nature of *tathatā* (suchness) is detached from the two paths of truth and delusion. If one wishes to discard delusion and return to truth, not only is truth impossible to recover, but it would ultimately fail.
It thus clearly constitutes the characteristic of non-existence; for it is the delusion within clarity—not something other—that constitutes the fault.
Therefore, the four negations are listed next to demonstrate the causes from which these characteristics of non-existence arise and the karma that brings them forth.

Jiyin [Zongjing] takes the preceding meaning of "separate from both 'is' and 'is not,' neither 'is' nor 'is not'" and applies it as a successive refutation of the phrases "neither arising nor abiding" and so forth in the passage below.
Furthermore, because the textual sequence is not continuous, it is not accepted.
Through successive arising, the power of birth manifests and perfumes [the mind] to form karma; similar karmas resonate with one another.
Due to this resonance, there is the mutual extinction and mutual generation of causes and effects. It is for this reason that sentient beings undergo perversion.
Ānanda, what is meant by the "inversion of the world"? It is that which exists as a mere semblance of existence, where fragmented delusions arise;
because of this realm, the non-cause is established as the cause, and the non-abiding is established as the abode.

Through this constant flux and lack of stability, the three periods of time and the four directions are formed, blending and interpenetrating one another to transform sentient beings into the twelve categories.

Supplement: Jingjue says that in the fourth fascicle, the phrase "the realms of phenomena interpenetrate and undergo threefold transformations" refers to the manifestation of the primary retribution (the six sense organs) in contrast to the secondary retribution (the environment), wherein each of the six faculties possesses twelve hundred merits.

Here, the interpenetration of the environments follows from the primary retribution to clarify the inverted nature of the world, thereby establishing the twelve classes of living beings. Since it was previously stated...
Regarding the phrase "merit" (guṇa) here being called "inversion" (viparyāsa), is it possible for the ancient masters to have used this to explain the first three layers?

As for the statement that "fragmented [existence] arises falsely, that which is not a cause is taken as cause, and that which has no abiding place is taken as abode, flowing on without staying"—this generally clarifies the meaning of the fourfold falsity: false arising, false abiding, the false mind, and false dharmas.
Therefore, in the world, sound exists because of movement; form exists because of sound; fragrance exists because of form; touch exists because of fragrance; taste exists because of touch;
and mental objects (*dharma*) are known because of taste. Since these six types of deluded conceptualization constitute the nature of karma, the twelve divisions revolve by means of this cycle.
Thus, the world’s sounds, fragrances, tastes, and touches exhaust the twelve transformations to become a single revolving cycle.
Supplement: The six faculties and the six objects constitute twelve divisions; when the faculties and their objects are summarized, they form twelve transformations.

To exhaust these twelve transformations is to return to the single rotation. Thus one knows that the karmic fruits of sentient beings continue in succession, circulating through the three realms without rest, due solely to the nature of inverted perceptions.
By riding upon this wheel of inverted characteristics, there exist worlds of egg-birth, womb-birth, moisture-birth, and transformation-birth;
those with form and those without form; those with perception and those without perception; those that are neither with nor without form, and those that are neither with nor without perception.
Supplement: The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states: "That which arises dependent on an egg is called birth from an egg (*aṇḍaja*); that which emerges from a womb is called birth from a womb (*jarāyuja*);
that which arises through the moisture of conditions is called birth from moisture (*saṃsvedaja*); and that which suddenly appears where there was nothing is called miraculous birth (*upapāduka*).

These four modes of birth take internal mental volitional karma as the cause and external eggs, wombs, and moisture as the conditions; they are categorized according to the predominance of these supporting conditions.
Developing from the few to the many in sequence: egg-birth possesses all four [elements], and for this reason it is placed first; womb-birth possesses three;
moisture-birth possesses two; and transformation-birth possesses only one.
Ānanda, due to the delusory cycle of the world caused by causal conditions, through the agitation of inverted views, the combination of vapors forms eighty thousand [beings].
Because there are four thousand such disordered thoughts of flying and sinking, there exist the egg-born and the *kalala* stages, circulating through various lands;
fish, birds, turtles, and snakes fill these realms.
Due to the causes of the world’s defiled saṃsāra and the perversions of desire, eighty-four thousand [beings] are formed through their union and growth.

Because such horizontal and vertical chaotic thoughts exist, there are the *kalala*, *arbuda*, and *peśī* stages of fetal development as they transmigrate through the lands of humans, animals, dragons, and immortals, filling all categories of existence.
Due to the world's attachment to the cycle of rebirth and its inverted inclinations, these elements combine with heat to form eighty-four thousand [types of beings].

Because such inverted and chaotic thoughts exist, there is the moist characteristic (*sneha-lakṣaṇa*) of the *bīśa* (flesh-mass) that transmigrates through the lands, teeming with crawling and wriggling creatures that fill every category.
Due to the world’s cycle of transformation and the false inversion of causes, these combine through contact to form eighty-four thousand [types of beings].

Because of such chaotic conceptions regarding the new and the old, there exist transformed forms (*kalala*) that flow through the lands, undergo metamorphosis, and fly about, their species filling the world.
Due to the causes of worldly attachment, obstruction, cyclic existence, hindrance, and inversion, these combine and coalesce to form eighty-four thousand [types of beings].

Because such is the case with the turbidity of radiance and distracted thoughts, there are forms characterized by *kalala* that circulate through the lands; their spirits of auspicious and inauspicious power fill every category.
Due to the causes of the world’s dissolution and the cycle of rebirth, and because of delusion and inversion, they combine with darkness to form eighty-four thousand [types].
Because such obscured and chaotic conceptions exist, there are formless *kalala* beings who transmigrate through the realms, dispersing, dissolving, and sinking into emptiness;
their kind fills these lands.
Due to the world’s causes of illusory transmigration and inverted reflections, they combine their memories to form eighty-four thousand [types].

Because they secretly harbor such disordered thoughts, there arise the *kalala* and *arbuda* stages characterized by conceptualization, which circulate through various lands; spirits, ghosts, and numinous entities of every kind fill these realms.
Due to the causes of the world’s dullness, cyclic existence, and deluded inversions, these combine with stubborn materiality to form eighty-four thousand [species].
Because withered and chaotic thoughts are thus, there exist the *kalala* of non-conceptualization (*asaṃjñika*) that circulate through the lands;
their spirits are transformed into earth, wood, metal, and stone, filling all categories thereof.
Due to the mutual dependence of the world and the false inversions of saṃsāra, they combine and form eighty-four thousand defiled states.

Because of such disordered thoughts, there exist non-material forms that take on material characteristics, such as the *kalala* and the floating lands of the ocean, including various sea-squirts that use shrimp as their eyes; these kinds of beings fill the world.

Due to the nature of inverted delusion caused by the mutual attraction of world-phenomena within the cycle of saṃsāra, mantras combine to form eighty-four thousand types of summoning and chaotic thoughts;
because of this, there exist those who are neither formless nor possessed of physical characteristics, such as the *kalala* stage of embryonic development, who transmigrate through various lands,
their species filling the realms with curses and malevolent incantations.
Because the world arises from the conjunction of causes with delusive saṃsāra and inverted views, various combinations form eighty-four thousand types of confused and mutually conflicting thoughts.
Thus, there exist the *kalala* and *arbuda* stages of thought-conception formed by the characteristics of "non-existence" and "existence.
In these realms of flowing transformation, creatures such as the *pulu* (maggots) are formed through the mutual transformation of different substances, their species filling every space.

Due to the causes of the world’s cycle of enmity and killing, and because of inverted views, these factors combine to produce eighty-four thousand types of beings who harbor the notion that they are eating their own parents.
Thus, there exist those with non-non-perceptive characteristics who circulate through lands as *kalala* (embryonic stages),
such as the earth-owl which fashions its young from clods of earth, and the mirror-cracking bird which uses the fruit of the poisonous *pi-bou* tree as its offspring.
The son completed his growth, yet both parents were devoured by him; his kind filled the world. Supplement:
Gushan says, according to the *Shiji*, "Basic Annals of Emperor Xiaowu," it states that for the sacrifice to the Yellow Emperor, one *xiao* bird and one *pojing* were used.
Meng Kang said: "The *xiao* is the name of a bird that devours its mother; the *pojing* devours its father. The Yellow Emperor wished to put an end to them."
Its kind is such that it is used for sacrifices to all hundred creatures; its broken mirror is like that of a *chū* (wild beast) with tiger-like eyes.
What is now called "bird" (*niǎo*) is an error by the translators; the character "bird" should have been "equal" (*děng*), and was later arbitrarily altered. I say:
while what Gu Shan has discussed is indeed excellent, I fear that among the birds and beasts there may be something distinct belonging to these four lands.
If one were to say that when both parents are encountered and eaten by their offspring, then the earth-owl does not eat only its mother and the "broken-mirror" bird does not eat only its father—
just as with the *bìluó* (pigeon) and other such species— then what further cause for doubt could there be?
These are called the twelve types of sentient beings.
The treatise states: *kalala* (translated as "congealed mucus"), *arbuda* (translated as "fetal membrane"), *peśī* (translated as "soft flesh"), and *ghana* (translated as "hard flesh").
Among those with *ghana* and perception (*saṃjñā-ghana*) are the seven classes of ghosts, spirits, and numinous beings.
(8) There are *kalala* [embryonic stages] that possess only ideation (*saṃjñā*) and lack ideation; these are earth, wood, metal, and stone, which are indeed *kalala* but lack ideation.

(9) There are *kalala* that possess form (*rūpa*); those such as the *siphonophora* (water mother) are *kalala* possessing form, yet they take the shrimp as their eyes to perceive the characteristics of color and form—thus they are neither "possessing form" in the primary sense, nor are they "without form."

The *kalala* of form and formlessness (10): Through incantations and curses, one may produce a *kalala* that is formless; yet it is still capable of manifesting transformation, so it is not without form.
The *kalala* of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (11): Like the *bhringa-rāja* (wasp) and others, these are originally of a different species;
they do not transmit life through the perception found in eggs or wombs, thus they are not "with perception," yet in the end, they achieve their mutual formation.
(12) It is not that they lack perception; nor is it that the *kalala* (embryonic stage) lacks perception. For example, creatures such as the earth-owl (*ulūka*) consume their parents;
yet this is not because they lack perception. However, a clod of earth or a poisonous fruit do not possess perception.

Because the womb arises through emotional attachment (*sneha*), it is called "defiled" (*saṃkleśa*), "desire" (*kāma*), and "nourishment" (*puṣṭi*). (1) Because the egg is formed through perception (*saṃjñā*), it is called "falsehood," "movement," and "instability."
It is merely *qi* (its ninth). Since dependent origination (*xiāngdài lúnhuí*) involves relying on provisional things, it is termed "artificial" (*wèi*).

(Its fourth) The cycle of transformation (*biànyì lúnhuí*) is of the same category as the cycle of birth-and-death through transformation (*biànyì shēngsǐ*); because this is not real, it is termed "provisional" (*jiǎ*).

However, while "dependent origination" should properly be called "provisional" (*jiǎ*) and "transformation" should properly be called "artificial" (*wèi*), perhaps the translator was mistaken. (Its third) Moisture is by way of conjunction.
Because of sensation, there is attachment; it awaits external warmth and merely touches the transformed body (5). Radiance arises from clarity, and clarity arises from awareness;
while awareness has no abiding characteristic, radiance possesses beauty, and is therefore called "obstructive attachment" (8).
Earth, wood, metal, and stone have form but no thought; because they take emptiness and dullness as their cause, they are delusion and inversion (6).

(7) Because the delusions of inverted perception arise from the causes of empty, scattered, dissolving, and sinking thoughts within the formless realm, spirits, ghosts, and numina have no substantial form;
thus they are called "phantoms" (*wangxiang*). Because they consist only of mental conceptions, they are called the "Land of Recollection.
When a state has chaotic omens, non-human beings are also in chaos; when an army has signs of victory, non-human beings also achieve victory; thus they are called "shadows" (*ying*).

(10) Mutual Induction: Samsara mutually induces one another; because this [nature] possesses the quality of existence and that [nature] is likewise capable of inducing it, it is called "Nature" (*xing*).

(11) Conjunction with Delusion: Samsara conjoins with delusion, causing those categories of self to transform delusion through delusion; therefore, it is called "Delusive" (*wang*). (12) Hostility and Harm:
Samsara is not a matter of constant principle; therefore, it is called "Strange" (*guai*). These [explanations] were all beyond the reach of ancient commentators, yet they are established by Dinglin.
This is attained by those who possess independent insight. "Puluo" refers to the *xie-weng* (wasp). Supplement:
Senghui Yin says that from the twelve categories of birth, delusion arises regarding the truth; if one wishes to restore the truth, one must apply remedies.
Since this is not yet the conclusion of the textual sequence, how could it extend beyond the scroll? Therefore, at the beginning of the eighth scroll, Wujin returns from delusion to the truth.
The true exposition of the characteristics of the stages (*bhūmi*) consists of one hundred and forty-one lines in total, which transition into the seventh fascicle.
Following the twelve categories, three gradual sequences (*krama*) are established. From this point, through gradual cultivation, the stages of the noble ones (*ārya*) are established;

continuing thus until the sequence of pure cultivation and realization, one enters ever more deeply. Mañjuśrī, already knowing the causes and effects and having completed his inquiry, now requests the clarification of the essential points.
The Buddha spoke these five names and commanded that they be upheld; this concludes the seventh fascicle. Furthermore, it is said that according to the original sūtra, the seven destinies are:
first, hell; second, hungry ghosts; third, animals; fourth, humans; fifth, *ṛṣis*; sixth, devas; and seventh, *asuras*.
By moving the *ṛṣis* to follow after the *asuras*, the human destiny and the celestial destiny are made to succeed one another, thereby establishing the sequential order of the ten destinies.

Regarding the structure of the text, it has its beginnings and endings, yet there is no confusion or interruption. A fool might say: "If one claims that the scroll must not be passed over until the narrative force has reached its conclusion, this is most certainly not so.
For instance, the "World-Ruling Sovereign’s Exquisite Adornment" chapter (*Lokēśvararāja-vyūha*) consists of five fascicles; the "World Systems" chapter (*Loka-dhātu*) consists of three fascicles;
the "Ten Transferences" chapter (*Daśa-prakṛti-parivarta*) consists of eleven fascicles; and the "Entry into the Dharma Realm" chapter (*Dharmadhātu-praveśa*) consists of twenty fascicles.
One scroll states that it is exactly as the seal says; it should also be joined together with the *Juer benjing* (The Scripture on the Seven Realms).

Since the seven realms have already been established as a fixed system, how can the five classes of immortals (*xiān*) be moved to follow the *asuras*? One does not know whether the realm of immortals is superior to humans or inferior to devas;
would it not be more appropriate to place them after the human realm and before the celestial realm? This is likely because of their power of cultivation...
Because their contemplation has not yet reached profound depth, they are confused by these teachings; there is no need to further debate other points.
