When one dwells in the cultivation and realization of perfect and luminous merit and virtue, such a class of beings is called the Heaven of Vast Results (Bṛhatphala).

If, regarding the previous mind, they simultaneously feel weary of both suffering and pleasure, and through the continuous, uninterrupted refinement of the mind of equanimity (upekṣā), they thoroughly exhaust the path of equanimity until body and mind are both extinguished,
and the mental faculties become ashen and motionless for five hundred kalpas— such a person, because they take birth and extinction as their cause, is unable to bring forth illumination.
Regarding the nature of non-arising and non-extinction: during the first half-aeon there is extinction, and during the latter half-aeon there is birth;
such a class of beings is called the Heaven of No-Thought (Āsaṃjñika-deva). Ānanda, these four superior streams cannot be moved by any worldly objects of suffering or pleasure.

Although they are not the unconditioned True Immovable Ground, because their minds still harbor a sense of attainment and their efforts have reached full maturity, they are called the Fourth Dhyāna. Ānanda.
Furthermore, within this realm, there are five classes of Non-returners (*anāgāmin*) for whom the nine grades of habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) in the lower realms are extinguished simultaneously;
for whom suffering and pleasure have both vanished; and who, having no further dwelling place below, establish their abode within the homogeneous class (*nikāya-sabhāga*) of equanimity.

Ānanda, with both suffering and pleasure extinguished and the mind of contention no longer active, such a category is named the Heaven of No Affliction (*Avṛha*). This is the essential mechanism [of its establishment].

Wandering alone with no ground for association—such a class is named the Heaven of No-Heat (*Atapa*). In the worlds of the ten directions, wondrous vision is perfectly clear and serene, with no further traces of dust or phenomena;
such a class is named the Heaven of Good Vision (*Sudṛśa*). Pure vision manifests before them, forging all things without obstruction;
such a class is named the Heaven of Good Appearance (*Sudarśana*). They have reached the ultimate limit of all subtle forms and exhausted the nature of matter.
The nature of nature enters into the boundless; such a class [of beings] is called the Heaven of Ultimate Form (Akaniṣṭha).
Ānanda, as for these Non-returners (Anāgāmin) in that heaven, those Kings of the Four Dhyāna Heavens can only hear of it with admiration, yet they cannot know or see it.
It is just as in this world where vast wildernesses, deep mountains, and sites of the Noble Path are all maintained by Arhats; therefore, the world is coarse [in contrast].

Ānanda, that which people cannot see—where these eighteen heavens move alone without companionship and have not yet exhausted the burden of the physical form—is, from this point downward, called the Realm of Form (rūpadhātu).
The treatise says: regarding the four dhyānas, there are four types: first, with outflows (sāsrava); second, without outflows (anāsrava); third, both with and without outflows; and fourth...
It is neither with-outflow (*sāsrava*) nor without-outflow (*anāsrava*). The *Abhidharmakośa* states that each of the first three dhyānas has three [levels], while the fourth dhyāna has eight;

this is because it does not differentiate the Heaven of Non-conceptualization (*asaṃjñisattva*) from the Vast Fruit (*bṛhatphala*). Maitreya says there are eighteen locations in the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*):

the Heaven of the Brahma-multitude (*brahmakāyika*), the Heaven of the Ministers of Brahma (*brahmapurohita*), and the Great Brahma Heaven (*mahābrahmā*)—these three arise from the lower, middle, and upper grades [of the first dhyāna].

By cultivating the first dhyāna through the lower, middle, and upper grades of fire-like refinement, there arise these three: Parīttābha (Limited Light), Apramāṇābha (Immeasurable Light), and Ābhāsvara (Utterly Pure Light).

By cultivating the second dhyāna through the lower, middle, and upper grades of fire-like refinement, there arise these three: Parīttaśubha (Limited Purity), Apramāṇaśubha (Immeasurable Purity), and Śubhakṛtsna (Universal Purity).
By cultivating the third dhyāna through the lower, middle, and upper grades of fire-like refinement, there arise Anabhraka (Cloudless), Puṇyaprasava (Born of Merit), and Bṛhatphala (Great Fruit).
The Heaven of Great Fruit (*Bṛhatphala*)—these three [heavens] arise from cultivating the fourth dhyāna through the weak, medium, and superior grades.

The Heaven of No-thought (*asaṃjñisattva*) is subsumed within the Heaven of Great Fruit and has no separate location. Furthermore, there are the five Pure Abodes (*śuddhāvāsa*), where noble beings dwell in a state distinct from others:
namely, the Unafflicted (*Avṛha*), the Heatless (*Atapa*), the Good-to-See (*Sudṛśa*), the Good-Appearing (*Sudarśana*), and the Ultimate Form (*Akaniṣṭha*). These arise from the weak... [grade].

Because he cultivated the fourth dhyāna with the highest of the high grades, Maitreya spoke of the "Brahma-foremost Beneficial Devas" (*brahmaviśeṣa*), which in this sutra refers to the Brahmapurohita Heaven;
and he spoke of the "Cloudless Devas" (*anabhraka*), which in this sutra refers to the Puṇyaprasava Heaven.
As for the division of the Puṇyaprasava Heaven into two branches, this describes the Āsaṃjñika (Non-percipient) Heaven. Question: Why?
The name has two diverging paths: if one proceeds directly, one reaches the Heaven of Vast Results (Bṛhatphala);
if one proceeds by a circuitous route, one reaches the Heaven of Non-conception (Āsaṃjñika). He asked again, "What is meant by 'Vast Results'? [The Master replied:

"From the moment of first generating the resolve for enlightenment, one does not harbor heterodox views but cultivates only the fundamental four dhyānas. Thus, one becomes free from the defilements of the lower stages and traverses the four levels."

Furthermore, the Heaven of Merit-Love (*Puṇyaprasava*) is that which further increases the superior meditative concentration of the Heaven of Vast Results (*Bṛhatphala*); it is the place of meritorious birth (*puṇyopaga*).
Again, he asked: "What is meant by the Heaven of Non-conception (*Asaṃjñisattva*)? He replied:

"If one, while still harboring heterodox views, suppresses the afflictions through the six practices, gradually becoming weary of and detached from them, and thus reaches the Heaven of Merit-Love, then by the power of having attained equanimity (*upekṣā*), the mind becomes perfectly integrated and no longer manifests [conceptual activity]."

Continuing to investigate the phenomena that were abandoned, even the mind of abandonment perishes; because one no longer reckons with body or mind, it is said that "body and mind are both extinguished.
Yet, one then clings to this as being *nirvāṇa*—this is precisely the characteristic of delusive thought (*vikalpa*).
To take this as the truth is merely because the sixth consciousness has temporarily ceased its activity, like a fish that has already been cast out from the water.
The characteristics of the mind are not known; one has merely not yet abandoned the arising and ceasing of subtle mental states. The *Abhidharmakośa* states:

"When these devas pass through the cycle of birth and death, there is a distinction regarding their initial birth. It takes half an eon (*kalpa*) for them to enter the maturation (*vipāka*) of non-conception (*asaṃjñika*).
Therefore, it is said that they cease after the first half-eon. Furthermore, when they are about to die, they do so from the maturation of non-conception."

Emerging again after another half-aeon (*kalpa*), the mental aspect (*citta-nimitta*) finally manifests, and only thereafter does transformation occur; hence it is said that one is born during the latter half-aeon.
Between births and deaths, for four hundred and ninety-nine aeons, there is a state of total non-conception (*asaṃjñika*).

How profound is the difficulty of separating from the *manas*! One attempts to treat it with the "attainment of non-conception" (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*), yet it persists; the combative mind does not cease.

When interacting, there is no contention; therefore, it is called "Without Affliction" (*Avṛha*). Since there is no ground for refining interactions, there is no friction; therefore, it is called "Without Heat" (*Atapa*).
Because there is wondrous vision, it is called "Good Vision" (*Sudarśana*). Because there is wondrous manifestation, it is called "Good Manifestation" (*Sudṛśa*).

Its mechanisms operate independently, without dependence. Refining interactions without ground means being without opposition. Casting and forging without obstruction enables transformation. Casting and forging...
It is simply water and fire: the essence-nature is water, and the seeing-nature is fire. To ultimately exhaust the myriad conditions is to reach the subtlest point of movement.

Herein, to ultimately exhaust the nature of form is for the nature of form to be emptiness; the nature of emptiness is awakening. When there is awakening, this is what is called the nature of the nature of form.
If one merely exhausts the nature of form, it is not the ultimate exhaustion of form. Form and emptiness are mutually...
Because it is his nature, the *Laṅkāvatāra* states: "Dwelling in the Heaven of the Ultimate Form (*Akaniṣṭha*), free from all faults, he attains perfect enlightenment there.
Furthermore, Ānanda, within this limit of form at the Peak of Existence (*Bhavāgra*), there are again two divergent paths.

If, within the mind of equanimity (*upekṣā*), one illuminates wisdom so that the light of insight becomes perfectly penetrating, one transcends the realm of dust to become an Arhat and enters the vehicle of the Bodhisattvas; such a class is called "Great Arhats who have turned their minds.

If, within the mind of equanimity, one achieves the relinquishing of aversion, perceives the body as an obstruction, and dissolves that obstruction to enter emptiness, such a class is called the "Sphere of Emptiness" (*ākāśāyatana*).
When all outflows have been exhausted, there is neither obstruction nor cessation; therein remains only the *ālaya-vijñāna* in its entirety, while the *manas* is present only in half its subtle form.

This class is called the Sphere of Infinite Consciousness (*vijñānānantyāyatana*). When the empty-form has vanished and the consciousness-mind is entirely extinguished, the ten directions are silent and utterly devoid of any destination.
This class is called the Sphere of Nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*). The nature of consciousness does not...
Moving toward extinction through exhaustive investigation within the inexhaustible, they proclaim the full realization of their nature;

as if existing yet not existing, as if exhausted yet not exhausted—such a class is called the Sphere of Neither Perception nor Non-Perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*). These have reached the limit of emptiness, yet do not exhaust the principle of emptiness.
Those who reach the limit through the holy path from the Heaven of No-Retreat (*anāgāmin*)—such a class is called the dull Arhat of non-retrogressive mind.

Ānanda, if a person from the Han land follows the various non-Buddhist practitioners of the Heaven of No-Thought (*asaṃjñisattva*), who exhaust themselves in the pursuit of emptiness yet fail to return [to the path], remaining deluded, leaking, and ignorant, they will immediately enter the cycle of rebirth.
Among these various heavens, each of those celestial beings is but an ordinary person whose karmic fruit has been requited;

once that requital is exhausted, they enter the cycle of rebirth. Those kings of the heavens are actually Bodhisattvas who, through their practice of *samādhi*, have gradually progressed and turned back [from worldly attachments].
Ānanda, the path of practice toward the noble stages consists of these four heavens of emptiness (*ārūpya*), where body and mind are extinguished and the nature of stability manifests before one;

from this point until the end, it is called the Formless Realm (*ārūpyadhātu*). All of these arise from failing to understand the wondrously enlightened, luminous mind, accumulating delusions that give rise to the three realms of existence.
Within them, delusions follow along as one sinks and drifts through the seven destinies, becoming a *pudgala*.
Each [class of being] follows its own kind.

The *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya* states: "In the heavens of the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), there are not four [physical elements]. Although there is no matter (*rūpa*) resulting from karma, there is matter resulting from meditative concentration (*samādhi*), which serves as the basis for matter.
Thus, the *Kośa* asks: "Why is it that the formless realm has no location? Maitreya replied: [Because it is based on the mind.]
It is said that there are four locations in the formless realm, or perhaps no location at all; however, for sentient beings, their physical dimensions are established as follows:
the human body in Jambudvīpa is of indefinite size, being sometimes tall and large and sometimes short and small, yet it is measured at three and a half cubits according to one's own cubit.
In Pūrvavideha to the east, the body size is fixed, also measuring three cubits according to one's own cubit.
The body size is likewise half [a krośa], yet it is also tall and large;
as it is with Pūrvavideha, so too is the body size in Aparagoyānī and Uttarakuru, increasing further in height and girth.
The body size of the gods of the Cāturmahārājakāyika realm is one-quarter of a krośa; the body size of the Trāyastriṃśa gods increases by another quarter-part.
When the body size of Śakra is half a krośa, the body size of the gods of the Heaven of the Thirty-three is likewise half of that;
all those above should be understood to increase gradually by one part each according to the body sizes of the desire-realm gods.
The body size of the Brahmakāyika gods is half a yojana; the body size of the Brahmapurohita gods is one yojana; the body size of the Mahābrahmā gods is one [yojana].
The body size of the gods in the Parīttābha (Limited Light) heaven is two yojanas;

for all the remaining heavens above this, the body sizes increase progressively by double each time, with the exception of the Anabhraka (Cloudless) heaven, where it should be known that the size decreases by three yojanas.
Furthermore, the body sizes of the great hells (*mahānāraka*) are indeterminate; however, for those who have committed extremely heavy, evil, and unwholesome deeds, their [bodies]...
It is perceived that the dimensions of their bodies are vast and great, whereas others are not so;
as it is with the great hells (*mahā-naraka*), so it is with the cold hells, the solitary hells, the neighboring hells, as well as with animals and hungry ghosts (*preta*).

As for the body dimensions of the non-gods (*asura*), they are like those of the Heaven of the Thirty-three (*trāyastriṃśa*); one should know that there are none in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).
Because it belongs to the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*), there is no measurement of the body; this can be trusted as known from Maitreya’s *Abhidharmakośa*.

Question: What are the two further types of divergent paths? Answer: Within the limit of the realm of form (*rūpāvacara*), if one is able to give rise to the light of wisdom, one will no longer ascend to the four heavens of the Sphere of Infinite Space, the Sphere of Infinite Consciousness, the Sphere of Nothingness, and the Sphere of Neither-Perception-nor-Non-Perception.

Therefore, they are called "Great Arhats who have turned their minds. If there were only the mind of equanimity, it would be the "Anāgāmin who delights in concentration," and thus it is called the Sphere of Infinite Space. Again, he asked: "What is meant by 'half-fine' and 'entirely subtle' manas?
He replied: "The eighth consciousness is the Ālayavijñāna; the seventh consciousness is the Manas. [It is] discrimination."
The *vastu-vijñāna* (object-consciousness) is the sixth consciousness. These three exist in mutual dependence, and the substance of the eight consciousnesses is neither identical nor different.
As for the characteristics of the six consciousnesses, they are divided into coarse and subtle: the coarse refers to externally perceiving all phenomena such as form and space;
the subtle refers to internally perceiving only the two, namely the *ālaya-vijñāna* and the *manas*. However, the mental activities (*ākāra*) of the *manas* alone are difficult to discern.
Although it is associated with the grasping of the mark of a self, along with ignorance, pride, craving, and views, when one investigates it thoroughly, no place of return is seen.
An ancient master used the metaphor of setting out a water vessel at midday: the water vessel is the eighth consciousness, and the sun is the six consciousnesses.
Because the sun takes the water within the vessel as its condition, [the reflections] float and move upon the walls.
Regarding the term "shadow-like manas" (*chāyā-manas*), here it refers to the manas in its entirety; this consciousness merely clings internally and does not perceive external objects.
As for the "subtle half," this refers to the subtle characteristics of two types: the six consciousnesses that internally perceive the *ālayavijñāna*, and the manas itself.
It is like a person eating an egg who, having peeled away the shell and divided it with their fingernails, observes the yolk within—the *ālaya*.
He also said: "This is what is called abiding in the whole while functioning as the *manas*.

It has already discarded the husk—the coarse aspects of the six consciousnesses that externally perceive all phenomena such as form and emptiness—yet its subtle membrane remains. Within its white portion, there is still a half-portion of extremely subtle aspects.
He asked again: "What is meant by 'appearing to exist yet not existing,' or 'exhausted yet not exhausted'? He replied: "Although it is seen..."

Consciousness remains present yet does not arise, as if existing and yet not existing. Although the objects of perception are exhausted, consciousness remains; thus, even if it appears exhausted, it is not truly exhausted.
It is called "Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception" because the nature of consciousness is immovable and the coarse perceptions of the sixth consciousness do not arise.
It is called "Non-Non-Perception" because although the coarse [perceptions] do not arise, the eighth consciousness continues its flow without ceasing. Furthermore, he asked: "What is 'Nothingness'?"

"Does the physical dimension have a lifespan? He replied: "Because that which is the retribution upon which consciousness relies is a conditioned phenomenon (*dharma*), and all conditioned phenomena must eventually reach their end;
therefore, even though it is called the 'Formless Realm,' it likewise possesses a lifespan. Maitreya said:
"The lifespan of the people of Jambudvīpa is not fixed. Those people take thirty days and nights as one month, and twelve such months [as one year]."
In one period their lifespan is one hundred years; in another period it is eighty years;
and in another period it gradually decreases until it reaches ten years.
The lifespan of the people of Pūrvavideha is fixed at two hundred and fifty years, while that of the people of Aparagoyānī is fixed at five hundred years.
In the northern continent of Uttarakuru, the lifespan of humans is fixed at one thousand years.
Furthermore, fifty human years constitute one day and night for the gods of the Cāturmahārājakāyika realm;
thirty such days and nights make one month, and twelve such months make one year. By this reckoning, the lifespan of the subsequent classes of gods is five hundred years in human terms.

One hundred years on earth constitutes one day and night for the gods of the Heaven of the Thirty-three (*Trāyastriṃśa*). With this day and night, as previously described, the lifespan of those gods is one thousand years.

In this manner, for all the remaining heavens up to the Heaven of Mastery over Others' Emanations (*Paranirmita-vaśavartin*), each subsequent day, night, and lifespan doubles that of the preceding one. Furthermore, such is the full lifespan of the gods of the Four Great Kings (*Cāturmahārājika*).
In this Saṃjīva Great Hell, one day and night is equivalent to thirty such days and nights;

twelve such months constitute one year. The lifespan in that Great Hell is five hundred years, which is equal to the lifespan of the gods of the Cāturmahārājakāyika realm. Thus is the lifespan in the Saṃjīva Great Hell established.
The lifespan of the Trāyastriṃśa gods constitutes the lifespan in the Kālasūtra great hell;
the lifespan of the Yāma gods constitutes the lifespan in the Saṃghāta great hell; the lifespan of the Tuṣita gods constitutes the lifespan in the Raurava great hell;
and the lifespan of the Nirmāṇarati gods constitutes the lifespan in the Mahāraurava great hell.
The lifespan in the hells should be understood as follows: the lifespan in the Saṃjīva (Reviving) hell is equal to the lifespan of the Paranirmita-vaśavartin gods;
the same applies to the Tapana (Heating) hell. In the Pratāpana (Intense Heating) hell, the lifespan of sentient beings is half an intermediate kalpa;
in the Avīci (Uninterrupted) hell, the lifespan of sentient beings is one intermediate kalpa. The lifespans of the non-gods (asuras) are like those of the three [classes of gods].
The life spans of the beings in the thirteen heavens, the animals, and the hungry ghosts are indefinite.
Furthermore, it should be understood that the life spans in the cold hells are successively half as long as those in the great hells when compared in order.
Additionally, the life spans of sentient beings born in the neighboring hells and the isolated hells are indefinite. The life span in the Heaven of the Brahma-multitude is twenty intermediate kalpas.

One kalpa is a *kalpa* prior to Brahmā; the lifespan of the gods in that realm is forty intermediate kalpas (*antarakalpa*). One kalpa is the lifespan of Mahābrahmā, which is sixty intermediate kalpas.
One kalpa is the lifespan of the Parīttābha (Limited Light) gods, which is eighty intermediate kalpas. Two kalpas [is the lifespan of the Ābhāsvara gods].

From this point upward, the lifespans of the remaining gods in the Form Realm (*rūpadhātu*) should be understood to increase progressively by double relative to one another, with the exception of the Anabhraka (Cloudless) gods. One should know this.
The lifespan of those devas is reduced by three eons: the lifespan in the Sphere of Infinite Space is twenty thousand eons;
in the Sphere of Infinite Consciousness, forty thousand eons; in the Sphere of Nothingness, sixty thousand eons; and in the Sphere of Neither-Perception-nor-Non-Perception, eighty thousand eons.
With the exception of the continent of Uttarakuru, all other realms include *pudgalas* who die prematurely.

This is called a *pudgala* (a "person" or "sentient being subject to rebirth"), meaning that ordinary beings, by virtue of the conditions of their wholesome or unwholesome karma, are born into the heavenly realms or fall into the three miserable states;
thus, they take up birth within the seven destinies without fixed duration. [Supplement]:

Regarding the lifespan discussed by Jiyin, it has not yet exhausted the calculations of the formation and destruction kalpas of the physical world (*bhājana-loka*), nor the increasing and decreasing of the lifespans within those seven destinies.
All of these take Jambudvīpa as the standard; furthermore, regarding one cycle of increase and decrease within a kalpa of abiding— comprising twenty such cycles of increase and decrease—
it is said that during a "kalpa of increase," when the lifespan of the people of Jambudvīpa has at various times decreased to a mere ten years,
a child born subsequently doubles it to fifteen years, gradually doubling again until it reaches eighty thousand years.
Because it lasts for four thousand years, it is called an *utsarpiṇī-kalpa* (increasing aeon) and an *avasarpiṇī-kalpa* (decreasing aeon).

For example, when the human lifespan decreases by one year per century, it gradually declines from eighty-four thousand years down to ten years; such a cycle of one increase and one decrease is termed a single *antarakalpa*.
Furthermore, during the decreasing aeon, when the human lifespan has decreased to thirty years, the *durbhikṣa-kalpa* (famine aeon) arises and lasts for seven [years].
When seven months and seven days of the [period of] famine have passed, human lifespan again decreases until it reaches twenty years, at which time the kalpa of disease arises;
after seven months and seven days, it ceases, and during this time people give rise to a middling degree of world-weariness (*saṃvega*). After this period of disease...
When the lifespan of humans has decreased again to ten years at the end of a kalpa, the *śastra-kalpa* (the age of weapons) arises and lasts for seven days before subsiding.
At that time, people give rise to a superior degree of weary detachment (*saṃvega*). Once this *śastra-kalpa* has passed, it is called a minor *tri-saṃvartanī-kalpa*.
This minor *tri-saṃvartanī-kalpa* destroys only sentient beings but does not destroy the physical world (*bhājana-loka*). As it is said: [text continues].
These twenty intermediate kalpas constitute the period of formation (*vivartakalpa*), which refers to the formation of the receptacle world (*bhājanaloka*).

When the receptacle world forms, it first forms from above in the third dhyāna heaven of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), and sequentially forms downward until the Yāma heaven of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
This is because those who dwell in the sky form from above downward. Following that, it first forms from below, starting with the wind-circle (*vāyumaṇḍala*).
The formation [of the world] from below up to the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven occurs because it relies upon the earth element; thus, having been formed from below, it becomes established above.

When these twenty intermediate kalpas of formation have been completed, there is the period of abiding (*sthiti-kalpa*). This means that once the world has been fully formed, it is capable of supporting sentient beings.
Within these twenty kalpas of abiding, each eon of increase (*utkarṣa-kalpa*) increases [the human lifespan] up to eighty-four thousand years.

At that time, there appeared a Wheel-Turning King who ruled over the world. During this period of decrease, within twenty kalpas of decline, one thousand Buddhas appear to transform the world, as occurred during the Bhadrakalpa when four Buddhas appeared in the ninth kalpa to transform the world.
When the lifespan decreased to sixty thousand years, Krakucchanda Buddha appeared to transform the world; it further decreased to—

When the human lifespan was forty thousand years, Konāgamana Buddha appeared to transform the world; when it further decreased to twenty thousand years, Kāśyapa Buddha appeared to transform the world;
and when it reached one hundred years, Śākyamuni Buddha appeared to transform the world.
During the eight preceding *kalpas*, no Buddhas appeared in the world; it was only upon reaching the tenth *kalpa* that the lifespan decreased to eight [thousand years].

During the ten thousand *kalpas* from the first to the fourteenth, Maitreya Buddha will appear to transform the world; during the eleventh through the fourteenth *kalpas*, no Buddhas will appear in the world.
During the fifteenth *kalpa*, nine hundred and ninety-four Buddhas will appear in succession to transform the world;
during the sixteenth through the nineteenth *kalpas*, no Buddhas will appear in the world. Then, during the twentieth *kalpa*, [the Buddha] Louzhi...

When a Buddha appears and transforms the world, within this world-system during the kalpa of abiding, there are one thousand Mount Sumerus, one thousand solar and lunar discs, and one thousand sets of four great continents, surrounded by a single Cakravāḍa mountain whose summit reaches up to the Second Dhyāna Heaven;
this is called a "small chiliocosm. One thousand small chiliocosms constitute a [medium] chiliocosm, surrounded by a single Cakravāḍa mountain whose summit reaches up to the Third [Dhyāna Heaven].

The dhyāna heavens are called a "small chiliocosm" (*sāhasra-cūḍika-lokadhātu*). A thousand small chiliocosms constitute one "middle chiliocosm," and its summit reaches up to the fourth dhyāna heaven;
this is called a "great trichiliocosm" (*trisāhasra-mahāsāhasra-lokadhātu*).
This is collectively termed the Sahā world, which is the realm transformed by a single Buddha and undergoes a single process of formation and destruction within each four-continent system.
Among these, there is one transformation body called the "thousand billion transformation bodies.

After remaining for twenty intermediate kalpas (*antarakalpa*), it is destroyed—meaning that the kalpa of abiding has reached its full term and the time for the kalpa of destruction (*saṃvartakalpa*) has arrived.

First, in the fire-kalpa, the co-arisen fire arises and destroys everything up to the second dhyāna heaven. Second, in the water-kalpa, the co-arisen water arises and destroys everything up to the third dhyāna heaven.

The three celestial wind-kalpas arise together with their co-nascent winds; they destroy everything up to the fourth dhyāna heaven, yet the fourth dhyāna heaven itself is not destroyed because it is characterized by the purity of equanimity and mindfulness.

These are called the great kalpas of the three calamities. These great kalpas of the three calamities destroy only the receptacle world (bhājana-loka) but do not destroy sentient beings; rather, sentient beings migrate to other realms or possess merit.
Those who possess the power of vows and samādhi are born among the gods of the Four Dhyāna Heavens.
Thus, after twenty intermediate kalpas of destruction, there is emptiness—meaning that the receptacle world has been destroyed and the kalpa of emptiness has arrived.

After the period of twenty empty kalpas has elapsed, the receptacle world is once again formed. In this way, the beginning and end of the receptacle world’s formation and destruction are linked together.
Because these cycles revolve in an unending stream, it is said that the total of eighty intermediate kalpas (antarakalpa) constitutes one great kalpa (mahākalpa).
Furthermore, Ānanda, within these three realms there are four classes of asuras; if they belong to the realm of hungry ghosts (preta),...

By the power of protecting the Dharma, they attain supernatural penetrations and enter into emptiness; these asuras are born from eggs and are categorized within the realm of hungry ghosts (preta-gati).
If they descend from the heavens due to a loss of merit and fall, their dwelling place is adjacent to the sun and moon;
these asuras are born from wombs and are categorized within the realm of humans (manuṣya-gati). There are asura kings who uphold the world, whose power is penetrating and fearless.
Able to contend for power with the Brahma King, Śakra Devendra, and the Four Heavenly Kings—these asuras arise through transformation and are subsumed within the heavenly realm, Ānanda.
Furthermore, there is a separate class of inferior asuras who are born from the depths of the great ocean and dwell at the mouths of underwater caverns;
they roam in the void by day and return to their watery abodes by night. These asuras arise from moisture and are thus categorized among the animal realm.

Included within the destinies: Ānanda, these seven destinies— namely hell-beings, hungry ghosts, animals, humans, seers and immortals, devas, and asuras— are all thoroughly investigated to be states of delusion,
characterized by all conditioned phenomena, where birth is received through false imagination and one follows karma through false imagination, [all occurring] within the Wondrous [Nature].
The perfectly luminous, unconditioned original mind is like flowers in the sky; fundamentally, it has nothing to which one can cling. It is merely a single delusion with no further root or thread.

Ānanda, these sentient beings do not recognize their original mind and thus undergo this saṃsāra for immeasurable kalpas, failing to attain true purity because they follow along with killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct. If they turn away from these three, they will instead give rise to liberation.

The absence of killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct is called the realm of ghosts; the presence [of these] is called the heavenly realm. As existence and non-existence incline toward one another, they give rise to the nature of saṃsāra.
If one attains the wondrous arousal of samādhi, then the wondrous is eternally quiescent; both existence and non-existence are absent, and even their non-duality ceases.

Since there is not even "non-killing, non-stealing, and non-sexual misconduct," how could one further follow after the matters of killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct? Ānanda, do not continue this way.
The three karmas each have their own private causes; because they arise from the various private aggregates and private commonalities, they are not without a fixed locus.

They are produced by one’s own delusions, yet this production of delusion has no cause and cannot be traced back to its origin. You must exert yourself in practice; if you wish to attain Bodhi, you must eliminate the three delusions.
If you do not exhaust these three delusions, even if you should attain supernormal powers, they will all be worldly, conditioned functions of habitual tendencies.
"Though one does not fall into the path of Māra, if one wishes to eliminate delusion yet instead redoubles one's falsehoods, the Tathāgata says such a person is to be pitied.
This delusion is self-created; it is not the fault of Bodhi. To speak thus is called the correct teaching;
if anyone speaks otherwise, that is the teaching of Māra."

Supplement: Regarding the various masters' judgments concerning the *parīndanā* (concluding) section for which no definitive consensus has been seen—some point to the passage following Mañjuśrī’s inquiry on the names in the eighth fascicle as the *parīndanā*;
some point to the section on the seven destinies in the ninth fascicle as the two-fold *parīndanā*;
and some point to the passage beginning "Ānanda, if there should be another person" in the tenth fascicle as the *parīndanā*. Now, if...

If the section following the inquiry into names were intended for the two types of circulation, why would Ānanda base his inquiry into the seven destinies upon the previously mentioned wondrously luminous and wondrous mind?

Furthermore, if the section following the seven destinies were intended for the two types of circulation, why would the Tathāgata specifically address the circulation of the gate of practice (*caryā-mukha*) at this point?
According to the sutra, it begins with Ānanda’s earnest and reverent request.
Regarding the initial expedient means for the sublime *śamatha*, *samādhi*, and *dhyāna*, up until [the stage of] the Tathāgata, [the Buddha] said to Ānanda:
"Although you possess a powerful memory and merely increase your extensive learning, you have not yet fully understood the subtle and secret contemplation of *śamatha* within the mind.
Subsequently, after he was about to conclude his discourse from the Dharma-seat, he again addressed the great assembly and Ānanda, saying: "You..."
It has not yet been recognized that the subtle demonic activities encountered while practicing *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā— from their beginning to their end—
do not transcend the essential principles of the contemplative practices of *śamatha*, *samādhi*, and *dhyāna*. From this,

one may know that from the section following the inquiry regarding the name until "If there be another person" below constitutes the *zhengzong* (the orthodox teaching), while the subsequent portion belongs to the *liutong* (the dissemination).
Question: What is meant by "having a name" in the realm of ghosts and "having no name" in the destiny of devas?
Answer: To follow and conform to killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct is "having" (the defilements); therefore, one falls into the four evil destinies, of which the realm of ghosts is one.

Conversely, to oppose these three—by not following and not conforming to killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct—is "not having" (the defilements); therefore, one is born into the three good destinies, of which the destiny of devas is one.
This is merely citing one example to establish the origins of the seven realms of existence.
Within the four evil and three good realms, there are distinctions between whether the three karmas are committed simultaneously or not; yet, though good and evil differ, saṃsāra is one and the same.
Thus, as good and evil mutually influence one another, beings transmigrate through the seven realms without rest. If one can skillfully give rise to samādhi...
If even those who uphold the precepts do not harbor a dualistic mind, how much less would they engage in acts of killing, stealing, or sexual misconduct?
The meaning of "Asura" is explained in the fifth fascicle, under the section "Those Who Possess Complete Merit."

Thereupon, the Tathāgata, having concluded his discourse from the Dharma-seat upon the lion throne, took up a seven-jeweled desk and turned toward the Purple Gold Mountain to lean against it once more.

He addressed the great assembly and Ānanda, saying: "You who are still in training—whether pratyekabuddhas or śrāvakas—who today have turned your minds toward the Great Bodhi and the unsurpassed, wondrous enlightenment: I have now expounded for you the method of true cultivation."
You still do not recognize the subtle demonic activities and the manifestation of demonic realms that arise during the cultivation of śamatha and vipaśyanā;
unable to discern them, you fail to purify your mind and instead fall into false views.
Whether it be the skandha-māra, the celestial māra, attachment to ghosts and spirits, or encounters with malevolent demons, your mind remains clouded, such that you mistake a thief for your own son.

Supplementary Note: The preceding text has already elucidated the characteristics of the turbid aggregates (*skandha*), yet it did not provide a detailed account of the sequence of the various demons (*māra*).
Now, these are presented again so that practitioners may dwell securely in *dhyāna* and *smṛti*, remaining unmoved by superior or wondrous states;
thus, the various demons will submit of their own accord without a battle. This is indeed the great purport of attaining Buddhahood.

Since ancient times, masters of the scholastic tradition have generally considered a broad mastery of the scriptures their primary task, rather than regarding the cultivation of samādhi as the essential secret;
consequently, they categorized it as merely for the purpose of dissemination.

Likewise, many enlightened practitioners of our own school have been intoxicated by polemical writings and have been unable to settle their spirits in the realm of refined investigation regarding the Three Decisions.
Because the definitions have lost their solemnity, one encounters circumstances and conditions that lead to being dismantled and distressed by Māra—how lamentable!
There are five kinds of *skandhas* (aggregates) which can shroud the true nature and cause ignorance to flourish; deluded conceptualization (*vikalpa*) is their root.

Thus, the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*) takes solidity to be deluded conceptualization, while the aggregate of sensation (*vedanāskandha*) takes vacuity and clarity to be deluded conceptualization. Regarding conceptualization...
The *āyatana* (spheres) take fusion and interpenetration as their delusive thought; the *skandha* of formations (*saṃskāra*) takes the obscure and hidden as its delusive thought;
and the *skandha* of consciousness (*vijñāna*) takes the indistinct, void, and inverted as its delusive thought.
Because one does not recognize the various demons that enter during *śamatha*, it is said that "cleansing the mind is not correct."

Furthermore, within this context, there are those who consider a small attainment to be sufficient—for instance, a monk of the fourth dhyāna who, lacking learning, falsely claims to have realized the state of an Arhat.
When his celestial retribution is exhausted and the signs of decline appear before him, he slanders the Arhats; his body then undergoes further existence and falls into the Avīci Hell.
You should listen attentively, for I shall now analyze this for you in detail. Ānanda rose from his seat, as did the rest of the assembly.
Together with the assembly of learners, they joyfully prostrated and humbly awaited his compassionate instruction.
The Buddha addressed Ānanda and the great multitude: "You should know that in this world of outflows, the twelve classes of beings possess a fundamentally enlightened and wondrous clarity;
the essence of their awakened, perfect mind is no different and not distinct from that of the Buddhas of the ten directions. It is only due to your deluded thoughts..."

Delusion regarding principle is the fault; from ignorance and craving, birth arises, and as birth repeatedly occurs, universal delusion ensues. Thus, although the nature of emptiness exists, the transformation of delusion does not cease, and the world-systems arise.
Consequently, these lands of the ten directions, as numerous as motes of dust, are all established through deluded, stubborn, and false imaginings, rather than being untainted.
You should know that empty space arises within your own mind, like a fragment of cloud appearing within the vast clarity of the great sky.
How much more so for all the worlds that exist within space? If even one of you develops true realization and returns to the source, this emptiness of the ten directions will entirely vanish;
how then could the lands existing within that space not tremble and shatter?
As you cultivate dhyāna and adorn your samādhi, the minds of the Bodhisattvas of the ten directions and the various stainless Great Arhats will penetrate in deep resonance with yours.
In that place, all was serene; yet the Māras, ghosts, spirits, and ordinary devas saw their palaces collapse and crack for no apparent reason, and the great earth tremble and split open.
Whether moving on land, in water, or through the air, none failed to be struck with terror. These ordinary beings, shrouded in darkness, did not perceive the calamity that had befallen them.
They all attained the five supernormal powers, yet—save for those who had exhausted their outflows—they remained attached to this world of dust and toil.
How could they possibly shatter that place? Therefore, when you are in samādhi, ghosts, spirits, celestial Māras, and all manner of demons and goblins come together to harass you.

Yet, though those Māras may be filled with great rage, within your wondrous enlightenment amidst their defilements, they are like wind blowing against light or a blade cutting through water; they do not touch you at all. You are like boiling water.
It is like solid ice that gradually encounters warm breath; it will melt away before long. To rely merely on the power of spiritual penetrations is to treat them as mere guests.
Because you allow the master of the five *skandhas* within your own mind to become deluded, these guests gain the upper hand.
If you abide in *dhyāna* and awaken without confusion, then those demonic affairs will be powerless against you; as the *skandhas* dissolve and enter into clarity, they will vanish.

Thus, those various evils all receive dark energy; yet clear wisdom can shatter darkness, and as it draws near, they will naturally perish. How could they dare remain to disturb your meditative concentration?
If you do not attain clear awakening and are deluded by these shadows, then you, Ānanda, will surely become a child of Māra and accomplish the work of Māra.
Compared to that Dengga, who was merely a sorceress who broke the Buddha’s precepts, you would be far more insignificant and inferior. She only cast spells upon you to destroy the Vinaya.
Among the eighty thousand practices, even if one violates but a single precept, because the mind remains pure, one has not yet fallen into ruin;

yet this [violation] destroys your entire body of precious enlightenment, like a high minister’s family suddenly encountering a total confiscation of property—left to wither away and fall apart beyond all hope of rescue.
The treatise says: A monk who has not heard the true Dharma, through unremitting diligence, attains the stages from the first dhyāna up to the fourth dhyāna.
Having become free from the eight calamities, he believes he has realized the fruit of arhatship and no longer cultivates further progress.

When it is time for his transformation, he perceives that within the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) of the fourth dhyāna there is still rebirth. Consequently, he suddenly gives rise to slander and thus falls into wrong view. This is the Heaven of No-Thought (*asaṃjñisattva-deva*).
Because one dies in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) and falls into the evil destinies, it is said that "one considers a little to be sufficient.

The World-Honored One, in this assembly, used Ānanda as an occasion to proclaim this profound mystery; yet, mindful that future generations might fall into the obstacle of limited learning, he spoke again of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), each from its coarsest to its subtlest aspect, until their dissolution. At the time of death, there are ten realms of perception, which are like this: [the following list follows].
The compassionate mother assisted her daughter as she ascended the carriage, earnestly admonishing her to guard against lapses and harboring deep anxiety for her. She asked:
"If one person awakens to the Truth and returns to the Source, the voids of the ten directions will all vanish; this is possible for me alone.
Yet you say that all the Demon Kings, ghosts, spirits, and ordinary devas see their palaces [vanish]..."
Therefore, why does it collapse and shatter? It is said: Whatever is originally non-existent and now exists cannot be trusted. Why? Because it is a provisional dharma (*prajñapti-dharma*).

Provisional dharmas depend on mental states (*citta*), and these states exist through conceptualization (*vikalpa*), like the moon in water; it is not apprehended by the sense-base of the eye, yet the mind conceives of it as existing.
If one awakens to the fact that the three realms are but mind-only, there is only one state of quiescent extinction (*śānta-nirvāṇa*).
Within the state of quiescent extinction, there may still exist the Māras, spirits, ordinary beings, and classes of devas;
it is like a single thread within a blazing furnace. Therefore it is asked: "How can the lands existing within space not tremble and shatter? The answer is:
You should know that space arises within your own mind, just as a fragment of cloud appears within the vast clarity of the great sky. Thus, [the lands] are contained therein.
"Emptiness arises within the Great Enlightenment, like a single bubble emerging from the ocean; how much more so the various worlds within empty space?

Thus, through delusion and falsehood there is empty space, and based upon that emptiness, the worlds are established. If even one among you awakens to the truth and returns to the source, this empty space of the ten directions will all vanish and perish.
Since the bubble has ceased, the emptiness was originally non-existent—how much less so the three realms?"

"It is so. Ānanda, you should know that when you sit at the site of enlightenment and cause all thoughts to fall away, once those thoughts are exhausted, then all states of clarity and brilliance that are free from thought will remain unmoved by motion or stillness;
recollection and forgetfulness will become one. You should abide in this state and enter *samādhi*."
It is like a person with clear vision situated in great darkness; though the essence of the mind is wondrously pure, its light has not yet emerged.

This is called the realm of the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*). If the eyes become bright and clear, so that the ten directions open up and there is no more gloom, this is called the exhaustion of the aggregate of form.
Such a person is then able to transcend the turbidity of the kalpa (*kalpa-kaṣāya*). If one examines its origin, one finds that it is rooted in the delusion of solidity.

Ānanda, if you should investigate this subtle clarity within with such intensity that the four elements no longer obstruct one another, and in a brief moment your body can pass through barriers—this is called the overflowing of refined energy into the objective field.
This is merely a temporary attainment resulting from your practice; it is not a holy realization.
If you do not regard it as a holy state, it is called a "wholesome realm"; if you mistake it for a holy realization, you will immediately be possessed by various demons.
Ānanda, if one again uses this mind to investigate the subtle clarity until it penetrates the interior of the body, that person may suddenly pick out roundworms or maggots from within their own body;
yet the physical form remains intact, without injury or damage. This is called the overflowing of refined spirit into the physical body;
it is merely a temporary attainment resulting from refined practice and is not a holy realization. If one does not claim it to be a holy realization, it is called wholesome.
If one interprets these objective realms as being the realization of a sage, one will immediately succumb to various heterodox influences.

Furthermore, when this mind is scrutinized with precision both internally and externally, the *po*, *hun*, *yi*, and *shen* spirits—excluding the body which they grasp and sustain—all enter into mutual interaction, each acting alternately as guest or host.
Suddenly, one may hear the sound of the Dharma being preached in the void, or hear it from the ten directions.
I shall likewise expound the profound meaning of this: when the vital essence and the spirit separate and then reunite, one achieves a virtuous seed and temporarily attains such states;

yet these are not the realization of a sage. If you do not conceive of them as the realization of a sage, they are called "auspicious realms"; if you interpret them as the realization of a sage, you will immediately succumb to various demonic influences.
Furthermore, when this mind is clear, luminous, and penetrating, illuminating both internally and externally, the ten directions everywhere take on the color of Jambūnada gold.

All manner of forms transform into Tathāgatas; at that moment, one suddenly beholds Vairocana seated upon a platform of celestial light, surrounded by a thousand Buddhas, appearing simultaneously with ten billion lands and lotus flowers.

This is called the heart-soul’s spiritual awakening and the illumination of the mind-light through refinement, which shines upon all worlds. To experience this momentarily is not yet a holy realization.
Not conceiving a holy mind is called a wholesome state; if one forms a holy interpretation, one will immediately succumb to various evils.

Furthermore, when this mind investigates the subtle brilliance with ceaseless observation, suppressing, subduing, restraining, and transcending, there may suddenly arise a time when the empty space of the ten directions becomes the color of the seven treasures or the hundred treasures, simultaneously filling all places.
When blue, yellow, red, and white appear purely and distinctly without obstructing one another, this is called the power of suppression exceeding its limit;

such a state may be attained temporarily, but it is not a realization of sainthood. If you do not conceive of it as a state of sainthood, it is a favorable condition; however, if you interpret it as a realization of sainthood, you will immediately be possessed by various demons.
Furthermore, by using this mind to investigate until it is transparent and pure, its refined radiance remains undisturbed;
suddenly, in the middle of the night within a dark room, one sees various objects no different from those seen in broad daylight, yet the objects in the dark room do not vanish.

This is called the mind being subtle and dense, its vision clarified so that what is seen penetrates the profound darkness; having attained such a state for a time, do not regard it as a holy realization, nor give rise to the thought of being a sage.
If one regards such a state as a "wholesome realm" and forms a holy understanding of it, one will immediately succumb to various demonic influences.
Furthermore, by means of this mind, one may enter a state of perfect emptiness and fusion such that the four limbs suddenly become like grass and wood;
even if burned by fire or cut with a blade, there is no sensation at all. Moreover, the flames cannot burn or heat, and even if one's flesh is sliced, it is just like carving wood.
This is called the simultaneous merging of sensory objects with the four great elements, wherein their natures temporarily attain such a state of pure uniformity; it is not a holy realization.
If one does not conceive of it as a holy attainment, it is called a "wholesome state"; if one interprets it as a holy realization, one will immediately succumb to various demonic influences.

Furthermore, as this mind achieves the perfection of pure and refined mental cultivation, suddenly the great earth, the mountains, and rivers of the ten directions are all seen to become Buddha-lands, complete with the seven treasures and filled with pervasive radiance.
One also sees Buddhas and Tathāgatas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges filling the void, their towers and palaces magnificent and resplendent;
looking down, one perceives the hells, and looking up, one beholds the celestial palaces, attaining unimpeded vision.
This is called the state of joy and aversion where focused contemplation deepens daily; as the contemplation lasts long, it transforms into something non-substantial. It is not a holy realization;
if one does not conceive of it as a holy attainment, it is called a "wholesome realm. If one takes it to be a holy realization, one will immediately succumb to various demonic influences.

Furthermore, using this mind to investigate the profound and far-reaching, one may suddenly see, in the middle of the night, distant marketplaces, streets, alleys, kinsmen, or relatives, or hear their voices.
This is called the "oppressed mind" (p'o-hsin); because it is driven to its extreme limit, it flies out, resulting in many such visions of things separated by distance.

This is not a realization of the sages; if one does not conceive the thought of attaining sagehood, it is called a favorable state. If one interprets it as the realization of a sage, one will immediately fall under the influence of various demonic influences.

Furthermore, if you use this mind to investigate with extreme intensity and perceive the physical form of a spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra) shifting and changing, undergoing various transformations in an instant without apparent cause, this is called a deluded mind harboring demons or being possessed by a celestial Māra entering its heart and belly.
Such a person may suddenly preach the Dharma and penetrate subtle meanings, yet these are not signs of saintly realization. If you do not regard them as such, the demonic activities will subside.
If one forms a holy interpretation of these states, one will immediately succumb to various demonic influences.

Ānanda, these ten kinds of manifested realms during *dhyāna* are all appearances resulting from the mutual interaction of the mind with the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*); thus these matters manifest.
When sentient beings are stubborn and deluded, failing to reflect upon themselves, they encounter these conditions and, being lost, fail to recognize them for what they are, saying:
To claim to have attained sainthood through a great falsehood is to fall into the Avīci Hell.

You all should, after the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa, during the age of the Final Dharma, proclaim and reveal this meaning so that no celestial Māras may find an opportunity; protect and sustain it, and thereby achieve the Unsurpassed Way.

Supplement: All demons dwell in dependence upon false conceptualization (*vikalpa*); the aggregates (*skandha*) belong to this conceptualization. When conceptualization ceases, the aggregates dissolve and the demons naturally go into hiding.
As long as the aggregates persist and conceptualization remains, the demons will find the opportunity to watch for a rift.

For one who enters *samādhi*, the essential point is not to be deluded regarding the master of the five aggregates, but to personally recognize the countenance of that master and know the place where he dwells. If...
If one recognizes their faces and knows their dwelling places, what power can the Māras possibly exert?
How could they wait for the gradual warming of their breath before being able to eliminate them? The World-Honored One said to Ānanda:
"If you do not recognize the location of the mind's eye, you will be unable to subdue the dust and toil of the senses. For this reason, the masters of old frequently called out to themselves.
The Master replied for himself, "Yes. He spoke again: "Stay alert! At a later time, do not allow others to deceive you!

Alas, this may be called true knowledge and true realization. Had he not attained such true knowledge and true realization, when encountering the manifest states of *dhyāna*, he would have followed the Tathāgata’s warning and not claimed the realization of sainthood.
Then one may hope for progress. Upon entering this aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*), all discursive thoughts dissolve and fall away;

movement and stillness do not shift [the mind], like a person with clear vision situated in great darkness because the mind has not yet emitted light. When one does not interweave with the four great elements, the body is able to pass through obstructions;
thus it flows over the objective realm. When the body penetrates inwardly, the physical characteristics remain distinct; thus it flows [back].
When it overflows within and without the physical form and is refined through intensive study, the internal and external act as guest and host to one another;
thus they alternate between separation and union. When clarity is revealed with pure transparency, it illuminates all worlds.

Because spiritual awakening is what colors the experience, observation never ceases, and thus its power exceeds ordinary limits. Because the refined light is not disordered, the vision is secretly clarified; therefore, whatever is beheld...
When one penetrates the profound mystery and enters the roundness of the void and fusion, one casts off the nature of the four great elements; therefore, there is nothing perceived.

When the function of stilling the mind reaches its ultimate limit, one attains non-obstruction; therefore, when concentrated contemplation deepens day by day and investigation becomes profound and far-reaching, one is so intensely pressed that one flies out.

Because of many obstructions to vision, when research reaches its most refined extreme, one comes to contain and receive even mountain spirits and demons; therefore, one preaches the Dharma without any apparent cause.

Furthermore, the kalpa-turbidity exists in dependence upon the aggregate of form; if this aggregate is exhausted, the ten directions open up in clarity, for it is not that space and vision are not distinct, but rather that one is able to transcend them.
The "Collected Explanation of the Four Limbs" treats them as the four parts of the body.

Ānanda, when that good man, while practicing samādhi and śamatha, has exhausted the aggregate of form (rūpa-skandha), he perceives the minds of all Buddhas appearing like reflections in a clear mirror. Although there is something attained, he is as yet unable to employ it;

he is like a person suffering from somnambulism whose hands and feet are perfectly present and whose sight and hearing are unconfused, yet whose mind is touched by an external evil spirit so that he cannot move. This, then, is...
This is called the domain of the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*). If the affliction of being stifled by a nightmare ceases, the mind departs from the body and looks back at its own face;

it can go or stay with freedom, no longer hindered by obstructions. This is called the exhaustion of the aggregate of sensation. Such a person is then able to transcend the turbidity of views (*dṛṣṭi-kaṣāya*).
Observing its origin, one finds that empty, luminous false imagination is its root.

Ānanda, that good man, while in this state, will attain a great radiance; his mind becomes luminous, yet because he suppresses it excessively within, a boundless compassion suddenly arises from that place.
Thus, even when looking at mosquitoes or gadflies, he regards them as his own infants, giving rise to a heart of pity and involuntarily shedding tears.
This is called the "excessive suppression and crushing of effort"; if one awakens to it, [it is not an obstacle].
Being free from fault does not constitute proof of saintliness; rather, it is the realization of awakening without delusion, which naturally dissipates over time.

If you mistake this for the attainment of sainthood, the demon of compassion will enter your heart and viscera; you will see people and weep boundlessly, losing correct meditative absorption (*samyaksamādhi*) and falling into ruin.

Ānanda, furthermore, within that state of concentration, those good sons who see the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) dissolve and the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*) become clear, and for whom superior signs manifest before them, may suddenly experience an excess of agitation.

Within this state, they give rise to boundless courage; their minds become fierce and sharp, and their resolve becomes equal to that of the Buddhas, thinking that the three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas* can be transcended in a single thought-moment.
This is called "the transgression of overreaching through effortful application" (*yònggōng lǐngshuài guòyuè*). If they awaken to it, [they will not fall].
"Being free from fault is not yet the realization of a sage; it is merely being awakened and free from delusion, which will naturally dissipate over time.
If you take this to be the attainment of sagehood, then a mad demon will enter your heart and viscera. When you see others, you will boast that your self-conceit is peerless.
Your mind will reach such a state that you neither look up to the Buddhas nor look down upon men; you will lose right concentration and inevitably fall into ruin."
Furthermore, within that samādhi, certain sons of good family perceive the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) dissolving and the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*) becoming clear.
Having nothing new to realize before them, they lose their hold on what they previously dwelt in; their power of wisdom declines and they fall into a state of desolation, seeing nothing at all.
Suddenly, a great parching thirst arises within their minds, and at all times they remain immersed in this recollection without dispersal, taking this very state to be the mark of diligent vigor.
This is called cultivating the mind without wisdom; though one may lose oneself, there is no fault in awakening. It is not a realization of the sages.

If you take this for a realization of sainthood, then the demon of recollection will enter your heart and viscera. Morning and evening it will seize the mind and suspend it in a single place, causing you to lose right concentration and leading you inevitably to fall into ruin.
Furthermore, within that samādhi, certain sons of good family perceive the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) dissolving and the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*) becoming clear and bright.

Because their power of wisdom exceeds the concentration, they lose its sharp intensity; harboring various superior natures within their minds, they themselves become suspicious that they are Vairocana, and taking this minor attainment as sufficient.
This is called losing constant discernment through the application of the mind, thereby drowning in intellectual views; yet if they awaken to this, there is no fault.
This is not a true realization of the holy state; if one mistakes it for such a realization, the demon of inferiority and easy contentment will enter one’s heart and marrow.
Seeing others speak of having attained the Unsurpassed Ultimate Truth (paramārtha-satya), one loses right concentration (samādhi) and shall surely fall away.

Furthermore, within that state of meditative absorption, those good sons see the aggregate of form (rūpa-skandha) vanish and the aggregate of sensation (vedanā-skandha) become clear, yet they have not yet attained a new realization.
Therefore, with the mind already lost, one surveys the two limits and naturally encounters hardship and peril.

Within the mind, an inexhaustible sorrow suddenly arises, like sitting upon an iron bed or drinking a poisonous drug; the heart has no desire to live and constantly seeks someone to end its life for the sake of early liberation.
This is called "losing the skillful means" in practice; if one awakens to it, there is no fault, yet it does not constitute a realization of sainthood.
If one forms a holy understanding [of these states], then a portion of the Māra of Constant Sorrow will enter their heart and viscera; grasping a sword or blade, they will cut their own flesh,
rejoicing in the relinquishing of their life-span, or being constantly sorrowful, they will flee into mountain forests, unable to bear seeing people,
and having lost right concentration (*samyaksamādhi*), they shall fall into ruin.

Furthermore, within that meditative concentration, when those good sons perceive the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) dissolving and the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*) becoming clear and pure, they experience a sense of security.
Suddenly, an infinite joy arises within their hearts, such that their delight cannot be restrained. This is called "light ease" (*praśrabdhi*).
If one lacks wisdom and fails to restrain oneself, there is no fault; however, it is not a realization of the holy ones. If one takes this to be a holy attainment, [it is a delusion].
Then there is a class of beings who are possessed by the demon of "delightful joy," which enters their hearts and viscera;

seeing people on the roadsides, they laugh, sing, and dance, claiming for themselves that they have attained unimpeded liberation, yet they have lost right concentration and are destined for downfall.

Furthermore, those good sons within meditative absorption see the aggregate of form (rūpa-skandha) dissolve and the aggregate of sensation (vedanā-skandha) become clear, whereupon they claim to be fully satisfied.

Suddenly, groundless and great conceit arises; thus it continues until conceit, excessive conceit, and even super-conceit—or overweening conceit, or the conceit of inferiority—all break out simultaneously.
Within the mind, one holds even the Tathāgatas of the ten directions in contempt, let alone those of lower rank such as Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas.
This is called "seeing oneself as superior. If there is no wisdom to save oneself, this is a fault; yet if one awakens to it, there is no blame.
This is not a sign of saintly realization; if one mistakes it for such realization, then a portion of the Great Māra of Arrogance will enter their heart and viscera.
They will fail to pay homage to stupas and temples and will destroy scriptures and images. They will say to donors, "These [images] are merely gold and copper, or perhaps clay and wood;
these scriptures are but tree leaves or layered flowers. Thus, while their own physical bodies are truly eternal, they fail to show them respect, yet instead venerate clay and wood.

This is indeed a perversion; those who have deep faith will, because of this destruction, bury it in the earth, leading deluded sentient beings into the Avīci Hell and causing them to lose right concentration and fall into ruin.
Furthermore, within that meditative concentration, those good sons see the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) dissolve and the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*) become clear and bright.

Within their refined spirit, they perfectly realize the principle of essence and attain great compliance. Suddenly, their minds give rise to immeasurable lightness and ease, whereupon they claim to have attained sainthood and achieved great self-mastery.
This is called "attaining various states of lightness and purity through wisdom. Such realization is without fault and does not constitute a false certification of sainthood.
If one takes this to be a realization of the holy, then a portion of the "light-and-pure" demon will enter their heart and viscera;

they will consider themselves satisfied and no longer seek further progress. Such people mostly become unlearned bhikṣus who mislead sentient beings, causing them to fall into the Avīci Hell and lose right concentration, thereby falling into ruin.

Furthermore, when those good sons within that samādhi perceive the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) dissolving and the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*) becoming clear and bright, they attain a nature of empty luminosity within their enlightened understanding.
Suddenly, they turn toward eternal extinction, repudiating cause and effect and entering exclusively into emptiness;
as this empty mind manifests before them, they develop a long-standing understanding of annihilationism. This is not a fault, nor is it a realization of the holy.

If one forms a holy understanding [of these experiences], then the "emptiness-demon" (śūnyatā-māra) will enter their heart and viscera; they will then slander those who uphold the precepts, calling them followers of the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna).

Believing they have realized emptiness, the Bodhisattva will think, "What is there to be held or transgressed? Consequently, they will constantly drink wine and eat meat, and engage extensively in sexual misconduct before faithful donors.
Due to the power of this demon, it will cause those people before them to harbor no suspicion or slander; thus, the ghost’s influence will long take hold.

Or, they may consume excrement, urine, wine, meat, and the like; as both [the practice and the result] are empty, they violate the Buddha’s disciplinary code, lead others into transgression, lose right concentration (*samyaksamādhi*), and shall surely fall into ruin.

Furthermore, within that state of meditative absorption, those sons of good family see the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*) dissolve and the aggregate of sensation (*vedanāskandha*) become clear and bright, savoring its empty luminosity.
When this state penetrates deep into the marrow and a sudden, boundless love arises within the mind, and the intensity of this love leads to madness, it becomes mere craving.

This is called the "state of concentration" (*samādhi-viṣaya*), which enters the mind with ease and compliance. If one lacks wisdom to maintain oneself and mistakenly enters into various desires, there is no fault upon awakening;
however, if one takes this to be a realization of sainthood (*ārya-siddhi*), then the demon of desire will enter one's heart and entrails, leading one to speak only of desire.
To transform laypeople for the sake of the path to Bodhi, he causes them to practice desire with equanimity; those who engage in sexual conduct are called "sons of the Dharma.

By the power of spirits and deities, during the final age, they gather together the ordinary and ignorant, their number reaching as many as one hundred, two hundred, five, six, or seven hundred, or even up to ten million. When the demons' minds become weary and detached, their physical bodies [perish].
Since their majestic virtue is lacking, they will fall into royal calamity; they will mislead sentient beings into the Avīci Hell and lose their right concentration, inevitably falling into ruin.

Ānanda, these ten kinds of present manifestations during *dhyāna* are all appearances resulting from the interaction between the mind and the *vedanā-skandha* (the aggregate of sensation). Thus they appear.

These beings are stubborn and deluded, failing to reflect upon themselves; encountering such causes and conditions, they remain confused and fail to recognize them for what they are, claiming instead that they have attained sainthood.

By committing this great falsehood, they fall into the Avīci Hell. You all should likewise take these words of the Tathāgata and, after my parinirvāṇa, transmit and reveal them during the Final Dharma age, so as to cause all beings everywhere to awaken to this meaning, and not allow celestial Māras to seize their opportunity.
Through skillful means, they maintain and protect [the mind] to accomplish the Unsurpassed Way.
Supplement: Entering this aggregate of sensation (vedanā-skandha), one perceives the minds of all Buddhas like images in a clear mirror;
yet because there is something apprehended that cannot yet be employed, one is like a person in a nightmare. Upon attaining great radiance, there is no longer any lingering obstruction.
When the supreme manifestation of boundless compassion appears before one, infinite joy arises;

when one is arrogant, transgressive, and the power of wisdom has declined, great parching thirst arises; when lacking wisdom and losing the power of wisdom due to over-transcending meditative concentration, one becomes satisfied with meager attainment;
and when mired in views and surveying the two extremes, inexhaustible sorrow arises—thus [the practitioner] is lost.
Because after finding peace in the mind through skillful means, limitless joy arises; because without wisdom, one restrains oneself and considers it sufficient, whereby great conceit arises;
because without wisdom, one seeks self-deliverance and perfects the subtle principle, thereby attaining various states of lightness and purity;
because having attained the nature of empty luminosity, one no longer seeks further progress and enters exclusively into emptiness; thus, [the path] is long severed.
When one extinguishes the understanding of its flavor and its void-brightness, limitless craving arises; thus, one mistakenly enters into various desires.

When this sensation is completely eliminated, one can detach from the body and contemplate it without further obstruction; therefore, one transcends the turbidity of views. The Ever-Bright One (Nityaprabha) bestowed these precepts, saying:
"If you see handsome men or women, regard them as if they were corpses; only then may you engage in sexual desire. It would be as if one were cutting out one's own heart."
If one’s liver feels like wood or stone, then one may eat meat; if drinking wine feels like consuming excrement or urine, then one may drink wine.
These are also words of skillful means. Viewed through the words of the Tathāgata, this is precisely because one has been entered by the demon of emptiness.
Alas! How lamentable it is! The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states: "The Māra can enter all assemblies."

They give rise to thoughts that cause them to take refuge in the factions of Māra, becoming as inseparable as glue or lacquer; they do not consider it difficult even to have their hands severed or their arms cut off.

Because they are possessed by the power of Māra, all people believe in and submit to them. The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* states: "Deeply attached to false and illusory dharmas, they stubbornly cling to them and refuse to relinquish them;
thus they slander those who uphold the precepts. This refers to such persons.
Ānanda, when that good man cultivates samādhi and the aggregate of sensation (vedanā-skandha) is exhausted, although his outflows (āsrava) are not yet ended,
his mind is detached from its physical form like a bird escaping from a cage. He is already able to achieve the body of intent-birth (manomaya-kāya),
ascending from this ordinary body through the sixty sagely stages of a Bodhisattva, proceeding everywhere without obstruction.

Supplement: Regarding the textual structure of the "Summation of Positions," there are three sections. Following the Ten Dedications (*daśa-pariṇāmanā*), it says: "All these constitute the forty-one minds;
next, one accomplishes the four kinds of wondrously perfect preparatory practices. Following the Ten Grounds (*daśa-bhūmi*), it says:
"Thus, by means of the three progressive advancements, one is well able to accomplish the fifty-five positions of the true path to Bodhi. This refers to the stage of Receiving [the Prediction].

Where the aggregates (skandhas) are exhausted, it is said that from this point onward, the ordinary person ascends through the sixty sacred stages of a Bodhisattva to attain the mind-born body (manomayakāya), proceeding everywhere without obstruction.
When the ignorant masses first read this sutra and reach this passage, they privately say to themselves:
"The preceding summary text categorized the Dry Wisdom, the Ten Faiths, the Ten Abidings, the Ten Practices, and the Ten Dedications as forty [stages]."
Once, when the four *anāgāmin* stages and the ten *bhūmis* were added to the [original] fifty, they became fifty-five;
this must mean that the three types of progress (*tri-vidha-viśeṣa*) and the two types of perfect enlightenment (*samyak-sambodhi*) constitute the sixty.

Later, reading the *Jijie*, I saw the words annotated by Gushan, which accorded with my own view as if fitting together like the two halves of a tally. I realized that in past lives, I too had once cultivated them with diligence.
I have examined this and read the *Wujin haiyan* (The Eye of the Infinite Ocean), which states: "This passage is an error of the translator;
moreover, there is no mention of 'sixty stages of sagehood,' and since the commentators have further forced a reconciliation, they only serve to obstruct the true principle.
Thus, he deleted the twenty-four characters: "Already able to achieve unimpededness wherever one goes. I am unable to know [the full extent of his reasoning].

These three advancements, situated beyond the four stages known as the "Instructions" (*śikṣā*) and preceding the initial stage of Dry Wisdom (*śuklavipaśyanā-bhūmi*), separately encompass a class of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) of great capacity;

therefore, it is said that "the flow is reversed and the six functions cease," and again, "this person immediately attains the patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*). Furthermore, it is subsequently stated: "All these are by means of the three advancements."
Because of this progressive advancement, one is well able to accomplish the fifty-five stages of the true path to Bodhi; how could this be in vain?

Since it is said that one ascends from this ordinary body through the sixty sacred stages of a Bodhisattva, is it not because these are combined and concluded by means of the three types of advancement (*tri-viśeṣa*) together with the two awakenings of Equality (*samatā*) and Subtlety (*pratyakṣa*)?
