If one were to establish only fifty-five stages, then...

Regarding the two types of awakening—the equal and the wondrous—where do they lead? Although all stages prior to the [first] bhūmi belong to the rank of the worthy (ārya), this stage is not a step ascended by celestial beings or non-Buddhists;
rather, it is the path traversed by the Tathāgatas of the three periods of time. Therefore, it is collectively termed "sage" (ārya).
This is because the forty-one minds and fifty-five stages have not yet reached the ultimate fruit. Thus, [the distinction is made].

This refers to the present exhaustion of the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*), which is like the delirious speech of one in deep sleep; as one approaches the ultimate state of sainthood (*ārya-pada*), these are therefore combined and summarized.
For example, suppose there is a person in deep sleep who speaks in their dreams; although this person has no distinct cognition, the words they utter are nonetheless formed.
The sequential order of phonemes causes those who cannot sleep to fully comprehend their meaning; this is called the realm of the *saṃskāra-skandha* (the aggregate of mental formations).

If all stirring thoughts are exhausted and floating imaginings are eliminated, such that the awakened, luminous mind is like a heart free from dust and grime, and one perfectly illuminates the beginning and end of the cycle of birth and death within a single category, this is called the exhaustion of the *saṃskāra-skandha*.
Such a person is then able to transcend the turbidity of afflictions (*kleśa-kaṣāya*) by observing its origin.
The fusion of delusive thoughts serves as its foundation.

Ānanda, when that virtuous man’s aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*) becomes void and subtle, and he is no longer beset by deviant thoughts, his perfect concentration manifests and he enters *samādhi*.

At that time, his heart comes to cherish this perfect clarity; he sharpens his refined contemplation and greedily seeks out skillful methods. It is then that the celestial Māra watches for an opportunity to seize him.

They then dispatch their refined essence to enter a person’s mouth to preach the Dharma; that person is unaware they are possessed by a demon and claims for themselves that they have attained unsurpassed *nirvāṇa*.
They come to the dwelling of a seeker of skillful means, a son of good family, where they arrange a seat and preach the Dharma.
For a brief moment, their form may appear as a bhikṣu so that the person may see them, or they may become Śakra, or a woman, or a [lay] brother.
A bhikṣuṇī may sleep in a dark room while her body emits light; such a person is deluded by folly and deceives others into believing she is a bodhisattva.

Trusting her teachings, they have their minds shaken and agitated, breaking the Buddha’s disciplinary code as they secretly practice lust. She delights in speaking of calamities, auspicious signs, and supernatural transformations;
she may claim that the Tathāgata has appeared in a certain place, or speak of the kalpa-ending conflagration, or describe the terrors of war.

If they cause a person’s family wealth to dissipate for no reason, this is called a "strange ghost" (*guǐkuài*). When old, it becomes a demon that harasses and disturbs the person until it feels satiated;
having developed such thoughts, it leaves the person's body. Both the disciple and the master will then fall into royal punishment.
You must be aware of this beforehand so as not to enter the cycle of rebirth; if you are deluded and unaware, you will fall into the Avīci Hell.

Ānanda, furthermore, when a good man’s aggregate of sensation (vedanā-skandha) becomes empty and subtle, and he is not beset by deviant thoughts, his perfect concentration gives rise to illumination within the *samādhi*. At that time, his mind may come to love wandering about, causing his refined thoughts to fly forth as he greedily seeks out experiences. Then, a celestial Māra waits for such an opportunity and sends forth his essence to possess a person, who speaks of sutras and dharmas; yet the person does not realize they are possessed by a Māra, and says: ... [The remainder of the passage continues with the description of the various forms of possession and the resulting delusions. ... Thus, Ānanda, these are the various demonic states arising from the aggregate of sensation. If one can recognize them and remain unmoved, one will transcend them. If one fails to recognize them and allows oneself to be moved, one will fall into the various realms of suffering. This is called the "Demonic State of the Aggregate of Sensation. If one can recognize it, one will transcend it; if one cannot recognize it, one will fall into it. Therefore, you should be careful to examine and distinguish them. Do not let your mind be moved, lest you fall into the net of demons and lose your original nature. You should now carefully observe these matters. If you do not understand them, you will surely fall into the path of demons. If you understand them, you will attain liberation. Thus, Ānanda, you should know that these are the various demonic states arising from the aggregate of sensation. If one can recognize them and remain unmoved, one will transcend them. If one fails to recognize them and allows oneself to be moved, one will fall into the various realms of suffering. This is called the "Demonic State of the Aggregate of Sensation. If one can recognize it, one will transcend it; if one cannot recognize it, one will fall into it. Therefore, you should be careful to examine and distinguish them. Do not let your mind be moved, lest you fall into the net of demons and lose your original nature. You should now carefully observe these matters. If you do not understand them, you will surely fall into the path of demons. If you understand them, you will attain liberation. Thus, Ānanda, you should know that these are the various demonic states arising from the aggregate of sensation. If one can recognize them and remain unmoved, one will transcend them. Since attaining unsurpassed *nirvāṇa*, whenever he visits the abodes of those sons of good family seeking the Way to spread his seat and preach the Dharma, his own form undergoes no change;
yet those who listen to the Dharma suddenly see themselves sitting upon jeweled lotus flowers, their entire bodies transformed into a mass of purple-gold light.
Each person in the assembly experiences this, attaining what they have never known before. These people, deluded by folly, take this to be [the attainment of Buddhahood].
The Bodhisattva’s mind becomes licentious and he violates the Buddha’s Vinaya, secretly practicing lustful desires. He delights in saying that various Buddhas have appeared in the world;

he claims that a certain person in a certain place must be the emanation of a certain Buddha come here, or that such-and-such a person is a certain Bodhisattva who has come to transform the human realm.
When people see him, their hearts become filled with longing and craving, and wrong views secretly arise, obstructing the seed of wisdom.
The eradication of this [demon] is the *pātra* ghost who, having grown old, becomes a *māra* to harass and disturb this person;
once it has become satiated, it leaves the person's body, and both the disciple and the teacher fall into royal peril. You should perceive this beforehand so as not to enter the cycle of rebirth;
if you are deluded and unaware, you will fall into the Avīci Hell.

Furthermore, when a good man’s aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*) has become empty and subtle, and he is no longer beset by perverse thoughts, his perfect concentration gives rise to illumination within *samādhi*.

At that time, if his mind becomes fond of a continuous, lingering state and he clarifies his refined contemplation, greedily seeking a point of accord with the truth, a celestial demon (*devaputra-māra*) will then watch for an opportunity to seize the moment.

He dispatches a refined spirit to possess a person, who then speaks the sutras and the Dharma. The possessed person is actually unaware they are under demonic influence, yet they also claim to have attained realization themselves.
When the Unsurpassed Nirvāṇa comes to the place where that seeker of union—a son of good family—is seated, it preaches the Dharma;

the form [of the Buddha] and those people listening to the Dharma undergo no external change or transformation. Yet, it causes those listeners, before they have even heard the Dharma, to attain spontaneous awakening in their own minds.

From moment to moment, they experience shifts and transformations: some obtain the power of recollecting past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛti*), some possess the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*), some see the hells, or some come to know the human world.
Regarding various matters of likes and dislikes, they may either recite verses aloud or chant sutras themselves; each finds such joy as they have never experienced before.
These people are deluded and confused; some, out of their long-standing affection for Bodhisattvas, violate the Buddha’s precepts and secretly engage in lustful desires.
They take pleasure in saying that there are "great" and "small" Buddhas—that a certain Buddha is a former Buddha and another is a later Buddha—and that among them, there are also...

Whether it be a true Buddha, a false Buddha, a male Buddha, or a female Buddha—the same applies to Bodhisattvas—if a person encounters such manifestations, they will wash away their original mind and easily fall into deviant realization.
This is called a "possessing ghost" (*māyā-ghost*) that becomes a "demon" (*māra*) with age to harass and disturb this person. Once it has become satiated, it leaves the person's body;
yet both the disciple and the teacher fall into royal calamity. You should be aware of this beforehand so as not to enter the cycle of rebirth.
Deluded and ignorant, they fall into the Avīci Hell.
Furthermore, when the *skandha* of goodness is empty and subtle, and one has not encountered perverse thoughts, the bright illumination of perfect concentration arises within the *samādhi*.

At this time, the mind becomes fond of the fundamental source; one exhaustively examines the transformations of things to the very end and beginning of their nature, refining and clarifying the mind while greedily seeking analytical discernment.
At that time, a celestial Māra, waiting for an opportunity, sent his refined essence to possess a person who then spoke the Dharma of the sutras.

That person was previously unaware they were possessed by a demon, yet he also claimed to have personally attained unsurpassed *nirvāṇa*. He came to the place where the seeker of the source, a good man, was seated, and having spread out a seat, he preached the Dharma.
His body possessed majestic spiritual power, which subdued the seeker and caused those in his audience—though they had not yet heard the Dharma—to submit.
Their minds were naturally subdued. These people took the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa and his bodhi-dharmakāya to be none other than their own present physical bodies;
they saw that fathers and sons, generation after generation, mutually producing one another, was itself the eternally abiding dharmakāya without interruption.
They pointed directly to the present as the Buddha-land, asserting there were no separate Pure Abodes nor any golden marks. Thus, these people accepted it with faith.
Having lost their original resolve, they take refuge in their own bodies and lives, attaining what they have never had before. These deluded ones mistake themselves for Bodhisattvas;
they examine their own minds and violate the Buddha’s precepts, secretly practicing lust.
They are fond of saying that the eyes, ears, nose, and tongue are all Pure Lands, and that the male and female organs are the true abode of Bodhi and Nirvana. Such are those who lack wisdom.
To believe such foul words is called the poison of *gū*, the evil spirits of nightmares, and demons that afflict the aged;
they disturb these people until they become weary and satisfied, at which point they leave the person's body. Both the disciple and the teacher will fall into royal peril.
You must be aware of this beforehand so as not to enter the cycle of rebirth; if you are deluded and unaware, you will fall into the Avīci Hell.

Furthermore, when a son of good family’s aggregate of feeling (vedanā-skandha) becomes empty and subtle, and he is not beset by deviant thoughts, his perfect concentration gives rise to illumination within the samādhi.

At this time, if his mind develops a fondness for suspended responses and he exhaustively investigates them with a craving for mysterious resonance, then a celestial Māra will watch for an opportunity to seize the advantage.

He dispatches a refined spirit to possess a person, who then speaks of sutras and dharmas; yet the person is fundamentally unaware that they are possessed by a Māra, and even claims to have attained realization themselves.
When the Unsurpassed Nirvāṇa approaches, he comes to the place where those seeking the response—worthy sons of good family—are seated;

there he spreads his seat and preaches the Dharma, enabling the listeners to behold his body for a time as if for hundreds of thousands of years. Their hearts give rise to such deep affection and attachment that they cannot bear to part from him.
They serve him as his slaves, providing the four requisites of life without ever feeling weary, each causing the people beneath his seat to recognize him as their former teacher.

This original spiritual friend separately gives rise to a craving for dharmas that is as sticky as glue or lacquer; having attained what he has never experienced before, this person is deluded by folly and takes himself to be a bodhisattva.
He draws near to others with such a mind that he violates the Buddha’s precepts and secretly practices lust. With his mouth, he delights in saying:
"In a previous life, during such-and-such a birth, I first delivered such-and-such a person; at that time, they were my wife, concubine, brother, or sister."
Now they come to deceive you, saying, "Follow me back to such-and-such a world to make offerings to such-and-such a Buddha," or claiming, "There is another Great Radiant Heaven where a Buddha dwells;
it is the place where all Tathāgatas rest. Those who do not recognize this for what it is will believe these false and deceptive words, losing their original mind.
This is called the "leprosy-demon" (rākṣasa), who has grown old and become a māra, coming to disturb and confuse such a person.
When a sense of satiety arises and they depart from the person's body, both the disciple and the teacher shall fall into royal calamity;
you must awaken first so as not to enter saṃsāra, for through delusion and ignorance, you will fall into the Avīci Hell.

Furthermore, when a son of good family’s aggregate of feeling (vedanā-skandha) becomes empty and subtle, and he is not beset by perverse thoughts, his perfect concentration gives rise to illumination within the samādhi.
At this time, his mind comes to love deep penetration; through diligent self-discipline, he delights in dwelling in the stillness of the aggregates and greedily seeks quietude.

Then, the celestial Māra watches for an opportunity, dispatches a refined spirit to possess a person, who then speaks of sutras and dharmas. That person originally does not realize they have been possessed by a demon.
It is also said that having personally attained unsurpassed *nirvāṇa*, he went to the place where those sons of good family seeking the aggregates were gathered;
there he arranged seats and preached the Dharma so that each listener came to know their own fundamental karma.

Or, at such a place, he might say to one person, "Though you have not yet died, you have already become an animal," and then command another person to step on his tail from behind, instantly causing the first person to rise up, unable to remain seated.
Thereupon, the entire assembly inclined their hearts toward him with admiration and submission. As soon as someone conceived a thought, he already knew its origin.
Beyond the Buddhist monastic discipline, he added further ascetic rigor. He slandered bhikṣus, reviled their followers, and exposed their private affairs without avoiding public censure.
His mouth was fond of speaking of future calamities and blessings; when the time arrived, not even a hair’s breadth of error occurred. This was the Great Powerful Ghost.
When old age causes them to become demons who harass and disturb this person, they will feel weary and satisfied, and their spirits will depart from that person's body;

both the disciple and the teacher will fall into royal calamity. You must be aware of this beforehand so as not to enter the cycle of rebirth; if you remain deluded and ignorant, you will fall into the Avīci Hell.

Furthermore, O Good Man, when the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*) becomes empty and subtle, and one is not beset by perverse thoughts, the perfect concentration (*samādhi*) will manifest its brilliance within the state of *samādhi*.

When one’s mind cherishes knowledge and views, diligently seeking and greedily craving past lives, at that time a celestial Māra watches for an opportunity and sends his essence to possess a person, who then speaks of the Dharma and sutras.
That person is entirely unaware they have been possessed by a Māra; they also claim to have personally attained unsurpassed *nirvāṇa*.
They come to the place of the good man who seeks such knowledge, arrange their seat, and preach the Dharma. This person does so without cause.

At the place where the Dharma is being preached, he obtains a great precious jewel. That Māra may at times transform himself into an animal with the jewel and various other treasures, such as books, talismans, and scrolls, held in its mouth; it first presents these to the person [preaching], and then attaches them to their body.
Or, it may entice the listeners and hide them underground, where there is a bright moon-jewel that illuminates that spot—all those who were listening.

Having obtained many medicinal herbs never before encountered, he does not partake of fine delicacies; sometimes he eats only one sesame seed and one grain of wheat per day, yet his body remains plump and robust because it is sustained by the power of Māra.
He slanders bhikṣus and reviles their followers, showing no regard for public censure.
In his mouth he delights in speaking of hidden treasures in other regions and the secret dwelling places of sages throughout the ten directions, leading those who follow him there.
Often one encounters strange and extraordinary people; these are known as spirits of mountain forests, local deities, city gods, rivers, peaks, and ghosts who have grown old and become demons.
Some preach debauchery and violate the Buddha’s precepts, secretly indulging in the five desires with those who serve them;
others are diligent practitioners who subsist solely on grasses and trees, yet their conduct is erratic, and they disturb such people until the latter develop a sense of weariness and revulsion.

When that person’s body has departed, both the disciple and the teacher will likely fall into royal calamity; you should be aware of this beforehand so as not to enter the cycle of rebirth, nor to fall into the Avīci Hell through delusion and ignorance.

Furthermore, O Good Man, when the aggregate of sensation (vedanā-skandha) becomes empty and subtle, and one is not beset by deviant thoughts, the perfect concentration will manifest and clarify within the state of samādhi.
With hearts fond of supernatural powers and various transformations, they study the source of such manifestations and greedily seek spiritual might.
At that time, a celestial Mara seizes the opportunity to fly his essence into a person, who then speaks of the Dharma and sutras. This person is truly unaware they are possessed by a demon;
they also claim to have attained supreme *nirvāṇa* themselves and come to the dwelling of those seekers of power, where they arrange seats and preach the Dharma.
This person may again hold a flame in his hand and take a portion of that light, placing it upon the heads of the fourfold assembly who are listening;
the flames atop the crowns of these listeners are all several feet long, yet they possess no heat and never burn.
Or he may walk upon water as if treading on level ground, or sit motionless in mid-air, or enter into a jar.
Sometimes he was inside a sack, sometimes he passed through windows or walls without any obstruction; yet regarding weapons, he could not exercise mastery.

He claimed to be a Buddha while wearing white lay clothing, accepted prostrations from bhikṣus, slandered dhyāna and vinaya, reviled his followers, and exposed private matters without avoiding public censure.
His mouth constantly spoke of supernatural powers and mastery, or else he caused others to...
Looking around at the Buddha-lands, one sees that those who delude people through the power of ghosts have no reality;
they praise sexual misconduct and do not condemn coarse behavior, taking all manner of lewd acts to be the transmission of the Dharma.

These are known as mountain spirits, sea spirits, wind spirits, river spirits, and earth spirits of the heavens and earth, or the accumulated essences and phantoms of plants and trees over many kalpas, or perhaps dragon spirits, or immortals whose lives have ended.
Those who return to life as *māra* spirits or immortals will, at the end of their allotted lifespan, face death; yet their forms do not decay, and they become possessed by other monsters.
As they grow old, they become demons who harass and disturb people until they grow weary and leave the person's body. Both the disciples and the masters often fall into royal punishment.
You should be aware of this beforehand so as not to enter the cycle of rebirth; if you are deluded and unaware, you will fall into the Avīci Hell.

Furthermore, when a good man’s *skandha* of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*) has become empty and subtle, and he is no longer beset by deviant thoughts, his perfect concentration gives rise to illumination within the *samādhi*.

At this time, if he loves the cessation of entry [into the state of extinction], investigating the nature of transformation and greedily seeking the profound emptiness, then a celestial demon will watch for an opportunity to seize the advantage.

A refined spirit will fly in and possess a person, who will orally proclaim sutras and dharmas; yet that person will never realize they are possessed by a demon, and will even claim to have attained realization themselves.

When he came to the place where that son of good family who sought emptiness was seated to preach the Dharma for the great assembly, his form suddenly became empty and the multitude could see nothing;
then, emerging abruptly from the void, he appeared and disappeared at will.
At times he manifested his body as transparent as lapis lazuli; at other times he extended his hands and feet, emitting the fragrance of sandalwood, or even passing excrement and urine.
As thick as rock honey, they slander the precepts and hold those who have left the household life in contempt.

Their mouths constantly preach that there is no cause and no effect, that once dead one is extinguished forever and never again has a subsequent body, and that there are neither ordinary beings nor sages. Though they may attain a state of empty stillness, they secretly practice lust;
those who receive their desire likewise claim to attain the empty mind. They deny cause and effect—this is called the eclipse of the sun and moon, the corruption of their vital energy.
Gold, jade, fungi, grasses, qilin, phoenixes, tortoises, and cranes live for thousands of myriad years without dying, acting as spirits;

yet when they are born into this human realm, they grow old and become demons, harassing and confusing people until they grow weary and leave the person's body. Both the disciples and the master often fall into royal punishment.
You should be aware of this beforehand so as not to enter the cycle of rebirth; if you are deluded and unaware, you will fall into the Avīci Hell.

Furthermore, when a son of good family’s aggregate of sensation (vedanā-skandha) has become empty and subtle, and he is no longer beset by deviant thoughts, his perfect concentration (samādhi) becomes luminous. Within this state of *samādhi*, his mind develops a fondness for longevity;

he laboriously investigates the subtle mysteries and greedily seeks eternal years, abandoning the coarse birth of the segmented body (*vipāka-deha*) and suddenly hoping for the permanence of the subtle characteristics of the transformed body (*nirmāṇa-deha*).
At that time, a celestial Māra seizes the opportunity and sends his refined essence to possess a person, who then speaks the Dharma of the sutras.
That person ultimately does not realize they are possessed by a māra; they also claim to have personally attained unsurpassed *nirvāṇa*.
They come to the place where that seeker of birth—a son of good family—resides, arrange their seat, and preach the Dharma.

They speak favorably of traveling to and from other regions without obstruction, or of returning in an instant after having traveled ten thousand *li*, claiming to have obtained goods from those distant lands. Or, while remaining in a single location within a house...
Within the space of a few steps, he caused them to go from the east to the western wall; though they walked with great haste for many years, they could not reach it.
Because of this, their minds were filled with faith and they doubted that the Buddha had appeared before them. They constantly said: "All sentient beings of the ten directions are my children;
I give birth to all Buddhas and I bring forth the worlds; I am the primordial Buddha who appears spontaneously in the world, not attained through cultivation."

This is called "Abiding in the World with Sovereignty. The celestial Māra may dispatch his retinue—such as Cāmunda, the Four Heavenly Kings, and the Piśāca youths who have not yet resolved for enlightenment—to take advantage of its empty clarity to consume the vital essence of the practitioner.
Alternatively, without relying on a teacher, the practitioner may personally behold them; they shall be called Vajradhara, grant you long life, and manifest in the form of beautiful women.
When greed prevails for no more than a year or two, their livers and brains will wither away and they will speak only to themselves, sounding like malevolent spirits.
Those who do not discern this in advance will fall into royal calamities; before even meeting their execution, they will already die of desiccation.
They will torment and confuse others until those others perish. You must perceive this beforehand so as not to enter saṃsāra; if you are deluded and ignorant, you will fall into the Avīci Hell.
Ānanda, you should know that these ten kinds of māras, during the time of the final age, will leave the household life to practice the Way within my Dharma;
some will possess the bodies of others, while others will manifest their own forms, all claiming to have already attained the realization of Right and Universal Enlightenment.
They will praise sexual desire and violate the Buddha’s Vinaya. These former evil māra-teachers and their disciples will transmit their lust from one to another; such are these perverse spirits.

They bewitch the hearts and innermost faculties of beings; those near them may be reborn for nine lifetimes, while many exceed a hundred generations. They cause those who truly practice cultivation to become the retinue of Māra.
After their lives end, they will surely become subjects of Māra, lose right and universal knowledge, and fall into the Avīci Hell. You need not yet seek nirvana first;
even if you have attained the stage of No-more-learning (aśaikṣa), remain with your vows to enter that Age of Dharma Decline and give rise to great compassion.
I deliver those sentient beings who possess a correct mind and deep faith, ensuring they are not ensnared by Māra and that they attain right knowledge and vision.
Now that I have delivered you from birth and death, if you follow the Buddha’s words, this shall be called repaying the Buddha’s kindness.

Ānanda, these ten kinds of meditative visions appearing during *dhyāna* all arise because the mind is applied in a state of interaction within the *saṃjñā-skandha* (aggregate of perception); thus, these phenomena manifest.

Beings are stubborn and deluded, failing to reflect upon themselves; encountering such conditions, they are confused and fail to recognize them for what they are, claiming instead that they have attained the state of a sage.
Having committed this great falsehood, they fall into the Avīci Hell. You must take the words of the Tathāgata as my [instruction].
After my parinirvāṇa, transmit and reveal this throughout the age of the final dharma, causing all sentient beings to awaken to this meaning;
do not allow celestial Māras to find any opportunity, but maintain and protect them so that they may achieve the unsurpassed way.
The treatise says: "There are seven kinds of pride (*māna*); why then does this text mention six? It replies: "Pride is a lack of respect. These are:

pride (*māna*), excessive pride (*atimāna*), pride beyond pride (*mānātimāna*), the pride of 'I' (*asmimāna*), overweening pride (*adhimāna*), inferiority pride (*ūnamāna*), and false pride (*mithyāmāna*).

Regarding 'excessive pride,' it means that one gives rise to pride because one has already surpassed others. As for 'pride beyond pride,' it combines two types of pride; since one lacks respect, one further acts [with arrogance]."

Because the mind overreaches [the object], one conceives of a self within the aggregates through the pride of "I" (*asmimāna*). Because of that pride toward them, one develops the pride of superiority (*abhimāna*), thinking oneself superior;
the pride of inferiority (*ūnamāna*), because one is actually superior; the pride of equality (*mānātimāna*), because one is actually inferior;

and the pride of falsity (*mithyāmāna*), because one takes the true Dharma as an object within meditative concentration. It is not called the pride of falsity because it does not involve false views. Furthermore, he asked: "What is meant by 'mind-born' (*manomaya*)?"
Regarding the body, the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* states that the "mind-made body" (*manomaya-kāya*) is a metaphor for the mind’s swift and unimpeded movement.
From the first stage (*bhūmi*) through the tenth, there are three types of mind-made bodies that proceed without obstruction wherever they go.
Furthermore, this mind, when separated from the physical body, is the very cause of the mind-made body. In the *Dhāraṇīsaṃgraha Sūtra*, there is the deity Cāmuṇḍā; Cāmuṇḍā...

The Vaiśya youths all consume vital essence (*ojas*). [Supplement: It is said that if one can enter this aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*) and cause the mind to detach from its physical form, one attains a mind-made body (*manomaya-kāya*), which is like the speech of a person in a dream.

This means that once a person already knows they will surely ascend through the stages of sainthood (*ārya-bhūmi*), their words become like established sounds and rhythms; those who fully comprehend such speech are like those who hear the utterances of a dreamer.
If the mind loves clarity and luminosity, it sharpens its refined contemplation, and thus greedily seeks skillful means;

if the mind loves wandering and roaming, it lets its refined contemplation fly, and thus greedily seeks experience; if the mind loves continuity and persistence, it clarifies its refined contemplation, and thus greedily seeks harmony;
if the mind loves the fundamental source, it exhausts the transformations of things, and thus greedily seeks [the ultimate].
Because the mind’s love for analytical discernment involves a pervasive and refined investigation, one greedily seeks profound resonance;

because the mind’s love for introspection involves self-discipline and arduous toil, one greedily seeks tranquil stillness; because the mind’s love for knowledge and vision involves diligent and painful inquiry, one greedily seeks past lives;
because the mind’s love for supernormal powers involves researching the source of transformations, one greedily grasps at the spirit.
If one enters cessation through the mind of power and love, it is because one investigates the nature of transformation; thus, one greedily seeks the profound emptiness of the mind.
If one loves longevity through the mind of power and love, it is because one laboriously investigates the subtlest workings; thus, one greedily seeks eternal years.

However, among these ten types of illuminating objects, there is no fault provided one remains undeluded and attains prior awakening. If this aggregate of darkness is exhausted within the mind of awakened clarity, [then liberation is attained].

Just as by removing dust and grime one can transcend the turbidity of afflictions, the former Chan Master Changlu Zu Zhaohe once perceived events within a radius of several tens of *li* while in meditative concentration (*samādhi*), yet no one had ever been aware of them.
Later, because a temple official reported his transgressions, the Master revealed them to the outside world and immediately entered *parinirvāṇa*. Furthermore, there was the Dharma Hall named Yan.
A monk was sitting in silent meditation within the Patriarch’s Hall when a radiant light permeated the doorway. Upon hearing this, the Chan Master took up his staff and went to investigate;
the monk raised his eyes, whereupon the Master struck him with his staff and drove him out of the monastery.

Such was the Master’s illumination through the Patriarchal tradition, ensuring that the outer precincts were not leaked and the assembly remained undeluded. Now, even in the practice of stillness and victory, one must still...
Failing to reach the realm of the ancients, they were anxious and preoccupied solely with the fear that others would not recognize them;
indeed, there have been instances where both disciple and master were caught together in royal calamity—how tragic!
The Combined Commentary on the Śūraṅgama Sūtra: The Great Buddha-Uṣṇīṣa Tathāgata’s Secret Cause for Cultivation and Realization, the Definitive Meaning of the Myriad Practices of All Bodhisattvas,
Volume Nine, Phonetic Transcriptions.
Xū (zhà yù qiè). Tián (yīn guō). Ruǎn (ér yuǎn qiè). Shàn (yīn jiàn). Mò (yīn mò). Yǐng (yīn mǐn). Chè (chǒu gé qiè). Jié (yīn jié).
Àn (with the initial *y* elided). Jiáo (pronounced *ráo*). Xì (qǐ jí qiè). Yàn (yú yǎn qiè). Zhōng duò (homophonous with huī). Yì (pronounced *yì*). Bié (pronounced *bō*).

The Combined Commentary on the Śūraṅgama Sūtra on the Ultimate Meaning of the Secret Cause of the Tathāgata’s Great Buddha-Uṣṇīṣa and the Myriad Practices of All Bodhisattvas, Volume Ten.
Ānanda, when that good man practicing samādhi has exhausted the aggregate of perception, his ordinary dreams and fantasies—

Extinguishing [delusion], one remains perpetually awakened and clear whether waking or sleeping; empty and still, like a cloudless sky, there are no longer the coarse and heavy shadows of external objects.
Contemplating the worlds, the great earth, mountains, and rivers, they are like reflections in a mirror—coming with nothing to adhere to and passing without leaving a trace.
Receiving illumination in emptiness, all former habits are utterly gone; there is only the single, pure reality. From this point, the root-source of birth and death [is severed].
One perceives all twelve classes of sentient beings throughout the ten directions, exhausting every category;

though one has not yet penetrated the individual threads of their destinies, one sees the common foundation of their births, which is like a shimmering mirage—agitated and clear—a fundamental pivot-hole for the floating sense organs and their objects.
This is called the realm of the *saṃskāra-skandha* (the aggregate of formations).
Supplement: The preceding text of the Sūtra begins here with the *saṃjñā-skandha*. If this *saṃjñā-skandha* persists, then in the waking state one grasps at images, and in sleep it becomes dreams.
If this *saṃjñā-skandha* is exhausted, then although there is waking and sleeping, there are no mental projections or dreams; hence it is said that "waking and sleeping are always one.
Once this is fully understood and no further [delusions] are presented, the description of the *saṃskāra-skandha* (the *saṃskāra-skandha*) is then set forth in its entirety. This means:
Since the root-source of arising and ceasing has thus been revealed, one sees that these twelve types all arise from the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*);
therefore, it is said they share a common basis of birth. "Wild horses" refers to drifting dust; "sparkling" refers to the light of fireflies.
This means that the subtle and continuous flux of the aggregate of formations is like the shimmering of motes of dust in a sunbeam.
Because one has thoroughly realized the absence of the characteristic of abiding, it is said: "The clear agitation flickers and quivers," and so forth.

If this flickering, clear agitation is fundamentally the nature of the essence, and that nature enters into the fundamental clarity—such that this single clarity is the original habituation, and the waves and ripples are extinguished and transform into still water—this is called the exhaustion of the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*).
Such a person is then able to transcend the sensory contact of sentient beings and contemplate its underlying cause.
Deep-seated delusive thoughts serve as its foundation.
Ānanda, you should know that when these good men attain right awareness within *śamatha*, their minds become concentrated, luminous, and upright;
at that time, the ten classes of celestial Māras cannot find an opportunity to interfere, and they are finally able to investigate exhaustively the root of all living beings among those very roots.

Regarding those who expose the source of birth: when they contemplate that profound, pure, and perfectly agitated source, if they give rise to conceptual calculations within that perfect source, such people fall into two theories of causelessness.
The first is when these people perceive that there is no fundamental cause. Why is this?
Because these people, having fully broken through the mechanism of their vital energy, rely upon the eight hundred merits of the eye-organ to see back eighty thousand kalpas.

There are sentient beings whose karmic streams meander and coil, dying here and being born there; they see only the cycle of rebirth within that place for eighty thousand kalpas, after which it becomes dark and nothing can be observed.
They then form this interpretation: "These sentient beings of the ten directions in this world have existed spontaneously without cause for eighty thousand kalpas.
By such deliberation, they lose correct universal knowledge and fall into the delusions of external paths.
Regarding the two aspects of the nature of Bodhi, these people perceive only the branches and deny the cause. Why is this?

Because such people, having already perceived the root of birth, know that humans produce humans and realize that birds produce birds; they see that crows have always been black and cranes have always been white.

Humans and devas were originally upright, while animals were originally horizontal. White was not made by washing, nor was black created by dyeing; from eighty thousand kalpas ago, there has been no further change.
If one changes [one's form], and now that this current form has ended, it is likewise so;
yet I have from the beginning never seen Bodhi—how could there be any further matter of attaining Bodhi? You should know that today all phenomena are fundamentally without cause.
From such conceptualization, one loses right universal knowledge and falls into the ways of external paths, deluding the nature of Bodhi; this is called the first [delusion].
The non-Buddhists establish a doctrine of causelessness.

Ānanda, these good sons within samādhi, having concentrated their clarity and set their minds upright so that Māra finds no opportunity, exhaustively investigate the root of all living beings and contemplate that profound, pure, and eternally agitated source.
Those who give rise to speculative calculations within this perfect and eternal reality are such persons.
Falling into the four types of theories on eternalism: The first is this person who investigates the nature of the mind and its objects and finds that both are without cause.

Through cultivation, they come to know that all sentient beings throughout the ten directions undergo birth and death within twenty thousand kalpas, which proceeds in a constant cycle without ever being lost;
they reckon this to be eternal. The second is this person who investigates the origin of the four great elements and finds that their four natures are eternally abiding. Through cultivation...

Third, they are able to know that throughout forty thousand kalpas, all births, deaths, formations, and disintegrations of sentient beings in the ten directions are fundamentally never lost or scattered,
and thus reckon them as permanent; furthermore, these persons exhaustively investigate the six sense faculties and the *manas* consciousness’s grasping and reception,
and because the fundamental source and locus within the *manovijñāna* are eternally constant by nature, through cultivation they are able to know everything within eighty thousand kalpas.
Sentient beings circulate in saṃsāra without losing their original, eternally abiding nature; though they exhaust themselves without losing this nature, they reckon it to be a permanent self.
[Supplement]: *Manas* is fully called *kliṣṭa-manas*, which here means "defiled grasping," referring to the eighth consciousness.
Jingjue says: "The eight consciousnesses are subtle and minute, known only by Buddhas and Bodhisattvas of the Eighth Ground."
Now, this person has suddenly exhausted the eight consciousnesses at the fundamental source of the *xing-yin* (the aggregate of formations);
because they perceive the subtle arising and ceasing there as being permanent, it does not mean that they have already seen the eighth consciousness within meditative concentration.
Fourth, this person has exhausted the source of ideation; in their fundamental nature, there is no longer any flowing, ceasing, moving, or revolving of thoughts and minds.

Now that these have been eternally extinguished, within this principle, the non-arising and non-ceasing state is spontaneously realized. Based on this, they take what is realized by the causal mind to be permanent.

Because of this calculation of permanence, they lose right and universal knowledge and fall into the ranks of external paths, deluding themselves regarding the nature of Bodhi. This is called... [the first stage of the four stages of delusion].
The second type of externalist establishes a doctrine of pervasive permanence. Furthermore,

among those sons of good family within samādhi who have stabilized their minds in right concentration, if they cannot resist the influence of Māra and, while investigating the root of all living beings,
contemplate that profound, pure, and eternal source of agitation, and thereby give rise to speculative calculations regarding self and others, such a person falls into [the error of permanence].
Regarding the first type of the "partial-universal-permanence-theory" among the four inverted views:

this person contemplates the wondrously luminous mind as pervading the ten directions, regarding its profound stillness as the ultimate *ātman*. From this, they calculate that this self pervades the ten directions, remaining concentrated, luminous, and unmoving;
they hold that all sentient beings are born and die within their own heart-mind, and thus [believe] their own heart-nature...
First, they designate that which undergoes arising and ceasing as "eternal," while regarding its true nature of arising and ceasing as "impermanent.

Second, these people do not contemplate their own minds, but instead observe the lands of the ten directions as numerous as the sands of the Ganges; seeing places where kalpas are destroyed, they designate this as the "nature of ultimate impermanence," and seeing places where kalpas are not destroyed, they designate this as "ultimate permanence.
Third, these people separately contemplate their own minds as being subtle, refined, minute, and secret.
It is like fine dust circulating throughout the ten directions; its nature does not shift or change, yet it can cause this body to arise and perish in an instant.
This indestructible nature is called the "constant nature of the self. All deaths and births flow forth from this self and are thus termed the "impermanent nature.

Fourth, when this person perceives that the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*) has ended and sees the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) flowing on, they reckon this constant flow of the formations to be the "constant nature."
Form, sensation, perception, and so forth have now been extinguished; this is called impermanence.

Because they calculate that one part is impermanent while another part is permanent, they fall into the ranks of the externalists and delude themselves regarding the nature of bodhi. This is called the third externalist doctrine:
the theory of partial permanence.
Furthermore, among those sons of good family within *samādhi*, there are those who stabilize their minds in right concentration so that Māra finds no opportunity.

They investigate the root of all living beings and contemplate that which is profound, pure, and eternally the source of agitation. Within this state of analysis, they engage in conceptual calculations;

such people fall into the four theories of finitude (*antagrāhika-dṛṣṭi*). The first is when a person calculates that the source of birth flows and functions without ceasing, and thus calculates regarding the past and the future.
First, they conceive of the continuous mind as having limits and name it "finite," while regarding it as "infinite" [in its continuity].

Second, these people observe eighty thousand kalpas and see that prior to those eighty thousand kalpas, sentient beings were silent, with nothing heard or seen; this state of no hearing or seeing is called "infinite," while the presence of sentient beings is called "finite.
Third, these people reckon that their own self possesses universal knowledge and attains the nature of infinity.
All those people appear within the scope of my knowledge, yet I have never known their cognitive nature;

thus they are said to lack the boundless mind and possess only a limited nature. Fourth, this person exhausts the emptiness of the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) by using the path of his own mind as a measure to calculate that within the single body of every sentient being, all things are half-born and half-extinguished.
They clarify that within all worlds, one half is finite and one half is infinite;

by such deliberation on finitude and infinity, they fall into the ways of external paths and delude the nature of bodhi. This is called the fourth external path, which establishes the doctrine of finitude.

Furthermore, among those good sons within samādhi who have stabilized their minds in right concentration, if Māra finds no opportunity and they exhaustively investigate the origin of all living beings,
observing that profound, pure, and eternal source of agitation and movement, yet give rise to conceptual calculations within their perceptions and views,
such persons fall into four kinds of inverted, "neither-dying-nor-chaotic" sophistry and pervasive false theorizing. The first is when such a person observes the source of transformation and change.
To perceive the place of flux is called "change"; to perceive the place of continuity is called "permanence"; to perceive the place of what is seen is called "arising";
to not perceive the place of seeing is called "ceasing. To perceive the place where the nature of the cause of continuity is uninterrupted is called "increase";
to perceive the place within the midst of correct continuity that is devoid [of such causes] is called "decrease"; and to perceive each respective place of arising—these are the various states.

That which is designated as "existence" is mutually absent in its various states, and that which is thus designated as "non-existence" is observed through principle yet perceived differently by the mind.
When seekers of the Dharma come to inquire about its meaning, I answer them by saying: "I am now both arising and ceasing, both existent and non-existent, both increasing and decreasing.
At all times, I confuse their speech so that those people before me lose the essential points of the text.
Second, this person contemplates the mind as being mutually non-existent; because there is nothing to be attained, they realize non-existence.

When someone comes to question them, they respond with only a single word, saying simply "non-existence," and beyond this non-existence, there is nothing further to be said. Third, this person contemplates the mind as having its own distinct locations;
because there is something to be attained, they realize existence. When someone comes to question them, they respond with only a single word.
They merely say that it is neither existent nor non-existent, having nothing further to say. Fourth, these people hold both views of existence and non-existence;
because their objects of perception are fragmented, their minds are likewise distracted. When someone comes to question them, they answer:

"It is both existent and non-existent, yet within being both existent and non-existent, it is not even 'both'. This is a form of evasive equivocation that allows no room for further interrogation, arising from such speculative reckoning.
Evasive, vacuous, and fallen into the ways of external paths, they delude the nature of bodhi; this is called the fifth class of externalists:
those of the four inverted natures who employ evasive speech of immortality and engage in pervasive, false theorizing.

Furthermore, among those sons of good family within samādhi who have stabilized their correct minds so that Māra finds no opportunity, they investigate the root of all living beings and contemplate that profound, pure, yet eternally agitated source.
Those who, amidst this inexhaustible flow, give rise to conceptual calculations fall into the view of "existence after death with form," leading to inverted resolve.
They may either cling to their own bodies, claiming "form is the self," or perceive the self as being pervasive.

Pervading all lands, one thinks, "I have form," or, following the preceding conditions, one turns back toward them and thinks, "Form belongs to me," or again, within the continuity of formations, one thinks, "I am in form. These are all conceptual reckonings that there are signs after death;
thus, circulating in this manner, there are sixteen such signs. From these, one may further reckon in terms of either ultimate affliction or ultimate enlightenment.
The two sexes proceed side by side without touching one another; from this conceptualization that there is existence after death, they fall into the heterodox paths and delude the nature of Bodhi.
This is called the sixth heterodox school’s theory of the inverted mind regarding the signs of existence after death within the five aggregates.
Furthermore, among those good sons within samādhi who have stabilized their minds in right concentration, the māras find no opportunity.

As they exhaustively investigate the source of all living beings and observe that profound, pure, and eternal state which is the root of agitation, there may be one who first eliminates form, sensation, and perception, yet still gives rise to conceptual calculations.
Such a person falls into the view of "formlessness after death," inverting their understanding by seeing that when form ceases, the physical body has no cause.

Contemplating the cessation of perception, one knows that the mind has no attachments; knowing the cessation of sensation, one finds there is no further connection. The nature of the aggregates dissolves and disperses;

even if the life-faculty remains, being devoid of sensation and perception, it is the same as grass and trees. Since this physical substance cannot be apprehended even while present before one, how could any signs exist after death?
Examining them through such a cycle, one finds that after death, these signs are non-existent. Thus the cycle continues.
There are eight signless states from which some may reckon that the causes and effects of nirvana are entirely empty, existing merely as names, and ultimately subject to total annihilation.
Because they speculate that there is nothing after death, they fall into the ranks of the non-Buddhists (tīrthikas), deluding themselves regarding the nature of bodhi.
This is called the seventh heterodox school, which establishes within the five aggregates a theory of post-mortem signlessness and mental perversion.
Furthermore, among those good sons within *samādhi* who have stabilized their minds in right concentration, the Māras find no opportunity.

They exhaustively investigate the root of all living beings and observe that source which is profoundly pure yet constantly subject to agitation. While abiding in the state of mental formations (*saṃskāra*), they simultaneously suppress sensation (*vedanā*) and perception (*saṃjñā*).

By dualistically calculating existence and non-existence, their own internal characteristics contradict one another, and these individuals fall into the nihilistic view that "both are non-existent after death," giving rise to inverted theories regarding form, sensation, and perception.

Seeing existence as non-existence, observing the flux of conditioned formations within, and contemplating that there is neither "is" nor "is not"—thus cycling through these states until the aggregates (*skandha*) and elements (*dhātu*) are exhausted—one encounters the eightfold characteristics of neither-being-nor-non-being.
Whichever single condition one attains, one claims that after death there are both characteristics and lack of characteristics.

Furthermore, calculating that the nature of all formations (*saṃskāra*) is subject to change and transformation, the mind gives rise to penetrating realization that both existence and non-existence are neither, and both the void and the real are lost; from this, such conceptualizations arise.

Because after death there is neither existence nor non-existence, and because the subsequent limit is shrouded in darkness such that it cannot be described, they fall into the path of externalists and delude themselves regarding the nature of Bodhi.
This is called the eighth externalist school’s inverted theory of the mind within the five aggregates, which posits that after death there is neither existence nor non-existence.

Furthermore, among those sons of good family within *samādhi* who have stabilized their minds in right concentration, Māra finds no opportunity; they exhaustively investigate the root of all living beings.

If one contemplates that profound clarity as being fundamentally subject to constant agitation, yet subsequently fails to apply discernment regarding the non-arising of phenomena, such a person falls into the seven theories of annihilationism.
They may speculate on the extinction of the body, or the extinction of desire, or the extinction of suffering, or the extinction of extreme bliss, or the extinction of extreme equanimity.
Thus they cycle through these states until the seven limits are exhausted; what appears before them is dissolved and extinguished, and once extinguished, nothing remains.
Based on this speculative reckoning that after death there is annihilation and falling away, one falls into the heterodox paths and becomes deluded regarding the nature of bodhi;
this is called the ninth heterodox doctrine, the inverted theory of mind which posits annihilation after death within the five aggregates.

The Treatise says: The established doctrine posits seven destinies, all of which ultimately undergo cessation. "Body" refers to humans and devas of the desire realm; the exhaustion of desire is the first dhyāna;
the exhaustion of suffering is the second dhyāna; supreme bliss is the third dhyāna;
and supreme equanimity is the fourth dhyāna and the formless realms. Regarding the statement here that "five things cease," the cessation of the body includes humans as well.
The two kinds of heavens consist of the ultimate equanimity combined with the four dhyānas and the two formless realms.

Furthermore, among those sons of good family within samādhi who have stabilized their correct minds so that Māra finds no opportunity, they exhaustively investigate the origin of all living beings and contemplate that profound, pure, yet eternally agitated source.
If, subsequently, they harbor conceptual calculations regarding future births, such persons fall into [the following states]:

Regarding the five theories on nirvana: some take the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) as the true basis for transformation (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*), because one perceives its perfect clarity and gives rise to a longing for it;
some take the first dhyāna, because its nature is free from sorrow (*daurmanasya*); some take the second dhyāna, because the mind is free from suffering (*duḥkha*);

some take the third dhyāna, because of the presence of extreme bliss (*prīti*); or some take the fourth dhyāna, because both suffering and pleasure have vanished, and its nature is not subject to the arising and ceasing of saṃsāra.

Deluded regarding the tainted heavens, they mistake them for the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*); taking these five abodes as secure and supreme pure refuges, they cycle through them until reaching their ultimate limit in these five places.
By such conceptualization, they calculate five kinds of present nirvana and fall into the ranks of externalists, confusing the nature of bodhi.
This is called the tenth heterodox school: the inverted doctrine of the mind that establishes five kinds of present nirvana within the five aggregates.
Ānanda, these ten kinds of deluded understandings arising from the *dhyāna* of the *saṃskāra-skandha* all appear because the mind’s application within this aggregate is in a state of mutual conflict.
When sentient beings, stubborn and deluded, fail to reflect upon themselves and encounter these manifestations, they mistake their confusion for enlightenment.
Claiming for themselves that they have attained the state of a sage, they commit the great falsehood and fall into the Avīci Hell.
Supplement: It is added that upon entering this skandha of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*), there is only a single, pure lucidity.

Although the various māras cannot find an opportunity, if one gives rise to conceptual calculations within this concentrated lucidity, one falls into the two kinds of causelessness and the four kinds of universal permanence.
If one gives rise to conceptual calculations within this firm concentration, one falls into the four perversions, the four [views of] finitude, and the four [views of] infinity.

The pervasive conceptualization of the four states of existence, the four signless states, the four states of neither-sign-nor-non-sign, the seven stages of annihilationism, and the five types of nirvana are all the doctrines of non-Buddhist outsiders (*tīrthika*).
If these aggregates (*skandha*) are exhausted, they are like waves that subside and vanish, transforming into clear water; thus, one is able to transcend the turbidity of sentient beings.
That which is inexhaustible is called "outflow" (*āsrava*). To grasp the body and refrain from practicing sexual desire is the ultimate state for humans and devas.
When the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) is empty and false wisdom prevails, all transgressions go unchecked and one will inevitably fall into ruin; thus the ancient masters said:
"A dull bird leaves its nest easily, but a numinous tortoise sheds its shell with difficulty."

You must certainly transmit the words of the Tathāgata to me after my parinirvāṇa throughout the age of the final dharma (*saddharmapratirūpaka*), causing all sentient beings to fully awaken to this meaning.
Do not allow the demons of the mind to give rise to deep calamities; maintain and protect [the teaching] to suppress false views, and instruct their bodies and minds to awaken to the true meaning.
In the unsurpassed path, do not encounter byways, and do not let the mind fall into vain prayers.
Attaining a small measure of realization and considering it sufficient, he acts as a Great Awakened King, providing a pure pointing-finger for others.

Ānanda, when that good man practices *samādhi* and the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) is exhausted, the subtle, clear, and restless commonality of all worldly natures—the vital impulse of birth—suddenly collapses like a fine mesh of cords; the *pudgala* [is freed from] the retribution of karma.
The profound pulse of resonance is suspended and severed.
[Supplement]: That which is called the nature of all worldly beings refers to the nature of the arising and ceasing of the twelve classes of living beings.

That which is called "profoundly clear yet agitated" refers to the turbid afflictions that momentarily clarify, only to be agitated again. That which is called "the generative mechanism of common allotment" refers to being identical with all [beings].

The mechanism of birth and extinction is categorized by its various types. Once the *saṃskāra-skandha* (the aggregate of formations) is exhausted, the subtle and pure commonality (*sabhāgatā*) and other such characteristics naturally dissolve along with it.
"Sinking and subtlety" refers to the source of the birth and extinction of the *saṃskāra-skandha*, which is like the main rope of a net or the button of a garment;
therefore, Changshui [Zongjing] took the "main rope and button" to represent the karmic cause, while the *pudgala* represents the karmic retribution. When the karmic cause perishes...
Then what draws forth the fruit? When the retribution of the fruit ceases, who is there to recompense it? Since cause and effect have vanished, the deep pulse is severed.
At the threshold of Nirvana, one is about to attain great awakening; like a rooster crowing at dawn, one looks toward the east where the first light of clarity already appears.
The six sense organs are empty and still, no longer wandering or escaping; internally and externally they are profoundly clear and bright, entering that which has nothing to enter.

One deeply penetrates the ten directions and the fundamental source from which the twelve classes of beings receive their life-force. By observing the source of grasping, one sees that none of these classes can summon one within the realms of the ten directions.
The essence of form does not sink away, and what was hidden and secret is revealed. This is called the domain of the *vijñāna-skandha* (consciousness aggregate).

If, having already attained the same state within the collective assembly, one has completely dissolved and refined the six sense-gates so that they are integrated and perfected, such that seeing, hearing,
and other faculties interpenetrate and function freely, and both the ten directions and one's own body and mind are as transparently clear inside and out as pure vaidūrya lapis lazuli,
this is called the exhaustion of the consciousness aggregate (*vijñāna-skandha*).
Supplementary Note: Upon entering this aggregate of consciousness (vijñāna-skandha), the six sense faculties become empty and still, no longer wandering or dissipated;

thus one can profoundly penetrate the fundamental source of the twelve types of life-receiving across the ten directions. Since both the environment and its inhabitants throughout the ten directions are manifestations of consciousness, when one contemplates the source from which they receive life and the root of what they grasp, within that state where there is neither sameness nor difference, a blazing diversity is formed.
Now that you have attained samādhi within this state, since there is no source from which it arises, others cannot summon you; this is called "returning to the origin.
Thus, all phenomena are but mind and consciousness alone, and the brilliant light of your own essence manifests—what darkness would not be illuminated?

Yet, you still remain within the domain of the *vijñāna-skandha*. If, among all categories of beings, you have already attained samādhi without being summoned, you can further grind away and polish this state.
When the six gates and so forth are mutually employed in purity, one reaches the exhaustion of this *vijñāna-skandha*, where there remains only the single essence of awakening;
thus, it is like vaidūrya. The *Zangjing yinyi* states: "Vaidūrya is the name of a precious gem. This gem is blue in color;
its substance is extremely hard, such that no sword among all precious metals can destroy it, nor can it be affected by smoke or flames."
Casting and smelting [metal] can only be accomplished as tools by spirits and deities who possess supernormal powers (*abhijñā*).

One source states that the eggs of the *garuḍa* (Golden-Winged Bird) are like this; the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* says: "Abiding in the perfection of generosity (*dāna-pāramitā*), one may transform worlds so that they are like vaidūrya."

Such a person is then able to transcend the turbidity of life (*āyuṣka-kaṣāya*) and contemplate its origins, [finding that] it is based upon the formless, the void, and inverted false imaginings (*viparyāsa-vikalpa*). Supplement:
Wujin says, "The ancient masters held that life-force (*āyuṣ*), warmth (*uṣman*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*) evolve simultaneously; since they are called 'consciousness'..."
Because life-force (*jīvita*) and warmth (*uṣman*) perish together, one transcends the turbidity of life-force; yet how does this differ from death when consciousness (*vijñāna*) has ceased?
Generally speaking, "life-force" refers to the subtle continuity of the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñānaskandha*), which is like the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*).

Now, since it is completely shattered and torn asunder, and the six sense-gates open and close while the body and mind become transparently clear, one thus transcends the turbidity of life-force. If one were to say that life-force and warmth perish together...
The following passage should not state: "He can cause his own body’s sense organs to join, separate, open, or close.

Ānanda, you should know that when this good man has exhausted all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) into emptiness and returned to the source within consciousness, he has already extinguished arising and ceasing;

yet, because his subtle and wondrous power of quiescent extinction (*śānti-nirvāṇa*) is not yet perfected, he can cause his own body’s sense organs to join, separate, open, or close, and likewise [interact] with those of the ten directions.

If one perceives that all categories of beings possess a universal consciousness capable of penetrating the fundamental source, and establishes this as a true, eternal cause for their refuge, thereby giving rise to resolute conviction, such a person falls into the attachment to causes and what is caused.
They become a companion to Śivaka who takes the obscure principle (*tattva*) as his refuge;
they are deluded regarding the Buddha’s Bodhi and have lost their insight. This is called the first instance of establishing a mind that clings to what is attained.

Having attained the fruit of their refuge, yet being far removed from perfect penetration, they turn their backs on the city of Nirvana and give rise to the seeds of external paths. Furthermore, Ānanda,
if a son of good family has exhausted the emptiness of all conditioned formations and already extinguished birth and death,

yet his subtle and wondrous state within quiescence is not yet perfected— if he regards that which he has taken as his refuge as his own self-body, encompassing all within the twelve categories of beings throughout the entirety of empty space— [he will fall into error].
If sentient beings all develop the superior understanding that they are born from a single category within my own body, such people fall into the grasping at "ability" and "inability.
They take Mahesvara as their companion by manifesting boundless bodies; they lose the Bodhi of the Buddha and forfeit their true knowledge and vision.
This is called the second [delusion]: establishing "ability" as the mind and achieving the fruit of "able deeds," which is far removed from perfect penetration and turns one's back on Nirvana.
"O son of good family, you were born in the city of Pāṇḍu as a deva of great pride, belonging to the lineage of Universal Perfection (Vibhu).

Furthermore, having exhausted all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) to the point of emptiness, you have already extinguished birth and death; yet, regarding the subtle and wondrous state of cessation (*nirvāṇa*), you have not yet reached full perfection.

If, within that which is the ultimate refuge, you harbor a sense of dependence and take it as a basis for reliance, you will doubt your own body and mind, believing they flow forth from that [state of cessation], and that the empty space of the ten directions likewise flows from it."

If they give rise to the notion that their own life-force is truly eternal and devoid of arising or ceasing at the very moment it arises—conceiving a body of true permanence within the ground of universal manifestation—they prematurely calculate permanence amidst what is subject to arising and ceasing. Thus, they are deluded regarding non-arising and confused about arising and ceasing.

Those who dwell in such deep-seated delusion yet maintain this superior resolve will fall into the attachment to permanence and non-permanence, taking the Lord of Sovereignty (*Īśvara*) as their companion.

To lose sight of the Buddha’s bodhi and forfeit one's true knowledge and vision is called the third [type of delusion]: establishing causes based on the mind to produce false conceptualizations of results;
it is far removed from perfect penetration and turns one's back on the city of nirvana, giving rise to the seeds of inverted perfection.

Furthermore, good son, having exhausted the emptiness of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) and extinguished birth-and-death, one may yet not have perfected the subtle and wondrous state of quiescent extinction (*śānti-nirvāṇa*).

If, regarding that which is known, one’s knowledge is universally pervasive, one establishes a view based on that knowledge such that all grasses and trees in the ten directions are called sentient beings, no different from humans.
One regards these grasses and trees as human beings; when they die, they return to becoming the grasses and trees of the ten directions. Thus, there is no discrimination in this universal knowledge.
Those who give rise to such superior understanding fall into the attachment of "knowing non-knowing" and the attachment of the Pāṭhas and Sainikas;

they take all-encompassing awareness as their companion, become deluded regarding the Buddha’s Bodhi, and lose their true knowledge and vision. This is called the fourth: calculating that the perfected mind achieves a false and erroneous fruit.
It is far removed from perfect penetration, turns its back on the city of Nirvana, and gives rise to the seeds of inverted knowledge.

Furthermore, good son, having exhausted the emptiness of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) and extinguished birth-and-death, yet while the subtle and wondrous state of quiescent extinction has not yet reached full perfection,

if one attains conformity within the mutual functioning of the circularly integrated sense organs, then one may seek the radiance of fire that gives rise to all things within the sphere of perfect transformation,
crave the purity of water, desire the pervasive circulation of wind, or fixate on the accomplishment of sensory objects, each venerating their respective domain.
Using these various sensory objects as the fundamental cause for their arousal, they establish a view of permanence. Such people fall into the dualistic attachment to birth and non-birth;
together with the Kāśyapas and Brahmins, they diligently exert their minds and bodies to serve fire and revere water, seeking to transcend birth and death.
They become companions in delusion regarding the Buddha’s Bodhi and lose their true knowledge and vision. This is called the fifth type of attachment: the fixation on revering external objects.

The deluded mind follows after external objects to establish false seeking; because it seeks falsely, it hopes for a false fruit. Thus it remains far removed from perfect penetration and turns its back on the city of Nirvana, giving rise to the seeds of perverted transformation.

Furthermore, O good son, having exhausted all conditioned phenomena to their emptiness, you have already extinguished birth and death; yet, regarding the subtle and wondrous state of quiescent extinction, you have not yet attained full perfection.

If, regarding this perfect luminosity, one reckons that the voidness within the light is not the cessation of the manifold transformations, and takes as one’s refuge the eternal cessation upon which they depend, thereby giving rise to a resolute conviction, such a person falls into the attachment of "seeking a refuge where there is no refuge.

They will become companions among the *śūnyatā* (void) beings in the Heaven of No-Thought, becoming deluded regarding the Buddha’s Bodhi and losing their true knowledge and vision. This is called the sixth: the mindless state of perfect voidness.
They will achieve the fruit of emptiness and non-existence, becoming estranged from perfect penetration and turning their backs on the city of Nirvana,

thereby giving rise to the seeds of annihilationism. Furthermore, O good sons, when one has exhausted the emptiness of all conditioned formations and extinguished birth and death, yet the subtle and wondrous state of quiescent extinction is not yet perfected— if one then forms a resolute conviction that the body is solid and permanent,
identical to the subtle and perfect essence, and remains forever without decaying or passing away— this is [the error of] generating such a superior understanding.
Such a person falls into the attachment to both craving and non-craving, becoming a companion to those Āsuras who seek long life;

they become deluded regarding the Bodhi of the Buddha and lose their true knowledge and vision. This is called the seventh [delusion]: clinging to the source of life, establishing a false cause for permanence, and heading toward the fruit of prolonged toil.
Supplement: Changshui (Changshui Baoche) changed "lao" (laborious) to "lao" (firm/stable), while Jingjue considered that interpretation to be correct.

However, I [the author] believe that since the preceding phrase already contains the character "gu" (solid/firm), there should not be another "lao" in the subsequent phrase. The general meaning is to prove the cause for establishing the persistence of delusion:
one does not shrink from diligent toil, desiring only that this body shall not collapse or pass away, like a fixed star.

Through the sincerity of observing the lunar fasts (*pi gu*) and refining the physical form, and through the practice of exhaling the old and inhaling the new (*tu gu na xin*), as well as the exercises of "bear-stretching" (*xiong jing*) and "bird-swaying" (*niao bi*), his will was set upon the completion of merit and the fulfillment of conduct;
that he might then shake out his robes and ascend lightly—is this not the fruit of long-term diligent effort?
Having strayed far from perfect penetration and turned one's back on the city of Nirvāṇa, they give rise to the seeds of delusive extension.

Furthermore, O son of good family, when you have exhausted all conditioned activities to the point of emptiness and have already extinguished birth and death, yet the subtle and wondrous state of quiescent extinction is not yet perfected, you may perceive that life-force and its functions are interpenetrating.
Fearing that the remnants of defilement might be entirely consumed, you may then sit within a lotus palace at this very juncture.
Extensively transforming the seven treasures, they increase many precious ladies, allowing their minds to run wild; yet those who give rise to superior resolve [attain liberation].
Supplement: Changshui says, "One contemplates the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*) as the life-source of the twelve classes of sentient beings.

Because my life permeates theirs and their life permeates mine, it is called 'mutual penetration. If the aggregate of consciousness were exhausted, the lives of all sentient beings throughout the ten directions would [likewise cease]."
If one’s life were to end immediately upon its exhaustion, who would realize the principle of true permanence? Who would be the sentient beings to be transformed?

Since there would be only true permanence but no one to realize it, one must therefore retain the afflictions (*kleśa*) to give rise to various realms of desire, freely enjoying sensual pleasures so that the life-force remains intact and does not perish.
This enables one to realize the truth and manifest transformative power to guide sentient beings; yet based on this, they cling to the fixed notion that [the self] does not exist.
To establish this consciousness as the "Superior Resolve" (adhimukti) is like appointing a beautiful woman as a concubine.
Such a person falls into the attachment to the real within the unreal; with Cakravartin kings as their companions, they lose sight of the Buddha’s Bodhi and forfeit true knowledge and vision.
This is called the eighth: giving rise to the cause of perverse thoughts and establishing the fruit of blazing dust, thereby remaining far removed from perfect penetration.
They turn their backs on the city of Nirvana and give birth to the lineage of devas and māras.

Furthermore, good sons who have exhausted the emptiness of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) and extinguished arising and ceasing, yet whose subtle and wondrous state of cessation has not yet reached full perfection, distinguish between the refined and the coarse within the clarity of life, and resolve the true and the false; they seek only for cause and effect to correspond, hoping for a response from the divine.

Regarding those who turn their backs on the path of purity—namely, those who see suffering, abandon its origin, realize cessation, and cultivate the path, yet having come to rest within cessation, no longer advance further and instead give rise to a fixed conviction (adhimokṣa)—[the commentary] adds:

because the aggregate of consciousness (vijñānaskandha) is manifest, it is called "life-illumination" (jīvitaprajñapti). Since consciousness contains both the seeds of outflows (sāsrava) and the seeds free from outflows (anāsrava), now...
