Within this context, the suffering and its origin (*duḥkha-samudaya*), which are with outflows (*sāsrava*), are termed "coarse" and "false," while the path and cessation (*mārga-nirodha*), which are without outflows (*anāsrava*), are termed "refined" and "true.

Because one discriminates and discards the coarse and false suffering and origin while retaining the refined and true path and cessation, it is called the "discrimination of the refined and the coarse.
As for the cultivation of the path (*bhāvanāmārga*), since its purpose is to realize and attain cessation, one should take up only these [refined and true factors]; therefore, it is said "only."
Seeking the fundamental cultivation of the perfect contemplation of the equality of the dharma-realm, free from the defilements of the two extremes, is called the path of purity;
now, because one has developed the understanding of the Lesser Vehicle’s joy in the sublime and aversion to the mundane, it is said that one "turns one's back.
Such a person falls into the company of those of fixed nature among the śrāvakas and those of overweening pride among the assembly of the unlearned, becoming their companion.

To lose sight of the Buddha’s Bodhi and forfeit one's true knowledge and vision is called the ninth stage: when the perfect essence fails to respond to the mind, it results in the fruit of a tranquilized state;
this is far removed from perfect penetration and turns its back on the city of Nirvana, giving rise to the seeds of entanglement within emptiness.

Furthermore, if a good man, having exhausted the emptiness of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) and extinguished birth and death, has not yet perfected the subtle and wondrous state of tranquil extinction (*śānti-nirvāṇa*),
and if he focuses his investigation upon the profound and subtle clarity of perfect, pure awakening, establishing himself in *nirvāṇa* without proceeding further and giving rise to a fixed resolve,
such a person falls among the class of Pratyekabuddhas of fixed nature— those solitary practitioners who do not turn their minds back toward the Great Vehicle.
Forming such a companion, they lose sight of the Buddha’s Bodhi and forfeit their true knowledge and vision; this is called the tenth:

the mind that has submerged in Perfect Enlightenment, achieving a fruit of profound clarity, yet remaining far removed from perfect penetration and turning its back on the city of Nirvana, giving rise to a seed of perfected luminosity that does not transform.

Supplement: It is said that when all formations (*saṃskāra*) are exhausted and emptiness is realized, although consciousness returns to its source, if one’s subtle and wondrous nature has not yet reached perfection and one gives rise to a superior understanding, one will fall into the eight attachments of the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*). These include the Śrāvaka who turns his back on the Way, and the Pratyekabuddha who extinguishes the mind and seeks no further advancement.

The eight attachments refer to: attachment to cause and what is caused; attachment to agent and what is not an agent; attachment to permanence and impermanence; and attachment to knowledge... [and so forth].

To grasp at non-knowledge as knowledge, to grasp at arising as non-arising, to grasp at that which has no refuge as having a refuge, to grasp at greed as non-greed, and to grasp at the unreal as real—this is it.
These inversions are perfected through false conceptualization. To take delusion as proof is inverted cognition.
To be entangled in emptiness is to be bound by quiescence. Not to transform one's firm attachment is not to turn back. "Inexhaustible" refers to the Buddhas.
To claim that what has not been transformed is not [the result] is an error; regarding practice, one speaks of the cause, while regarding failure, one speaks of the effect.
Sāṃkhyāyana and Pātañjali are the names of two non-Buddhist teachers; Asita is translated here as "Long Life."
Ānanda, these ten kinds of *dhyāna* may cause one to become deranged midway through their practice due to confusion;
this occurs because one mistakes what is incomplete for a realization of fulfillment. This state arises from the mutual interaction of the mind with the *vijñānakāya*.
When sentient beings encounter this manifestation, being stubbornly deluded and failing to reflect upon themselves, they each seek rest by means of their own cherished prior habits and deluded minds.
Claiming that you have attained the ultimate state of refuge and that you have personally realized unsurpassed enlightenment constitutes a great falsehood;

such will cause you to be influenced by external paths and demonic spirits, and when your karma is exhausted, you will fall into the Avīci Hell. You Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas shall not achieve further progress.
Therefore, maintain your resolve and uphold the Way of the Tathāgata, and after my parinirvāṇa, transmit this Dharma-gate to the final age.
May all sentient beings universally awaken to and understand this meaning, so that they do not encounter Māra or create deep calamities for themselves. May they be protected, comforted, and rescued;
may their perverse conditions be quelled, and may their bodies and minds enter the Buddha’s knowledge and vision. From their initial accomplishment, may they not encounter divergent paths.
Such a Dharma gate has, throughout kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges in the past, enabled dust-mote-like Tathāgatas to open their minds by relying upon it.
"One attains the Unsurpassed Way.
[Supplementary Note: Regarding the statement that there are ten kinds of demonic activities (*māra-karman*) within each of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), this is merely a general outline.

If one investigates the underlying cause, they all arise from the mutual interference of mental applications, thereby giving rise to these deep-seated calamities. Were it not for the Tathāgata’s prophetic revelation, [these would remain hidden].
In future generations, if all sentient beings were to awaken to this meaning and reach this supreme and wondrous realm, who would not be [liberated from] Māra and externalists?
Alas! From the former Buddhas to the later Buddhas, there is no gift of the Dharma greater than this;
even grinding one’s bones to powder would not suffice to repay it with sincerity, just as Yongjia said regarding those who first give rise to resolute understanding.
Master De once said: "As soon as there is something held as important, it becomes a fixed trap. He also said: "Simply exhaust all mundane sentiments;
apart from this, there is no other superior understanding"—it cannot go beyond this.

If the consciousness aggregate (*vijñāna-skandha*) is exhausted, then your present sense faculties will function interchangeably; from within this mutual functioning, you can enter the stage of a Bodhisattva.
The adamantine wisdom of dry insight (*vimalā-jñāna*) is perfectly luminous; from within this refined essence, transformation arises like a precious moon contained within pure lapis lazuli.

Thus, one transcends the stages of the ten faiths, ten abidings, ten practices, ten transferences, and the four preparatory minds (*prayoga-citta*), as well as the conduct of the Bodhisattvas through the ten adamantine grounds (*bhūmi*).
Upon reaching Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*), one attains perfect luminosity and enters the Tathāgata’s ocean of wondrous adornment, thereby fulfilling Bodhi.
"Returning to the realization of non-attainment.

[Supplementary Note: The meaning of this section reveals the power of the mutual functioning of the sense faculties (*indriya*) at the point where the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*) is exhausted.
It means that once the five aggregates have been exhausted, one is able to enter the Bodhisattva’s initial stage of the Great Vehicle, the adamantine dry-wisdom (*vajra-śuṣka-prajñā*).
The perfectly luminous, refined mind is like a vajra, indestructible and unbreakable; yet within it, transformative power arises like a precious moon contained within pure lapis lazuli.
This is what is called "not giving rise to a single thought," whereby the boundaries of past and future are severed and one is named a Buddha.
Therefore, without dwelling in the stages of external or internal ordinary beings, one enters directly into the wondrously adorned realm of the Tathāgata.

Yanhai’s claim that the "perfectly bright, refined mind" (*yuanming jingxin*) of the *Vajra-śīkṣā* constitutes the "uninterrupted path" (*ānantarya-mārga*) following the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*) is erroneous.
It is only when one transcends from this state and reaches the perfect brightness of Equal Enlightenment that it truly becomes the uninterrupted path.
If one were to take the *Vajra-śīkṣā* as the [uninterrupted path], [it would be a mistake].

Regarding the "one word" (*yī zì*) that transcends the intermediate path, to what principle does its meaning ultimately refer? There are four instances where *liú lí* (lapis lazuli) is raised as a metaphor.
First, in the section on the three progressive stages, it describes the reversal of the flow and the rotation of the six functions so that they no longer operate, stating:
"It is like a bright moon suspended within lapis lazuli. This reveals how an ordinary person with the Great Mind suddenly achieves perfect contemplation; therefore—

The text below states: "All the secret, perfect, pure, and wondrous [qualities] of all Tathāgatas appear therein; this person immediately attains the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
Next, in the second stage of the dwelling-position (*vihāra*), describing the arising of clear wisdom within the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*), it says:
"Like pure lapis lazuli revealing refined gold within. This reveals that through the power of cultivation and refinement, one subdues those afflictions (*kleśa*).

Because it constitutes an obstruction, the subsequent text says: "By taking the previous wondrous mind as the ground and treading upon it to form the stages, they are called the Dwelling of Cultivating the Ground.

Next, at the point where the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*) is exhausted, the text describes the mutual functioning of seeing, hearing, and the other faculties in their pure state, stating:
"It is like vaidūrya, transparent and clear inside and out. This reveals that the luminous voidness shines by itself, without depending on the power of wisdom. Therefore, below...
The inscription states: "Observe its origins: it takes the formless and the void as its foundation.

Furthermore, regarding those who follow next, whose various faculties function interchangeably, and who manifest transformation from within their perfectly enlightened, refined mind, it says: "It is like pure lapis lazuli containing a precious moon within.
This reveals the path of liberation through which one ascends directly from the mutual functioning of the faculties to the stage of Sublime Enlightenment (*Abhisambodhi*). Therefore...
The subsequent text states: "In this way, one transcends the stages such as the stage of faith and enters the Tathāgata’s ocean of wondrous adornment.

This indicates that at the beginning, the fruit is complete within the cause, and at the end, the cause and fruit are complete within the fruit. While the virtues of the fruit were not yet manifest, it was merely called the "moon";
once the virtues of the fruit have become manifest, it is encompassed by the term "jewel. The rest is understandable. Regarding the term "vajra":

Regarding the "Ten Grounds" (*daśabhūmi*), Jiyin said: "Because diamond (*vajra*) has subtlety as its essential nature and can destroy all things, and because the Ten Grounds realize *tathatā* by destroying hindrances and delusions, the Ten Grounds are called the 'Vajra-treasury' (*vajragarbha*).
Furthermore, their wisdom is called the 'extremely subtle realm,' and their object is also called the 'extremely subtle. Therefore, they are termed the 'Diamond Ten Grounds.'"
Changshui said: "Because his merit is sufficient, he is named 'Wondrous Adornment'; because his wisdom is sufficient, he is 'Ocean-like Wisdom.
Because the principle of Bodhi is perfected, he returns to non-attainment.
This is the analytical discernment of the clarity of awareness through *vipaśyanā* within *śamatha*, as practiced by the World-Honored Buddhas of the past."
Subtle demonic activities and demonic realms will appear before you; you shall be able to recognize them and wash away the defilements of the mind, so that you do not fall into false views.
The *skandha-māra* will be extinguished, the *deva-māra* will be shattered, and powerful spirits and deities will lose heart and flee. *Chi-mei* and *wang-liang* demons shall no longer be born.
Until you reach Bodhi, you shall lack nothing; your inferior states will be transcended as you advance toward Great Nirvana.

If your mind is not deluded or distressed, and if there are sentient beings in the final age who are dull-witted and ignorant—those who do not yet recognize *dhyāna* (meditative concentration), do not know how to preach the Dharma, yet delight in practicing *samādhi*—you should fear they might fall into heterodoxy;
therefore, with a single-minded resolve, you should exhort them to uphold this *dhāraṇī-mantra* from the crown of my Buddha-head.
If they are unable to recite it, have it written down and place it in their meditation hall, or carry it upon their person; then no demons whatsoever will be able to move them.
"You should reverently honor the ultimate cultivation and final instructions left by the Tathāgatas of the ten directions.
Ānanda immediately rose from his seat; having heard the Buddha’s instruction, he prostrated himself in worshipful reception, memorizing it without loss.
In the midst of the great assembly, he addressed the Buddha once more: "As the Buddha has said, within the characteristics of the five aggregates, the five kinds of delusion serve as the root."

We, the assembly, have not previously received the Tathāgata’s subtle and detailed instruction. Furthermore, regarding these five aggregates (*skandhas*), are they to be eliminated simultaneously or exhausted sequentially?
To what extent do these five layers extend as their respective boundaries?
We only pray that the Tathāgata will manifest great compassion to clarify the minds and eyes of this assembly, thereby serving as a guiding eye for all sentient beings of future ages.

The Buddha told Ānanda: "The essence of the Tathāgata is the subtle, true, wondrous clarity of original enlightenment, perfectly pure and free from the retention of birth and death, as well as all defilements—even up to empty space—all of which arise solely due to deluded thoughts. This is fundamentally the wondrous, clear, true essence of original enlightenment;
it is through delusion that the various vessel-worlds are produced. It is like the case of Yajñadatta, who, losing his head, mistook a reflection for it; such delusion has no fundamental cause."
Within the realm of deluded thoughts, one establishes the nature of causes and conditions; those who are confused about causes and conditions call it "spontaneity.
That nature of space is like a real illusion arising from causes and conditions; both spontaneity and causes and conditions are all the conceptual reckonings of the deluded minds of sentient beings.

Ānanda, you know that these arise from delusion and speak of the causes and conditions of delusion; yet if delusion were fundamentally non-existent, then speaking of the causes and conditions of delusion would be fundamentally nothing at all—how much more so this case!

Because you do not understand that you are merely pushing against the natural order, the Tathāgata has clarified for you that the original cause of the five aggregates is likewise nothing but false imagination.

Your physical body was initially produced through the imagination of your parents; had your mind not been characterized by imagination, it could not have entered into this state of imagination to transmit life.

Supplement: Question: What is meant by "destiny" (*ming*)? Answer: Destiny exists in dependence upon consciousness (*vijñāna*). Therefore, when consciousness moves, ideation (*saṃjñā*) arises; when ideation arises, destiny is established;
when destiny is established, the vital breath (*prāṇa*) follows; and when the vital breath follows, the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) are complete.
These three—destiny, warmth, and consciousness—are precisely this. Indeed, the moving nature of consciousness is the root of ideation. The Confucians say, "Know your destiny."
The Way is called "returning the mandate," and this is called "transmitting the mandate. Thus, what should the student take as knowing, what as returning, and what as transmitting?
Only by penetrating this may one enter the Way of neither arising nor ceasing.
As I previously stated: when the mind conceives of the taste of vinegar, saliva flows from the mouth; when the mind conceives of ascending a high precipice, the soles of the feet tingle with acid.
Though the cliff does not exist and the vinegar has not arrived, your physical body is certainly not false, for it functions in common with others.
How could this water in the mouth emerge simply because of speaking of vinegar? Therefore, you should know that your present material body is called the first false conception of solidity.

This very state you have described—whereby the mind’s contemplation of heights causes your physical form to truly experience a sensation of astringency, and through the arising of that sensation, moves the substance of your body—is what you now manifest as the second deluded thought, called "empty brightness. It is driven by the alternation of the present conditions of benefit and harm.
It is caused by your mental reflections which drive your physical body; yet the body is not of the same category as thought. For what reason does your body exist?
Following after recollection, various mental images arise; when the mind is awake, these forms correspond to thought, and when one sleeps, they become dreams.
Thus, the movement of your thoughts and deluded sentiments is called "interfusion," the third false imagination.

Transformation-principle does not abide; it shifts and moves in secret. The nails grow and the hair grows; the vital breath wanes and the face wrinkles. Day and night they alternate and replace one another.
Ānanda, you have never awakened to this: if this were not you, why would its essence undergo change? If it were truly you, why would you lack awareness?
Thus, your various mental formations (*saṃskāra*) that ceaselessly shift from moment to moment are called the "hidden" fourth delusion.

Furthermore, as for that which you call "luminous and pure," "tranquil and unmoving," and "eternal"—if it truly exists within the body, it must not transcend seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing. If it were real...

The essence of purity admits no admixture of habitual delusion; for what reason, Ānanda, have you never before seen a marvelous object such that, though years have passed, it is neither remembered nor forgotten?
Yet, if later you suddenly behold that former marvel again, the memory is as vivid as ever, without any loss.
Thus, within this pure, lucid, and unshakable state, there is a continuous permeation by thought after thought—how could there be any calculation of its limits? Ānanda!

You should know that this stillness is not True Suchness (tathatā). It is like looking at a rapid torrent that appears tranquil; though the flow is swift and you do not see it, it is not that there is no flow.
If this were not the source of perception, how could one ever undergo the habitual tendencies of delusion?

Since these false imaginings within your six sense-faculties—opening and closing—are never extinguished, they have become deeply ingrained through repeated practice within your current seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing. How, then, could this stillness be realized?
Having understood that the internal is formless, void, and non-existent, one reaches the fifth stage: the subtle and refined perception of inversion.

Ānanda, these five aggregates of clinging are formed by these five types of false imagination. If you now wish to know the depth of their causal realms: only form and emptiness constitute the limit of form;
only contact and its cessation constitute the limit of sensation; and only recollection and forgetfulness constitute the limit of perception.
The limits are merely cessation and arising; this is the limit of formations. To enter deeply into stillness and merge with stillness is to return to the limit of consciousness.

These five aggregates originally arise in overlapping succession: their arising has consciousness as its cause, and their cessation begins with form. In principle, one may achieve sudden enlightenment, whereby everything is eliminated simultaneously with that awakening;
yet in practice, things are not suddenly removed, but are exhausted through gradual stages. I have already shown you how the knots were tied in the *kārpāsa* cloth; what further do you wish to know?
I do not understand; please inquire further so that you may penetrate the root of this deluded thought and transmit it to future practitioners of the Dharma-ending age,
enabling them to recognize its falsity, develop a profound weariness with it, realize the existence of Nirvana within themselves,
and no longer cling to the three realms.

The treatise states: The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* contains ten thousand verses as numerous as motes of dust, yet Zao Bo (Dharmarakṣa) extracted its essentials to compose the *Treatise on Dependent Origination*.
It describes its causal arising through twelve aspects, which in reality are the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*).
Therefore, the World-Honored One reiterated this here so that [beings] may know that all these arise from the power of the sentient beings' own mental formations.
When one achieves the purity of mindfulness through hearing, supernatural powers and radiance will cause ordinary people to realize the truth;

when mindfulness is defiled by impurities, one abandons birth within the three realms and six paths as previously shown. By means of the two methods of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*, one refines the five aggregates;
thus, internally, one attains the merits of the six sense faculties, and externally, one transcends the evil world of the five turbidities.

When the power of concentration is refined and strict, one departs from the fifty kinds of demonic activities (*mārakarman*), and the principles become brilliantly clear; students should contemplate this deeply.

[Supplementary Note: Although the aggregates (*skandha*) were previously identified as belonging to perception (*saṃjñā*), the root source of perception and the shallow and deep levels of the realms (*dhātu*) had not yet been described.
Therefore, Ānanda (Pǐngxǐ) again presented his inquiry, and the World-Honored One answered it in full. This concludes the [first] chapter.

The fifth state, where one remains unmoving in profound stillness, is described as follows: this stillness is not true suchness; it is like a rapid torrent that appears tranquil from a distance because the current flows so swiftly that it cannot be seen.
If this were not the source of thought, how could it ever receive the habit-energy of delusion? It is not the mutual functioning of your six sense-faculties, nor their opening and closing.
This delusive thought can never be extinguished; only when it is recognized as such is it called "subtle, inverted, and refined thought. This is what the student must understand.

At this point, one should realize that this perception is the very root of the skandhas, and apply the power of contemplative observation daily to extinguish it entirely—just as one removes weeds by pulling out their roots.
If one realizes this but fails to apply the power of contemplative observation and does not extinguish it, then it is no different from not having realized it at all;
what benefit would there be? Therefore it is said: "In principle, there is sudden realization; one rides upon realization..."
"Simultaneous elimination" refers to the meaning of "the six dissolving into one and forgetting. Since birth exists because of consciousness, extinction follows from the removal of form;
this depends solely on the depth of contemplative observation. Once the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) is shattered, the rest will be resolved as easily as a blade cutting through wood.
Therefore it is said: "Matters are not eliminated all at once, but are exhausted through successive stages"—this is the previous conclusion based on the sequence.
This is the meaning that must now be understood sequentially by the Honorable One. Therefore, the text below says: "I have already shown you the knots made with the *kārpāsa* cloth;
what is it that you do not understand that you must inquire about again? The principle here is evident. [The questioner] asks:
"In the previous account, the six sense-gates were successively dissolved, combined, opened, and established; how does this differ from the mutual application of opening and closing described here?"
The previous statement described how the function of mutual interpenetration first becomes manifest at the limit of the consciousness-aggregate (*vijñāna-skandha*);

this present passage describes how the fundamental source of perception (*saṃjñā-mūla*) is extinguished by relying on the power of that mutual interpenetration. This fundamental source of perception cannot be extinguished without the power of such mutual interpenetration.
As for the mention of the five aggregates of clinging (*pañca-upādāna-skandha*), these are the phenomena through which sentient beings receive retribution; therefore, they are treated collectively.
The meaning of "receiving the profound penetration and merging with the profound" is explained at the end of the third fascicle.
Ānanda, suppose there were a person who filled all the empty space throughout the ten directions with the seven treasures and offered them to as many Buddhas as there are motes of dust,
serving and making offerings to them without a single thought being in vain— what do you think of this person?
"By the causal conditions of this gift to the Buddha, will one not obtain much merit? Ānanda replied, "The void is inexhaustible and precious jewels are boundless.
In the past, there were sentient beings who gave the Buddha seven coins; by relinquishing their bodies, they still obtained the rank of a Wheel-Turning King.

How much more so for one who, in the presence [of the Buddha], gives precious jewels until the void is exhausted and the Buddha-lands are filled? Even if one were to contemplate this for an entire kalpa, it would still not suffice."
"How could there be any limit to such merit?
The Buddha told Ānanda, "The words of all Buddhas and Tathāgatas are not false.
If there were a person who committed the four grave offenses or the ten pārājikas, even for a mere instant, they would pass through the Avīci Hell of this world and other worlds until the very end."

There is nowhere throughout the ten directions that they have not traversed; able to take this Dharma-door with a single thought and reveal it to those who have not yet studied during the final eon, the karmic obstacles of such a person shall be extinguished at that very moment.

The suffering of their imprisonment in hell shall be transformed into a land of peace and bliss, and the merit they obtain shall surpass that of the previous donor by a hundredfold, a thousandfold, ten thousandfold, a hundred millionfold, or even more.
Thus it continues until it reaches that which cannot be fathomed by calculation or analogy. Ānanda,

if there are sentient beings who can recite this sutra and uphold this mantra as I have extensively explained— exhausting an entire kalpa without end— and who act according to my instructions and practice the Way as taught,
they will directly attain Bodhi, and no further demonic activities shall arise.
When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, the bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, upāsikās,
and all those in the world— gods, humans, asuras, as well as the bodhisattvas from other directions, the noble ones of the two vehicles, the sages, the youths,
and the powerful ghosts and spirits who had first resolved their minds— all rejoiced greatly, paid homage, and departed.

The Commentary states: Generally, when a sutra reaches its conclusion, it says that the merit obtained is "extraordinary. This is because the World-Honored One, out of his compassionate heart, gathers in those of various dispositions.
There is a class of bodhisattvas who are attached to merit; hearing the meaning of emptiness, they give rise to false attachments and risk falling back.
Therefore, the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā* says: "Subhūti, a bodhisattva practices the non-abiding mark."
The merit of giving is likewise thus inconceivable. Wuzhuo said:
"It is for the sake of enabling a certain class of bodhisattvas who are attached to merit to become capable of receiving the profound, subtle, and vast Dharma.

If it were not stated that giving without dwelling on signs possesses great merit, it would result in nihilism; it would not only fail to extensively encompass those of inferior faculties," [but would also exclude others].
Furthermore, it would also cause one to lose one's own tenet regarding the dharma of non-abiding.
Generally speaking, the reason sentient beings transmigrate through the three realms and rise and fall within the six destinies is that desire serves as their foundation; specifically, sexual desire.
It is for this that he provides a summary: where feelings attach and conceptions rely, one dreams of death and lives in intoxication; how could such a state transcend the world?
The World-Honored One, using the great compassionate vessel to ferry beings across this sea of suffering, desired to proclaim the wondrous Dharma to universally awaken all sentient beings.
Foreknowing that the time had arrived, he joyfully concealed his person within a brothel in order to manifest it for their sake.
It is said that "the Dharma does not arise in isolation.

I have once studied this sutra with great diligence, from the point where Mañjuśrī exhorted Ānanda to return to the presence of the Tathāgata, prostrate, weep with grief, and earnestly request instruction on the initial expedient means for attaining the wondrous *śamatha*, *samādhi*, and *dhyāna* through which the Tathāgatas of the ten directions achieve Bodhi; yet the World-Honored One did not answer, but merely—
At the outset, upon generating the aspiration for enlightenment, you suddenly renounced all affection and love after witnessing a most extraordinary sign.
Furthermore, you realized that the continuous cycle of birth and death for all sentient beings since beginningless time arises entirely from their failure to know the eternally abiding true mind.
Subsequently, because they do not recognize the location of the mind’s source, I interrogated them regarding the seven internal and external locations, employing both concession and refutation.

What is the reason? I humbly examine the Tathāgata’s intention: it is to lead Ānanda to the realm where the Tathāgata himself has arrived, and to cause sentient beings of the末代 (final age) to see for themselves and awaken for themselves just as Ānanda did. This is the path of direct pointing, which cannot be reached through contemplative observation (*vipaśyanā*).
If one cannot find a mutual resonance like a needle meeting its eye or a magnet attracting its pin, and instead fails to grasp it through spiritual intuition and mental understanding, then...

The Tathāgata, having no choice but to manifest the path for entering *samādhi* and to dispel the delusions of the demon of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), established this as his final instruction.
Alas! The Tathāgata’s heart of compassion may truly be called ultimate; yet the purport of the sutra is subtle and profound, not easily elucidated.
From the time it was translated during the Shenlong era and received by the Venerable Fang (Xuanzang), it has been transmitted through the Tang dynasty.
To this day, over several centuries, the scholarship of commentary and sub-commentary has not been lacking in number;

yet these works generally elevate some points while neglecting others, each possessing both strengths and weaknesses. Our dynasty’s Venerable Jiyin, having attained great practical benefit from this sūtra, subsequently composed the *Zuǒdǐng Fǎlùn* (Treatise on the Dharmas of the Usnīṣa) to refute divergent views and elucidate its profound meanings. It is a pity that [this work] remains...
It was transmitted and entered into perfect stillness. Zen Master Yuanwu happened to see it and sighed, saying, "This is truly the eye of the celestial vision.
He immediately provided a generous sum of one hundred strings of cash and encouraged Peng Gong Siyu of Huxiang to have it carved into blocks at Nanchang.
After the Jianyan era, the woodblocks were no longer extant; in the early Shaoxing period, his disciple Zhiju raised funds for their reproduction.
It was carved again for circulation in Gaoyang, but it has since been lost; if this treatise were not in the world today, its merit would have been squandered.
Only the Chief Seat Shao-mi of Sanshan preserved it alone. After I, a fool, requested it repeatedly, he finally opened the ten layers of its casket.
Observing its text, I find it concise yet its meaning vast and manifest; it shatters the darkness of ignorance with a brilliant torch and breaks the shackles of confinement.
The net of doubt is severed by the precious sword; though my hands may fumble and fail to let go, I have compiled these teachings into a continuous sequence.
To provide clarity, I have analyzed them beneath the main text as a "Comprehensive Discussion" (*He-lun*).
Where the principles did not reach their full depth, I have supplemented them; where the phrasing was unstable, I have revised it.

The characters therein contained errors and corruptions; I have corrected them. In the *Yisi* year of the Chongxu era, I merely completed a provisional compilation, as I had not yet had the leisure to circulate it.

In the *Renzi* year of the Shaoxing era, I submitted the *Fandeng Lu* (Record of the Universal Lamp) and took up residence at Jiyuan Hermitage on the outskirts of the capital, where I struck my staff.
The following winter, I moved to Yongshou Monastery in Wuxing, where I dwelt among the springs and rocks.
Amidst a state of serene detachment, following a full meal and a sound sleep, he shook off the decayed and corrupt [manuscripts] and finally accomplished his purpose.
Regarding the small characters that were neither original nor supplementary, he provided them so that readers might have something to refer to.

Initially, Jiyin composed this treatise, but Lingyuan sent him a letter objecting to it, claiming that it blocked the gate for later generations to attain self-awakening; therefore, Jiyin later wrote in his preface that there was someone who...
In this context, to refer to the staff and shouts of the Patriarchs is called Chan; to set aside the staff and shouts and rely on the sutras and treatises is called Teaching.
Is there such a distinction of acceptance and rejection within the ultimate reality? Those who have not yet attained realization consider these two to be contradictory.
Baojue once shared the teaching seat with Master Laonan at Huangbo to enlighten future generations; subsequently, he followed Leshan.
Chan Master Tanyue was entrusted with the essentials of this sutra. While serving under Huanglong and later residing at Haitang, he read this sutra without ceasing.
Each time he closed the volume and struck the desk, he would tell his disciples: "This is the marrow of Chan.
Those who understand it know that the mutual exhortations between the masters of former generations could not have been otherwise; it is not easy to view them as being different."
Jiyin’s taboo name was Dehong; Juefan was his courtesy name. He was a native of Junyang who received the Dharma from Zhenjing.
The Layman Zhang Shangying, known as Wujin, was in complete accord with him. His life story is recorded in the *Xu sengbao zhuan* (Continued Biographies of the Jewel of the Sangha).
"Jiyin" was the honorific title he used for himself, while "Ganlu Mie" was another of his alternative names. When Wujin resigned from the相位 (prime ministership), [he became...]

The Guest-Banisher Jiyin was likewise detained in a place of punishment; it was at that time that he composed this treatise. Formerly, when King Wen was imprisoned in Youli, he re-examined the six lines of the *Yi* (Book of Changes);
had it not been for Youli, [the *Yi* would not have been enriched]. When Confucius was in Chen, his playing of the zither and singing never ceased;

had it not been for Chen, [his teachings might have perished]. Later, during the Qin dynasty, Dharma Master Zhao also completed the *Baocang lun* (Treatise on the Precious Treasury) while within the circular prison walls.
Huì burned his official documents and fled to Méiyáng, where he composed the *Zhèngfǎyǎnzàng*.
Amidst the hardships faced by sages and worthies, there was no situation in which he did not find self-contentment; Jìyīn was likewise so. From youth, he was exceptionally gifted;

having shaved his head as a Confucian scholar, his literary compositions became a staple on people's lips, such that the world eventually regarded him as a "poet-monk. When Dàhuì was among the assembly, he often held Jìyīn in high esteem.
When the Master was residing at Shuangjing, [Liu] Zhi painted his portrait and composed a eulogy for it. Upon returning from his place of banishment to Tong’an, he first repaired the Master’s stupa.
Recently, there have been those who engage in public debate, venting their pens with insults and disparagement; they mostly reveal their own lack of discernment.
Nevertheless, Jiyin asked: regarding the matter of King Virūḍhaka’s accession to the throne and his slaughter of the Śākya clan, how could this—?
In this assembly, the Buddha was just beginning to give his father the parable of pointing out the river, while Ānanda had already recounted the circumstances of his son’s death;
from this it is known that what was spoken at a later time after the naming of himself was specifically compiled by the redactors and joined together as a single sutra.
Furthermore, from the time the Tathāgata preached this sutra until the end of his life at Nirvāṇa, eighteen years passed.
It cannot be argued that because [the teachings] are inexhaustible, they may not be discussed at once;
yet, to edit this sutra—which serves as the pure Sea-Eye—by deleting passages concerning the pointing-out of the river and other matters, would be a great error. Alas!

If one were to claim that the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* could be edited, then which of the Tripiṭaka and Twelve Divisions of Scripture would not be subject to such editing? National Teacher Qingliang composed the commentary on the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*.
In order to verify the errors of the translators, I have recorded them at the end of the sutra even though I did not obtain the Sanskrit original.

For instance, it says "The Third Leaf, Tenth Line of the First Fascicle of the Chapter on the Inconceivable Dharma of the Buddhas," yet the word "all" (sarva) has been omitted from "all buddhas" in the old version;
furthermore, it says "great lapis lazuli jewel" (*mahā-vaiḍūrya-maṇi*), which likely refers to *vaidūrya* jewel. Guifeng [Zongmi] followed Yuan [Zhao].

In the *Juewu ruzuo shuchao* (Commentary on the Entry into Enlightenment), he sought to change the phrase "all realize perfect enlightenment" (*jie zheng yuanjue*) to "all possess perfect enlightenment" (*jie ju yuanjue*).

He reviled this most vehemently, saying: "If all sentient beings possessed perfect enlightenment yet did not realize it, then not a single person would ever develop the true aspiration to return to the source;
ordinary people would have no need to seek liberation. Confucius, for this reason— [The text here appears to be incomplete.]
Taking the rectification of names as his own responsibility, Confucius composed the *Spring and Autumn Annals* based on the records of the state of Lu;

although he embedded the principles of editorial revision—like the chisel and the brocade—within the span of two hundred and forty-two years, instances such as recording "the fifth month of summer" or "Duke Guo" were merely the preservation of existing texts, transmitting what was certain with certainty and what was doubtful with doubt. How much more so, then, regarding the scriptures of the Great Sage of the West?
That this is not comparable to worldly books—who would say it is? Within the Confucian gate he was a great master; within the garden of awakening he was a great lay practitioner (*upāsaka*).
Yet, to have arbitrarily excised and altered this sutra—how can one call this anything but a profound lack of reflection!
Is it only this? The *Awakening of Mahāyāna* states: "This deluded mind cannot exist without the six sense-objects. This is the very essence of the Chan school.
It may be acceptable to take the six characters as a single phrase for the sake of convenience, yet Danzhi Nan considered it improper to treat them as a fixed sentence.
This is because, according to the Tathāgata’s intention, deluded mind arises only when the sense faculties (*indriya*) and their objects (*viṣaya*) come together;

to now claim that deluded mind exists first would invert the original meaning—how could such a thing be expected? Even though the Buddha expounds the Dharma with a single voice, [the capacity to understand varies].
Sentient beings each attain understanding according to their own kind; while it is acceptable to take the meaning as the understanding, it is not permissible to take the phrasing as definitive.
When Chan Master Lingyan An read this sutra to the passage: "When knowledge and vision establish knowledge (phrase), that is the root of ignorance (phrase);
when knowledge and vision are without seeing (phrase), this is nirvana (phrase)," he broke the reading to: "Knowledge and vision establish (phrase)."
"Knowing is itself ignorance" (phrase); "fundamentally knowing and seeing non-existence" (phrase); "seeing this is itself nirvana" (phrase).
After one has attained such profound and clear awakening, can later generations take these as fixed, definitive phrases?
Prince Zhaoming of the Liang dynasty divided the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* into thirty-two sections, yet the masters of his time still criticized him, saying it was a "fragmentation."
How much more so for Fashen Kuṇa, who served as a master of doctrinal studies, to have recklessly determined the punctuation in this manner—it was indeed a great error.
Since the *Qīngjìng hǎiyǎn jīng* (Sūtra of the Pure Ocean Eye) by the monk Huìyìn of Kuàijī has already been published, it will only further confuse future generations;
therefore, I, the humble one, cannot help but rectify and rescue its errors in this *Yúanjué lüèshū* (Brief Commentary on the Perfect Enlightenment Sūtra). Therein...
It is said: "Because one does not afflict others with what one excels in, there is no doctrine of exclusion;
because one does not conceal others for what they have not yet attained, there is no doctrine of arbitrary opinion. Now, I, the fool, am not like this;

I affirm what I deem right and deny what I deem wrong—what hesitation can there be regarding the doctrine of exclusion? I take existing principles as a basis and append my own views to them—what hesitation can there be?
Regarding the arguments presented here, I have set forth the general outlines of their strengths and weaknesses within these volumes,
so as to further ensure that Jiyin’s critique emerges with pure consistency, free from even the slightest flaw or blemish that could be pointed out—
is this not indeed praiseworthy? Should there be anything that remains unconvincing, I leave it for future sages to judge.

Preface to the Combined Commentary on the Śūraṅgama Sūtra: The Ultimate Meaning of the Secret Cause for Cultivation and Realization of the Tathāgata’s Great Uṣṇīṣa and the Myriad Practices of All Bodhisattvas, Volume Ten.
It states: Following the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, the World-Honored One preached this scripture, fully exhausting the profound meanings contained within all other sūtras.

Regarding the essential purport of the One Vehicle: originally, Nāgārjuna read it in the Dragon Palace and recited it from memory upon his departure. For generations, the sovereigns of the Five Indias held it as a profound secret and did not transmit it.
When the Tiantai Master Zhizhe was expounding the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, he could not understand the meaning of the "merits of the six sense faculties.
He set down his pen and contemplated this; then, a Brahman monk said to him, "Only the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi-sūtra* elucidates this meaning clearly; you may use it for verification."

The *Cheng* does not require further explanation. On this day, the wise [master] faced west and performed two prostrations morning and evening, vowing that [the teaching] would soon be transmitted to this land;
yet he passed away before it could be seen. During the Shénlóng era of the Táng dynasty, Mīghaśikṣā arrived in Guǎngzhōu with the Sanskrit manuscript.
Fáng Róng, the Prefectural Governor, translated it on the spot. Shortly thereafter, a messenger was dispatched by the King of Kāpiśī to retrieve it, so that it nearly failed to be transmitted.
The translation was completed. After Empress Wu presented it to the court, Emperor Zhongzong ascended the throne; however, he had no leisure to promulgate it.
The monk Shenxiu received it while dining within the imperial palace and brought it back to Yuquan Monastery in Jingzhou.

From its transmission until the present, there have been no fewer than ten families of scholars who have produced commentaries and exegeses. Nevertheless, their judgments regarding the fundamental tenets differ widely, and as for the text—
Failing to penetrate the underlying meaning, I have long observed that [the interpretations] are obscure;

having grasped the intent of the World-Honored One beyond the various commentaries and treatises, I intended to compose a śāstra to refute divergent views and rectify the purport of the sūtras. However, bound by worldly circumstances, I lacked the leisure to spare my pen.
In the tenth month of the first year of the Zhenghe era, while suffering persecution for propagating the Dharma, I was exiled from the capital to Zhuya (Zhiye). There, I... [continued].
In the second month of that year, I arrived at Hainan and stayed at Kaiyuan Temple in Qiongshan. The temple was as empty as an abandoned household;
the ruined shrines contained nothing but this scripture. I said to myself: "Is Heaven intending to fulfill my resolve regarding this scripture?

Were it not for having been cast away in these remote regions due to my transgressions, who could have composed their mind to investigate and contemplate such profound discourse? While I was still drafting my preliminary notes...
Having been granted imperial favor, I returned north to rely upon my former teacher; thus, another two years passed before the vihāra was successfully completed.
My disciples then asked, "The sūtras and śāstras each have their own lineages of transmission; how can you speak of the sūtras and śāstras from the perspective of the Chan school?

I replied, "Aśvaghoṣa and Nāgārjuna were the patriarchs of the Western Heaven (India); they composed śāstras and commented on sūtras in numbers as vast as mountains and oceans, which have been transmitted here."
The Master of Earth (Dongshan) esteemed several million words; yet Dharma, the Patriarch of this land at Caoxi, when preaching the Dharma, said:
"Only the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* can seal the mind and transmit the mind. He then explained the meaning of the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā*.
Are the hearts and mouths of the Buddhas and Patriarchs ever at variance? There is someone who... [text ends]
This refers to the Patriarchs employing the "stick and shout," which is called Chan; setting aside the stick and shout, the sutras and treatises are called Teaching (Jiao).
Within the ultimate reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), does one accept or reject these? Xiansha said: "The Chan school and the vehicle of the teachings revolve from the tip of your own tongue;

how could there be any real duality? National Teacher Shaorou cited a verse on people of today looking at ancient teachings: "Seeking the Buddha within the scriptures, One is like a dog gnawing a bone. If you wish to see the Buddha, Look at the Buddha’s own body."
He addressed the assembly, saying: "Everyone, what do you call 'teaching'? Do not say that you have seen or heard even a single word of teaching;
if you say so, you are stuck within the teaching. My school does not function in this way—do not err! It is not that the teaching causes people to be deluded;
rather, it is people who are deluded by the teaching. Take these five thousand and forty-eight fascicles: if you recognize them, there is not a single word in excess and not a single word lacking."

If there is one word in excess, the Buddha-dharma increases; if there is one word lacking, the Buddha-dharma decreases. Yet, in truth, the Buddha-dharma possesses no principle of increase or decrease.
Furthermore, it is said: "The Patriarchs are disciples of the Buddha; if you can exhaustively fathom the words of the Buddha and the words of the Patriarchs, they will naturally manifest before you.
This is truly a famous saying of the world. Alas! How difficult was the arrival of the scriptures!
Thus it was transmitted within families, yet these lineages were subsequently muddied by them.
Since students have not received the teachings with excellence, they harbor doubts regarding the Dharma-vehicle; their self-obstruction is such as this, which is truly lamentable.
As I explain this treatise, may those who are able to illuminate their own minds therein and realize the Buddha’s intent, vow to take the Dharma as their kin throughout all lifetimes.
By the power of his original vows, he brings universal salvation to all beings and transforms them so that they may attain Buddhahood. On the first day of the fifth month of the eighth year,

I respectfully record this postscript to the *Zongchi Zhongkai Zunding Falun* (The Dharma Discourse on the Reopening of the Honored Crown), dedicating all roots of goodness toward the great ocean of skillful means of the stage of wisdom for those who study well, as found in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*.
I vow that, through wondrous eloquence, I shall extensively expound for all sentient beings according to their capacities so that they may fully understand;
for the Tathāgata, by means of the seal of impartial compassion, manifests the supreme ultimate truth of both mundane and supramundane phenomena.

It is not otherwise than through transcendent eloquence that one may dispel heterodox interpretations and false attachments, causing the distinction between objects and wisdom to become clearly manifest, thereby conforming to the cessation of ignorance.
Those who remain in the long sleep of birth and death merely obstruct themselves in vain.

Therefore, when a Bodhisattva on the Stage of Excellent Intelligence (*sādhumatī-bhūmi*) acts as a Great Dharma Master to expound all phenomena, they must do so by means of immeasurable skillful wisdom, giving rise to the four kinds of unimpeded great eloquence (*catasraḥ pratisaṃvidaḥ*).
These four are that which is demonstrated through various forms of knowledge to turn the wheel of the Dharma in its entirety. From this, one knows that eloquence arises from [wisdom].

The ground of wisdom benefits sentient beings without ever abandoning them for even a moment, for its penetrating realization is like the waters of Lake Anavatapta, flowing everywhere without obstruction;
thus, within my Dharma, there is no conceptual proliferation. The Venerable Master Jiyin Baojue Yuanming Chan, from his very birth, possessed the ambition to soar toward the heavens;
subsequently, he received the Dharma from Wen Guansi, whose heroic influence spread in all four directions.
The ocean of wisdom is serene, from which the light of insight emerges; with samādhi as his brush and ink, he sports with sovereign ease.

Thus, what appears in his writings are all the remnants of the Way. Nevertheless, when used to adorn the vehicles of the Teaching and to illuminate their essential mysteries, they are as brilliant and vibrant as if the grounds were interspersed with incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) jewels and exquisite ornaments—such that all who see or hear them [are moved].
These individuals were inspired and elevated, each attaining realization according to their own faculties; was this not what is called "great eloquence"?

Yet those who remain stuck in mere outward traces fail to investigate the ultimate destination, often lamenting that such people are constrained by Confucian habits, knowing them only for their ability to produce waves of literary brilliance with their speech and brush. Alas! It is like a pearl rolling upon a platter.
The jewel rolling upon a tray is entirely unrestricted; yet to recklessly debate its arbitrary movements or its curvature and straightness—is this truly knowing the Silent Sound (Jiyin)?

Is it not nearly falling into frivolous discourse (prapañca)? I have observed that the commentaries on this sutra are dedicated exclusively to the gate of entering the Way by thoroughly knowing one’s own mind, and to the essential decision for attaining Buddhahood;
thus they establish the fundamental tenets and penetrate both the nature and characteristics [of reality].
Whether sudden or gradual, his realizations were all fully realized; his words were concise yet reached the ultimate principle, exhaustive yet clear, not merely venturing into empty rhetoric.

He investigated and explored with such precision that he reached what previous masters had not attained. Grasping its fundamental limit, he achieved internal integration and took it as his personal responsibility to propagate the Dharma.
Thus, his discernment regarding the Path flowed spontaneously from the very core of his being, proceeding forth without hesitation.
During the Jiānyán era, after Jìyīn had passed away, his elder brother Sīyǔ was serving in the administration at Xùjiāng.

Delighted by the request of Jìyīn’s disciples, Fǎguǒ Chánshī also contributed one hundred thousand [coins] to have the woodblocks carved at Nánchāng. Not long after, they were destroyed by the "Guān" troops.
For nearly twenty years, the work was almost lost until it was preserved through the resolute efforts of the eminent disciple Zhìjù, who took great pains to restore it.
He hurried to Gao'an to recruit further support for its publication. When Tu Yuanzhi of Qingjiang saw it, he contributed his wealth to lead the way, and those who joined in harmony were numerous.
Within less than a few months, the project was completed. Though Jiyin’s Way had suffered setbacks, it became even more pervasive;
though obscured, it became even more brilliant. Thus, the power of their collective vows was fulfilled, thereby continuing the legacy of the tradition and reviving the family’s reputation.
It may be said that he was free from any lingering regret. In the past, Zhu Daosheng attained an awakening to the profound meanings of various sutras that had not yet been transmitted;
consequently, his fellow lecturers harbored resentment and jealousy, falsely accusing him of propagating heterodox teachings. Daosheng made a solemn oath before the assembly, saying:

"If what I have preached does not accord with the meaning of the scriptures, I shall deserve punishment according to the Vinaya; if it truly accords with the Buddha’s mind, I vow to remain forever upon the lion throne. Thereupon, he set up a stone pillar.

The assembly listened with their minds resolved upon him, and Congshi nodded in agreement; subsequently, as he ascended the seat, his voice was fluent and mellifluous, falling like rain upon the dust and transforming it.
Alas! Sheng’s complete possession of wisdom and realization may be called a profound discernment of the Way, one who possesses self-confidence and nothing to guard against.
Jiyin once discussed this point, saying that what Sheng perceived was entirely blunt and whole.
As for those who study the doctrines and yet conspire together to suppress it—those of petty intelligence who act out of self-interest—it is not surprising.

Through this, I know that the synchronicity of the "beak and peck" between Sheng and Jiyin was tacitly understood across a thousand years; that their paths met like two carts on the same track surely follows its own inherent way.
I consider Jiyin to be a brother of the same school as myself. Thus, I have taken the errors and omissions in the old edition and corrected them by hand.

This was transcribed in small clerical script for the convenience of students to read and practice; having completed this scripture, I have further extracted its essential points to record at the end of the volume.
Written respectfully on the first day of the New Year in the Dingsu year of the Shaoxing era by Peng Yiming of Shuangxi.
